title: APIs, schemas and authentication
questions:
  - id: http-methods
    prompt: Which HTTP methods are conventionally safe (read-only)?
    options:
      - id: get
        text: GET and HEAD
        correct: true
      - text: POST and PUT
      - text: DELETE and PATCH
      - text: All methods
    explanation: Classifying agent tools by HTTP semantics is a quick first risk assessment.
  - id: idempotent-methods
    prompt: Which HTTP methods are defined as idempotent?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: get
        text: GET
        correct: true
      - id: put
        text: PUT
        correct: true
      - id: delete
        text: DELETE
        correct: true
      - text: POST
    explanation: POST is not idempotent by definition — use idempotency keys for retried creates.
  - id: status-codes
    prompt: A tool receives HTTP 429. What should it do?
    options:
      - text: Retry immediately in a tight loop
      - text: Treat it as success
      - id: backoff
        text: Back off and retry later (respecting Retry-After), or report rate limiting to the agent
        correct: true
      - text: Delete the request
    explanation: 429 means Too Many Requests. 4xx errors other than 408/429 usually should not be retried.
  - id: json-schema
    prompt: What is JSON Schema used for in agent systems?
    options:
      - text: Styling JSON
      - id: describe
        text: Describing the shape of tool parameters and structured outputs so models can produce valid arguments and applications can validate them
        correct: true
      - text: Compressing JSON
      - text: Encrypting JSON
    explanation: Function calling, MCP and structured outputs all use JSON Schema.
  - id: required-enum
    prompt: "In a tool schema, what does `\"enum\": [\"low\", \"medium\", \"high\"]` on a `priority` parameter do?"
    options:
      - text: Sets the default to low
      - text: Makes the parameter optional
      - text: Sorts the values
      - id: restrict
        text: Restricts valid values to those three, guiding the model and enabling validation
        correct: true
    explanation: Tight schemas reduce invalid tool calls.
  - id: oauth
    prompt: What is OAuth 2.x primarily for?
    options:
      - id: delegated
        text: Delegated authorisation — letting an application act on a user's behalf with scoped, revocable tokens without handling the user's password
        correct: true
      - text: Encrypting databases
      - text: Hashing passwords
      - text: Load balancing
    explanation: MCP's authorisation for remote servers builds on OAuth.
  - id: scopes
    prompt: What are OAuth scopes?
    options:
      - text: Telescope settings
      - id: scopes
        text: Named permissions requested by a client, limiting what an access token allows
        correct: true
      - text: Code blocks
      - text: Network ranges
    explanation: Request the narrowest scopes an agent needs.
  - id: api-keys
    prompt: Why are long-lived API keys risky for agents?
    options:
      - text: They expire too quickly
      - text: They are hard to type
      - id: leak
        text: If leaked (logs, prompts, repositories) they grant broad access until manually rotated; short-lived scoped tokens limit the damage
        correct: true
      - text: They cannot be used over HTTPS
    explanation: Keep secrets out of prompts and traces.
  - id: async
    prompt: Why do agent runtimes rely on asynchronous I/O?
    options:
      - text: It makes models smarter
      - text: It is required by JSON
      - text: It reduces token counts
      - id: waiting
        text: Agents spend most time waiting on model and tool calls; async I/O lets one process handle many concurrent runs efficiently and run independent calls in parallel
        correct: true
    explanation: In .NET, `async`/`await` with `CancellationToken`; in Python, `asyncio`.
  - id: state-machine
    prompt: Why model long-running agent tasks as explicit state machines or durable workflows?
    options:
      - id: durable
        text: So tasks can pause for approvals, survive restarts and resume from known states rather than restarting from scratch
        correct: true
      - text: Because LLMs are state machines
      - text: To avoid using a database
      - text: It is only for games
    explanation: Graph-based workflow engines in agent frameworks provide this.
  - id: webhooks
    prompt: What is a webhook?
    options:
      - text: A fishing tool
      - text: A browser plugin
      - id: callback
        text: An HTTP callback — a service calls your endpoint when an event happens, instead of you polling
        correct: true
      - text: A type of SQL join
    explanation: Useful for resuming agents when external events (approvals, payments) complete.
---
## Learning objectives

- Classify tools by HTTP semantics and idempotency
- Write precise JSON Schemas
- Understand OAuth, scopes and secrets handling
- Know why agents are asynchronous and stateful

## A precise tool schema

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "title":    { "type": "string", "maxLength": 120 },
    "priority": { "type": "string", "enum": ["low", "medium", "high"] },
    "due":      { "type": "string", "format": "date" }
  },
  "required": ["title", "priority"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}
```

## Sources

- RFC 9110, "HTTP Semantics" — <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110>
- JSON Schema — <https://json-schema.org/>
- OAuth 2.1 draft — <https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1/>
- MCP specification, "Authorization" — <https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification>

title: Defining AI agents
questions:
  - id: definition
    prompt: Which definition of an AI agent is most useful for builders?
    options:
      - text: Any chatbot
      - text: A model with more parameters
      - id: loop
        text: A system in which an LLM directs its own process — choosing actions and tool calls in a loop, observing results — to accomplish a goal
        correct: true
      - text: A robot with a body
    explanation: Simon Willison's short form — "an LLM agent runs tools in a loop to achieve a goal" — captures the same idea.
  - id: components
    prompt: According to the Databricks course description, which core components make up an agent?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: llm
        text: An LLM for reasoning
        correct: true
      - id: tools
        text: Tools for acting and retrieving information
        correct: true
      - id: memory
        text: Memory
        correct: true
      - id: workflow
        text: Workflows or control logic
        correct: true
    explanation: Different sources slice it differently, but these four recur.
  - id: vs-chatbot
    prompt: How does an agent differ from a plain chatbot?
    options:
      - id: acts
        text: A chatbot responds with text; an agent can decide to take actions through tools, observe results and continue over multiple steps toward a goal
        correct: true
      - text: Agents are always smarter models
      - text: Chatbots cannot use LLMs
      - text: There is no difference
    explanation: The ability to act is what creates both value and risk.
  - id: vs-traditional
    prompt: How do LLM agents differ from traditional rule-based automation (e.g. RPA)?
    options:
      - text: Agents are fully deterministic
      - text: RPA cannot click buttons
      - text: Agents never need integration work
      - id: flexible
        text: Agents handle unstructured inputs and unanticipated situations flexibly, but are non-deterministic and harder to verify; RPA is brittle but predictable
        correct: true
    explanation: Many good systems combine both — deterministic steps where possible, LLM judgment where needed.
  - id: autonomy
    prompt: Which statement about agent autonomy is accurate?
    options:
      - text: Agents are either fully autonomous or not agents
      - id: spectrum
        text: Autonomy is a spectrum — from a single LLM call, through fixed workflows and routers, to agents that plan and choose tools freely
        correct: true
      - text: More autonomy is always better
      - text: Autonomy is set by the model vendor
    explanation: Choose the least autonomy that solves the problem.
  - id: agent-washing
    prompt: What is "agent washing"?
    options:
      - text: Cleaning agent logs
      - text: Retraining agents daily
      - id: rebrand
        text: Rebranding existing chatbots, RPA or assistants as "agents" without real agentic capability; Gartner estimated only about 130 of thousands of "agentic AI" vendors were genuine in 2025
        correct: true
      - text: A security attack
    explanation: Ask vendors what the system decides by itself and what tools it can call.
  - id: goal
    prompt: Why does an agent need a clear goal and stopping condition?
    options:
      - text: For marketing copy
      - id: termination

        correct: true
      - text: Models require a goal parameter
      - text: To reduce the number of tools
    explanation: Combine a goal with explicit limits on steps, time and cost.
  - id: agent-not-new
    prompt: Is the concept of a software "agent" new?
    options:
      - text: Yes, it was invented in 2023
      - text: Yes, by Databricks
      - text: Yes, by OpenAI
      - id: old
        text: No — agents (perceive, decide, act) are a classic AI concept, central to Russell and Norvig's textbook; LLMs made general-purpose agents practical
        correct: true
    explanation: Older concepts — environments, policies, rewards — remain useful for thinking about LLM agents.
  - id: enterprise-components
    prompt: In an enterprise setting, what makes an agent "production-ready" beyond the loop itself?
    type: multiple

      - id: evaluation
        text: Evaluation showing it meets a quality bar

      - id: observability

        correct: true

        correct: true
    explanation: The Databricks course stresses evaluation and governance; they apply on any platform.

## Learning objectives

- Define an AI agent precisely
- Distinguish agents from chatbots and traditional automation
- Recognise agent washing

## The minimal agent loop

```text
goal ─► LLM decides ─┬─► final answer ─► stop
         ▲           └─► tool call ─► execute ─► observation
         └────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

```python
messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": goal}]
for step in range(MAX_STEPS):
    reply = llm(messages, tools=TOOLS)
    if not reply.tool_calls:
        return reply.content
    for call in reply.tool_calls:
        result = run_tool(call.name, call.arguments)
        messages += [reply.as_message(), {"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id, "content": result}]
raise RuntimeError("step budget exhausted")
```

## Sources

- Databricks, "AI Agent Fundamentals" course — <https://www.databricks.com/training/catalog/ai-agent-fundamentals-4482>
- Databricks blog, "Master AI Agents with New Databricks Training", 2025 — <https://www.databricks.com/blog/master-ai-agents-new-databricks-training>
- Simon Willison, "I think 'agent' may finally have a widely enough agreed upon definition", 2025 — <https://simonwillison.net/2025/Sep/18/agents/>
- Gartner press release, June 2025 — <https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-06-25-gartner-predicts-over-40-percent-of-agentic-ai-projects-will-be-canceled-by-end-of-2027>
- Russell and Norvig, *Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach*, 4th ed.

FILE: content/books/ai-agent-fundamentals/01-what-agents-are/02-workflows-versus-agents.md
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
---
title: Workflows versus agents
questions:
  - id: anthropic-distinction
    prompt: In Anthropic's "Building effective agents" (2024), what distinguishes workflows from agents?
    options:
      - id: control
        text: In workflows, LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths; in agents, the LLM dynamically directs its own process and tool usage
        correct: true
      - text: Workflows use smaller models
      - text: Agents cannot call tools
      - text: Workflows are only for data engineering
    explanation: Both are "agentic systems"; the difference is who decides the control flow.
  - id: augmented-llm
    prompt: What is the "augmented LLM" building block?
    options:
      - text: An LLM with more GPUs
      - text: A fine-tuned LLM
      - id: augmented
        text: An LLM enhanced with retrieval, tools and memory, which it can use itself
        correct: true
      - text: Two LLMs in a row
    explanation: Every pattern in this book is built from augmented LLM calls.
  - id: when-workflow
    prompt: When is a workflow preferable to an autonomous agent?
    options:
      - text: When the task is open-ended and unpredictable
      - id: predictable
        text: When the task's steps are well understood and predictable, so fixed paths give consistency, lower cost and easier testing
        correct: true
      - text: Never
      - text: When you have a large budget
    explanation: Most production "agents" are actually workflows with a few LLM decisions — and that is a good thing.
  - id: when-agent
    prompt: When is an autonomous agent most justified?
    options:
      - text: When you need deterministic output
      - text: When the steps are always identical
      - text: When errors are very costly and cannot be checked
      - id: open-ended
        text: When the number and order of steps cannot be predicted in advance, the environment gives feedback, and you trust the model's decisions in that domain
        correct: true
    explanation: Coding agents fit — tests and compilers give feedback at every step.
  - id: start-simple
    prompt: What does Anthropic's guidance recommend as a starting point?
    options:
      - id: simplest
        text: Start with the simplest solution — often a single well-prompted LLM call with retrieval — and add complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes
        correct: true
      - text: Start with a multi-agent framework
      - text: Start by fine-tuning
      - text: Start with full autonomy and restrict later
    explanation: "\"Success in the LLM space isn't about building the most sophisticated system. It's about building the right system for your needs.\""
  - id: frameworks
    prompt: What caution does the same guidance give about agent frameworks?
    options:
      - text: Never use them
      - text: Always use the most popular one
      - id: understand
        text: Frameworks speed up starting but add abstraction that can obscure prompts and responses; understand what happens underneath, and start with direct API calls if possible
        correct: true
      - text: Frameworks guarantee correctness
    explanation: Many patterns are a few dozen lines of code.
  - id: spectrum
    prompt: Order these from least to most autonomous.
    options:
      - text: Agent → router → single call → chain
      - text: Chain → agent → single call → router
      - text: Router → agent → chain → single call
      - id: order
        text: Single LLM call → prompt chain → router → autonomous agent
        correct: true
    explanation: Each step up adds flexibility, cost, latency and unpredictability.
  - id: deterministic-steps
    prompt: In a hybrid design, which steps should stay deterministic code?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: auth
        text: Authorisation checks
        correct: true
      - id: money
        text: Calculations involving money
        correct: true
      - id: validation
        text: Validation of tool inputs and outputs
        correct: true
      - text: Interpreting free-text customer complaints
    explanation: Use LLMs where language understanding is needed; use code where correctness must be guaranteed.
---
## Learning objectives

- Distinguish workflows from agents
- Choose the least autonomy that solves the problem
- Use frameworks with understanding

## A routing workflow (not an agent)

```python
category = llm_classify(ticket, ["billing", "technical", "account"])
match category:
    case "billing":   reply = billing_flow(ticket)
    case "technical": reply = technical_flow(ticket)
    case _:           reply = escalate_to_human(ticket)
```

The LLM makes one decision; code owns the control flow. This is easy to test and cheap to run.

- LangChain, "How to think about agent frameworks", 2025 — <https://blog.langchain.com/how-to-think-about-agent-frameworks/>

title: When not to build an agent
questions:
  - id: gartner
    prompt: What did Gartner predict in June 2025 about agentic AI projects?
    options:
      - text: All will succeed by 2026
      - id: forty
        text: Over 40% will be cancelled by the end of 2027 due to escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls
        correct: true
      - text: Agents will replace all software by 2027
      - text: No change from traditional projects
    explanation: Predictions are not facts, but the stated reasons — cost, value, risk — are the ones to plan against.
  - id: compounding
    prompt: Each step of a 20-step agent task succeeds independently with 95% probability. Roughly how likely is the whole task to succeed?
    options:
      - text: 95%
      - text: 75%
      - id: thirty-six
        text: About 36% (0.95²⁰)
        correct: true
      - text: 5%
    explanation: Errors compound across steps. Reliability per step must be very high, or steps must be verified and recoverable.
  - id: red-flags
    prompt: Which are red flags that an agent is the wrong tool?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: deterministic
        text: The process is fully specified and deterministic
        correct: true
      - id: zero-error
        text: Errors are catastrophic and cannot be checked or undone
        correct: true
      - id: no-eval
        text: There is no way to tell whether the agent succeeded
        correct: true
      - id: latency
        text: Strict low-latency requirements in a user-facing path
        correct: true
    explanation: Each pushes toward code, workflows or human processes instead.
  - id: cheaper-alternatives
    prompt: A team wants an agent to "answer questions about our sales data". What should they consider first?
    options:
      - id: simpler
        text: Whether a dashboard, a governed text-to-SQL tool (like a Genie space) or a few parameterised reports already meet the need
        correct: true
      - text: A five-agent system
      - text: Fine-tuning a model on the sales database
      - text: Nothing; agents are always best
    explanation: Agents should earn their complexity.
  - id: process-first
    prompt: Why does automating a broken process with an agent rarely work?
    options:
      - text: Agents refuse broken processes
      - text: Agents only work on new processes
      - text: It is illegal
      - id: amplify
        text: Agents amplify the process's ambiguity and data problems; redesigning the process often delivers more value than automating it
        correct: true
    explanation: Workflow redesign was the strongest predictor of value in several 2025 enterprise surveys.
  - id: reliability-metric
    prompt: Sierra's τ-bench introduced pass^k. What does it measure?
    options:
      - text: The pass rate on the first attempt only
      - id: consistency
        text: The probability that an agent succeeds on all k independent trials of the same task — exposing inconsistency that single-run accuracy hides
        correct: true
      - text: The number of passes through a loop
      - text: Password strength
    explanation: Agents that succeed 60% of the time on one try can succeed far less often when consistency across 8 tries is required.
  - id: human-cost
    prompt: Which costs are often missed when estimating an agent's ROI?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: review
        text: Time humans spend reviewing and correcting agent outputs
        correct: true
      - id: incidents
        text: Cost of incidents caused by wrong actions
        correct: true
      - id: maintenance
        text: Ongoing evaluation and maintenance as models and tools change
        correct: true
      - text: The agent's salary
    explanation: If reviewing takes as long as doing, the agent adds cost.
---
## Learning objectives

- Recognise when an agent is the wrong tool
- Understand compounding error and consistency
- Account for hidden costs

## Decision checklist

| Question | If "no" |
|---|---|
| Can we define and measure success? | Don't build yet |
| Are steps unpredictable enough to need LLM planning? | Use a workflow |
| Can wrong actions be detected and undone? | Add human approval or don't automate |
| Is per-step reliability high on our tasks? | Narrow the scope |
| Is the process itself sound? | Fix the process first |

## Learning objectives

- Understand what the LLM does and does not do in an agent
- Choose models for agentic workloads
- Practise context engineering

## What the model actually emits

```json
{
  "role": "assistant",
  "tool_calls": [
    { "id": "call_1", "type": "function",
      "function": { "name": "lookup_order", "arguments": "{\"order_id\": \"A-1042\"}" } }
  ]
}
```

The model proposes; your code disposes. Everything about safety follows from that boundary.

title: Tools and function calling
questions:
  - id: function-calling
    prompt: How does function (tool) calling work?
    options:
      - text: The model connects to your database over the network
      - id: schema
        text: You describe tools (name, description, JSON Schema parameters); the model returns a structured request to call one; your code validates and executes it and returns the result
        correct: true
      - text: The model downloads and runs your code
      - text: The provider executes your functions
    explanation: Some providers host built-in tools (web search, code execution), but for your own tools execution is always on your side.
  - id: tool-types
    prompt: Which are common categories of agent tools?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: retrieval
        text: Retrieval — search, vector search, SQL queries
        correct: true
      - id: action
        text: Actions — send email, create ticket, update records
        correct: true
      - id: compute
        text: Computation — code execution, calculators
        correct: true
      - id: human
        text: Human interaction — ask for clarification or approval
        correct: true
    explanation: Read-only tools are far less risky than action tools; classify every tool accordingly.
  - id: descriptions
    prompt: Why do tool names and descriptions matter so much?
    options:
      - text: They are shown to end users
      - text: They are only for documentation
      - id: selection
        text: The model chooses tools based on them; vague or overlapping descriptions cause wrong tool choices
        correct: true
      - text: They determine billing
    explanation: Anthropic recommends writing tool descriptions as you would for a new colleague, with examples and edge cases.
  - id: validation
    prompt: The model calls `refund(order_id="A-1042", amount=5000)`. What must the tool layer do?
    options:
      - text: Execute it; the model decided
      - id: validate
        text: Validate arguments and enforce business rules and the user's permissions (e.g. refund cap, order ownership) before executing
        correct: true
      - text: Ask the model if it is sure
      - text: Log it and execute
    explanation: Tool arguments are untrusted input.
  - id: too-many-tools
    prompt: What happens when an agent is given 200 tools?
    options:
      - text: It becomes 200 times more capable
      - text: Nothing changes
      - text: The provider rejects the request
      - id: degrade
        text: Tool-selection accuracy tends to drop, tool definitions consume context and tokens, and behaviour becomes harder to test; group tools, retrieve relevant tools dynamically, or split into specialised agents
        correct: true
    explanation: Fewer, well-designed tools beat many thin wrappers.
  - id: granularity
    prompt: Which tool design is usually better for agents?
    options:
      - id: task-level
        text: Task-level tools (e.g. `schedule_meeting(attendees, duration)`) that encapsulate several API calls and return concise, relevant results
        correct: true
      - text: One tool per REST endpoint, returning raw JSON
      - text: A single `execute_sql(any_query)` tool for everything
      - text: Tools that return entire database tables
    explanation: Tools designed for agents differ from APIs designed for programs — they should be meaningful units with token-efficient outputs.
  - id: errors
    prompt: How should tools report errors to the agent?
    options:
      - text: Crash the agent
      - text: Return an empty string
      - id: informative
        text: Return clear, actionable error messages (e.g. "order_id must look like A-1234; did you mean A-1042?") so the model can correct itself
        correct: true
      - text: Return a stack trace

  - id: parallel-calls

      - text: Retrying a failed call
      - id: parallel

        correct: true
      - text: Calling the same tool twice
    explanation: Only safe when calls are independent; actions with ordering dependencies must run sequentially.
  - id: idempotent

    options:
      - id: retry

        correct: true
      - text: To make them faster
      - text: Models require it
      - text: To reduce token count
    explanation: The same rule applies to any distributed system with retries.
  - id: code-tools
    prompt: What is the main risk of giving an agent a general code-execution or shell tool?
    options:
      - text: It is too slow
      - text: Models cannot write code
      - id: blast-radius

    explanation: Sandboxing is non-negotiable for code tools.

## Learning objectives

- Explain the function-calling protocol
- Design tools that agents use well
- Validate and sandbox tool execution

## A tool definition

```json
{
  "name": "lookup_order",
  "description": "Look up one order by its ID (format A-1234). Returns status, items and total. Use when the user references a specific order.",
  "parameters": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": { "order_id": { "type": "string", "pattern": "^A-\\d{4}$" } },
    "required": ["order_id"]
  }
}
```

## The execution boundary

```text
LLM ──proposes call──► Tool layer: parse → validate schema → check user's permission
                                 → enforce business rules → execute (sandboxed)
                                 → shape result (concise) ──► back to LLM
```

title: Memory and context
questions:
  - id: short-term
    prompt: What is an agent's short-term (working) memory?
    options:
      - id: context

        correct: true
      - text: The model's weights
      - text: A database of all users
      - text: The GPU cache

  - id: long-term

      - text: Fine-tuning the model nightly
      - text: A larger context window
      - id: persisted
        text: Information persisted outside the model (databases, vector stores, files) and retrieved into context when relevant across sessions
        correct: true

  - id: memory-types

    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: episodic

        correct: true
      - id: semantic
        text: Semantic — facts about the world or user
        correct: true
      - id: procedural
        text: Procedural — how to do things (prompts, code, skills)
        correct: true
      - text: Hydraulic — memory stored in pipes

  - id: overflow

    type: multiple

        correct: true
      - id: offload

        correct: true
      - id: subagents

        correct: true
      - text: Increase temperature
    explanation: Summaries lose detail; decide what must be preserved verbatim.
  - id: memory-poisoning

    options:
      - text: Corrupting RAM chips

        correct: true
      - text: Forgetting old conversations
      - text: Running out of memory

  - id: privacy

        correct: true
      - id: sensitive
        text: Sensitive categories may need to be excluded or protected
        correct: true
      - text: Memory is exempt from privacy law

  - id: state

    options:
      - text: Only in the model's context
      - text: In the model's weights
      - id: system-of-record

        correct: true
      - text: In the system prompt

  - id: stateless-api

      - text: Because of HTTP limits
    explanation: This is why cost grows roughly quadratically with step count unless context is managed.

## Learning objectives

- Distinguish short-term and long-term memory
- Manage growing context
- Secure and govern memory

## Memory architecture

```text
┌──────────── context window (short-term) ────────────┐
│ system prompt · recent turns · tool results · notes  │
└───────────────▲──────────────────────────┬───────────┘
                │ retrieve relevant        │ write selected facts
┌───────────────┴──────────────────────────▼───────────┐
│ long-term stores: user profile · episodic log ·       │
│ vector memory · files · system-of-record databases    │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

title: Planning and ReAct
questions:
  - id: react

    options:
      - text: React.js and Python

        correct: true

      - text: Reinforcement learning and actors

  - id: plan-execute

    options:
      - text: Executing without a plan
      - text: Asking the user for a plan
      - id: plan-first
        text: A planner produces a multi-step plan up front; an executor carries out steps (possibly with a cheaper model), and the plan is revised if steps fail
        correct: true
      - text: Running the same step repeatedly

  - id: reflection

    options:

        correct: true
      - text: Mirroring the user's tone
      - text: Reflecting data into another table
      - text: A security attack
    explanation: Shinn et al., 2023. Self-critique works best with external feedback (tests, validators); without it, models may confidently "fix" correct answers.
  - id: feedback

    options:
      - text: Code is easy
      - text: Programmers write better prompts
      - text: Coding models are larger
      - id: verifiable

        correct: true

  - id: stuck

    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: loop-detect
        text: Detecting repeated actions and intervening
        correct: true
      - id: budgets
        text: Step, time and token budgets
        correct: true
      - id: escalate
        text: Escalating to a human when stuck
        correct: true
      - text: Raising the step limit to infinity
    explanation: Loops are a common, expensive failure mode.
  - id: decomposition
    prompt: What is task decomposition?
    options:
      - text: Deleting tasks
      - id: subtasks
        text: Breaking a complex goal into smaller sub-tasks that are easier to solve and verify individually
        correct: true
      - text: Splitting a model into layers
      - text: Compressing context
    explanation: Decomposition can be fixed in code (workflow) or produced by the model (planning).
  - id: ask-user
    prompt: When should an agent ask the user instead of proceeding?
    options:
      - text: Never; autonomy means no questions
      - text: Before every step
      - id: ambiguity
        text: When the request is ambiguous in a way that changes the outcome, or before irreversible actions
        correct: true
      - text: Only when the model's confidence is above 90%
    explanation: Give the agent an explicit `ask_user` tool and guidance on when to use it.
  - id: tree-search
    prompt: What does Tree of Thoughts add?
    options:
      - id: explore

        correct: true
      - text: A visual tree diagram for users
      - text: A database index
      - text: Storing thoughts in a B-tree
    explanation: Yao et al., 2023. Powerful for puzzles; often too expensive for routine business tasks.

## Learning objectives

- Explain ReAct, plan-and-execute and reflection
- Design feedback and stopping conditions
- Know when to ask the user

## ReAct trace

```text
Thought: The user wants the delivery date for order A-1042.
Action: lookup_order(order_id="A-1042")
Observation: {"status": "shipped", "carrier": "UPS", "tracking": "1Z999"}
Thought: I need the carrier's estimate.
Action: track_shipment(carrier="UPS", tracking="1Z999")
Observation: {"eta": "2026-11-14"}
Answer: Your order shipped with UPS and should arrive on 14 November.
```

## Sources

- Yao et al., "ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models", 2022 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629>

FILE: content/books/ai-agent-fundamentals/03-architectures-and-protocols/01-workflow-patterns.md
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
---
title: Workflow patterns
questions:
  - id: chaining
    prompt: What is prompt chaining?
    options:
      - text: Running the same prompt many times
      - id: sequence
        text: Decomposing a task into a fixed sequence of LLM calls, each processing the previous output, optionally with programmatic checks ("gates") between steps
        correct: true
      - text: Linking prompts with a blockchain
      - text: Combining prompts into one long prompt
    explanation: Example — generate an outline, check it meets criteria, then write the document.
  - id: routing
    prompt: What is the routing pattern?
    options:
      - text: Network routing
      - text: Load balancing between identical models
      - id: classify
        text: Classifying an input and directing it to a specialised follow-up prompt, tool or model
        correct: true
      - text: Sending every request to every model
    explanation: Routing also enables cost savings — easy questions to small models, hard ones to large.
  - id: parallelization
    prompt: Which two variants of parallelisation does Anthropic describe?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: sectioning
        text: Sectioning — splitting a task into independent subtasks run in parallel
        correct: true
      - id: voting
        text: Voting — running the same task several times for diverse outputs or consensus
        correct: true
      - text: Sharding the model across GPUs
      - text: Running two users' requests together
    explanation: Example of sectioning — one call answers the question while another screens for inappropriate content.
  - id: orchestrator
    prompt: What characterises the orchestrator-workers pattern?
    options:
      - id: dynamic
        text: A central LLM dynamically breaks down a task, delegates subtasks to worker LLMs and synthesises their results — subtasks are not predefined
        correct: true
      - text: A fixed DAG of tasks
      - text: Workers that never return results
      - text: A Kubernetes operator
    explanation: It differs from parallelisation because the orchestrator decides the subtasks at runtime.
  - id: evaluator-optimizer
    prompt: When does the evaluator-optimizer pattern fit?
    options:
      - text: When there are no evaluation criteria
      - text: For single-word answers
      - text: When latency must be minimal
      - id: criteria
        text: When clear evaluation criteria exist and iterative refinement measurably improves results — e.g. translation or writing against a rubric
        correct: true
    explanation: One LLM generates; another evaluates and gives feedback; repeat until it passes or a limit is reached.
  - id: gates
    prompt: What is a "gate" in a chain?
    options:
      - text: A firewall
      - id: check
        text: A programmatic check between steps that stops or redirects the flow if an intermediate output fails validation
        correct: true
      - text: A paywall
      - text: A UI component
    explanation: Gates catch errors early instead of letting them compound.
  - id: pattern-match
    prompt: Match each scenario to the best pattern. Which pairings are sensible?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: support-routing
        text: Customer messages of distinct types → routing
        correct: true
      - id: code-review-voting
        text: Security review of code where missing an issue is costly → voting across several reviews
        correct: true
      - id: research-orchestrator
        text: Research across an unknown number of sources → orchestrator-workers
        correct: true
      - text: Extracting one field from a form → five-agent debate
    explanation: Use the simplest pattern that fits.
  - id: latency-tradeoff
    prompt: Which pattern typically increases latency the most?
    options:
      - text: A single call
      - text: Routing
      - id: iterative
        text: Iterative patterns such as evaluator-optimizer loops and multi-step orchestration
        correct: true
      - text: Parallel sectioning
    explanation: Parallel sectioning can reduce latency; loops add round trips.
---
## Learning objectives

- Recognise the five workflow patterns
- Choose patterns by task structure
- Use gates to stop error propagation

## Patterns at a glance

```text
Chaining:           A ──► gate ──► B ──► C
Routing:            in ──► classifier ──┬─► flow 1
                                        └─► flow 2
Parallelisation:    in ──┬─► A ─┐
                         └─► B ─┴─► aggregate
Orchestrator:       in ──► orchestrator ──► (workers decided at runtime) ──► synthesise
Evaluator-optimizer: generate ⇄ evaluate (until pass or limit)
```

## Sources

- Anthropic, "Building effective agents", 2024 — <https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents>
- Anthropic cookbook, agent patterns — <https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-cookbook/tree/main/patterns/agents>

title: Multi-agent systems
questions:
  - id: definition
    prompt: What is a multi-agent system in the LLM sense?
    options:
      - id: several
        text: Several agents — each with its own instructions, tools and context — collaborating, often coordinated by a supervisor or through hand-offs
        correct: true
      - text: One agent with many users
      - text: Several copies of the same model behind a load balancer
      - text: Agents competing in a game
    explanation: The Databricks course introduces multi-agent systems; Agent Bricks offered a multi-agent supervisor template.
  - id: why
    prompt: Which are legitimate reasons to use multiple agents?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: specialisation
        text: Specialisation — different tools, permissions and prompts per domain
        correct: true
      - id: context-isolation
        text: Context isolation — sub-agents explore in fresh contexts and return condensed results
        correct: true
      - id: parallel
        text: Parallel exploration of independent sub-problems
        correct: true
      - text: Because more agents are always smarter
    explanation: Each reason has a cost; justify it with evaluation.
  - id: anthropic-research
    prompt: What did Anthropic report about its multi-agent research system (2025)?
    options:
      - text: It used fewer tokens than a single agent
      - id: tokens
        text: It outperformed a single agent substantially on breadth-first research tasks but used many times more tokens — roughly 15× a chat interaction
        correct: true
      - text: It failed completely
      - text: It worked best for coding tasks with tight dependencies
    explanation: Multi-agent designs pay off when the task's value justifies the token cost and the work parallelises.
  - id: cognition
    prompt: Cognition's essay "Don't Build Multi-Agents" (2025) argued what?
    options:
      - text: Multi-agent systems are always best
      - text: Agents should not use tools
      - id: context-sharing
        text: Splitting work across agents that do not share full context leads to conflicting assumptions and fragile results; single-threaded agents with good context management are often more reliable
        correct: true
      - text: Agents should be written in Rust
    explanation: The two positions are compatible — parallelise read-only research; keep tightly coupled decisions in one context.
  - id: supervisor
    prompt: In a supervisor (hierarchical) architecture, what does the supervisor do?
    options:
      - id: delegate
        text: Interprets the request, delegates to specialised agents, and combines their outputs into a response
        correct: true
      - text: Monitors GPU temperature
      - text: Writes all answers itself
      - text: Approves expenses
    explanation: The supervisor's routing quality caps the whole system's quality.
  - id: handoff
    prompt: What is a hand-off pattern?
    options:
      - text: Passing a request to a human
      - text: Ending the conversation
      - text: Sharing API keys
      - id: transfer
        text: One agent transfers control of the conversation to another agent better suited to continue, along with relevant context
        correct: true
    explanation: Used in customer-service designs (triage → billing agent).
  - id: failure-modes
    prompt: Research on multi-agent failures (Cemri et al., 2025) identified which categories?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: spec
        text: Specification and system design problems
        correct: true
      - id: misalignment
        text: Inter-agent misalignment — agents ignoring or misunderstanding each other
        correct: true
      - id: verification
        text: Weak task verification and premature termination
        correct: true
      - text: Agents unionising
    explanation: Their taxonomy (MAST) found many failures arise from design, not model capability.
  - id: debugging
    prompt: Why are multi-agent systems harder to debug?
    options:
      - text: They do not produce logs
      - id: emergent
        text: Behaviour emerges from interactions; errors propagate between agents, and you need end-to-end traces across all of them
        correct: true
      - text: They run on different clouds
      - text: They cannot be tested
    explanation: Tracing that links spans across agents is essential.
  - id: cost-multi
    prompt: A two-level supervisor with four worker agents handles each request. Compared with one agent, what should you expect?
    options:
      - text: Lower cost and latency
      - text: Identical cost
      - text: Cost depends only on the supervisor
      - id: higher
        text: Higher token cost and latency, justified only if quality gains are measured
        correct: true
    explanation: Measure cost per successful task for both designs.

## Learning objectives

- Explain supervisor, hand-off and parallel multi-agent designs
- Weigh the evidence for and against multi-agent systems
- Recognise multi-agent failure modes

## Supervisor sketch

```text
User ──► Supervisor ──┬─► Sales-data agent (Genie / SQL tools, read-only)
                      ├─► Policy agent (document retrieval)
                      └─► Ticketing agent (create/update tickets, needs approval)
                 ◄── combine results ──
```

---
title: Protocols — MCP and A2A
questions:
  - id: mcp-what
    prompt: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?
    options:
      - text: A proprietary Databricks API
      - id: open
        text: An open protocol, introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, standardising how AI applications connect to tools, data and prompts through MCP servers
        correct: true
      - text: A model compression format
      - text: A messaging queue
    explanation: Often described as "USB-C for AI applications" — one integration works with many hosts.
  - id: mcp-problem
    prompt: Which integration problem does MCP address?
    options:
      - text: Slow GPUs
      - text: Token pricing
      - id: m-times-n
        text: The M×N problem — every AI application writing custom integrations for every tool — becoming M+N with a common protocol
        correct: true
      - text: Model hallucination
    explanation: Tool providers implement a server once; any MCP-capable client can use it.
  - id: primitives
    prompt: Which are MCP server primitives?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: tools
        text: Tools — functions the model can call
        correct: true
      - id: resources
        text: Resources — data the application can read into context
        correct: true
      - id: prompts
        text: Prompts — reusable templates
        correct: true
      - text: GPUs
    explanation: Clients can also offer capabilities to servers, such as sampling (asking the client's model to generate) and elicitation (asking the user for input).
  - id: transports
    prompt: Which transports does MCP define?
    options:
      - text: FTP and SMTP
      - id: stdio-http
        text: stdio for local servers launched as subprocesses, and Streamable HTTP for remote servers (which replaced the earlier HTTP+SSE transport in 2025)
        correct: true
      - text: Only WebSockets
      - text: Bluetooth
    explanation: Local stdio servers run with the user's privileges — a security consideration.
  - id: governance-mcp
    prompt: Where is MCP governed as of 2026?
    options:
      - text: Solely by Anthropic
      - text: By the W3C
      - text: Nobody governs it
      - id: aaif
        text: Anthropic donated MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation in December 2025
        correct: true
    explanation: Neutral governance encouraged adoption across OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Databricks and others.
  - id: mcp-risks
    prompt: Which are known MCP security risks?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: tool-poisoning
        text: Tool poisoning — malicious instructions hidden in tool descriptions
        correct: true
      - id: rug-pull
        text: "\"Rug pulls\" — a server changing tool definitions after approval"
        correct: true
      - id: confused-deputy
        text: Confused-deputy and token-passthrough problems in authorisation
        correct: true
      - id: untrusted-servers
        text: Installing untrusted local servers that run arbitrary code
        correct: true
    explanation: Treat MCP servers like third-party dependencies — vet, pin, sandbox and monitor them. The specification adopted OAuth-based authorisation for remote servers.
  - id: mcp-not
    prompt: What does MCP NOT do by itself?
    options:
      - id: not-safe
        text: Make tools safe or decide what an agent should be allowed to do — permissions and policies are still your responsibility
        correct: true
      - text: Define how tools are described
      - text: Allow remote servers
      - text: Support tool calling
    explanation: A protocol standardises connections, not trust.
  - id: a2a
    prompt: What is the Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol?
    options:
      - text: A protocol for agents to call databases
      - text: A replacement for MCP
      - id: agents-talk
        text: An open protocol (introduced by Google in April 2025, now under the Linux Foundation) for agents built on different frameworks to discover each other and collaborate on tasks
        correct: true
      - text: An authentication standard
    explanation: MCP connects an agent to tools and data; A2A connects agents to other agents. They are complementary.
  - id: agent-card
    prompt: In A2A, what is an Agent Card?
    options:
      - text: A business card for developers
      - id: card
        text: A JSON document (served at a well-known URL) describing an agent's identity, skills, endpoint and authentication requirements, used for discovery
        correct: true
      - text: A GPU accelerator
      - text: A credit card for agent purchases
    explanation: A2A also defines tasks with lifecycle states, messages and artifacts, with support for long-running work and streaming.
  - id: mcp-vs-a2a
    prompt: When would you use A2A rather than MCP?
    options:
      - text: To give an agent access to a file system
      - text: To call a calculator
      - text: To read a database table
      - id: opaque-agents
        text: When delegating a task to another autonomous agent (possibly from another vendor) that manages its own reasoning and tools, rather than calling a deterministic tool
        correct: true
    explanation: In practice MCP adoption has been much broader than A2A so far.
---
## Learning objectives

- Explain MCP's architecture, primitives and transports
- Recognise MCP's security risks
- Distinguish MCP from A2A

## MCP architecture

```text
Host application (IDE, chat app, agent)
 └─ MCP client ──(stdio | Streamable HTTP, JSON-RPC 2.0)──► MCP server
                                                            ├─ tools
                                                            ├─ resources
                                                            └─ prompts
```

## A2A at a glance

```text
Client agent ──GET /.well-known/agent-card.json──► Remote agent
             ──send message / create task─────────► (works autonomously)
             ◄─status updates, artifacts (streaming)─
```

- Anthropic, "Introducing the Model Context Protocol", November 2024 — <https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol>
- MCP specification — <https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification>
- Linux Foundation, "Agentic AI Foundation" announcement, December 2025 — <https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-announces-the-formation-of-the-agentic-ai-foundation>
- Invariant Labs, "MCP Security Notification: Tool Poisoning Attacks", 2025 — <https://invariantlabs.ai/blog/mcp-security-notification-tool-poisoning-attacks>
- A2A protocol — <https://a2a-protocol.org/>
- Linux Foundation, "Linux Foundation Launches the Agent2Agent Protocol Project", June 2025 — <https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-launches-the-agent2agent-protocol-project-to-enable-secure-intelligent-communication-between-ai-agents>

## The Agent Bricks idea

```text
Describe the task ──► connect data (Unity Catalog tables, volumes, Genie spaces, MCP)
        │
        ▼
Generated evaluation set + LLM judges ◄── expert feedback (natural language)
        │
        ▼
Optimise (prompts, models, retrieval, fine-tuning) for quality and cost
        │
        ▼
Deploy with governance (Unity Catalog, AI gateway, tracing)
```

## A Unity Catalog function as a tool

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION main.support.order_status(order_id STRING)
RETURNS TABLE (status STRING, carrier STRING, eta DATE)
COMMENT 'Look up the status, carrier and estimated delivery date of an order by ID (format A-1234).'
RETURN SELECT status, carrier, eta FROM main.sales.orders WHERE id = order_id;

GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION main.support.order_status TO `support-agents`;
```

## Logging and deploying a code-first agent

```python
import mlflow
from databricks import agents

with mlflow.start_run():
    info = mlflow.pyfunc.log_model(
        name="agent",
        python_model="agent.py",
        registered_model_name="main.support.order_agent",
    )

agents.deploy("main.support.order_agent", info.registered_model_version)
```

APIs evolve; check the current docs for the recommended deployment target.

title: Evaluating agents
questions:
  - id: levels
    prompt: Which levels of agent evaluation are useful?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: outcome

        correct: true

        correct: true

  - id: state-check

title: The lethal trifecta
questions:
  - id: trifecta
    prompt: Which three capabilities form Simon Willison's "lethal trifecta" for AI agents?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: private
        text: Access to private data
        correct: true
      - id: untrusted
        text: Exposure to untrusted content
        correct: true
      - id: exfil

  - id: why-dangerous

      - text: Because it is expensive
      - text: Because it slows the agent down

  - id: rule-of-two

        correct: true
      - id: approval

        correct: true
      - text: Telling the model to ignore malicious instructions

  - id: real-incidents

      - text: MCP forbids read-only tools

- Recognise the lethal trifecta and the Rule of Two
- Design agents that remove at least one leg
- Understand why prompt instructions are not a defence

## The trifecta

```text
        Private data
           ▲    ▲
          /      \
 Untrusted ─────── External
  content          communication
   (all three together = exfiltration risk)
```

## Action classes

| Class | Examples | Control |
|---|---|---|
| Read | Search, lookup | Scoped to user's permissions |

title: Failure modes and runaway costs
questions:
  - id: modes

        correct: true

        correct: true

        text: Stopping early and claiming success
        correct: true
      - id: drift

        correct: true

  - id: hallucinated-tool

        correct: true
      - text: The agent should crash
      - text: The model should be retrained

  - id: budgets

    type: multiple

      - id: steps
        text: Maximum steps or tool calls
        correct: true
      - id: tokens
        text: Maximum tokens or cost
        correct: true
      - id: time
        text: Maximum wall-clock time
        correct: true
      - text: Maximum number of users

  - id: reward-hacking

    options:
      - text: A good solution
      - text: A compiler bug
      - id: specification-gaming
        text: Specification gaming (reward hacking) — satisfying the literal objective instead of the intended one
        correct: true
      - text: A network error
    explanation: Protect evaluators (tests, checks) from modification and review diffs.
  - id: cost-growth
    prompt: Why can agent cost grow faster than linearly with the number of steps?
    options:

        text: Each step resends the growing context, so total input tokens grow roughly with the square of the step count unless context is managed or cached
        correct: true
      - text: Providers charge more per step
      - text: Tools charge per character
      - text: It cannot
    explanation: Prompt caching and context compaction flatten the curve.
  - id: error-propagation
    prompt: An early tool returns subtly wrong data, and the agent builds its whole answer on it. How do you limit this?
    options:
      - text: Use higher temperature
      - text: Add more steps
      - text: Hide tool outputs from the model
      - id: validate
        text: Validate tool outputs, cross-check critical facts with a second source, and design checkpoints where results are verified
        correct: true
    explanation: The agent cannot know a tool lied; your validation can.
  - id: graceful
    prompt: What should an agent do when it cannot complete a task?
    options:
      - id: escalate
        text: Stop, explain what it tried and what is missing, and hand off to a human or ask the user — not guess or fake completion
        correct: true
      - text: Keep trying forever
      - text: Return a plausible answer
      - text: Silently fail
    explanation: Make "I could not do this" a valid, rewarded outcome in prompts and evaluations.

## Learning objectives

- Recognise typical agent failure modes
- Bound runs with budgets and validation
- Escalate gracefully

## A guarded loop

```python
for step in range(budget.max_steps):
    if budget.tokens_used > budget.max_tokens or clock() > budget.deadline:
        return escalate("budget exhausted", trace)
    reply = llm(context.render(), tools=allowed_tools)
    if reply.final:
        return verify_or_escalate(reply)
    for call in reply.tool_calls:
        if call.name not in allowed_tools:
            context.add_error(f"Unknown tool {call.name}. Available: {list(allowed_tools)}")
            continue
        if loop_detector.seen(call):
            return escalate("repeated action", trace)
        context.add_result(call, execute_validated(call))
return escalate("step limit", trace)
```

    explanation: Vertical agents tend to show clearer ROI because success is easier to define.
  - id: customer-facing
    prompt: What extra considerations apply to customer-facing agents?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: liability
        text: The company is liable for what the agent says (cf. Moffatt v. Air Canada)
        correct: true
      - id: disclosure
        text: Disclosure that the customer is talking to AI
        correct: true
      - id: escalation
        text: Easy escalation to a human
        correct: true
      - text: No logging is needed
    explanation: Internal pilots first, then limited external rollout.

## Learning objectives

- Identify strong agent use cases
- Interpret productivity evidence critically
- Plan customer-facing deployments responsibly

|---|---|---|

## Learning objectives

- Build an honest ROI model for agents
- Use controlled comparisons
- Define stop criteria

## An ROI sketch

```text
Benefit per month = tasks × (baseline cost per task − agent cost per successful task) − cost of agent errors
Agent cost per successful task = (inference + tools + review time × wage + rework) / successful tasks
Payback = (build + integration + evaluation) / monthly benefit
```

## A minimal tool-using agent

```csharp
using System.ClientModel;
using System.ComponentModel;
using Microsoft.Extensions.AI;
using OpenAI;

var openAi = new OpenAIClient(
    new ApiKeyCredential(Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("DATABRICKS_TOKEN")!),
    new OpenAIClientOptions { Endpoint = new Uri($"{workspaceUrl}/serving-endpoints") });

IChatClient chat = openAi.GetChatClient(chatEndpointName)
    .AsIChatClient()
    .AsBuilder()
    .UseFunctionInvocation()
    .UseOpenTelemetry(sourceName: "Terlingua.Agents")
    .Build();

ChatOptions options = new() { Tools = [AIFunctionFactory.Create(OrderTools.GetStatus)] };

ChatResponse response = await chat.GetResponseAsync(
    [new(ChatRole.System, "You answer questions about orders. Use tools; never guess."),
     new(ChatRole.User, "Where is order A-1042?")],
    options);

Console.WriteLine(response.Text);

public static class OrderTools
{
    [Description("Gets status, carrier and ETA for an order ID in the format A-1234.")]
    public static OrderStatus GetStatus([Description("Order ID, e.g. A-1042")] string orderId) =>
        OrderId.TryParse(orderId, out var id)
            ? OrderRepository.Find(id)
            : throw new ArgumentException("Order IDs look like A-1234.", nameof(orderId));
}

public sealed record OrderStatus(string Status, string Carrier, DateOnly Eta);
```

## With dependency injection

```csharp
builder.Services.AddChatClient(sp => sp.GetRequiredService<OpenAIClient>()
        .GetChatClient(builder.Configuration["Ai:ChatModel"]!)
        .AsIChatClient())
    .UseFunctionInvocation()
    .UseOpenTelemetry();
```

## An MCP server

```csharp
using System.ComponentModel;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting;
using ModelContextProtocol.Server;

var builder = Host.CreateApplicationBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IOrderRepository, OrderRepository>();
builder.Services.AddMcpServer().WithStdioServerTransport().WithToolsFromAssembly();
await builder.Build().RunAsync();

[McpServerToolType]
public static class OrderMcpTools
{
    [McpServerTool, Description("Gets status, carrier and ETA for an order ID in the format A-1234.")]
    public static async Task<OrderStatus> GetOrderStatus(
        IOrderRepository orders,
        [Description("Order ID, e.g. A-1042")] string orderId,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken) =>
        await orders.GetStatusAsync(OrderId.Parse(orderId), cancellationToken);
}
```

```csharp
using ModelContextProtocol.Client;
```

## Learning objectives

- Use C# 15 unions and closed hierarchies to model agent outcomes

## Modelling outcomes with a union

```csharp
public sealed record Answered(string Text, IReadOnlyList<Uri> Sources);
public sealed record NeedsApproval(string Action, string Reason, Guid IdempotencyKey);
public sealed record Escalated(string Reason);

public union AgentOutcome(Answered, NeedsApproval, Escalated);

public static IResult ToHttp(AgentOutcome outcome) => outcome switch
{
    Answered a => Results.Ok(new { a.Text, a.Sources }),
    NeedsApproval n => Results.Accepted(value: new { n.Action, n.Reason, n.IdempotencyKey }),
    Escalated e => Results.Json(new { e.Reason }, statusCode: StatusCodes.Status202Accepted),
};
```

## A deterministic core around the model

```csharp
public sealed class RefundTool(IOrderRepository orders, IRefundPolicy policy, TimeProvider clock)
{
    [Description("Requests a refund for an order. Amounts above the policy limit require human approval.")]
    public async Task<AgentOutcome> RequestRefundAsync(string orderId, decimal amount, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        var order = await orders.GetAsync(OrderId.Parse(orderId), cancellationToken);
        return policy.Evaluate(order, amount, clock.GetUtcNow()) switch
        {
            RefundDecision.Allowed => new Answered($"Refund of {amount:C} submitted.", []),
            RefundDecision.NeedsApproval => new NeedsApproval("refund", "Above automatic limit", Guid.CreateVersion7()),
            RefundDecision.Denied d => new Escalated(d.Reason),
        };
    }
}
```

The model decides *whether* to request a refund. The policy, in tested C#, decides *what happens*.

## Ten-year checklist for .NET agents

- `IChatClient` and `AIFunction` at the boundary; vendor SDKs only in the composition root
- MCP for tools you share; OpenTelemetry for traces
- Records for tool contracts; unions for outcomes
- `CancellationToken` and `TimeProvider` everywhere
- Evaluation suites in CI; regression cases from production traces
- Model names and limits in configuration
- Target LTS releases for long-lived services; keep code compiling on the current STS

## Sources

## Terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Augmented LLM | LLM + retrieval + tools + memory |
| Workflow | Predefined code paths orchestrating LLM calls |
| ReAct | Interleaved reasoning and acting |
| Orchestrator-workers | Runtime decomposition and delegation |
| Context engineering | Curating what enters the context each step |
| Excessive agency | More capability or permission than needed |
| Rule of Two | At most two of: untrusted input, sensitive access, external action |
| On-behalf-of-user | Agent acts with the invoking user's permissions |

## Learning objectives

- Apply the book's ideas to mixed scenarios

## Twelve rules for agents

1. Start with the simplest thing; add autonomy only when evaluation demands it.
2. The model proposes; code disposes.
3. Design tools for agents — task-level, concise, validated.
4. Bound every run: steps, tokens, time.
5. Verify outcomes in the environment, not in the agent's words.
6. Evaluate trajectories and consistency, not one lucky run.
7. Trace everything, with privacy controls.
8. Never combine the lethal trifecta without supervision.
9. Agents act with the user's permissions, never more.
10. Approvals for irreversible actions, with real information.
11. Depend on abstractions and protocols; isolate frameworks.
12. Measure cost per successful task against a baseline.

## Sources

- See the sources listed in each section of this book.

## Learning objectives

- Describe Regions, Availability Zones, Local Zones and edge locations
- Know which services are zonal, regional or global
- Design for AZ-level failure

## The hierarchy

| Concept | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| Region | A geographic area such as `us-east-1` (N. Virginia) or `eu-central-1` (Frankfurt); fully isolated from other Regions |
| Availability Zone | Isolated data-centre group within a Region, e.g. `eu-central-1a`; Regions have at least three |
| Local Zone / Wavelength | Extensions placing compute closer to specific metros or 5G networks |
| Edge location | Points of presence for CloudFront, Route 53 and Global Accelerator |

## Scope of common services

| Scope | Examples |
|-------|----------|
| Global | IAM, Route 53, CloudFront, Organizations |
| Regional | S3 buckets, DynamoDB tables, Lambda functions, VPCs, SQS queues |
| Zonal | EC2 instances, EBS volumes, subnets, NAT gateways |

## Designing for failure

> "Everything fails, all the time." — Werner Vogels, Amazon CTO

- Run at least two instances in **different AZs** behind a load balancer
- Use Multi-AZ databases
- Prefer regional, managed services (S3, DynamoDB, Lambda, SQS) that are multi-AZ by design
- Consider multi-Region only when requirements justify the cost and complexity

## Choosing a Region

Latency to users, data residency law, service and feature availability, and price all vary by
Region. New services often launch first in `us-east-1`.

## Learning objectives

- Apply the shared responsibility model to different services
- Use the six Well-Architected pillars to review designs

## Shared responsibility by service type

| Service | AWS manages | You manage |
|---------|-------------|------------|
| EC2 (IaaS) | Hardware, hypervisor, facilities | Guest OS, patches, runtime, app, security groups, data |
| RDS (managed) | Plus OS, database engine patching, backups infrastructure | Schema, users, parameters, network access, data |
| Lambda, S3, DynamoDB (serverless) | Almost all infrastructure and runtime | Code, IAM permissions, data, configuration |

Always yours: **data classification, identity and access, encryption choices and configuration**.
Most cloud breaches are misconfigurations — public buckets, over-permissive IAM — not failures of
the provider.

## The six pillars

| Pillar | Focus |
|--------|-------|
| Operational Excellence | Automate, observe, improve operations |
| Security | Identity, detection, data protection, incident response |
| Reliability | Recover from failure, scale to demand |
| Performance Efficiency | Use the right resources efficiently |
| Cost Optimization | Avoid unnecessary cost |
| Sustainability | Minimise environmental impact |

The free **AWS Well-Architected Tool** walks a workload through questions per pillar and tracks
improvement items. Specialised **lenses** (Serverless, SaaS, Machine Learning, ...) add
domain-specific guidance.

title: Accounts and AWS Organizations
questions:

    options:

      - text: Share its password with the whole team

        correct: true
      - text: Delete it
    explanation: The root user has unrestricted access to the account. Daily work should use IAM Identity Center or roles.
  - id: scp
    prompt: What does a Service Control Policy (SCP) do?
    options:
      - text: Grants permissions to users in member accounts
      - id: guardrail
        text: Sets the maximum permissions available to principals in the accounts it applies to, without granting anything itself
        correct: true
      - text: Encrypts S3 buckets
    explanation: An action must be allowed by IAM policies and not blocked by any SCP in the hierarchy.
  - id: multi-account
    prompt: Why do organisations use multiple AWS accounts?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Accounts are strong security and blast-radius boundaries
        correct: true
      - text: Separate accounts per environment simplify cost attribution
        correct: true
      - text: Service quotas apply per account, so workloads don't compete
        correct: true
      - text: AWS charges less per resource in new accounts forever
    explanation: The account is the fundamental isolation boundary in AWS.
---
## Learning objectives

- Structure workloads across multiple accounts
- Apply guardrails with Organizations and SCPs
- Protect the root user

## Why many accounts

An AWS account is a hard boundary for security, billing and quotas. A typical structure:

```text
Management account (billing, Organizations only — no workloads)
├── Security OU      log-archive, security-tooling
├── Infrastructure OU shared networking
├── Workloads OU
│   ├── Prod OU      shop-prod
│   └── NonProd OU   shop-dev, shop-staging
└── Sandbox OU       per-developer experiments
```

**AWS Control Tower** sets up such a landing zone with best-practice guardrails.

## Service Control Policies

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Sid": "DenyOutsideApprovedRegions",
    "Effect": "Deny",
    "NotAction": ["iam:*", "organizations:*", "route53:*", "cloudfront:*", "sts:*", "support:*"],
    "Resource": "*",
    "Condition": { "StringNotEquals": { "aws:RequestedRegion": ["eu-central-1", "eu-west-1"] } }
  }]
}
```

SCPs never grant permissions; they cap what IAM policies in member accounts can allow. **Resource
control policies (RCPs)** complement them by capping what can be done *to* resources, such as
denying access to S3 buckets from outside the organisation.

## The root user

- Enable MFA (ideally a hardware key or passkey)
- No access keys
- Use only for tasks that require it (such as changing account settings or closing the account)

## Workforce access

Use **IAM Identity Center** for people: single sign-on from your identity provider into each
account with permission sets, and short-lived credentials for the console and CLI
(`aws sso login`). Avoid long-lived IAM users with access keys.

title: IAM fundamentals
questions:
  - id: role
    prompt: What is an IAM role?
    options:
      - text: A user with a permanent password
      - id: assumable

        correct: true

      - text: A billing category
    explanation: Roles have no long-term credentials. AWS STS issues temporary credentials when the role is assumed.
  - id: trust

    options:
      - id: who
        text: Who (which principals or services) is allowed to assume the role
        correct: true
      - text: What the role can do once assumed
      - text: Which Region the role lives in
    explanation: The trust policy controls who can assume; permission policies control what the role can do.
  - id: least
    prompt: Which practices follow IAM best practices?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Grant least privilege, starting narrow and adding permissions as needed
        correct: true
      - text: Use roles and temporary credentials for workloads instead of long-term access keys
        correct: true
      - text: Use IAM Access Analyzer to find unused access and generate policies from activity
        correct: true
      - text: Attach `AdministratorAccess` to every application role to avoid errors
    explanation: Broad permissions turn small bugs into large incidents.
---
## Learning objectives

- Distinguish users, groups, roles and policies
- Understand trust policies and temporary credentials
- Apply least privilege

## Principals

| Principal | Description | Credentials |
|-----------|-------------|-------------|
| Root user | Owner of the account | Password + MFA; avoid |
| IAM user | Long-lived identity | Password and/or access keys; avoid for people (use Identity Center) |
| IAM group | Collection of users | — |
| IAM role | Assumable identity | Temporary credentials from STS |
| Federated user | Signed in through an identity provider | Temporary credentials |

## A role for a Lambda function

Trust policy — who can assume it:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": { "Service": "lambda.amazonaws.com" },
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRole"
  }]
}
```

Permission policy — what it can do:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["dynamodb:GetItem", "dynamodb:PutItem", "dynamodb:Query"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:dynamodb:eu-central-1:111122223333:table/Orders"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["sqs:SendMessage"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:eu-central-1:111122223333:order-events"
    }
  ]
}
```

## Policy types

| Type | Attached to | Purpose |
|------|-------------|---------|
| Identity-based | Users, groups, roles | What the principal can do |
| Resource-based | Resources (S3 bucket, SQS queue, KMS key) | Who can access this resource, including other accounts |
| Permissions boundary | Users, roles | Maximum permissions identity policies can grant |
| SCP / RCP | Accounts, OUs | Organisation-wide guardrails |
| Session policy | An assumed-role session | Further restrict a session |

## Least privilege in practice

Start with AWS managed policies for exploration, then replace them with customer managed policies
scoped to specific actions and resource ARNs. IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from a role's
actual CloudTrail activity.

---
title: How AWS evaluates permissions
questions:
  - id: default
    prompt: If no policy mentions an action, is the request allowed?
    options:
      - text: Yes, everything is allowed by default
      - text: Only for the root user and only in us-east-1
      - id: implicit-deny
        text: No — requests are implicitly denied unless an applicable policy allows them
        correct: true
    explanation: AWS starts from deny. An explicit Allow is required (the root user is the special exception within its own account).
  - id: explicit-deny
    prompt: An identity policy allows `s3:DeleteObject`, but an SCP explicitly denies it. What is the result?
    options:
      - text: Allowed, because the identity policy is more specific
      - id: denied
        text: Denied, because an explicit deny in any applicable policy overrides every allow
        correct: true
      - text: It depends on which policy was created first
    explanation: Explicit deny always wins.
  - id: cross-account
    prompt: Which statements about cross-account access are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Access generally requires permission on both sides — the caller's identity policy and the resource policy or role trust policy
        correct: true
      - text: A common pattern is for the other account to assume a role in your account
        correct: true
      - text: Condition keys such as `aws:PrincipalOrgID` can restrict access to principals in your organisation
        correct: true
      - text: Any AWS account can access your S3 bucket unless you block it
    explanation: S3 buckets are private by default, and Block Public Access is on by default for new buckets.
---
## Learning objectives

- Trace how AWS decides to allow or deny a request
- Use conditions to narrow permissions
- Reason about cross-account access

## The evaluation logic (simplified)

1. Start with **implicit deny**
2. Any applicable **explicit deny** (identity, resource, SCP, RCP, boundary, session) → **deny**
3. Organization guardrails (SCPs/RCPs) must allow the action
4. Permissions boundaries and session policies, if present, must allow it
5. An **identity-based or resource-based policy must allow** it → **allow**
6. Otherwise → **deny**

## Conditions

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": "s3:GetObject",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-invoices/*",
  "Condition": {
    "StringEquals": { "aws:PrincipalTag/department": "finance" },
    "Bool": { "aws:SecureTransport": "true" }
  }
}
```

Common keys: `aws:SourceIp`, `aws:PrincipalOrgID`, `aws:RequestedRegion`, `aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent`,
`aws:SourceArn`, and resource or principal tags for attribute-based access control (ABAC).

## Resource policies and the confused deputy

When allowing a service to act on your resource, scope it to your source:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": { "Service": "sns.amazonaws.com" },
  "Action": "sqs:SendMessage",
  "Resource": "arn:aws:sqs:eu-central-1:111122223333:orders",
  "Condition": { "ArnEquals": { "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:sns:eu-central-1:111122223333:order-events" } }
}
```

Without the condition, any SNS topic could be configured to send to your queue.

## Debugging access

- The error message names the action and often which policy type denied it
- **IAM Policy Simulator** tests policies without making real calls
- **CloudTrail** records the denied API call with the principal and error code

## Learning objectives

- Understand the SDK's default credential chain
- Give workloads roles instead of keys
- Configure the AWS SDK for .NET with dependency injection

## The default credential chain

The AWS SDKs look for credentials in a well-defined order, including:

1. Environment variables (`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, ... or web identity token settings)
2. Shared config and credentials files (`~/.aws/config`) — profiles, including IAM Identity Center (SSO) profiles
3. Container credentials (ECS/Fargate task role, EKS Pod Identity)
4. Instance profile credentials from the EC2 instance metadata service

Your code stays the same everywhere: locally it uses your SSO profile, in AWS it uses the role.


`Profile` so the role is used.

- **GitHub Actions / GitLab** — OIDC federation to an IAM role
- **On-premises servers** — IAM Roles Anywhere with X.509 certificates

## EC2 metadata security

Require **IMDSv2** (session-token based) on instances; it mitigates SSRF attacks that tried to steal
credentials from the metadata endpoint.

## Learning objectives

- Choose instance types and purchasing options
- Build self-healing, elastic fleets with Auto Scaling
- Run .NET on EC2 sensibly

## Instance families

| Family | Optimised for | Example |
|--------|---------------|---------|
| M, T | General purpose (T = burstable) | `m7g.large`, `t4g.small` |
| C | Compute | `c7i.xlarge` |
| R, X | Memory | `r7g.2xlarge` |
| I, D | Storage I/O | `i4i.large` |
| P, G, Inf, Trn | Accelerated (GPU, ML chips) | `g5.xlarge` |

The `g` suffix in `m7g` denotes Graviton (Arm). .NET runs natively on Arm64, so Graviton is
often an easy price-performance win.

## Purchasing options

| Option | Discount | Commitment | Use for |
|--------|----------|------------|---------|
| On-Demand | None | None | Spiky, unpredictable, short-term |
| Savings Plans | Significant | 1 or 3 years of $/hour spend | Steady baseline (also covers Fargate and Lambda for Compute Savings Plans) |
| Reserved Instances | Significant | 1 or 3 years, specific instance attributes | Steady, predictable usage |
| Spot | Up to 90% | None; interruptible | Fault-tolerant batch and stateless work |

## Auto Scaling

```bash
aws autoscaling create-auto-scaling-group \
  --auto-scaling-group-name shop-web \
  --launch-template LaunchTemplateName=shop-web,Version='$Latest' \
  --min-size 2 --max-size 10 --desired-capacity 2 \
  --vpc-zone-identifier "subnet-aaa,subnet-bbb,subnet-ccc" \
  --target-group-arns arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:...:targetgroup/shop-web/abc \
  --health-check-type ELB --health-check-grace-period 120

aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy --auto-scaling-group-name shop-web \
  --policy-name cpu50 --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling \
  --target-tracking-configuration '{"PredefinedMetricSpecification":{"PredefinedMetricType":"ASGAverageCPUUtilization"},"TargetValue":50}'
```

A **launch template** defines the AMI, instance type, security groups, IAM instance profile and
user data. **Target tracking** keeps a metric near a target value.

## Treat servers as cattle

Bake images (EC2 Image Builder), keep instances stateless, store state in managed services and
replace instances rather than patching them by hand. Use **Systems Manager Session Manager** for
shell access instead of opening SSH to the internet.
