## Learning objectives

- Understand Lambda's execution model and limits
- Build .NET Lambda functions, including ASP.NET Core APIs
- Tune performance and cost

## Execution model

An event (HTTP request, SQS message, S3 upload, schedule, ...) triggers your handler in an
**execution environment**. Environments are reused for later invocations ("warm"); new ones must be
initialised ("cold start").

| Limit | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Timeout | Up to 15 minutes |
| Memory | 128 MB – 10,240 MB (CPU scales with memory) |
| Ephemeral storage `/tmp` | 512 MB – 10,240 MB |
| Package | Zip (50 MB zipped / 250 MB unzipped) or container image up to 10 GB |

## A .NET handler with Lambda Annotations

```csharp
public sealed class Functions(IOrderService orders)
{
    [LambdaFunction]
    [HttpApi(LambdaHttpMethod.Get, "/orders/{id}")]
    public async Task<IHttpResult> GetOrder(int id, ILambdaContext context)
    {
        var order = await orders.FindAsync(id);
        return order is null ? HttpResults.NotFound() : HttpResults.Ok(order);
    }
}

[LambdaStartup]
public class Startup
{
    public void ConfigureServices(IServiceCollection services) =>
        services.AddSingleton<IOrderService, DynamoOrderService>();
}
```

The Annotations source generator creates the boilerplate handler and CloudFormation (SAM) template entries.

## ASP.NET Core on Lambda

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddAWSLambdaHosting(LambdaEventSource.HttpApi);
var app = builder.Build();
app.MapGet("/health", () => "ok");
app.Run();
```

`Amazon.Lambda.AspNetCoreServer.Hosting` lets a minimal API run locally with Kestrel and on
Lambda behind API Gateway or a function URL.

## Processing queues

```csharp
public async Task<SQSBatchResponse> Handler(SQSEvent evt, ILambdaContext context)
{
    var failures = new List<SQSBatchResponse.BatchItemFailure>();
    foreach (var record in evt.Records)
    {
        try { await ProcessAsync(record.Body); }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            context.Logger.LogError(ex, "Failed {MessageId}", record.MessageId);
            failures.Add(new SQSBatchResponse.BatchItemFailure { ItemIdentifier = record.MessageId });
        }
    }
    return new SQSBatchResponse(failures);
}
```

With *ReportBatchItemFailures* enabled on the event source mapping, only failed messages are retried.

## Tuning

- Initialise SDK clients and connections **outside** the handler so warm invocations reuse them
- Right-size memory with AWS Lambda Power Tuning — more memory can be cheaper if it finishes faster
- Use **Native AOT** (on the `provided.al2023` runtime) or **SnapStart** for faster cold starts
- Use **Graviton (arm64)** for lower cost per GB-second

## ECR

```bash
aws ecr create-repository --repository-name shop-api
aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin 111122223333.dkr.ecr.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com
dotnet publish src/Shop.Api -c Release -t:PublishContainer \
  -p ContainerRegistry=111122223333.dkr.ecr.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com -p ContainerRepository=shop-api
```

Enable image scanning and lifecycle policies to remove old images.

## ECS concepts

| Concept | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| Cluster | Logical grouping of capacity and services |
| Task definition | Blueprint: image, CPU/memory, ports, environment, roles, logging |
| Task | A running instance of a task definition |
| Service | Keeps N tasks running, integrates with load balancers and auto scaling |
| Capacity provider | Fargate, Fargate Spot, or EC2 Auto Scaling groups |

```json
{
  "family": "shop-api",
  "requiresCompatibilities": ["FARGATE"],
  "networkMode": "awsvpc",
  "cpu": "512",
  "memory": "1024",
  "runtimePlatform": { "cpuArchitecture": "ARM64", "operatingSystemFamily": "LINUX" },
  "executionRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/ecsTaskExecutionRole",
  "taskRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/shop-api-task",
  "containerDefinitions": [{
    "name": "api",
    "image": "111122223333.dkr.ecr.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com/shop-api:1.4.0",
    "portMappings": [{ "containerPort": 8080 }],
    "secrets": [{ "name": "ConnectionStrings__Shop", "valueFrom": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:eu-central-1:111122223333:secret:shop-db" }],
    "logConfiguration": { "logDriver": "awslogs", "options": { "awslogs-group": "/ecs/shop-api", "awslogs-region": "eu-central-1", "awslogs-stream-prefix": "api" } }
  }]
}
```

Secrets are injected as environment variables at start-up; the execution role needs permission to
read them, and the task role is what the app uses at runtime.

## ECS or EKS?

| | ECS | EKS |
|-|-----|-----|
| API | AWS-native | Kubernetes |
| Operational effort | Lower | Higher (add-ons, upgrades) |
| Portability | AWS-specific | Kubernetes ecosystem |
| Fargate support | Yes | Yes |

Start with ECS on Fargate unless you already run Kubernetes or need its ecosystem.

## Learning objectives

- Understand buckets, objects, durability and consistency
- Secure buckets and share objects safely
- Optimise cost with storage classes and lifecycle rules

## Basics

- **Buckets** have globally unique names and live in one Region
- **Objects** are up to 5 TB; use multipart upload for large objects (single PUT max 5 GB)
- Designed for **99.999999999% (11 nines) durability** across multiple AZs (except One Zone classes)
- **Strong read-after-write consistency**

## Storage classes

| Class | Use |
|-------|-----|
| Standard | Frequently accessed data |
| Intelligent-Tiering | Unknown or changing access patterns |
| Standard-IA / One Zone-IA | Infrequent access (One Zone = single AZ, cheaper, less resilient) |
| Glacier Instant Retrieval | Archive with millisecond access |
| Glacier Flexible Retrieval | Archive, minutes to hours retrieval |
| Glacier Deep Archive | Lowest cost, hours retrieval |
| Express One Zone | Single-digit-millisecond latency for hot data in one AZ |

## Working with S3 from .NET

```csharp
await s3.PutObjectAsync(new PutObjectRequest
{
    BucketName = "acme-uploads",
    Key = $"users/{userId}/avatar.png",
    InputStream = stream,
    ContentType = "image/png"
}, ct);

using var response = await s3.GetObjectAsync("acme-uploads", $"users/{userId}/avatar.png", ct);
await response.ResponseStream.CopyToAsync(destination, ct);
```

## Presigned URLs

```csharp
var url = await s3.GetPreSignedURLAsync(new GetPreSignedUrlRequest
{
    BucketName = "acme-uploads",
    Key = $"incoming/{Guid.CreateVersion7()}.pdf",
    Verb = HttpVerb.PUT,
    Expires = DateTime.UtcNow.AddMinutes(10),
    ContentType = "application/pdf"
});
```

## Protecting data

- **Versioning** — keep every version; protects against overwrites and deletes
- **Object Lock** — write-once-read-many retention for compliance
- **Replication** — same-Region or cross-Region copies
- **Bucket policies** — require TLS (`aws:SecureTransport`), restrict to your organisation or VPC endpoint
- **CloudFront with Origin Access Control** — serve public content without making the bucket public

## Lifecycle rules

```json
{
  "Rules": [{
    "ID": "logs",
    "Status": "Enabled",
    "Filter": { "Prefix": "logs/" },
    "Transitions": [
      { "Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA" },
      { "Days": 180, "StorageClass": "GLACIER" }
    ],
    "Expiration": { "Days": 2555 }
  }]
}
```

## Learning objectives

- Choose between EBS, instance store, EFS and FSx
- Understand EBS volume types and snapshots

## Options at a glance

| Service | Type | Scope | Use |
|---------|------|-------|-----|
| EBS | Block | One AZ, one instance (mostly) | Boot volumes, databases on EC2 |
| Instance store | Block, ephemeral | The host | Caches, scratch space |
| EFS | File (NFS) | Regional, many clients | Shared content for Linux, containers |
| FSx for Windows File Server | File (SMB) | Many Windows clients | Windows shares, .NET Framework apps |
| FSx for Lustre / NetApp ONTAP / OpenZFS | File | Specialised | HPC, enterprise NAS migrations |
| S3 | Object | Regional | Almost everything else |

## EBS volume types

| Type | Characteristics |
|------|-----------------|
| gp3 | General-purpose SSD; baseline performance with independently provisioned IOPS and throughput — the default choice |
| io2 Block Express | Highest IOPS and durability for critical databases |
| st1 / sc1 | Throughput-optimised / cold HDD for large sequential workloads |

## Snapshots

```bash
aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-0abc --description "pre-upgrade"
```

Snapshots are incremental and stored in S3. Use **Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager** or **AWS Backup**
to schedule and retain them, and copy them to another Region for disaster recovery.

## EFS for containers

EFS volumes can be mounted by ECS tasks, EKS pods and Lambda functions, which makes them a simple way
to share files between stateless compute — though for most application data, S3 or a database is
a better fit than a shared file system.

## Learning objectives

- Choose between RDS engines and Aurora
- Design for availability and read scaling
- Connect securely from .NET

## RDS

Managed relational databases: provisioning, patching, backups, monitoring and failover are handled
for you. Engines: **PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Db2**.

| Feature | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| Multi-AZ | Automatic failover to a synchronous standby |
| Read replicas | Asynchronous copies to scale reads (also cross-Region) |
| Automated backups | Point-in-time restore within the retention window |
| Snapshots | Manual backups kept until deleted |

## Aurora

Aurora re-architects MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible databases on a distributed storage layer:

- Six copies across three AZs; tolerates the loss of an AZ for writes
- Up to 15 low-lag read replicas with a reader endpoint
- **Aurora Serverless v2** scales capacity in fine-grained increments
- **Global Database** for low-latency cross-Region reads and fast regional failover

## Connecting from .NET

```csharp
builder.Services.AddNpgsqlDataSource(builder.Configuration.GetConnectionString("Shop")!);
```

```json
{
  "ConnectionStrings": {
    "Shop": "Host=shop.cluster-abc.eu-central-1.rds.amazonaws.com;Database=shop;Username=shop_app;SSL Mode=VerifyFull"
  }
}
```

Keep the password out of configuration files: inject it from **Secrets Manager** (with automatic
rotation) or use **IAM database authentication**, where the app generates a short-lived token with
its role instead of a password.

## Networking

Place databases in **private subnets**, allow inbound traffic only from the application's security
group, and never make production databases publicly accessible.

## Serverless options

For spiky or unpredictable workloads, Aurora Serverless v2 avoids paying for idle capacity, and
Aurora DSQL offers a distributed, serverless PostgreSQL-compatible database for active-active
multi-Region designs.

title: Amazon DynamoDB
questions:
  - id: query-scan
    prompt: Why should you prefer `Query` over `Scan` in DynamoDB?
    options:
      - id: efficient
        text: Query reads only the items with a given partition key (optionally filtered by sort key), while Scan reads the entire table
        correct: true
      - text: Scan is not supported by the .NET SDK
      - text: Query returns results in random order
      - text: Scan costs nothing
    explanation: Scans consume capacity for every item they read, even if a filter discards most of them.
  - id: consistency
    prompt: What is the default read consistency for DynamoDB `GetItem` and `Query`?
    options:
      - id: eventual
        text: Eventually consistent; strongly consistent reads can be requested per call (not on global secondary indexes)
        correct: true
      - text: Always strongly consistent
      - text: Read-uncommitted
    explanation: Strongly consistent reads cost twice as much read capacity as eventually consistent reads.
  - id: indexes
    prompt: Which statements about DynamoDB secondary indexes are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: A global secondary index (GSI) can have a different partition key from the base table
        correct: true
      - text: GSIs can be added after the table is created
        correct: true
      - text: Local secondary indexes (LSIs) must be defined when the table is created
        correct: true
      - text: GSIs support strongly consistent reads
    explanation: GSI reads are always eventually consistent; LSIs share the table's partition key and allow strong consistency.
  - id: item-size
    prompt: What is the maximum size of a single DynamoDB item?
    options:
      - text: 64 KB
      - id: kb400
        text: 400 KB
        correct: true
      - text: 16 MB
      - text: 5 GB
    explanation: Store large blobs in S3 and keep a reference in the item.
---
## Learning objectives

- Model data around access patterns with partition and sort keys
- Use queries, indexes and conditional writes
- Choose capacity modes

## Keys

| Key | Role |
|-----|------|
| Partition key | Determines the partition; items with the same value form an *item collection* |
| Sort key (optional) | Orders items within a partition; enables range queries |

## Single-table modelling

| PK | SK | Attributes |
|----|----|-----------|
| `CUSTOMER#42` | `PROFILE` | name, email |
| `CUSTOMER#42` | `ORDER#2026-11-01#1001` | total, status |
| `CUSTOMER#42` | `ORDER#2026-11-05#1007` | total, status |

"Get a customer and their recent orders" becomes one `Query` on `PK = CUSTOMER#42`.

## .NET SDK

```csharp
var response = await dynamo.QueryAsync(new QueryRequest
{
    TableName = "Shop",
    KeyConditionExpression = "PK = :pk AND begins_with(SK, :prefix)",
    ExpressionAttributeValues = new Dictionary<string, AttributeValue>
    {
        [":pk"] = new() { S = "CUSTOMER#42" },
        [":prefix"] = new() { S = "ORDER#2026-11" }
    },
    ScanIndexForward = false,
    Limit = 20
}, ct);
```

## Conditional writes

```csharp
await dynamo.PutItemAsync(new PutItemRequest
{
    TableName = "Shop",
    Item = item,
    ConditionExpression = "attribute_not_exists(PK)"   // create only if new
}, ct);
```

Conditions give optimistic concurrency and idempotency without locks. `TransactWriteItems` makes
up to 100 actions atomic.

## Capacity modes

| Mode | Billing | Use when |
|------|---------|----------|
| On-demand | Per request | Unknown or spiky traffic; the default for new workloads |
| Provisioned (with auto scaling) | Per provisioned RCU/WCU | Predictable traffic at lower cost |

## Other features

- **Streams** — ordered change log per item, triggering Lambda for event-driven processing
- **TTL** — automatically expire items such as sessions
- **Global tables** — multi-Region, multi-active replication
- **Point-in-time recovery** — restore to any second in the retention window

## Design rule

List your access patterns **first**, then design keys and indexes to serve them. DynamoDB rewards
up-front modelling and punishes ad-hoc querying.

## Learning objectives

- Choose between SQS, SNS, EventBridge and Step Functions
- Build reliable consumers
- Orchestrate workflows

## Which service?

| Service | Model | Use for |
|---------|-------|---------|
| **SQS** | Queue (pull) | Decoupling producers and consumers, buffering, work distribution |
| **SNS** | Pub/sub (push) | Fan-out to many subscribers (SQS, Lambda, HTTP, e-mail, SMS) |
| **EventBridge** | Event bus with rules | Event-driven architectures, SaaS and AWS service events, scheduling |
| **Kinesis Data Streams** | Ordered, replayable stream | High-volume streaming analytics |
| **Step Functions** | State machine | Orchestrating multi-step workflows with retries and compensation |

## SQS consumer in .NET

```csharp
while (!ct.IsCancellationRequested)
{
    var response = await sqs.ReceiveMessageAsync(new ReceiveMessageRequest
    {
        QueueUrl = queueUrl,
        MaxNumberOfMessages = 10,
        WaitTimeSeconds = 20,          // long polling
        VisibilityTimeout = 60
    }, ct);

    foreach (var message in response.Messages ?? [])
    {
        await handler.HandleAsync(message.Body, ct);
        await sqs.DeleteMessageAsync(queueUrl, message.ReceiptHandle, ct);
    }
}
```

Delete only after successful processing. Handlers must be **idempotent**, since standard queues
deliver at least once. (In SDK v4, unset collections may be `null`, hence `?? []`.)

## EventBridge

```json
{
  "source": ["shop.orders"],
  "detail-type": ["OrderPlaced"],
  "detail": { "total": [{ "numeric": [">", 1000] }] }
}
```

This rule pattern matches large orders and can route them to a fraud-check Lambda, while other rules
send all orders to analytics — publishers don't know or care.

```csharp
await events.PutEventsAsync(new PutEventsRequest
{
    Entries = [new PutEventsRequestEntry
    {
        EventBusName = "shop",
        Source = "shop.orders",
        DetailType = "OrderPlaced",
        Detail = JsonSerializer.Serialize(orderPlaced)
    }]
}, ct);
```

**EventBridge Scheduler** runs one-off or recurring invocations (cron) of thousands of targets, and
**EventBridge Pipes** connects sources to targets with filtering and enrichment.

## Step Functions

State machines (defined in Amazon States Language) coordinate Lambda functions, ECS tasks and
direct service integrations, with built-in retries, timeouts, parallel branches, waits for human
approval and error handling — ideal for sagas such as "reserve stock → charge card → ship, or
compensate".

## Learning objectives

- Design a VPC with public and private subnets across AZs
- Control traffic with security groups and NACLs
- Reach AWS services privately with VPC endpoints

## A standard layout

```text
VPC 10.0.0.0/16 (eu-central-1)
├── AZ a: public 10.0.0.0/24  │ private-app 10.0.10.0/24 │ private-data 10.0.20.0/24
├── AZ b: public 10.0.1.0/24  │ private-app 10.0.11.0/24 │ private-data 10.0.21.0/24
└── AZ c: public 10.0.2.0/24  │ private-app 10.0.12.0/24 │ private-data 10.0.22.0/24

Public subnets:  load balancers, NAT gateways   (route 0.0.0.0/0 → internet gateway)
App subnets:     ECS tasks, Lambda ENIs, EC2     (route 0.0.0.0/0 → NAT gateway in same AZ)
Data subnets:    RDS, ElastiCache                (no internet route)
```

## Security groups

```text
sg-alb:  inbound 443 from 0.0.0.0/0
sg-app:  inbound 8080 from sg-alb
sg-db:   inbound 5432 from sg-app
```

Referencing security groups instead of IP ranges builds a least-privilege chain that keeps working
as instances come and go.

## Security groups vs NACLs

| | Security group | Network ACL |
|-|----------------|-------------|
| Level | Network interface | Subnet |
| State | Stateful | Stateless |
| Rules | Allow only | Allow and deny, evaluated in number order |
| Typical use | Primary control | Coarse subnet-wide blocks |

## VPC endpoints

| Type | Services | Cost |
|------|----------|------|
| Gateway endpoint | S3, DynamoDB | Free |
| Interface endpoint (PrivateLink) | Most AWS services, your own services | Hourly + data |

Endpoints keep traffic off the internet and can carry endpoint policies restricting which resources
can be reached.

## Connecting networks

VPC peering (one-to-one), **Transit Gateway** (hub-and-spoke for many VPCs and on-premises),
Site-to-Site VPN and **Direct Connect** (dedicated private links).

## Visibility

Enable **VPC Flow Logs** to record accepted and rejected traffic for troubleshooting and security analysis.

## Learning objectives

- Choose the right Elastic Load Balancer
- Route traffic globally with Route 53
- Accelerate and protect content with CloudFront

## Elastic Load Balancing

| Type | Layer | Highlights |
|------|-------|------------|
| Application Load Balancer | 7 | Path/host/header routing, WebSockets, HTTP/2, authentication, Lambda targets |
| Network Load Balancer | 4 | TCP/UDP/TLS, millions of requests per second, static IPs, ultra-low latency |
| Gateway Load Balancer | 3 | Inserting third-party network appliances (firewalls) |

Target groups perform **health checks**; unhealthy targets stop receiving traffic, and Auto Scaling
replaces them.

## Route 53

```text
example.com        A  ALIAS → d1234.cloudfront.net
api.example.com    A  ALIAS → shop-alb-123.eu-central-1.elb.amazonaws.com  (latency record, eu-central-1)
api.example.com    A  ALIAS → shop-alb-456.us-east-1.elb.amazonaws.com     (latency record, us-east-1)
```

| Policy | Use |
|--------|-----|
| Simple | One resource |
| Weighted | Canary releases, A/B splits |
| Latency | Send users to the lowest-latency Region |
| Failover | Active-passive disaster recovery |
| Geolocation / geoproximity | Compliance or localisation by user location |

## CloudFront

CloudFront caches content at edge locations worldwide and terminates TLS close to users:

- **Origins** — S3 (with Origin Access Control, keeping the bucket private), ALBs, API Gateway, any HTTP server
- **Cache behaviours** — per path pattern TTLs and policies
- **AWS WAF** and **Shield** — filter malicious traffic; Shield Standard DDoS protection is included at no extra cost
- **CloudFront Functions / Lambda@Edge** — lightweight logic such as redirects and header manipulation

A static Blazor WebAssembly app is a natural fit: S3 for the files, CloudFront in front, and a
custom error response that serves `index.html` for unknown paths so client-side routing works.

## CloudWatch

| Feature | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| Metrics | Built-in service metrics plus custom metrics |
| Logs + Logs Insights | Centralised logs with a query language |

```text
fields @timestamp, @message
| filter level = "Error"
```

## Instrumenting .NET with OpenTelemetry

```csharp
builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry()
    .ConfigureResource(r => r.AddService("shop-api"))
    .WithTracing(t => t
        .AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation()
        .AddHttpClientInstrumentation()
        .AddAWSInstrumentation()
        .AddOtlpExporter())
    .WithMetrics(m => m.AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation().AddOtlpExporter());
```

The **AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT)** collector or the CloudWatch agent receives OTLP and
forwards traces to X-Ray/CloudWatch and metrics to CloudWatch. Write logs as structured JSON to
stdout; container and Lambda platforms ship them to CloudWatch Logs.

## Learning objectives

- Deploy infrastructure declaratively with CloudFormation
- Write infrastructure in C# with the CDK
- Preview changes safely

## CloudFormation

Templates (YAML or JSON) describe resources; CloudFormation creates them as a **stack**, ordering
operations by dependencies and rolling back on failure.

```yaml
Resources:
  OrdersTable:
    Type: AWS::DynamoDB::Table
    Properties:
      BillingMode: PAY_PER_REQUEST
      AttributeDefinitions:
        - { AttributeName: PK, AttributeType: S }
        - { AttributeName: SK, AttributeType: S }
      KeySchema:
        - { AttributeName: PK, KeyType: HASH }
        - { AttributeName: SK, KeyType: RANGE }
      PointInTimeRecoverySpecification:
        PointInTimeRecoveryEnabled: true
```

## CDK in C#

```csharp
public sealed class ShopStack : Stack
{
    public ShopStack(Construct scope, string id, IStackProps? props = null) : base(scope, id, props)
    {
        var table = new Table(this, "Orders", new TableProps
        {
            PartitionKey = new Attribute { Name = "PK", Type = AttributeType.STRING },
            SortKey = new Attribute { Name = "SK", Type = AttributeType.STRING },
            BillingMode = BillingMode.PAY_PER_REQUEST,
            RemovalPolicy = RemovalPolicy.RETAIN
        });

        var api = new Function(this, "Api", new FunctionProps
        {
            Runtime = Runtime.DOTNET_8,
            Architecture = Architecture.ARM_64,
            Handler = "Shop.Api",
            Code = Code.FromAsset("../src/Shop.Api/bin/Release/publish"),
            MemorySize = 1024,
            Environment = new Dictionary<string, string> { ["TABLE_NAME"] = table.TableName }
        });

        table.GrantReadWriteData(api);
    }
}
```

`GrantReadWriteData` writes a least-privilege IAM policy for you. (Use the newest managed .NET
runtime your CDK version offers.)

```bash
cdk bootstrap aws://111122223333/eu-central-1
cdk diff
cdk deploy
```

## Other tools

- **AWS SAM** — CloudFormation extension focused on serverless, with local testing (`sam local`)
- **Terraform** — popular multi-cloud alternative

Whatever the tool: everything in Git, deployed by pipelines, previewed before applying, and no
manual console changes in production. **Drift detection** finds resources changed outside IaC.

## Learning objectives

## Encryption with KMS

**AWS KMS** manages encryption keys used by S3, EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, Secrets Manager and more.
Services use **envelope encryption**: data keys encrypt data, and a KMS key encrypts the data keys.
Customer managed keys let you control key policies, rotation and cross-account use; every key use
is logged in CloudTrail.

## Secrets

| Service | Use |
|---------|-----|
| Secrets Manager | Credentials with rotation, cross-account sharing |
| Systems Manager Parameter Store | Configuration values and simple secrets (`SecureString`) |

```csharp
var secret = await secretsManager.GetSecretValueAsync(new GetSecretValueRequest { SecretId = "shop/db" }, ct);
var credentials = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<DbCredentials>(secret.SecretString);
```

Cache secrets in memory and refresh periodically rather than calling the API per request.

## Detection and posture

| Service | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| GuardDuty | Threat detection from logs and runtime signals |
| Security Hub | Aggregated findings and best-practice checks |
| Inspector | Vulnerability scanning for EC2, container images and Lambda |
| Macie | Discover sensitive data (PII) in S3 |
| IAM Access Analyzer | External and unused access findings |
| AWS WAF / Shield | Web exploits and DDoS protection |

Enable these organisation-wide from a delegated security account.

## Cost management

- **Cost Explorer** — analyse by service, account, Region and tag
- **Budgets** — alerts on actual or forecast spend
- **Cost Anomaly Detection** — machine-learning alerts on unusual spend
- **Compute Optimizer** and **Trusted Advisor** — right-sizing and idle resources
- **Savings Plans / Reserved Instances** — commitments for steady usage
- **Spot and Graviton** — cheaper compute where workloads allow

Common hidden costs: NAT gateway data processing (use gateway endpoints for S3/DynamoDB),
cross-AZ data transfer, unattached EBS volumes, old snapshots, idle load balancers and verbose
CloudWatch Logs retained forever.

> Treat cost like any other metric: tag it, watch it, alert on it, and review it in your
> engineering rituals.

---
title: What is Blazor WebAssembly?
questions:
  - id: runtime
    prompt: Where does a Blazor WebAssembly app's C# code run?
    options:
      - text: On the web server, with UI updates sent over a socket
      - id: browser
        text: In the browser, on a .NET runtime compiled to WebAssembly
        correct: true
      - text: In a browser plugin that must be installed separately
    explanation: Blazor WebAssembly downloads the .NET runtime and your assemblies, then runs them directly in the browser's WebAssembly sandbox.
  - id: static-hosting
    prompt: Which statements about hosting a standalone Blazor WebAssembly app are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: It can be served from a static file host such as GitHub Pages
        correct: true
      - text: It requires ASP.NET Core on the server
      - text: The browser downloads the app's assemblies before it starts
        correct: true
      - text: Every click makes a round trip to the server
    explanation: A standalone app is just static files. Once downloaded, it runs entirely on the client.
---
Blazor is a .NET framework for building interactive web UIs with C# instead of JavaScript.
The **WebAssembly** hosting model runs your app directly in the browser.

## How it works

When a visitor opens the site, the browser downloads:

1. A small JavaScript loader, `blazor.webassembly.js`
2. The .NET runtime, compiled to WebAssembly
3. Your app's assemblies and their dependencies

From then on, your C# code executes on the client. There is no server process rendering pages.

## Why that matters

Because the output is plain static files, you can host the app anywhere that serves files —
including GitHub Pages, which is exactly how this site is deployed.

> The trade-off is a larger first download. After that, navigation is instant.

|------|---------|

```csharp
var builder = WebAssemblyHostBuilder.CreateDefault(args);
builder.RootComponents.Add<App>("#app");
builder.Services.AddScoped<IBookService, BookService>();
await builder.Build().RunAsync();
```

Services registered here can be injected into any component with `@inject`.

FILE: content/books/blazor-basics/02-components/02-lifecycle.md
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
---
title: Component lifecycle
questions:
  - id: async-load
    prompt: Which lifecycle methods are good places to load data asynchronously?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: "`OnInitializedAsync`"
        correct: true
      - text: "`OnParametersSetAsync`"
        correct: true
      - text: The component constructor
    explanation: Use `OnInitializedAsync` for one-time loads and `OnParametersSetAsync` when the data depends on parameters that can change.
  - id: js-interop
    prompt: When is it safe to call JavaScript interop that touches the rendered DOM?
    options:
      - text: In `OnInitialized`
      - text: In `OnAfterRenderAsync`
        correct: true
      - text: In `SetParametersAsync`
---
Every component goes through the same sequence of lifecycle methods:

1. `SetParametersAsync` — parameters arrive from the parent
2. `OnInitialized` / `OnInitializedAsync` — runs once
3. `OnParametersSet` / `OnParametersSetAsync` — runs whenever parameters change
4. `OnAfterRender` / `OnAfterRenderAsync` — runs after the DOM is updated

## Reacting to route changes

When the user navigates between two URLs handled by the **same** page, Blazor reuses the
component instance. `OnInitialized` does not run again, but `OnParametersSet` does — so load
route-dependent data there.

FILE: content/books/clean-code/01-introduction/01-what-is-clean-code.md
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
---
title: What is clean code?
questions:
  - id: read-write
    prompt: Why is readability usually more important than writing speed?
    options:
      - text: Compilers optimise readable code better
      - text: Readable code always uses fewer lines
      - text: Code reviews are only done on readable code
      - id: read-more
        text: Code is read far more often than it is written, so reading cost dominates
        correct: true
    explanation: Every change starts with reading and understanding existing code. Making that cheap pays off on every future change.
  - id: qualities
    prompt: Which qualities describe clean code?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: It does one thing and its intent is obvious
        correct: true
      - text: It is covered by tests that document its behaviour
        correct: true
      - text: It contains clever one-liners that only experts understand
      - text: It has minimal duplication
        correct: true
    explanation: Clarity, tests and low duplication are recurring themes. Cleverness that hides intent is the opposite of clean.
  - id: tech-debt
    prompt: What is "technical debt"?
    options:
      - id: future-cost
        text: The extra future cost created by choosing an expedient solution now
        correct: true
      - text: Money owed for software licences
      - text: The cost of hiring senior developers
    explanation: Ward Cunningham's metaphor — shortcuts accrue interest in the form of slower, riskier future changes.
---
"Clean code" is not a style guide. It is code whose **intent is obvious** to the next reader — who
is usually you, six months later.

## Learning objectives

- Describe the properties of clean code
- Explain why readability has economic value
- Understand technical debt as a trade-off, not a sin

## Same behaviour, different cost

```csharp
public List<int[]> Get(List<int[]> l)
{
    var r = new List<int[]>();
    foreach (var x in l) if (x[0] == 4) r.Add(x);
    return r;
}
```

```csharp
public IReadOnlyList<Cell> FlaggedCells(IEnumerable<Cell> board) =>
    board.Where(cell => cell.IsFlagged).ToList();
```

Both compile. Only the second tells you what it does. The magic number `4` became a named concept,
the anonymous `int[]` became a `Cell` type, and the name says *why* the method exists.

## Properties of clean code

- **Readable** — reads like well-written prose; names reveal intent
- **Focused** — each function, class and module does one thing
- **Tested** — behaviour is pinned down and documented by tests
- **Unsurprising** — it does what its name says and nothing else
- **Free of duplication** — each piece of knowledge lives in one place

## Technical debt

Ward Cunningham coined the debt metaphor: shipping a quick solution is like borrowing. Debt is
fine when deliberate and repaid. It becomes dangerous when nobody tracks it and the "interest" —
slower, riskier changes — grows until the team spends most of its time working around old
decisions.

> "Any fool can write code that a computer can understand. Good programmers write code that humans
> can understand." — Martin Fowler

FILE: content/books/clean-code/01-introduction/02-meaningful-names.md
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
---
title: Meaningful names
questions:
  - id: best-name
    prompt: Which variable name best reveals intent?
    options:
      - text: "`d`"
      - text: "`days`"
      - text: "`data`"
      - id: elapsed
        text: "`elapsedTimeInDays`"
        correct: true
    explanation: A good name answers why it exists, what it does and how it is used. Units are part of the meaning.
  - id: conventions
    prompt: Which follow standard .NET naming conventions?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: "`PascalCase` for types, methods and public properties"
        correct: true
      - text: "`camelCase` for parameters and local variables"
        correct: true
      - text: Interfaces prefixed with `I`, such as `IOrderRepository`
        correct: true
      - text: Hungarian notation such as `strName` and `iCount`
    explanation: .NET conventions use PascalCase, camelCase and the `I` prefix for interfaces. Hungarian notation is discouraged because the type system already tells you the type.
  - id: booleans
    prompt: Which is the clearest name for a boolean property?
    options:
      - text: "`ActiveFlag`"
      - id: is-active
        text: "`IsActive`"
        correct: true
      - text: "`Status`"
    explanation: Prefixes such as `Is`, `Has`, `Can` and `Should` make booleans read like questions.
  - id: async-suffix
    prompt: What convention does .NET use for methods that return an awaitable `Task`?
    options:
      - text: Prefix the name with `Await`
      - id: suffix
        text: Suffix the name with `Async`, as in `SaveAsync`
        correct: true
      - text: No convention exists
    explanation: The `Async` suffix tells callers they need to await the result.
---
Names are the first and most frequent documentation a reader sees.

## Learning objectives

- Choose names that reveal intent
- Apply .NET naming conventions consistently
- Avoid disinformation and encodings

## Reveal intent

```csharp
// Before
int d; // elapsed time in days
if (u.s == 2) { }

// After
int elapsedTimeInDays;
if (user.Status == AccountStatus.Suspended) { }
```

If a name needs a comment, the name is not finished.

## .NET conventions

| Element | Convention | Example |
|---------|------------|---------|
| Types, methods, properties | PascalCase | `OrderService`, `PlaceOrder`, `TotalPrice` |
| Parameters, locals | camelCase | `orderId`, `lineCount` |
| Private fields | `_camelCase` (common team convention) | `_orders` |
| Interfaces | `I` + PascalCase | `IClock` |
| Async methods | `Async` suffix | `LoadAsync` |
| Booleans | `Is`/`Has`/`Can` | `IsExpired`, `HasChildren` |

## Avoid disinformation

- Do not call something `accountList` if it is a `HashSet`
- Avoid names that differ in tiny ways: `XmlControllerForHandlingStrings` vs `XmlControllerForStorageOfStrings`
- Avoid noise words: `ProductInfo`, `ProductData` and `Product` usually mean the same thing

## Use domain language

Use the words your business experts use: `Invoice`, `Shipment`, `Policyholder`. Where a technical
concept is clearer, use the pattern name: `OrderFactory`, `PriceCalculator`, `CustomerRepository`.

## Scope and length

A short name is fine in a tiny scope (`i` in a three-line loop, `x` in `x => x.IsActive`). The
larger the scope, the more descriptive the name must be. Methods should be verbs (`Calculate`,
`Send`); classes should be nouns (`Invoice`, `Calculator`).

FILE: content/books/clean-code/02-functions/01-small-and-focused.md

---
title: Small and focused
questions:
  - id: one-thing
    prompt: How can you tell that a function does more than one thing?
    options:
      - text: It contains more than one line
      - id: extract
        text: You can extract another function from it with a name that is not merely a restatement of its implementation
        correct: true
      - text: It has a return value
      - text: It is called from more than one place
    explanation: If meaningful sub-steps can be extracted and named, the function is doing several things at different levels.
  - id: abstraction-level
    prompt: "What does \"one level of abstraction per function\" mean?"
    options:
      - text: Each function may only call functions in the same class
      - id: mixing
        text: A function should not mix high-level steps like "charge customer" with low-level details like string concatenation
        correct: true
      - text: Functions must be declared in order of abstraction
    explanation: Mixing levels forces readers to switch between "what" and "how" constantly.
  - id: guard
    prompt: Which techniques reduce nesting and make a function easier to read?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Guard clauses that return early for invalid cases
        correct: true
      - text: Extracting the body of a loop into a well-named function
        correct: true
      - text: Replacing nested ifs with pattern-matching switch expressions where appropriate
        correct: true
      - text: Adding more `else` branches
    explanation: Early returns, extraction and switch expressions flatten code. Additional `else` branches usually deepen nesting.
---
## Learning objectives

- Write functions that do one thing
- Keep each function at one level of abstraction
- Reduce nesting with guard clauses and extraction

## A function that does everything

```csharp
public string Register(string email, string password)
{
    if (email != null)
    {
        if (email.Contains('@'))
        {
            if (password.Length >= 12)
            {
                var hash = Convert.ToBase64String(SHA256.HashData(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(password)));
                _db.Execute("INSERT INTO Users ...", new { email, hash });
                _smtp.Send("noreply@example.com", email, "Welcome", "Hi!");
                return "ok";
            }
            return "weak password";
        }
    }
    return "bad email";
}
```

## Refactored

```csharp
public async Task<RegistrationResult> RegisterAsync(string email, string password, CancellationToken ct)
{
    if (!EmailAddress.IsValid(email)) return RegistrationResult.InvalidEmail;
    if (!PasswordPolicy.IsStrong(password)) return RegistrationResult.WeakPassword;

    var user = User.Create(email, _passwordHasher.Hash(password));
    await _users.AddAsync(user, ct);
    await _welcomeMailer.SendAsync(user, ct);
    return RegistrationResult.Success;
}
```

The new function reads as a list of steps at one level. Details — hashing, SQL, SMTP — live in
collaborators. (It also fixes a security bug: a bare SHA-256 is not a password hash. Use a slow,
salted algorithm such as ASP.NET Core Identity's `PasswordHasher<T>`, PBKDF2, bcrypt or Argon2.)

## Guard clauses

Return early for the special cases so the main path is not indented:

```csharp
decimal Discount(Customer? customer)
{
    if (customer is null) return 0m;
    if (!customer.IsActive) return 0m;
    return customer.Tier switch
    {
        Tier.Gold => 0.15m,
        Tier.Silver => 0.05m,
        _ => 0m
    };
}
```

## How small?

There is no magic line count. A function should fit in your head: you should be able to read its
name and body and predict exactly what it does. When you need to scroll, or when you find yourself
writing a comment above a block to explain it, extract that block and let the name be the comment.

FILE: content/books/clean-code/02-functions/02-arguments-and-side-effects.md
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
---
title: Arguments, side effects and command–query separation
questions:
  - id: cqs
    prompt: What does command–query separation (CQS) recommend?
    options:
      - id: separate
        text: A method should either change state (command) or return information (query), but not both
        correct: true
      - text: Every method should be both a command and a query
      - text: Queries must be asynchronous
      - text: Commands must be stored in a database
    explanation: Bertrand Meyer's CQS makes code predictable — asking a question should never change the answer.
  - id: flag-argument
    prompt: Why are boolean flag arguments like `Render(true)` considered a smell?
    options:
      - id: two-things
        text: They signal that the function does two different things, and the call site is unreadable
        correct: true
      - text: Booleans use more memory than integers
      - text: C# does not allow boolean parameters on public methods
    explanation: Split into two well-named functions, or use an enum or named argument to make the call site self-explanatory.
  - id: hidden-side-effects
    prompt: A method named `CheckPassword` also initialises the user's session. Which problems does this cause?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Callers may start a session accidentally just by validating a password
        correct: true
      - text: The name lies about what the method does
        correct: true
      - text: It creates a temporal coupling where checking must happen at a particular moment
        correct: true
      - text: It improves performance by doing two things at once
    explanation: Hidden side effects make names untrustworthy and couple behaviour to call order.
  - id: many-args
    prompt: A constructor takes eight primitive parameters. What is usually the best refactoring?
    options:
      - text: Make all of them optional
      - text: Replace them with a `Dictionary<string, object>`
      - id: parameter-object
        text: Group related parameters into meaningful types such as `Address` or `DateRange`
        correct: true
    explanation: Parameter objects give names to concepts and make invalid combinations harder to construct.
---
## Learning objectives

- Keep argument lists short and meaningful
- Eliminate hidden side effects
- Apply command–query separation

## Fewer, better arguments

```csharp
// Hard to call correctly
var unclear = new Booking("Ada", "Lovelace", "10 Downing St", "London", "SW1A 2AA",
                          new DateOnly(2026, 12, 1), new DateOnly(2026, 12, 5), 2);

// Concepts made explicit
var booking = new Booking(
    guest: new GuestName("Ada", "Lovelace"),
    address: new Address("10 Downing St", "London", "SW1A 2AA"),
    stay: new DateRange(new DateOnly(2026, 12, 1), new DateOnly(2026, 12, 5)),
    guests: 2);
```

## Flag arguments

```csharp
report.Render(true);                 // what does true mean?
report.RenderForPrint();             // two functions
report.Render(RenderMode.Print);     // or an enum
```

## Side effects

A side effect is a hidden change in state. Make effects visible in names or remove them:

```csharp
public bool CheckPassword(User user, string password)
{
    var ok = _hasher.Verify(user.PasswordHash, password);
    if (ok) _sessions.Initialize(user); // hidden!
    return ok;
}
```

Rename it `CheckPasswordAndStartSession`, or better, let the caller start the session explicitly.

## Command–query separation

```csharp
// Violates CQS: changes state and returns whether the key existed
public bool Set(string key, string value) { /* ... */ return true; }

// Separated
public bool Contains(string key) => _items.ContainsKey(key);
public void Set(string key, string value) => _items[key] = value;
```

Pragmatic exceptions exist — `Stack<T>.Pop` and `Dictionary.TryAdd` are deliberate, well-known
idioms — but your own APIs should default to CQS.

title: Comments that earn their place
questions:
  - id: good-comment

    options:
      - id: why

        correct: true
      - text: "`// increment i` above `i++;`"
      - text: "`// changed by Bob on 3 May` above a method"
      - text: A block of commented-out code kept just in case
    explanation: Good comments explain *why* — constraints and decisions the code cannot express. Version control already records who changed what.
  - id: commented-out
    prompt: What should you do with commented-out code?
    options:
      - text: Keep it so others can restore it
      - text: Move it to a `#region` named Old
      - id: delete
        text: Delete it; version control keeps the history
        correct: true
    explanation: Commented-out code rots, confuses readers and is never trusted. Git remembers it for you.
  - id: xml-docs

    type: multiple

    explanation: Document public contracts. Restating obvious names on private code is noise.

## Learning objectives

- Distinguish helpful comments from noise
- Replace explanatory comments with better code
- Use XML documentation where it adds value

## Comments are a failure to express — usually

```csharp
// Check to see if the employee is eligible for full benefits
if ((employee.Flags & HourlyFlag) != 0 && employee.Age > 65) { }
```

```csharp
if (employee.IsEligibleForFullBenefits()) { }
```

The extracted method says the same thing, and unlike a comment, it cannot drift out of date
with the code.

## Comments worth writing

| Kind | Example |
|------|---------|
| Intent or reasoning | `// Use insertion sort: n is always < 10 and this is a hot path` |
| External constraints | `// Regulators require amounts rounded half away from zero` |
| Warnings | `// Not thread-safe: callers must hold _gate` |
| Public API documentation | `/// <summary>` on library members |
| TODOs tracked elsewhere | `// TODO(OPS-981): remove after v2 migration` |

## Comments to delete

- Restating code: `// return the total`
- Journal comments: `// 2024-01-02 fixed bug`
- Commented-out code
- Closing-brace markers: `} // end if`

## XML documentation

```csharp
/// <summary>Calculates the shipping cost for an order.</summary>
/// <param name="order">The order; must contain at least one line.</param>
/// <returns>The cost in the order's currency.</returns>
/// <exception cref="ArgumentException">The order has no lines.</exception>
public Money ShippingCost(Order order) { /* ... */ }
```

Enable `<GenerateDocumentationFile>true</GenerateDocumentationFile>` in library projects so the
compiler warns about missing or malformed docs on public members.

## The newspaper metaphor

A source file should read like a newspaper article: the headline (class name) first, then the
high-level summary (public methods), then the details (private helpers) in the order they are used.

```csharp
public sealed class InvoiceGenerator(ITaxCalculator tax)
{
    public Invoice Generate(Order order)
    {
        var lines = BuildLines(order);
        return new Invoice(order.Id, lines, Total(lines));
    }

    private IReadOnlyList<InvoiceLine> BuildLines(Order order) =>
        order.Lines.Select(l => new InvoiceLine(l.Sku, l.Quantity, l.Price, tax.For(l))).ToList();

    private static decimal Total(IEnumerable<InvoiceLine> lines) =>
        lines.Sum(l => l.Quantity * l.Price + l.Tax);
}
```

## Automate it

Formatting debates are a waste of review time. Commit an `.editorconfig`:

```ini
root = true

[*.cs]
indent_style = space
indent_size = 4
csharp_style_namespace_declarations = file_scoped:warning
csharp_prefer_braces = true:warning
dotnet_sort_system_directives_first = true
```

Then enforce it in CI:

```bash
dotnet format --verify-no-changes
```

Combine this with `<TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>` and
`<EnforceCodeStyleInBuild>true</EnforceCodeStyleInBuild>` to make the build itself the style
checker.

## Consistency beats preference

The specific style matters much less than everyone using the same one. A codebase that looks like
one person wrote it is easier to read than one where every file has its own dialect.

title: Exceptions and result types
questions:

    options:
      - text: "`throw ex;`"
      - text: "`throw new Exception(ex.Message);`"
      - id: throw
        text: "`throw;`"
        correct: true
      - text: "`return ex;`"
    explanation: "`throw;` rethrows the current exception unchanged. `throw ex;` resets the stack trace to the current line."
  - id: when-exception
    prompt: When is an exception the most appropriate way to signal a problem?
    options:
      - text: When a user types an invalid e-mail address into a form
      - text: For normal control flow such as ending a loop
      - id: exceptional
        text: When a method cannot fulfil its contract for an unexpected reason, such as a lost database connection
        correct: true
    explanation: Expected validation outcomes are better modelled as return values. Exceptions are for situations the caller does not expect as part of the normal flow.
  - id: good-practice
    prompt: Which are good exception-handling practices in .NET?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Catch only exceptions you can actually handle
        correct: true
      - text: Use exception filters such as `catch (HttpRequestException ex) when (ex.StatusCode == HttpStatusCode.NotFound)`
        correct: true
      - text: Wrap low-level exceptions in domain exceptions and keep the original as `InnerException`
        correct: true
      - text: Catch `Exception` everywhere and ignore it so the app never crashes
    explanation: Swallowing exceptions hides failures. Catch narrowly, add context and let unknown failures reach a global handler.
---
## Learning objectives

- Use exceptions for exceptional situations
- Model expected failures with result types
- Rethrow and wrap exceptions correctly

## Exceptions are for the unexpected

```csharp
try
{
    await _payments.ChargeAsync(order.Total, ct);
}
catch (HttpRequestException ex) when (ex.StatusCode == HttpStatusCode.ServiceUnavailable)
{
    throw new PaymentProviderUnavailableException(order.Id, ex);
}
```

Catch only what you can handle, add context, preserve the inner exception, and let everything else
bubble up to a global handler (`UseExceptionHandler` in ASP.NET Core) that logs it once.

## Do not lose the stack trace

```csharp
catch (Exception ex)
{
    _logger.LogError(ex, "Import failed for {File}", path);
    throw;      // preserves the stack trace
    // throw ex; would reset it
}
```

## Expected failures as values

A user entering a duplicate username is not exceptional; it is a normal outcome. Model it as data:

```csharp
public abstract record RegistrationResult
{
    public sealed record Success(UserId Id) : RegistrationResult;
    public sealed record UsernameTaken(string Username) : RegistrationResult;
    public sealed record WeakPassword(IReadOnlyList<string> Problems) : RegistrationResult;
}

var message = await registration.RegisterAsync(form, ct) switch
{
    RegistrationResult.Success s => $"Welcome! Your id is {s.Id}",
    RegistrationResult.UsernameTaken t => $"'{t.Username}' is taken",
    RegistrationResult.WeakPassword w => string.Join(", ", w.Problems),
    _ => throw new UnreachableException()
};
```

The compiler and the type system now force callers to consider every outcome, and the happy path
does not pay the cost of exceptions.

## Guard clauses for programmer errors

```csharp
public void Ship(Order order, int quantity)
{
    ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(order);
    ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegativeOrZero(quantity);
}
```

Throw helpers such as `ThrowIfNull` and `ThrowIfNegativeOrZero` (.NET 8+) keep guards short and
consistent.

title: Taming null
questions:
  - id: nrt
    prompt: What do nullable reference types (`<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`) do?
    options:
      - text: They make the runtime throw when a null reference is assigned
      - text: They replace all reference types with structs
      - text: They remove null from the language
      - id: static
        text: They let the compiler warn about possible null dereferences based on annotations like `string?`
        correct: true
    explanation: Nullable reference types are a compile-time analysis. At runtime, references can still be null.
  - id: bang
    prompt: What does the null-forgiving operator `!` (as in `name!.Length`) do?
    options:
      - text: Throws if `name` is null
      - id: suppress
        text: Suppresses the compiler's nullable warning without any runtime check
        correct: true
      - text: Converts null to an empty string
    explanation: It tells the compiler "trust me". Overusing it reintroduces the bugs the feature is meant to prevent.
  - id: techniques
    prompt: Which techniques reduce null-related bugs?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Return empty collections instead of null
        correct: true
      - text: Use `required` members so objects cannot be created half-initialised
        correct: true
      - text: Use the null-coalescing operators `??` and `??=` for defaults
        correct: true
      - text: Return null from every method that might fail, without documenting it
    explanation: Empty collections, required members and explicit defaults remove ambiguity. Undocumented nulls create surprises.
---
Tony Hoare called the null reference his "billion-dollar mistake". Modern C# gives you tools to
contain it.

## Learning objectives

- Enable and respond to nullable reference type warnings
- Avoid returning null where better options exist
- Use the null operators idiomatically

## Nullable reference types

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
</PropertyGroup>
```

```csharp
public Customer? Find(int id) => _customers.GetValueOrDefault(id);

var customer = repository.Find(42);
Console.WriteLine(customer.Name);   // warning CS8602: possible null dereference
if (customer is not null) Console.WriteLine(customer.Name); // fine
```

The `?` in the signature is documentation the compiler enforces.

## Prefer empty over null

```csharp
public IReadOnlyList<Order> OrdersFor(int customerId) =>
    _orders.TryGetValue(customerId, out var orders) ? orders : [];
```

Callers can iterate without checking. The `[]` collection expression creates an empty list.

## Required members

```csharp
public sealed class CreateUserRequest
{
    public required string Email { get; init; }
    public string? DisplayName { get; init; }
}

var request = new CreateUserRequest { Email = "ada@example.com" }; // omitting Email is a compile error
```

## Null operators

```csharp
var city = order.Customer?.Address?.City ?? "Unknown";
_cache ??= new Dictionary<string, string>();
```

C# 14 also allows the null-conditional operator on the left of an assignment:

```csharp
customer?.LastSeen = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow; // assigns only when customer is not null
```

Avoid the `!` operator except where you have knowledge the compiler cannot have, and prefer
fixing the annotation instead.

title: Objects, data structures and the Law of Demeter
questions:
  - id: demeter
    prompt: "Which line violates the Law of Demeter?"
    options:
      - id: train
        text: "`order.GetCustomer().GetAddress().GetCountry().TaxRate`"
        correct: true
      - text: "`order.Total()`"
      - text: "`customer.PlaceOrder(cart)`"
      - text: "`items.Where(i => i.IsActive).ToList()`"
    explanation: Reaching through several objects couples the caller to the internal structure of each. Fluent LINQ chains return new objects of the same abstraction and are not considered violations.
  - id: tell-dont-ask
    prompt: What does "tell, don't ask" encourage?
    options:
      - text: Avoiding all getters in every class
      - text: Logging every method call
      - id: tell
        text: Telling an object to perform behaviour rather than pulling its data out and deciding for it
        correct: true
    explanation: Behaviour should live next to the data it needs, which keeps invariants inside the object.
  - id: anemic
    prompt: Which statements describe an anemic domain model?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Entities are bags of public getters and setters with no behaviour
        correct: true
      - text: Business rules are scattered across service classes
        correct: true
      - text: Invariants such as "total cannot be negative" are enforced inside the entity
    explanation: In an anemic model, rules live outside the objects, so nothing prevents invalid state.
---
## Learning objectives

- Distinguish objects (behaviour, hidden data) from data structures (exposed data, no behaviour)
- Apply the Law of Demeter and "tell, don't ask"
- Recognise and fix anemic models

## Two different things

| Objects | Data structures |
|---------|-----------------|
| Hide data, expose behaviour | Expose data, have little behaviour |
| Easy to add new types | Easy to add new functions |
| `Account.Withdraw(amount)` | `record AccountDto(int Id, decimal Balance)` |

Both are useful. DTOs crossing a network boundary *should* be plain data. Domain objects that guard
business rules should hide their state.

## The Law of Demeter

A method should only talk to its immediate friends: its own fields, its parameters, objects it
creates, and its own methods.

```csharp
// Train wreck
var rate = order.GetCustomer().GetAddress().GetCountry().TaxRate;

// Ask the object that knows
var taxRate = order.TaxRate();
```

## Tell, don't ask

```csharp
// Asking — the rule lives outside the object
if (account.Balance >= amount)
{
    account.Balance -= amount;
}

// Telling — the object protects its own invariant
account.Withdraw(amount);

public sealed class Account
{
    public decimal Balance { get; private set; }

    public void Withdraw(decimal amount)
    {
        ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegativeOrZero(amount);
        if (amount > Balance) throw new InsufficientFundsException(Balance, amount);
        Balance -= amount;
    }
}
```

With a private setter, the only way to reduce the balance is through `Withdraw`, so the rule
cannot be bypassed.

title: Immutability and encapsulation

    type: multiple

    options:

      - id: mutate

        correct: true

## Learning objectives

- Use records and `init` for immutable data
- Model value objects that are always valid
- Protect collections inside aggregates

## Why immutability

Immutable objects are thread-safe, easy to reason about and impossible to corrupt after
construction. In C#, records make them cheap to write:

```csharp
public sealed record Money(decimal Amount, string Currency)
{
    public static Money Zero(string currency) => new(0m, currency);

    public Money Add(Money other) =>
        other.Currency == Currency
            ? this with { Amount = Amount + other.Amount }
            : throw new CurrencyMismatchException(Currency, other.Currency);
}
```

Records provide value-based equality, so `new Money(5, "EUR") == new Money(5, "EUR")` is `true`.

## Always-valid value objects

```csharp
public sealed record EmailAddress
{
    public string Value { get; }

    private EmailAddress(string value) => Value = value;

    public static EmailAddress Parse(string input)
    {
        var trimmed = input?.Trim() ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(input));
        if (!MailAddress.TryCreate(trimmed, out _)) throw new FormatException($"'{input}' is not a valid e-mail address");
        return new EmailAddress(trimmed.ToLowerInvariant());
    }

    public override string ToString() => Value;
}
```

Once you hold an `EmailAddress`, you never need to validate it again. This replaces "primitive
obsession" — passing raw `string`s everywhere and validating them repeatedly.

## Encapsulating collections

```csharp
public sealed class Order
{
    private readonly List<OrderLine> _lines = [];
    public IReadOnlyList<OrderLine> Lines => _lines;

    public void AddLine(Product product, int quantity)
    {
        ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegativeOrZero(quantity);
        if (_lines.Count >= 100) throw new OrderTooLargeException();
        _lines.Add(new OrderLine(product.Sku, product.Price, quantity));
    }
}
```

The order controls every change to its lines, so its rules always hold.

## Learning objectives

- Structure tests with Arrange–Act–Assert
- Name tests after behaviour
- Make tests deterministic

## A clean test

```csharp
public class ShoppingCartTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Adding_the_same_product_twice_increases_the_quantity()
    {
        // Arrange
        var cart = new ShoppingCart();
        var book = new Product("SKU-1", 12.50m);

        // Act
        cart.Add(book);
        cart.Add(book);

        // Assert
        var line = Assert.Single(cart.Lines);
        Assert.Equal(2, line.Quantity);
    }
}
```

The name reads as a specification. One behaviour per test, and the assertion checks an observable
outcome.

## FIRST

| Letter | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| Fast | Run in milliseconds so they run constantly |
| Independent | No shared state; any order works |
| Repeatable | Same result on every machine, every time |
| Self-validating | Pass or fail, no manual inspection |
| Timely | Written alongside (or before) the code |

## Controlling time

```csharp
public sealed class TrialService(TimeProvider time)
{
    public bool IsExpired(DateTimeOffset startedAt) => time.GetUtcNow() - startedAt > TimeSpan.FromDays(14);
}

[Fact]
public void Trial_expires_after_fourteen_days()
{
    var time = new FakeTimeProvider(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 1, 15, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
    var service = new TrialService(time);

    Assert.True(service.IsExpired(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero)));
}
```

`FakeTimeProvider` comes from the `Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing` package and lets
tests control the clock.

## Parameterised tests

```csharp
[Theory]
[InlineData("", false)]
[InlineData("short", false)]
[InlineData("correct-horse-battery", true)]
public void Password_strength(string password, bool expected) =>
    Assert.Equal(expected, PasswordPolicy.IsStrong(password));
```

---
title: Test-driven development
questions:
  - id: cycle
    prompt: What is the order of the TDD cycle?
    options:
      - text: Green, red, refactor
      - id: red-green-refactor
        text: Red, green, refactor
        correct: true
      - text: Refactor, red, green
      - text: Write all tests, then write all code
    explanation: Write a failing test (red), make it pass with the simplest code (green), then improve the design with tests as a safety net (refactor).
  - id: doubles
    prompt: What is the difference between a stub and a mock?
    options:
      - id: stub-mock
        text: A stub supplies canned answers; a mock also verifies that expected interactions happened
        correct: true
      - text: There is no difference
      - text: Mocks are only used for databases
    explanation: Prefer stubs and fakes for most tests; use mocks when the interaction itself is the behaviour you care about.
  - id: benefits
    prompt: Which are benefits of TDD?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: It pushes toward small, decoupled units that are easy to test
        correct: true
      - text: It produces a regression suite as a side effect
        correct: true
      - text: It forces you to think about the API from the caller's point of view first
        correct: true
      - text: It guarantees the software has no bugs
    explanation: TDD improves design and gives confidence, but tests can only find bugs that someone thought to test.
---
## Learning objectives

- Practice the red–green–refactor cycle
- Choose between stubs, fakes and mocks
- Understand what TDD does and does not guarantee

## Red, green, refactor

1. **Red** — write a test for behaviour that does not exist yet; watch it fail
2. **Green** — write the simplest code that makes it pass
3. **Refactor** — clean up duplication and naming with the tests protecting you

```csharp
[Fact]
public void Empty_string_returns_zero() => Assert.Equal(0, StringCalculator.Add(""));
```

```csharp
public static class StringCalculator
{
    public static int Add(string numbers) => 0;
}
```

The next test forces real behaviour:

```csharp
[Theory]
[InlineData("1", 1)]
[InlineData("1,2", 3)]
[InlineData("4,5,6", 15)]
public void Sums_comma_separated_numbers(string input, int expected) =>
    Assert.Equal(expected, StringCalculator.Add(input));
```

```csharp
public static int Add(string numbers) =>
    string.IsNullOrEmpty(numbers) ? 0 : numbers.Split(',').Sum(int.Parse);
```

## Test doubles

| Double | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| Dummy | Fills a parameter, never used |
| Stub | Returns canned answers |
| Fake | A working, simplified implementation (in-memory repository) |
| Spy | Records calls for later assertions |
| Mock | Pre-programmed with expectations it verifies |

Over-mocking couples tests to implementation details. A hand-written fake is often clearer:

```csharp
public sealed class InMemoryOrderRepository : IOrderRepository
{
    private readonly Dictionary<int, Order> _orders = [];
    public Task AddAsync(Order order, CancellationToken ct) { _orders[order.Id] = order; return Task.CompletedTask; }
    public Task<Order?> FindAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct) => Task.FromResult(_orders.GetValueOrDefault(id));
}
```

## What TDD does not do

TDD does not prove correctness, and it does not replace integration tests, exploratory testing or
thinking. It is a design and feedback technique that leaves a useful test suite behind.

title: Common code smells
questions:
  - id: feature-envy
    prompt: "A method in `InvoicePrinter` reads ten properties of `Customer` to compute a discount. Which smell is this?"
    options:
      - text: Long parameter list
      - text: Shotgun surgery
      - text: Dead code
      - id: envy
        text: Feature envy
        correct: true
    explanation: The method is more interested in another class's data than its own. Move the logic to `Customer`.
  - id: shotgun
    prompt: Every time a new currency is supported, you edit eight files in different folders. Which smell is this?
    options:
      - text: Primitive obsession
      - text: Lazy class
      - id: shotgun
        text: Shotgun surgery
        correct: true
    explanation: One conceptual change requires many scattered edits, a sign that the knowledge is not cohesive.
  - id: smell-facts
    prompt: Which statements about code smells are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: A smell is a hint that something may be wrong, not proof of a bug
        correct: true
      - text: The term was popularised by Kent Beck and Martin Fowler in "Refactoring"
        correct: true
      - text: Duplicated code is one of the most common smells
        correct: true
      - text: Every smell must be fixed immediately, regardless of context
    explanation: Smells guide attention. Whether to act depends on cost, risk and how often that code changes.
---
## Learning objectives

- Recognise the most common code smells
- Connect each smell to a refactoring

A **code smell** is a surface symptom that often points to a deeper design problem. The catalogue
was popularised by Kent Beck and Martin Fowler in *Refactoring*.

## A field guide

| Smell | Symptom | Typical refactoring |
|-------|---------|---------------------|
| Duplicated code | Same logic in several places | Extract method/class |
| Long method | You scroll to read it | Extract method |
| Large class | Many fields, many responsibilities | Extract class |
| Long parameter list | Many arguments, often primitives | Introduce parameter object |
| Primitive obsession | `string email`, `decimal amount` everywhere | Introduce value object |
| Feature envy | Method uses another class's data more than its own | Move method |
| Shotgun surgery | One change, many files | Move related code together |
| Divergent change | One class changes for many reasons | Extract class (SRP) |
| Switch statements | Same switch duplicated | Replace conditional with polymorphism |
| Speculative generality | Abstractions "for later" | Inline class, remove parameter |
| Dead code | Unused members | Delete |

## Example: primitive obsession

```csharp
public void Transfer(string fromIban, string toIban, decimal amount, string currency) { }
```

```csharp
public void Transfer(Iban from, Iban to, Money amount) { }
```

The second signature cannot be called with arguments in the wrong order, and validation lives in
`Iban` and `Money` once.

## Let tools help

Roslyn analyzers flag many smells automatically — unused members (IDE0051), unused parameters
(IDE0060), and complexity rules such as CA1502 (excessive cyclomatic complexity) when enabled.
Treat analyzer warnings as conversation starters in review, not as noise.

title: Refactoring safely
questions:
  - id: definition

    options:
      - text: Rewriting a system from scratch in a new language
      - text: Adding new features while cleaning up code
      - text: Any change that makes code shorter
      - id: behaviour
        text: Changing the internal structure of code without changing its observable behaviour
        correct: true
    explanation: Refactoring preserves behaviour. Adding features is a separate activity — do not mix them in one step.
  - id: boy-scout
    prompt: What does the Boy Scout Rule say?
    options:
      - text: Never touch code you did not write
      - text: Refactor the whole module before every feature
      - id: cleaner
        text: Leave the code a little cleaner than you found it
        correct: true
    explanation: Small, continuous improvements prevent decay without large, risky rewrites.
  - id: safe-steps
    prompt: Which practices make refactoring safe?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Take small steps and run tests after each one
        correct: true
      - text: Use automated IDE refactorings such as Rename and Extract Method
        correct: true
      - text: Commit refactorings separately from behaviour changes
        correct: true
      - text: Refactor and add a feature in the same large commit to save time
    explanation: Small, tested, separately committed steps keep reviews simple and make it easy to find a mistake.
---
## Learning objectives

- Define refactoring precisely
- Use small, tool-assisted steps
- Make continuous improvement part of daily work

## What refactoring is

> Refactoring: a change made to the internal structure of software to make it easier to understand
> and cheaper to modify without changing its observable behaviour. — Martin Fowler

Kent Beck's "two hats": at any moment you are either adding functionality **or** refactoring.
Switch hats deliberately, never wear both.

## A worked example: replace conditional with polymorphism

```csharp
public decimal Pay(Employee e) => e.Type switch
{
    EmployeeType.Salaried => e.MonthlySalary,
    EmployeeType.Hourly => e.HoursWorked * e.HourlyRate,
    EmployeeType.Commissioned => e.BaseSalary + e.Sales * e.CommissionRate,
    _ => throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(e))
};
```

Steps, running tests after each:

1. Create `abstract class Employee { public abstract decimal Pay(); }`
2. Create one subclass and move its branch into `Pay()`
3. Repeat for each branch
4. Replace the switch with `e.Pay()` and delete the type code

```csharp
public sealed class HourlyEmployee(decimal hours, decimal rate) : Employee
{
    public override decimal Pay() => hours * rate;
}
```

## Use the tools

Visual Studio, Rider and VS Code (C# Dev Kit) provide automated Rename, Extract Method,
Extract Interface, Introduce Parameter and Inline. Automated refactorings are behaviour-preserving
by construction and much faster than manual edits.

## The Boy Scout Rule

Leave the campground cleaner than you found it. Rename one unclear variable, extract one
function, delete one dead method each time you touch a file. Over months this compounds into a
codebase that improves instead of decays — without anyone scheduling a "refactoring sprint".

## Legacy code

Michael Feathers defines legacy code as **code without tests**. To change it safely: find a seam,
write characterisation tests that capture current behaviour, then refactor under their protection.

title: What Dapper is and when to use it
questions:
  - id: what
    prompt: What is Dapper?
    options:
      - id: micro-orm
        text: A micro-ORM that adds extension methods to ADO.NET connections for executing SQL and mapping results to objects
        correct: true
      - text: A full ORM with change tracking and migrations
      - text: A database engine
      - text: A replacement for ADO.NET providers such as Microsoft.Data.SqlClient
    explanation: Dapper sits on top of any ADO.NET provider. You write the SQL; Dapper handles parameters and mapping.
  - id: origin
    prompt: Where did Dapper originate?
    options:
      - text: It is part of Entity Framework Core
      - text: It was released by Oracle
      - id: stack-overflow
        text: It was built by the Stack Overflow team to make their data access fast
        correct: true
    explanation: Dapper was created at Stack Overflow and is open source under the Apache 2.0 licence.
  - id: when
    prompt: In which situations is Dapper a particularly good fit?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Read-heavy endpoints where you want precise control over SQL
        correct: true
      - text: Existing databases with complex queries, views or stored procedures
        correct: true
      - text: The read side of a CQRS design, alongside EF Core for writes
        correct: true
      - text: When you want the library to generate and apply schema migrations
    explanation: Dapper has no migrations or change tracking; pair it with a migration tool or EF Core when you need those.
---
## Learning objectives

- Describe what Dapper does and does not do
- Compare Dapper with raw ADO.NET and EF Core
- Decide when Dapper is the right tool

## The problem Dapper solves

Raw ADO.NET is fast but verbose:

```csharp
await using var command = new SqlCommand("SELECT Id, Name, Price FROM Products WHERE Id = @Id", connection);
command.Parameters.AddWithValue("@Id", id);
await using var reader = await command.ExecuteReaderAsync(ct);
Product? product = null;
if (await reader.ReadAsync(ct))
{
    product = new Product
    {
        Id = reader.GetInt32(0),
        Name = reader.GetString(1),
        Price = reader.GetDecimal(2)
    };
}
```

With Dapper:

```csharp
var product = await connection.QuerySingleOrDefaultAsync<Product>(
    "SELECT Id, Name, Price FROM Products WHERE Id = @Id", new { Id = id });
```

Same SQL, same provider, same performance characteristics — without the boilerplate.

## Dapper versus EF Core

| | Dapper | EF Core |
|-|--------|---------|
| You write | SQL | LINQ (SQL generated) |
| Change tracking | No | Yes |
| Migrations | No | Yes |
| Relationships | Manual (multi-mapping) | Navigation properties |
| Overhead | Very low | Low to moderate |
| Learning curve | SQL knowledge | EF concepts + SQL knowledge |

They are not rivals. Many teams use EF Core for writes and aggregates, and Dapper for hot read
paths and reporting queries.

## What Dapper does

- Opens and closes connections when needed
- Converts anonymous objects to command parameters
- Maps result columns to properties or constructor parameters by name
- Caches mapping information so repeated queries are fast

## What it does not do

No change tracking, no identity map, no lazy loading, no LINQ, no schema migrations. You own the
SQL — which is precisely the point.

## Learning objectives

- Install Dapper and a provider
- Run queries and map results to classes and records
- Manage connection lifetime correctly

## Install

```bash
dotnet add package Dapper
dotnet add package Microsoft.Data.SqlClient   # or Npgsql, MySqlConnector, Microsoft.Data.Sqlite
```

`System.Data.SqlClient` is deprecated; use `Microsoft.Data.SqlClient` for SQL Server.

## A sample table

```sql
CREATE TABLE Products (
    Id INT IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    Name NVARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    Category NVARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    Price DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,
    CreatedAt DATETIME2 NOT NULL DEFAULT SYSUTCDATETIME()
);
```

## First queries

```csharp
using Dapper;
using Microsoft.Data.SqlClient;

public sealed class Product
{
    public int Id { get; init; }
    public string Name { get; init; } = "";
    public string Category { get; init; } = "";
    public decimal Price { get; init; }
}

await using var connection = new SqlConnection(connectionString);

IEnumerable<Product> books = await connection.QueryAsync<Product>(
    "SELECT Id, Name, Category, Price FROM Products WHERE Category = @Category ORDER BY Name",
    new { Category = "Books" });

int count = await connection.ExecuteScalarAsync<int>("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Products");
```

`@Category` in the SQL matches the `Category` property of the anonymous object. Values are sent as
real parameters, never concatenated into the SQL text.

## Mapping to records

```csharp
public sealed record ProductSummary(int Id, string Name, decimal Price);

var summaries = await connection.QueryAsync<ProductSummary>(
    "SELECT Id, Name, Price FROM Products");
```

For constructor mapping, column names must match the parameter names (case-insensitively) and the
column types must be compatible with the parameter types — for example, a `BIGINT` column will not
map to an `int` parameter. Explicit casts or aliases in SQL fix mismatches.

## Async and cancellation

Use the `...Async` methods in server applications. To pass a cancellation token, use a
`CommandDefinition`:

```csharp
var command = new CommandDefinition(
    "SELECT Id, Name, Price FROM Products WHERE Price > @Min",
    new { Min = 10m },
    cancellationToken: ct);

var expensive = await connection.QueryAsync<ProductSummary>(command);
```
