        correct: true
    explanation: "The chapter describes draining requests before GC, restarting processes “before they accumulate enough long-lived objects”, and languages like Swift (reference counting) and Rust (lifetimes)."
---
Time-of-day clocks jump; monotonic clocks don't but can't be compared across machines. Synchronization
is imperfect, and relying on it is dangerous. Processes can also pause at any moment.

## Learning objectives

- Distinguish time-of-day and monotonic clocks and when to use each
- List sources of clock error and their magnitudes
- Explain why LWW with wall clocks loses data and why logical clocks are safer
- Explain confidence intervals, TrueTime and Spanner's commit wait
- Identify causes of process pauses and why leases need care

## In a nutshell

- Durations: monotonic clock. Points in time: time-of-day clock (synchronized, but may jump).
- 200 ppm drift ≈ 17 s/day; internet NTP ≈ 35 ms at best, spikes to seconds.
- Faulty clocks fail silently — monitor offsets and evict outliers.
- A clock reading is an interval; Spanner waits out the uncertainty.
- GC, VM suspension, steal time, paging, SIGSTOP and laptop lids can pause a thread for seconds.

## Connections to today

- **AWS ClockBound and Azure/Google precision time services** expose bounded clock error to customers,
  bringing TrueTime-like ideas to everyone.
- **The end of leap seconds** — scheduled to stop by 2035 — will remove one classic clock bug source.
- **.NET's `Stopwatch` and `TimeProvider`** separate monotonic elapsed time from wall-clock time, and
  `TimeProvider` makes time mockable for tests.

---
A node can only guess about others from messages. Quorums decide, fencing tokens stop zombies, system
models make assumptions explicit, and testing techniques check the result.

## Learning objectives

- Explain why a node can't trust its own judgment and why quorums decide
- Use fencing tokens to make leases safe, including with leaderless storage
- Explain Byzantine faults and when BFT is (not) worth it
- Name timing and failure system models and safety vs liveness
- Compare model checking, fault injection and deterministic simulation testing

## In a nutshell

- A node declared dead by a quorum must step down.
- Leases + pauses = zombies; fencing tokens (monotonic numbers) let storage reject stale writers.
- Most systems assume crash-recovery nodes in a partially synchronous model.
- Safety must always hold; liveness may depend on conditions.
- TLA+ models, Jepsen, and DST (FoundationDB, TigerBeetle, Antithesis) find bugs tests miss.

## Connections to today

- **S3 conditional writes** (`If-Match`/`If-None-Match`) now allow fencing and leader election directly
  on object storage, as the chapter notes.
- **Deterministic simulation** is spreading: Antithesis, TigerBeetle's VOPR and Rust's MadSim.
- **AI-generated code** benefits from property-based and simulation testing that explores states humans
  wouldn't think to write tests for.

Two philosophies: expose replication to the application (eventual consistency) or hide it (strong
consistency). This chapter makes "strong" precise and shows how to achieve it with consensus.

## Learning objectives

- Contrast eventual and strong consistency philosophies and when each fits

## In a nutshell

- Offline editing forces eventual consistency.
- Fast, reliable links make strong consistency affordable.
- Strong consistency = linearizability; fault-tolerant linearizability needs consensus.

## Connections to today

- **Global SQL databases** let teams choose per-region strong reads versus faster stale reads — the
  philosophical choice made per query.

---
Make a replicated system look like one copy with atomic operations: a recency guarantee. Useful for
locks, uniqueness, and cross-channel races — but expensive.

## Learning objectives

- Define linearizability and apply it to timing diagrams
- Distinguish linearizability from serializability
- Identify when linearizability is required
- Judge which replication methods can be linearizable
- Explain CAP, its flaws, and the latency cost of linearizability

## In a nutshell

- Once any read sees a new value, all later reads must too.
- Serializability: multi-object transactions in some serial order; linearizability: single-object recency. Both = strict serializability.
- Needed for leader election, hard uniqueness constraints, and cross-channel dependencies.
- Single-leader (reads on leader) and consensus: potentially linearizable; multi-leader: not; Dynamo-style: assume not.
- CAP is "either consistent or available when partitioned" and mostly of historical interest.
- Linearizable latency ∝ network delay uncertainty (Attiya–Welch).

## Connections to today

- **etcd v3** provides linearizable reads by default, while ZooKeeper reads may be stale — a practical
  difference for Kubernetes operators.
- **S3 strong read-after-write consistency** (since 2020) removed a common cross-channel race in data
  pipelines.
- **Push notification races** in mobile apps — notification arrives, fetch hits a stale replica — are the
  chapter's example in everyday apps.

      - id: o7dd914
        text: "Clocks are too slow"
    explanation: "“how does a node know whether its own timestamp is the lowest? To be sure, it needs to hear from every other node ... this system would grind to a halt ... We need consensus.”"
---
Unique IDs that also tell you order are surprisingly subtle. Distributed schemes give uniqueness but
weak ordering; Lamport and hybrid logical clocks give causal order; linearizable IDs need a single
authority or bounded clocks.

## Learning objectives

- Compare single-node, sharded, block, UUID and timestamp-based ID schemes
- Explain Lamport clocks and hybrid logical clocks, and how they differ from vector clocks
- Explain why causal IDs can still leak a private photo, and how linearizable IDs fix it
- Explain why logical clocks alone can't implement locks

## In a nutshell

- Single-node autoincrement: linearizable but a SPOF, slow cross-region, a bottleneck.
- UUIDv7, Snowflake, ULID: unique, roughly time-ordered, not linearizable.
- Lamport: (counter, node ID), advance on receive; total order consistent with causality.
- HLC: physical-time-like, monotonic, causal — used by CockroachDB.
- Vector clocks detect concurrency at the cost of size.
- Timestamp oracles (TiDB) or Spanner's commit wait give linearizable IDs.

## Connections to today

- **UUIDv7** (RFC 9562) is now the common default for new primary keys; .NET 9 added
  `Guid.CreateVersion7()`.
- **TiDB's PD timestamp oracle** is the chapter's single-node linearizable ID generator in production.

---
Getting nodes to agree. Many problems — CAS, shared logs, fetch-and-add, atomic commit — turn out to be
consensus in disguise. Raft, Paxos, Zab and VR solve it with epochs and quorums; coordination services
package it for applications.

## Learning objectives

- State FLP and why consensus is still achievable in practice
- State the four properties of consensus and which are safety vs liveness
- Explain equivalences: CAS, shared log/total order broadcast, fetch-and-add (consensus number 2), atomic commit
- Explain epochs and two rounds of quorum voting; contrast with 2PC
- Weigh the costs of consensus and the uses of coordination services

## In a nutshell

- FLP: no deterministic algorithm always terminates in the asynchronous model; timeouts or randomness escape it.
- Uniform agreement, integrity, validity (safety) + termination (liveness, needs a majority).
- Most systems expose a shared log; state machine replication follows.
- Within each epoch the leader is unique; higher epoch wins.
- Consensus = "single-leader replication done right"; costs: majority required, no throughput scaling, timeout tuning.
- ZooKeeper/etcd: leases, fencing tokens, sessions, notifications — for slow-changing metadata.

## Connections to today

- **Kafka KRaft** and **Kubernetes on etcd** are consensus in everyday infrastructure.
- **Raft pre-vote and check-quorum** settings exist because of the flapping-leadership edge cases the
  chapter mentions.
- **Unclean leader election** in Kafka is the explicit availability-over-consistency switch the sidebar
  describes.

        text: "Humans can't make mistakes in batch jobs"
    explanation: "“If you introduce a bug into the code and the output is wrong or corrupted, you can simply roll back to a previous version of the code and rerun the job ... The idea of being able to recover from buggy code has been called human fault tolerance.”"

  - id: batch-downsides
    prompt: "Which are challenges of batch processing?"
    type: multiple

      - id: oc1e1ef

    options:

---
Online systems answer requests fast; batch jobs read immutable inputs and regenerate outputs from
scratch. That simple discipline buys "human fault tolerance".

## Learning objectives

- Contrast online and batch systems and their performance measures
- Explain the benefits of immutable inputs and side-effect-free jobs
- Place MapReduce in history

## In a nutshell

- Batch: throughput matters; online: response time matters.
- Bad code? Roll back and rerun — or switch back to old output (time travel).
- Downsides: output available only when the job finishes; any input change means reprocessing everything.
- MapReduce is largely obsolete; Spark, Flink and cloud warehouses replaced it; Airflow/Dagster/Prefect replaced Oozie.

## Connections to today

- **Iceberg/Delta time travel** makes "keep the old output and switch back" a table-format feature.
- **Spot instances** make batch cheap precisely because jobs can be retried.

A five-command pipeline finds the most popular pages in a log, and teaches the sort-versus-hash
trade-off that distributed systems reuse.

## Learning objectives

- Explain each stage of the log-analysis pipeline
- Compare in-memory hash aggregation with sorting
- Explain how GNU sort scales beyond memory

## In a nutshell

- awk extracts, sort groups, uniq -c counts, sort -rn ranks, head trims.
- Hash table: working set = distinct keys; fine if it fits in memory.
- Sorting spills to disk and parallelizes; the limit becomes disk read speed and one machine.

## Connections to today

- **DuckDB** applies the same choices (hash aggregation with spilling) on a single machine and often
  beats clusters for tens of gigabytes.

Distributed batch frameworks are like a distributed OS: a filesystem (DFS or object store), a scheduler,
and programs connected by data. Workflows chain jobs; fault handling retries tasks.

## Learning objectives

- Map OS components (storage, scheduler, pipes) to distributed equivalents
- Compare distributed filesystems with object stores
- Explain orchestrator components and why scheduling is hard
- Explain workflow DAGs and how frameworks handle task failures

## In a nutshell

- DFS: large blocks (HDFS 128 MB), data nodes, a metadata service (NameNode), replication or erasure coding.
- Object stores: immutable objects, prefix listing, no atomic rename, compute separate from storage.
- Orchestrators: executors (kubelet, NodeManager), resource manager, scheduler; heuristics for an NP-hard problem.
- Workflows of 50–100 jobs are common; Airflow/Dagster/Prefect manage dependencies.
- Spot/preemptible capacity suits batch; retries happen per task.

## Connections to today

- **S3-compatible APIs** (MinIO, R2, Tigris, B2) are the de facto storage protocol for analytics engines.
- **Kubernetes batch scheduling** (Kueue, Volcano) adds gang scheduling and quotas for AI training jobs.
- **DeepSeek's 3FS** — named in the chapter — is a modern DFS for AI workloads.

        text: "Each event looks up the user over the network"
    explanation: "“The shuffle then ensures that a reducer function can access a particular user’s date of birth and all of that user’s page view events at the same time ... This technique is known as a secondary sort.”"
  - id: join-memory
    prompt: "Why does the sort-merge join need little memory and no network requests in the reducer?"
    options:
      - id: ob40c7a
        text: "It reads from a remote database"
      - id: o39e10b
        text: "The reducer processes one user's records at a time, keeping only one user record in memory"
        correct: true
      - id: o033ccc
        text: "It uses Bloom filters"
      - id: of1f227
        text: "It caches the whole user table"
    explanation: "“Since a reducer processes all the records for a particular user ID in one go, it needs to keep only one user record in memory at any one time, and it never needs to make any requests over the network.”"
  - id: sql-benefits
    prompt: "Why did batch systems embrace SQL?"
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: o6f0731

      - id: o6a5206

      - id: oe62fa0

        correct: true
    explanation: "SQL is “the lingua franca for batch processing” and “High-level query languages don’t just make the humans using the system more productive; they also improve job execution efficiency at a machine level.”"
  - id: not-sql

      - id: o38e19d

  - id: warehouse-cost
    prompt: "Why might you run a large job on Spark rather than a cloud warehouse?"
    options:
      - id: oc7a515

  - id: distributed-df
    prompt: "What surprise can occur when moving from Pandas to distributed DataFrames?"
    options:
      - id: o985605
        text: "Local DataFrames are indexed and ordered, but distributed ones generally aren't"
        correct: true
      - id: od14641

      - id: oc4f416

      - id: o3f5291
        text: "Pandas runs lazily"
    explanation: "“local DataFrames are usually indexed and ordered, while distributed DataFrames are generally not. This can lead to performance surprises”. Also, “Spark first translates all the DataFrame API calls into a query plan and runs query optimization”."
---
MapReduce's map–sort–reduce, the dataflow engines that replaced it, the shuffle that powers joins and
grouping, and the SQL and DataFrame interfaces on top.

## Learning objectives

- Map the Unix pipeline onto MapReduce
- List dataflow engines' advantages over MapReduce
- Explain the shuffle and a sort-merge join with secondary sort
- Explain why SQL and DataFrames improve both productivity and execution

## In a nutshell

- Mapper: stateless per record; reducer: per key over sorted values.
- Dataflow engines (Spark, Flink) treat a whole workflow as one job: sort only where needed, fuse operators, keep state local, pipeline.
- Shuffle = distributed sort, not random.
- Sort-merge join: both sides keyed by user ID; reducer sees the profile first, then events.
- Warehouses and batch frameworks have converged; DataFrames go distributed (but are unordered).

## Connections to today

- **Spark Connect and DataFrame APIs in BigQuery and Snowflake (Snowpark)** show the convergence the
  sidebar describes.
- **Polars and Daft** offer lazy, optimized DataFrames that plan queries before executing, like Spark.

  matter.

Batch processing assumes bounded input. Real data is unbounded, so we process events continuously as
they arrive.

## Learning objectives

- Explain why sorting needs bounded input
- Define a stream and where the concept appears

## In a nutshell

- Daily batches mean day-old results; streams process events as they happen.
- A stream is data made available incrementally over time.

## Connections to today

- **Real-time features** — fraud scoring, personalization, LLM agent event triggers — are pushing many
  pipelines from nightly batch to streaming.

---
Events, producers, consumers and topics; direct messaging versus brokers; AMQP/JMS-style queues versus
log-based brokers like Kafka.

## Learning objectives

- Define events, producers, consumers and topics
- Ask the two key questions about any messaging system
- Compare direct messaging, traditional brokers and log-based brokers
- Explain load balancing vs fan-out, acknowledgments, redelivery reordering and DLQs
- Explain offsets, retention as a ring buffer, and replay

## In a nutshell

- Overload options: drop, buffer, or backpressure; durability costs throughput.
- Traditional brokers delete on ack; logs keep messages and track consumer offsets.
- Load balancing + redelivery reorders messages.
- Log shards: total order within a shard, consumer parallelism ≤ shard count, head-of-line blocking.
- A slow log consumer affects only itself; replay from any offset makes streams batch-like.

## Connections to today

- **Kafka share groups** (queue-style consumption) and **diskless/object-storage Kafka** (WarpStream,
  Bufstream) are the convergence and tiering the chapter describes.
- **Webhooks** remain the default integration mechanism for SaaS events — with all the loss caveats of
  direct messaging.
- **Azure Service Bus and SQS dead-letter queues** are standard tools for poison messages.

---
Every database write is an event. Change data capture turns a database into a stream source; event
sourcing makes the stream the source of truth. State and logs are two sides of the same coin.

## Learning objectives

- Explain the race and failure problems of dual writes
- Describe CDC, initial snapshots, log compaction and the outbox pattern
- Contrast CDC with event sourcing
- Explain the state/stream duality and the benefits and limits of immutability

## In a nutshell

- Dual writes: interleaving makes systems permanently inconsistent; partial failure too.
- CDC makes the database the leader and derived systems followers, preserving order.
- Snapshots must align with a log position; log compaction keeps the latest value per key.
- CDC exposes schemas as public APIs; outbox tables decouple them.
- State = integral of events; changelog = derivative of state.
- Immutability aids auditing, recovery and multiple views; deletion needs excision or crypto-shredding.

## Connections to today

- **Debezium** — the chapter's main example — plus managed CDC (AWS DMS, Google Datastream, Azure
  Data Factory CDC) are standard ingestion paths into lakehouses.
- **Transactional outbox** libraries in .NET (MassTransit, Wolverine) implement the outbox pattern.
- **Postgres logical replication slots** must be monitored — a stuck consumer causes WAL growth.

---
What to do with a stream: write it to storage, push it to people, or transform it into other streams. The
section covers uses, time, windows, joins and fault tolerance.

## Learning objectives

- Distinguish CEP, stream analytics, materialized view maintenance and stream search
- Explain incremental view maintenance
- Distinguish event time from processing time and handle stragglers
- Compare tumbling, hopping, sliding and session windows
- Explain stream–stream, stream–table and table–table joins and their time dependence
- Achieve exactly-once effects with microbatching, checkpoints, transactions or idempotence

## In a nutshell

- CEP and stream search store queries and run data past them.
- Approximation (HyperLogLog, Bloom filters) is an optimization, not inherent to streaming.
- IVM (Materialize, RisingWave, Feldera) updates views incrementally.
- Processing-time windows create fake spikes; event-time windows face stragglers.
- Joins need state; cross-stream ordering makes them nondeterministic unless versioned (SCD).
- Effectively-once = discard partial output: microbatches, checkpoints, internal transactions, idempotent writes.

## Connections to today

- **Flink SQL and Kafka Streams** are mainstream; **streaming databases** blur stream processors and
  warehouses.
- **Real-time feature pipelines** for ML and LLM retrieval (fresh embeddings) are stream–table joins.
- **Idempotency keys** in payment APIs (Stripe-style) are the chapter's idempotence technique applied to
  external side effects.

        correct: true
      - id: o94fe32
        text: "Trains are like databases"
    explanation: "Tracks were converted “to dual gauge or mixed gauge by adding a third rail ... allowing the old and new versions to exist side by side, makes it possible to change the gauge gradually”."
  - id: gradual-migration
    prompt: "Why is migrating via two derived views safer than a sudden switch?"
    options:
      - id: o6341c9
        text: "It is cheaper"
      - id: o393e2d
        text: "It needs no extra storage"
      - id: ofc47ee
        text: "Each stage is reversible, so you always have a working system to go back to"
        correct: true
      - id: o6df700
        text: "It avoids testing"
    explanation: "“The beauty of such a gradual migration is that every stage of the process is easily reversible if something goes wrong; you always have a working system to go back to.”"
  - id: unify
    prompt: "Which features does unifying batch and stream processing require?"
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: obcb112
        text: "Exactly-once semantics for stream processors"
        correct: true
      - id: o536e22
        text: "Windowing by event time, not processing time"
        correct: true
      - id: obc424d
        text: "Separate code bases for batch and stream"
      - id: oe67a50
        text: "Replaying historical events through the same engine"

---
No single tool fits all uses, so applications compose tools. The chapter argues for deriving data
through ordered event logs rather than distributed transactions, and for using batch and stream together.

## Learning objectives

- Explain why tool composition is inevitable
- Reason about which systems are sources and which are derived
- Compare log-based derived data with distributed transactions
- Explain the limits of total ordering and capturing causality
- Explain how reprocessing enables evolution and what unifying batch and stream requires

## In a nutshell

- Decide on a total order of writes (CDC or event log) and derive everything else from it.
- Derived data vs distributed transactions: idempotent retry vs atomic commit; derived data is usually asynchronous.
- Total order breaks down with sharding, multiple regions, microservices and offline clients.
- Asynchrony contains faults; distributed transactions amplify them.
- Reprocessing lets you run old and new views side by side, like dual-gauge railways.
- Kappa-style unification needs replay, exactly-once, and event-time windows.

## Connections to today

- **Zero-ETL integrations** in cloud platforms are vendor-managed derived-data pipelines.
- **Blue/green data migrations** with shadow reads are the chapter's gradual evolution.
- **Apache Beam** — named in the chapter — remains the canonical unified batch/stream API.

---
Treat the organization's dataflow as one giant database whose indexes are separate systems kept in
sync by logs. Then design applications as derivation functions over streams, and extend the write path
all the way to the user's screen.

## Learning objectives

- Contrast the Unix and relational philosophies
- Relate CREATE INDEX to followers and CDC bootstrapping
- Distinguish federated databases (unifying reads) from unbundled databases (unifying writes)
- Explain why log-based integration loosely couples systems and teams
- Explain dataflow application design, the write/read path boundary, and reads as events

## In a nutshell

- Batch and stream processors are like triggers, stored procedures and view maintenance at organization scale.
- Unbundling is about breadth, not depth — use one product if it does everything you need.
- Application code is a derivation function; keep it separate from state, but subscribe to state changes.
- Dataflow replaces synchronous RPC with stream joins against local state.
- Caches, indexes and views shift the boundary between write and read paths; clients can be subscribers too.

## Connections to today

- **Trino and Postgres FDWs** are federated reads; **Debezium + Kafka + IVM engines** are unbundled writes.
- **Live queries** in Firebase, Convex, Supabase Realtime and sync engines extend the write path to UIs.
- **React/Blazor state management** already re-renders on state changes — the missing piece is server push.

---
Strong database guarantees don't make an application correct. End-to-end request IDs, log-based
constraint checking, integrity over timeliness, and auditing get closer.

## Learning objectives

- Explain why serializable transactions don't prevent duplicate requests from users
- State the end-to-end argument and apply it to dedup, checksums and encryption
- Enforce uniqueness and multi-shard operations with sharded logs and request IDs
- Distinguish timeliness from integrity and use compensating transactions
- Explain "trust, but verify" and designing for auditability

## In a nutshell

- TCP and DB transactions dedupe only within their scope; a client-generated request ID must flow end to end.
- Uniqueness needs consensus; shard by the unique value and process sequentially.
- Multi-shard payments: atomicity comes from appending one request event; downstream steps dedupe by request ID.
- Timeliness violations are temporary; integrity violations are permanent.
- Many "hard" constraints are business-negotiable with apologies.
- Coordination-avoiding systems: strong integrity, weak timeliness.
- Verify continually: read data back, test restores, recompute derived state.

## Connections to today

- **Idempotency keys** in payment APIs and ASP.NET Core idempotency middleware implement end-to-end
  request IDs.
- **Certificate Transparency** — cited in the chapter — is a production Merkle-tree audit log.
- **Data quality checks** (Great Expectations, dbt tests) are a form of continuous end-to-end auditing.

  - id: collusion
    prompt: "What happened when German gas stations adopted algorithmic pricing?"
    options:
      - id: oc51909
        text: "Prices fell sharply"
      - id: o2ee4cc
        text: "Algorithms learned to collude, reducing competition and raising prices"
        correct: true
      - id: of3e361
        text: "Stations went out of business"
      - id: o392491
        text: "Nothing changed"
    explanation: "“when gas stations in Germany introduced algorithmic prices, competition was reduced and prices for consumers went up because the algorithms learned to collude.”"
  - id: systems-thinking
    prompt: "What approach helps anticipate feedback loops?"
    options:
      - id: o3087db
        text: "More data collection"
      - id: occ5751
        text: "Systems thinking — considering the whole system including the people interacting with it"
        correct: true
      - id: o3e2e4f
        text: "Unit testing"
      - id: o18492b
        text: "Faster deployment"
    explanation: "“many consequences can be predicted by thinking about the entire system (not just the computerized parts, but also the people interacting with it)—an approach known as systems thinking.”"
---
Every system has intended and unintended consequences, and many datasets are about people. Predictive
analytics can exclude people unfairly, launder bias, evade accountability and create feedback loops.

## Learning objectives

- Explain why ethics is a participatory process, not a checklist
- Explain "algorithmic prison" and why organizations err on the side of "no"
- Explain how ML can learn and amplify bias, including via proxies
- Discuss accountability, recourse and the limits of probabilistic predictions
- Recognize feedback loops and apply systems thinking

## In a nutshell

- Technology isn't good or bad in itself; how it's used matters.
- Predictions about people have direct effects on their lives.
- "Machine learning is like money laundering for bias."
- Credit scores ask "How did you behave?"; predictive analytics ask "How did people like you behave?"
- Feedback loops: credit scores in hiring, algorithmic price collusion.

## Connections to today

- **The EU AI Act** classifies credit scoring and hiring systems as high-risk, imposing requirements on
  data governance, transparency and human oversight.
- **LLM-based screening tools** inherit biases in training data — the same "past codified" problem.
- **Recommendation feedback loops** shape what news and videos people see.

When tracking serves advertisers instead of users, data collection becomes surveillance. Consent is
often not meaningful, privacy is a decision right transferred to companies, data is a hazardous asset,
and we need both regulation and a culture shift.

## Learning objectives

- Explain when tracking serves the user and when it becomes surveillance
- Critique consent as practiced, and GDPR's consent requirements
- Define privacy as a decision right and explain its transfer to companies
- Explain why data is a "toxic asset" and why future governments matter
- Draw lessons from the Industrial Revolution and weigh legislation against self-regulation

## In a nutshell

- Replace "data" with "surveillance" and see how the sentence sounds.
- Users can't consent meaningfully to what they can't understand; data about one user reveals others.
- Opting out of essential services isn't a free choice.
- "Data is the pollution problem of the information age."
- Minimize collection, purge data you no longer need — data you don't have can't leak.

## Connections to today

- **AI training on user content** has revived debates over consent and opt-outs across major platforms.
- **Data brokers** remain the subject of regulatory action in the US and EU.
- **Retention policies and TTLs** in modern data platforms (e.g., Delta/Iceberg vacuum, Kafka retention)
  are the technical side of data minimization.

## Learning objectives

- Recall the probability, vector and ML basics behind LLMs
- Recognise evaluation pitfalls inherited from classic ML

## Softmax with temperature

```python
import numpy as np

def softmax(logits: np.ndarray, temperature: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray:
    z = logits / temperature
    z = z - z.max()
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum()

logits = np.array([2.0, 1.0, 0.1])
print(softmax(logits, 1.0))
print(softmax(logits, 0.2))
```

At low temperature almost all probability goes to the top token.

title: The AI family tree
questions:
  - id: nesting
    prompt: Which nesting is correct?
    options:
      - text: Machine learning ⊃ AI ⊃ deep learning ⊃ generative AI
      - text: Generative AI ⊃ deep learning ⊃ machine learning ⊃ AI
      - id: nest
        text: AI ⊃ machine learning ⊃ deep learning ⊃ (most of today's) generative AI
        correct: true
      - text: They are four unrelated fields
    explanation: Generative models predate deep learning (for example Markov chains, Gaussian mixture models), but today's GenAI is deep-learning based.
  - id: ml-def
    prompt: What distinguishes machine learning from rule-based AI?
    options:
      - id: learn
        text: ML learns patterns from data rather than following rules explicitly written by people
        correct: true
      - text: ML always uses neural networks
      - text: ML cannot make predictions
      - text: Rule-based systems are always worse
    explanation: Rule-based systems are still the right answer for many deterministic tasks — tax rules, validation, routing.
  - id: generative-discriminative
    prompt: What is the difference between discriminative and generative models?
    options:
      - text: Generative models are always larger
      - text: Discriminative models generate images
      - text: There is no difference
      - id: gen-disc
        text: Discriminative models learn to separate classes (p(y|x)), e.g. spam or not; generative models learn the data distribution well enough to produce new samples (p(x) or p(x|context))
        correct: true
    explanation: An LLM is generative — it models the probability of the next token given the previous ones.
  - id: modalities
    prompt: Which are examples of generative AI output modalities?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: text
        text: Text and code
        correct: true
      - id: images

        correct: true
      - id: audio
        text: Speech and music
        correct: true
      - id: structured
        text: Structured data such as JSON or synthetic tables
        correct: true
    explanation: Multimodal models accept and produce several modalities in one model.
  - id: foundation-model
    prompt: What is a foundation model?
    options:
      - text: A model for building foundations in construction
      - id: fm
        text: A large model trained on broad data at scale that can be adapted to many downstream tasks
        correct: true
      - text: The first model a company trains
      - text: A small model for a single task
    explanation: The term was popularised by Stanford's Center for Research on Foundation Models in 2021 (Bommasani et al.).
  - id: llm
    prompt: What does the "large" in "large language model" refer to?
    options:
      - text: The physical size of the server
      - text: The length of answers

        correct: true
      - text: The number of languages supported
    explanation: Parameter counts for frontier proprietary models are mostly undisclosed; open-weight models publish them.
  - id: diffusion
    prompt: Which architecture underlies most modern image generators?
    options:
      - text: Decision trees
      - text: Recurrent neural networks
      - text: Linear regression
      - id: diffusion
        text: Diffusion models, which learn to reverse a gradual noising process, often combined with transformers
        correct: true
    explanation: LLMs are transformer-based autoregressive models; image generation mostly uses diffusion. The two converge in multimodal systems.
  - id: not-genai
    prompt: Which of these tasks usually does NOT need generative AI?
    options:
      - text: Drafting a reply to a customer email
      - text: Summarising a long contract
      - id: forecast

        correct: true
      - text: Generating product descriptions
    explanation: Classical ML and statistics often beat LLMs on tabular prediction at a fraction of the cost. Use GenAI where language or content generation is the job.
  - id: ai-agents-link

    options:
      - id: built-on

      - text: Agents replaced LLMs
      - text: Agents are a type of database
    explanation: The AI Agent Fundamentals book covers this in depth.

## Learning objectives

- Place generative AI within AI, ML and deep learning
- Distinguish generative from discriminative models
- Recognise tasks that do not need GenAI

## The family tree

```text
Artificial intelligence  — systems performing tasks that need "intelligence"
└── Machine learning     — learns from data
    └── Deep learning    — multi-layer neural networks
        └── Generative AI — models that produce new content
            ├── Large language models (text, code)
            ├── Diffusion models (images, video)
            └── Multimodal models (several modalities)
```

## Choosing the right tool

| Task | Usually best |
|---|---|
| Deterministic business rules | Code |
| Tabular prediction (churn, demand) | Classical ML (gradient boosting) |
| Search over known documents | Search engines, plus embeddings |
| Drafting, summarising, extracting from text | LLMs |
| Open-ended conversation | LLMs |

## Sources

- Bommasani et al., "On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models", 2021 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.07258>
- Ho, Jain, Abbeel, "Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models", 2020 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239>
- Databricks, Generative AI Fundamentals — <https://www.databricks.com/learn/training/generative-ai-fundamentals-accreditation>

title: A short history
questions:
  - id: transformer-year
    prompt: Which 2017 paper introduced the transformer architecture?
    options:
      - text: "\"ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks\""
      - id: attention
        text: "\"Attention Is All You Need\" (Vaswani et al., Google)"
        correct: true
      - text: "\"Deep Residual Learning\""
      - text: "\"Generative Adversarial Nets\""
    explanation: The transformer replaced recurrence with self-attention, allowing parallel training on huge datasets.
  - id: why-transformer
    prompt: Why did transformers scale better than recurrent neural networks (RNNs)?
    options:
      - text: They use less memory for long sequences
      - id: parallel
        text: All positions in a sequence are processed in parallel during training, which suits GPUs; RNNs process tokens sequentially
        correct: true
      - text: They do not need training data
      - text: They are rule-based
    explanation: Self-attention's cost grows quadratically with sequence length, which is why long context remains expensive.
  - id: gpt
    prompt: What does GPT stand for?
    options:
      - text: General Purpose Transformer
      - text: Graph Processing Technique
      - id: gpt
        text: Generative Pre-trained Transformer
        correct: true
      - text: Global Prediction Tool
    explanation: OpenAI's GPT-1 (2018) showed generative pre-training plus fine-tuning worked; GPT-3 (2020, 175B parameters) showed in-context few-shot learning.
  - id: bert
    prompt: How did BERT (2018) differ from GPT?
    options:
      - id: encoder
        text: BERT is an encoder-only model trained to fill in masked tokens, strong for understanding tasks and embeddings; GPT is decoder-only and generates text left to right
        correct: true
      - text: BERT generated images
      - text: BERT was rule-based
      - text: There is no difference
    explanation: Encoder models remain widely used for classification and embeddings.
  - id: chatgpt
    prompt: What made ChatGPT (November 2022) a turning point?
    options:
      - text: It was the first neural network
      - text: It was open source
      - text: It ran on phones without internet
      - id: chat
        text: Instruction-tuning and RLHF turned a base model into a helpful conversational assistant, exposed through a free chat interface — reaching a reported 100 million users in about two months
        correct: true
    explanation: The underlying capabilities existed in GPT-3.5; the interface and alignment made them usable by everyone.
  - id: scaling-laws
    prompt: What do neural scaling laws describe?
    options:
      - text: How to scale a Kubernetes cluster
      - id: power-law
        text: Predictable improvements in loss as model size, data and compute increase, roughly following power laws (Kaplan et al., 2020)
        correct: true
      - text: Laws regulating AI
      - text: The speed of light limit for GPUs
    explanation: Chinchilla (Hoffmann et al., 2022) showed many models were under-trained; compute-optimal training uses roughly 20 tokens per parameter.
  - id: open-weights
    prompt: Which model families made open-weight LLMs mainstream?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: llama
        text: Meta's Llama
        correct: true
      - id: mistral
        text: Mistral's models
        correct: true
      - id: qwen-deepseek
        text: Qwen (Alibaba) and DeepSeek
        correct: true
      - text: Microsoft Excel
    explanation: "Open weights is not the same as open source: training data and code are often unreleased and licences may restrict use."
  - id: reasoning-models
    prompt: What characterises "reasoning models" such as OpenAI o1 (2024) and successors?
    options:
      - text: They use no neural networks
      - text: They cannot produce text
      - id: think
        text: They are trained, often with reinforcement learning, to generate long intermediate reasoning before answering, trading more inference compute for better results on maths, code and multi-step problems
        correct: true
      - text: They guarantee correct answers
    explanation: This shifted some scaling from training compute to "test-time compute". They are slower and costlier per answer.
  - id: hype-cycles
    prompt: Which statement about AI history is accurate?
    options:
      - text: AI progress has been steady and uninterrupted since 1950
      - text: Deep learning was invented in 2022
      - id: winters
        text: AI has had "winters" — periods of reduced funding after over-promising (notably the 1970s and late 1980s) — a reminder that expectations and capabilities can diverge
        correct: true
      - text: AI has never been over-hyped
    explanation: Current capabilities are real; so is the tendency to overestimate near-term impact.
  - id: deepseek
    prompt: What did DeepSeek-R1 (January 2025) demonstrate?
    options:
      - id: efficient
        text: That a competitive open-weight reasoning model could be trained with reinforcement learning at reportedly much lower cost than assumed, intensifying price competition
        correct: true
      - text: That transformers do not work
      - text: That RL is useless for LLMs
      - text: That closed models are always better
    explanation: Reported training costs excluded prior research and infrastructure; still, it shifted assumptions about cost and openness.

## Timeline

| Year | Milestone |
|---|---|
| 2013 | word2vec — word embeddings |
| 2014 | GANs; sequence-to-sequence with attention |
| 2017 | Transformer ("Attention Is All You Need") |
| 2018 | GPT-1, BERT |
| 2020 | GPT-3; scaling laws; RAG paper; diffusion models |
| 2022 | InstructGPT/RLHF; Chinchilla; ChatGPT |
| 2023 | GPT-4; Llama; open-weight explosion |
| 2024 | Long context; multimodal; reasoning models (o1); MCP |
| 2025 | DeepSeek-R1; agents mainstream; MLflow 3 |
| 2026 | Agent platforms, protocols under foundations; regulation phases in |

title: Tokens and tokenization
questions:
  - id: token
    prompt: What is a token?
    options:
      - text: A password for the API
      - text: Always exactly one word
      - text: Always exactly one character
      - id: subword
        text: A unit of text — often a word piece — from the model's fixed vocabulary; models read and write sequences of token IDs
        correct: true
    explanation: Most LLMs use subword tokenisers such as byte-pair encoding (BPE), so common words are one token and rare words are split.
  - id: rule-of-thumb
    prompt: For English text, roughly how many characters is one token on average with common tokenisers?
    options:
      - text: "1"
      - id: four
        text: About 4 (roughly ¾ of a word)
        correct: true
      - text: About 20
      - text: About 100
    explanation: OpenAI's rule of thumb. Other languages, code and numbers often use more tokens per character.
  - id: why-matters
    prompt: Why do tokens matter in practice?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: billing
        text: APIs bill per input and output token
        correct: true
      - id: context
        text: Context windows are measured in tokens
        correct: true
      - id: latency
        text: Output generation time scales with the number of output tokens
        correct: true
      - text: Tokens determine the model's licence
    explanation: Counting tokens is the basis of GenAI cost estimation.
  - id: language-tax
    prompt: Why can the same message cost more in Hindi or Burmese than in English?
    options:
      - text: Providers charge more for non-English languages by policy
      - text: Non-English text is compressed
      - id: tokenizer-bias
        text: Tokenisers trained mostly on English split many other scripts into more tokens per word, so the same content uses more tokens — a documented fairness issue
        correct: true
      - text: It does not; tokens are language-neutral
    explanation: Studies (e.g. Petrov et al., 2023) measured up to an order of magnitude more tokens for some languages.
  - id: strawberry
    prompt: Why did LLMs famously miscount the letter "r" in "strawberry"?
    options:
      - text: They cannot read English
      - id: no-letters
        text: The model sees tokens, not letters; character-level tasks require knowledge the token representation hides
        correct: true
      - text: The word was not in the training data
      - text: A bug that was fixed in all models
    explanation: The same blind spot affects spelling, character counting and some arithmetic on long numbers. Tools (code execution) fix it reliably.
  - id: numbers
    prompt: How does tokenisation affect arithmetic?
    options:
      - text: It has no effect
      - text: Numbers are always single tokens
      - text: LLMs compute with a built-in calculator
      - id: chunked
        text: Numbers may be split into irregular chunks, making digit-level arithmetic harder; models are unreliable calculators unless given a tool
        correct: true
    explanation: For exact computation, have the model call code or a calculator.
  - id: special-tokens
    prompt: What are special tokens used for?
    options:
      - id: structure
        text: Marking structure such as the start/end of a message, roles (system, user, assistant) and tool calls in chat templates
        correct: true
      - text: Encrypting prompts
      - text: Counting money
      - text: Formatting Markdown
    explanation: Chat APIs hide templates from you, but they are why you send structured messages rather than raw text.
  - id: vocab
    prompt: Typical modern LLM vocabularies contain how many tokens?
    options:
      - text: About 100
      - text: About 1,000
      - id: tens-of-thousands
        text: Tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand
        correct: true
      - text: Billions
    explanation: Larger vocabularies encode text more efficiently but enlarge the embedding and output layers.
  - id: output-pricing
    prompt: Most APIs price output tokens higher than input tokens. Why?
    options:
      - text: Output tokens are longer
      - id: sequential
        text: Input tokens are processed in parallel; output tokens are generated one at a time, each needing a forward pass, which costs more compute per token
        correct: true
      - text: To discourage questions
      - text: Output tokens are stored forever
    explanation: Asking for concise outputs is one of the simplest cost controls.

## Learning objectives

- Explain tokens and subword tokenisation
- Estimate token counts and costs
- Recognise tasks tokenisation makes hard

## See tokens

```python
import tiktoken
enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")
ids = enc.encode("Unbelievably, Databricks tokenises strawberries.")
print(len(ids), [enc.decode([i]) for i in ids])
```

Different model families use different tokenisers — always count with the target model's tokeniser.

## Cost arithmetic

```text
cost = input_tokens × input_price + output_tokens × output_price
1,000 requests × (1,500 in + 300 out) at $1 / $4 per million tokens
= 1.5M × $1 + 0.3M × $4 = $1.50 + $1.20 = $2.70
```

- Petrov et al., "Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages", 2023 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.15425>

title: Embeddings and attention
questions:
  - id: embedding
    prompt: What is an embedding?
    options:
      - text: An image embedded in a document
      - id: vector
        text: A dense vector of numbers representing meaning, where semantically similar items are close together in the vector space
        correct: true
      - text: A compressed zip file
      - text: A database index on text columns
    explanation: Embedding models power semantic search and RAG; LLMs also use embeddings internally for every token.
  - id: similarity
    prompt: Which measure is most commonly used to compare text embeddings?
    options:
      - text: Edit distance
      - text: File size
      - id: cosine
        text: Cosine similarity (or dot product on normalised vectors)
        correct: true
      - text: Alphabetical order
    explanation: Cosine similarity measures the angle between vectors, ignoring magnitude.
  - id: analogy
    prompt: The famous word2vec example "king − man + woman ≈ queen" illustrates what?
    options:
      - id: directions
        text: Directions in embedding space can encode semantic relationships
        correct: true
      - text: That embeddings are exact
      - text: That models understand monarchy
      - text: That arithmetic on words is always meaningful
    explanation: Such analogies are cherry-picked; they also showed that embeddings absorb societal biases (e.g. gender-occupation associations; Bolukbasi et al., 2016).
  - id: attention
    prompt: What does self-attention do in a transformer?
    options:
      - text: Monitors whether the user is paying attention
      - text: Stores the training data
      - id: weigh
        text: For each token, computes weighted combinations of other tokens' representations, so context (e.g. which noun "it" refers to) shapes each token's meaning
        correct: true
      - text: Translates text to images
    explanation: Queries, keys and values are learned projections; attention weights come from query–key similarity.
  - id: quadratic
    prompt: How does the cost of standard self-attention scale with sequence length n?
    options:
      - text: Constant
      - text: Linear, O(n)
      - id: quadratic
        text: Quadratic, O(n²)
        correct: true
      - text: Logarithmic
    explanation: Engineering (FlashAttention, sparse/linear attention, KV caching) mitigates this, but long context is still costlier.
  - id: decoder-only
    prompt: Most chat LLMs are decoder-only transformers. What does "causal" masking mean there?
    options:
      - text: The model explains causes
      - id: causal
        text: Each position can attend only to earlier positions, so the model learns to predict the next token from what came before
        correct: true
      - text: The model is trained on causal inference
      - text: Tokens are shuffled
    explanation: This is why generation is left-to-right, one token at a time.
  - id: parameters
    prompt: What are a model's parameters?
    options:
      - text: The options passed in an API call
      - text: The training documents
      - text: The number of users
      - id: weights
        text: The learned numeric weights (matrices) of the network, adjusted during training
        correct: true
    explanation: Don't confuse them with generation parameters like temperature, also casually called "parameters".
  - id: embedding-models
    prompt: Why use a dedicated embedding model rather than a chat LLM for semantic search?
    options:
      - id: purpose
        text: Embedding models are trained to produce vectors where similarity reflects relevance, and are far cheaper and faster per document
        correct: true
      - text: Chat LLMs cannot read text
      - text: Embedding models write better answers
      - text: There is no reason
    explanation: Choose embedding models by retrieval benchmarks (such as MTEB) and, more importantly, by tests on your documents.
  - id: model-mismatch
    prompt: You indexed documents with embedding model A, then switch queries to model B. What happens?
    options:
      - text: Search improves automatically
      - text: Nothing changes
      - id: incompatible
        text: Retrieval breaks — vectors from different models live in different spaces, so the whole corpus must be re-embedded with B
        correct: true
      - text: The index converts automatically
    explanation: Record the embedding model and version alongside the index. Plan re-embedding cost when upgrading.
  - id: mixture-of-experts
    prompt: What is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model?
    options:
      - text: A panel of human experts reviewing outputs
      - text: An ensemble of separate chatbots
      - text: A model trained only on expert-written text
      - id: moe
        text: A model where a router activates only a subset of expert sub-networks per token, so total parameters are large but compute per token is lower
        correct: true
    explanation: Many recent large models (e.g. Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3) use MoE. Memory requirements still reflect total parameters.
---
## Learning objectives

- Explain embeddings and similarity
- Describe self-attention and causal masking
- Avoid embedding-model mismatches

## Embeddings in code

```python
import numpy as np

def cosine(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> float:
    return float(a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b)))

q = embed("How do I reset my password?")
d1 = embed("Steps to change your account password")
d2 = embed("Quarterly revenue grew 12%")
print(cosine(q, d1), cosine(q, d2))
```

## Attention, intuitively

In "The trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because **it** was too big", attention lets the
representation of "it" draw mostly on "trophy". Change "big" to "small" and it shifts to
"suitcase". That context-sensitivity is what earlier word embeddings lacked.

- Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need", 2017 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762>
- Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) — <https://huggingface.co/spaces/mteb/leaderboard>
- Jay Alammar, "The Illustrated Transformer" — <https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-transformer/>

title: Pretraining, fine-tuning and alignment
questions:
  - id: pretraining-objective
    prompt: What is the pretraining objective of a GPT-style LLM?
    options:
      - text: Answer questions correctly
      - text: Classify sentiment
      - id: next-token
        text: Predict the next token across enormous amounts of text (self-supervised learning)
        correct: true
      - text: Follow instructions
    explanation: Everything else — knowledge, grammar, some reasoning — emerges as useful for predicting text.
  - id: base-vs-instruct
    prompt: What is the difference between a base model and an instruction-tuned model?
    options:
      - id: base-continues
        text: A base model continues text; an instruction-tuned model has been further trained to follow instructions and behave as an assistant
        correct: true
      - text: Base models are larger
      - text: Instruction models cannot generate text
      - text: There is no difference
    explanation: Ask a base model "What is the capital of France?" and it may continue with more quiz questions.
  - id: sft
    prompt: What is supervised fine-tuning (SFT)?
    options:
      - text: Training without data
      - text: Training by a supervisor watching the GPU
      - text: Pruning weights
      - id: sft
        text: Further training on curated input–output examples (such as instruction–response pairs) so the model imitates desired behaviour
        correct: true
    explanation: Quality beats quantity — small, high-quality SFT datasets can change behaviour substantially.
  - id: rlhf
    prompt: How does reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) work at a high level?
    options:
      - text: Humans rewrite the model's weights by hand
      - id: rlhf
        text: Humans rank model outputs; a reward model learns those preferences; the LLM is optimised (e.g. with PPO) to produce outputs the reward model scores highly
        correct: true
      - text: The model reads human feedback forms at runtime
      - text: Users click thumbs up to retrain the model instantly
    explanation: Described in OpenAI's InstructGPT paper (Ouyang et al., 2022). A 1.3B InstructGPT was preferred by labellers over 175B GPT-3.
  - id: dpo
    prompt: What does Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) change compared with classic RLHF?
    options:
      - text: It removes the need for preference data
      - text: It requires more human labellers
      - id: no-reward-model
        text: It optimises the model directly on preference pairs without training a separate reward model or running RL, which is simpler and more stable
        correct: true
      - text: It only works for images
    explanation: Rafailov et al., 2023. Many open models use DPO or related methods.
  - id: sycophancy
    prompt: Which side effect is linked to optimising for human approval?
    options:
      - text: Faster inference
      - text: Smaller models
      - id: syco
        text: Sycophancy — telling users what they want to hear, agreeing with mistaken premises, or flattering
        correct: true
      - text: Better arithmetic
    explanation: Anthropic researchers documented sycophancy across RLHF-trained assistants (Sharma et al., 2023). Ask models to critique, and phrase questions neutrally.
  - id: rlvr
    prompt: What is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards?
    options:
      - id: verifiable
        text: RL where rewards come from automatically checkable outcomes — unit tests passing, maths answers matching — rather than human preference; central to training reasoning models
        correct: true
      - text: RL verified by lawyers
      - text: A blockchain technique
      - text: Training on verified Twitter accounts
    explanation: It works best where correctness is checkable, which is one reason reasoning models improved fastest at maths and code.
  - id: data-sources
    prompt: Which statements about pretraining data are accurate?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: web
        text: Much of it is filtered web crawl (e.g. derived from Common Crawl), plus code, books and papers
        correct: true
      - id: undisclosed
        text: Frontier labs rarely disclose their exact training data
        correct: true
      - id: litigation
        text: Use of copyrighted material in training is the subject of ongoing lawsuits
        correct: true
      - text: All training data is licensed and public domain
    explanation: The legal landscape is unsettled and varies by jurisdiction; see the governance chapter.
  - id: cutoff
    prompt: What is a model's knowledge cut-off?
    options:
      - text: The maximum answer length
      - text: The date the model is retired
      - id: cutoff
        text: The approximate date after which events are not represented in its training data
        correct: true
      - text: The maximum context length
    explanation: Models also struggle near the cut-off because recent events are sparsely represented. Use retrieval or search for current facts.
  - id: cost-pretraining
    prompt: Why do almost no enterprises pretrain their own LLMs?
    options:
      - text: It is illegal
      - text: It requires no data
      - text: It is trivial and not worth mentioning
      - id: cost
        text: Pretraining competitive models costs tens to hundreds of millions of dollars in compute, data and expertise; adapting existing models is far cheaper
        correct: true
    explanation: Databricks' own DBRX (2024) is a reminder — a capable model was overtaken within months and later retired.
---
## Learning objectives

- Describe pretraining, SFT and preference optimisation
- Understand side effects of alignment such as sycophancy
- Know why enterprises adapt rather than pretrain

## The pipeline

```text
Raw text (trillions of tokens) ──pretraining──► Base model (predicts text)
        curated instructions ──SFT──────────► Instruction-tuned model
     human / AI preferences ──RLHF / DPO───► Aligned assistant
     verifiable tasks (code, maths) ──RL───► Reasoning model
```

## Why this matters to users

- A model's "personality" — helpful, cautious, verbose, agreeable — is trained behaviour.
- Agreeableness can become sycophancy: prefer neutral questions ("evaluate this plan") over
  leading ones ("this plan is great, right?").
- Knowledge is frozen at the cut-off; behaviour can change silently when the provider updates the model.

## Sources

- Ouyang et al., "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback", 2022 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155>
- Rafailov et al., "Direct Preference Optimization", 2023 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290>
- Sharma et al., "Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models", 2023 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548>
- DeepSeek-AI, "DeepSeek-R1", 2025 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948>

---
title: Generation and decoding
questions:
  - id: autoregressive
    prompt: How does an LLM produce a response?
    options:
      - text: It retrieves a stored answer from a database
      - text: It writes the whole response at once
      - id: one-token
        text: It repeatedly computes a probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next token, picks one, appends it, and repeats until a stop condition
        correct: true
      - text: It searches the internet
    explanation: This autoregressive loop is why responses stream token by token.
  - id: temperature
    prompt: What does the temperature parameter control?
    options:
      - text: GPU temperature
      - id: randomness
        text: How peaked or flat the next-token distribution is before sampling — low temperature favours the most likely tokens, high temperature increases variety
        correct: true
      - text: The length of output
      - text: The model's knowledge
    explanation: Low temperature for extraction and classification; higher for brainstorming. Temperature 0 reduces but does not always eliminate variation.
  - id: top-p
    prompt: What is top-p (nucleus) sampling?
    options:
      - text: Choosing the top p percent of users
      - text: Picking the first p tokens of the prompt
      - id: nucleus
        text: Sampling only from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p (e.g. 0.9)
        correct: true
      - text: A pricing tier
    explanation: Top-k limits to the k most likely tokens. Providers generally advise tuning temperature or top-p, not both.
  - id: greedy
    prompt: What is greedy decoding?
    options:
      - id: argmax
        text: Always choosing the single most probable next token
        correct: true
      - text: Generating as many tokens as possible
      - text: Charging more per token
      - text: Sampling at random
    explanation: Greedy decoding can produce repetitive text and is not guaranteed to find the most probable overall sequence.
  - id: nondeterminism
    prompt: Why can the same prompt at temperature 0 sometimes produce different outputs via an API?
    options:
      - text: Temperature 0 means random
      - id: infra
        text: Floating-point non-associativity, batching with other requests, hardware differences and silent model updates can change results
        correct: true
      - text: The model learns from each request
      - text: It cannot; outputs are always identical
    explanation: Design systems to tolerate variation, and pin model versions where providers allow.
  - id: context-window
    prompt: What is the context window?
    options:
      - text: The UI window where you type
      - text: The training data size
      - text: The number of users at once
      - id: max-tokens
        text: The maximum number of tokens (input plus output) the model can consider in one request
        correct: true
    explanation: Windows grew from about 2K tokens (GPT-3) to hundreds of thousands or millions. Bigger is not automatically better — see "lost in the middle".
  - id: stateless
    prompt: Does a chat model remember previous conversations by itself?
    options:
      - text: Yes, it learns from every chat
      - id: stateless
        text: No — each API call is stateless; the application resends conversation history (or uses a memory feature) each turn
        correct: true
      - text: Only on weekends
      - text: Only if temperature is 0
    explanation: Long chats cost more because the history is re-sent, and old turns get truncated or summarised.
  - id: kv-cache
    prompt: What is the KV cache?
    options:
      - text: A key-value database for prompts
      - text: A cache of user passwords
      - id: kv
        text: Stored attention keys and values for already-processed tokens, so each new token does not recompute the whole prefix
        correct: true
      - text: A CDN for model weights
    explanation: Prompt caching by providers reuses prefixes across requests, cutting cost and latency for repeated system prompts.
  - id: latency-metrics
    prompt: Which latency metrics matter for LLM applications?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: ttft
        text: Time to first token
        correct: true
      - id: tps
        text: Output tokens per second
        correct: true
      - id: e2e
        text: End-to-end latency including retrieval and tool calls
        correct: true
      - text: Number of parameters
    explanation: Streaming improves perceived latency by showing tokens as they arrive.
  - id: max-tokens
    prompt: A response is cut off mid-sentence and the finish reason is "length". What happened?
    options:
      - text: The model crashed
      - text: The user's network failed
      - text: The model chose to stop
      - id: limit
        text: The output hit the max-tokens limit set in the request (or the context limit)
        correct: true
    explanation: Check finish reasons in code; a truncated JSON response will not parse.
  - id: quantization
    prompt: What does quantisation do to a model?
    options:
      - id: lower-precision
        text: Stores weights at lower precision (e.g. 8- or 4-bit) to reduce memory and speed inference, usually with some quality loss
        correct: true
      - text: Increases the number of parameters
      - text: Adds quantum computing
      - text: Encrypts the weights
    explanation: Quantisation is how large open models run on smaller GPUs or laptops. Measure quality on your task.
---
## Learning objectives

- Explain autoregressive generation
- Use temperature, top-p and max tokens deliberately
- Understand context windows, statelessness and latency

## Decoding parameters

| Parameter | Low value | High value | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| temperature | Focused, repeatable | Varied, creative | 0–0.3 extraction; 0.7–1 ideation |
| top_p | Few candidate tokens | Many | Leave at default unless needed |
| max_tokens | Short, truncation risk | Long, costly | Set per task |

```python
response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model=model,
    temperature=0.1,
    max_tokens=300,
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "Extract the invoice number and total as JSON."},
        {"role": "user", "content": invoice_text},
    ],
)
```

title: Hallucination
questions:
  - id: definition
    prompt: What is a hallucination in LLM terms?
    options:
      - text: A visual glitch in image models only
      - id: def
        text: Fluent, confident output that is false or unsupported by the provided sources
        correct: true
      - text: Any creative writing
      - text: A model refusing to answer
    explanation: Some researchers prefer "confabulation". Either way, plausibility is not truth.
  - id: why
    prompt: Why do LLMs hallucinate?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: objective
        text: They are trained to produce probable text, not verified facts
        correct: true
      - id: incentive
        text: Training and benchmarks often reward guessing over saying "I don't know"
        correct: true
      - id: gaps
        text: Rare facts are poorly represented in training data
        correct: true
      - text: They are deliberately programmed to lie
    explanation: OpenAI's 2025 paper "Why Language Models Hallucinate" argues evaluation that penalises abstention encourages confident guessing.
  - id: avianca
    prompt: In Mata v. Avianca (2023), what happened?
    options:
      - text: An airline's chatbot sold free tickets
      - text: A model leaked passenger data
      - id: fake-cases
        text: Lawyers filed a brief citing non-existent court cases invented by ChatGPT, and were sanctioned
        correct: true
      - text: A court banned AI
    explanation: Hundreds of similar incidents have been documented since. Verification is the user's responsibility.
  - id: air-canada
    prompt: In Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024), what did the tribunal decide about the airline's chatbot?
    options:
      - text: The chatbot was a separate legal entity, so the airline was not liable
      - id: liable
        text: The airline was responsible for its chatbot's incorrect statement about bereavement fares and had to compensate the customer
        correct: true
      - text: Chatbots cannot make statements
      - text: The customer should have known better
    explanation: Organisations own what their AI tells customers.
  - id: mitigations
    prompt: Which techniques reduce hallucination?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: grounding
        text: Grounding answers in retrieved sources and requiring citations
        correct: true
      - id: abstain
        text: Instructing and allowing the model to say it does not know
        correct: true
      - id: tools
        text: Using tools (search, calculators, databases) for facts and computation
        correct: true
      - id: verify
        text: Automated groundedness checks and human review for high-stakes outputs
        correct: true
    explanation: None eliminates hallucination; combined, they reduce it to manageable rates for many uses.
  - id: rag-not-cure
    prompt: Does RAG eliminate hallucinations?
    options:
      - text: Yes, completely
      - text: No, it makes them worse in all cases
      - text: Only for images
      - id: reduces
        text: No — it reduces them, but models can still misread, over-generalise or ignore retrieved context, and bad retrieval feeds wrong context
        correct: true
    explanation: Stanford researchers found legal research tools marketed as "hallucination-free" still hallucinated in 17–33% of queries (Magesh et al., 2024).
  - id: citations-fake
    prompt: A model's answer includes a citation. What should you assume?
    options:
      - id: verify
        text: The citation might be fabricated or not support the claim; check that the source exists and says what is claimed
        correct: true
      - text: It is correct, because models cannot invent citations
      - text: Citations prove the answer
      - text: Only URLs can be fake
    explanation: In RAG systems, constrain citations to IDs of retrieved chunks so they can be validated mechanically.
  - id: confidence
    prompt: Is a model's stated confidence ("I am certain") reliable?
    options:
      - text: Yes, models know when they are right
      - id: not-calibrated
        text: Not reliably — verbal confidence is poorly calibrated, especially after alignment training
        correct: true
      - text: Only at temperature 0
      - text: Only for maths
    explanation: Use external verification, not the model's self-assessment, for important claims.
  - id: summary-halluc
    prompt: Can a model hallucinate when summarising a document you provide?
    options:
      - text: No, because the source is in the prompt
      - text: Only if the document is in another language
      - id: can-hallucinate
        text: Yes — adding details not in the document, merging facts, or inverting a negation are documented failure modes
        correct: true
      - text: Only for documents over 1 million tokens
    explanation: Vectara's hallucination leaderboard measures exactly this; rates differ substantially between models.
---
## Learning objectives

- Define hallucination and explain its causes
- Learn from real cases
- Apply layered mitigations

## Defence in depth

```text
Question
  │
  ├─ retrieve authoritative sources ─► ground the answer, cite chunk IDs
  ├─ use tools for facts & maths
  ├─ allow "I don't know"
  ├─ check groundedness automatically (LLM judge or NLI model)
  └─ human review where errors are costly
```

- Kalai et al. (OpenAI), "Why Language Models Hallucinate", 2025 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04664>
- Mata v. Avianca, Inc., S.D.N.Y. 2023 — <https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/new-york/nysdce/1:2022cv01461/575368/54/>
- Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149 — <https://www.canlii.org/en/bc/bccrt/doc/2024/2024bccrt149/2024bccrt149.html>
- Magesh et al., "Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools", 2024 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.20362>
- Vectara hallucination leaderboard — <https://github.com/vectara/hallucination-leaderboard>

---
title: Bias, context and reasoning limits
questions:
  - id: bias-source
    prompt: Where does bias in LLM outputs come from?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: data
        text: Patterns in training data reflecting societal biases and over-representation of some languages and cultures
        correct: true
      - id: labelling
        text: Choices made by annotators and alignment processes
        correct: true
      - id: deployment
        text: How the model is prompted and deployed, including which users it serves
        correct: true
      - text: Nowhere; models are neutral by construction
    explanation: Bias testing on your use case — for example comparing outputs across demographic variations — is part of responsible deployment.
  - id: lost-middle
    prompt: What did the "Lost in the Middle" study find?
    options:
      - text: Models forget the beginning of long prompts
      - id: middle
        text: Models used information at the beginning and end of long contexts better than information in the middle
        correct: true
      - text: Models perform equally across positions
      - text: Long context always improves accuracy
    explanation: Liu et al., 2023. Newer models improved, but "context rot" — degradation as inputs grow — is still observed. Put key instructions and evidence where they count and keep context lean.
  - id: needle
    prompt: Why is a "needle in a haystack" score a weak measure of long-context ability?
    options:
      - text: It is too hard
      - text: It uses images
      - id: easy
        text: Finding one verbatim sentence is much easier than reasoning across many scattered facts; models that ace it can still fail realistic long-context tasks
        correct: true
      - text: It measures cost, not quality
    explanation: Benchmarks like RULER and multi-hop tests show larger drops than simple retrieval.
  - id: reasoning
    prompt: Which statement about LLM reasoning is best supported by evidence?
    options:
      - text: LLMs never reason
      - text: LLMs reason exactly like humans
      - id: brittle
        text: LLMs can solve many multi-step problems, but performance can be brittle — sensitive to irrelevant details or rephrasing — suggesting partial reliance on pattern matching
        correct: true
      - text: Reasoning ability is fixed and cannot improve
    explanation: Apple's GSM-Symbolic study (Mirzadeh et al., 2024) showed drops when numbers or irrelevant clauses changed. Reasoning models narrowed but did not close such gaps.
  - id: cot-faithful
    prompt: Does a model's displayed chain of thought faithfully show how it reached its answer?
    options:
      - text: Yes, always
      - id: not-always
        text: Not necessarily — research shows stated reasoning can omit factors that actually influenced the answer
        correct: true
      - text: Chains of thought are random text
      - text: Only for small models
    explanation: Anthropic (2025) found reasoning models often did not mention hints they used. Treat reasoning text as helpful but not as an audit log.
  - id: drift
    prompt: Your prompt worked last month but quality dropped this week without code changes. What is a plausible cause?
    options:
      - text: Prompts expire
      - text: The internet changed
      - text: Tokens wore out
      - id: model-update
        text: The provider updated the model behind an alias; behaviour of the "same" model can drift over time
        correct: true
    explanation: Chen, Zaharia and Zou (2023) documented GPT-4 behaviour changes over months. Pin versions and run regression evaluations.
  - id: math
    prompt: What is the most reliable way to get exact arithmetic from an LLM application?
    options:
      - text: Ask the model to double-check
      - text: Use a larger model
      - text: Set temperature to 0
      - id: tool
        text: Have the model call a code interpreter or calculator and use the tool's result
        correct: true
    explanation: Tools convert a probabilistic problem into a deterministic one.
  - id: injection-link
    prompt: Why can't an LLM reliably tell instructions from data in its context?
    options:
      - id: one-stream
        text: Everything — system prompt, user input, retrieved documents — is one token sequence; there is no hard boundary separating "code" from "data"
        correct: true
      - text: It can, perfectly
      - text: Because of temperature
      - text: Because it is stateless
    explanation: This is the root of prompt injection, covered in the next chapter.
  - id: anthropomorphism
    prompt: Why is anthropomorphising chatbots risky?
    options:
      - text: It is not risky
      - id: overtrust
        text: Human-like language encourages over-trust, emotional reliance and attributing understanding or intent that may not be there
        correct: true
      - text: It makes models slower
      - text: It violates copyright
    explanation: The "ELIZA effect" was observed in 1966 with a far simpler program.
---
## Learning objectives

- Recognise sources of bias
- Understand long-context degradation
- Know what research says about LLM reasoning and its faithfulness

## Practical rules

- Keep prompts focused; more context is not always better
- Put critical instructions at the start (and repeat key constraints at the end for long inputs)
- Use tools for computation and lookups
- Pin model versions and run regression evaluations on every change
- Test outputs across demographic and linguistic variations

## Sources

- Liu et al., "Lost in the Middle", 2023 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172>
- Hsieh et al., "RULER: What's the Real Context Size of Your Long-Context Language Models?", 2024 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654>
- Mirzadeh et al., "GSM-Symbolic", 2024 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.05229>
- Anthropic, "Reasoning models don't always say what they think", 2025 — <https://www.anthropic.com/research/reasoning-models-dont-say-think>
- Chen, Zaharia, Zou, "How Is ChatGPT's Behavior Changing over Time?", 2023 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09009>
- Chroma, "Context Rot", 2025 — <https://research.trychroma.com/context-rot>
