title: Type 2 diabetes
questions:
  - id: dpp
    prompt: In the Diabetes Prevention Program (2002), intensive lifestyle change aiming for 7% weight loss and 150 minutes of activity weekly reduced progression to type 2 diabetes by how much?
    options:
      - text: 5%
      - id: fifty-eight
        text: 58%, compared with 31% for metformin
        correct: true
      - text: 100%
    explanation: Similar results came from the Finnish Diabetes Prevention Study. Benefits partly persisted over 15+ years of follow-up.
  - id: direct
    prompt: What did the DiRECT trial in UK primary care show?
    options:
      - id: remission
        text: A total diet replacement programme followed by food reintroduction led to diabetes remission in 46% of participants at one year, and in 86% of those who lost at least 15 kg
        correct: true
      - text: Diet has no effect on type 2 diabetes
      - text: Type 2 diabetes was cured permanently in everyone
    explanation: Remission (normal glucose without medication) declined over five years as weight was regained, but remained much higher than control. Remission is most likely early in the disease.
  - id: type1
    prompt: Can diet cure type 1 diabetes?
    options:
      - text: Yes, with a raw vegan diet
      - text: Yes, with cinnamon
      - id: no-cure
        text: No — type 1 diabetes is autoimmune destruction of insulin-producing cells; people with it require insulin, and stopping insulin can be fatal
        correct: true
    explanation: Children have died when parents replaced insulin with diet or faith-based "cures". Diet helps manage type 1 diabetes alongside insulin.
  - id: sugar-cause
    prompt: Does eating sugar directly cause type 2 diabetes?
    options:
      - text: Yes, sugar is the only cause
      - id: indirect
        text: Not directly as a single cause; excess weight and visceral fat are the main drivers, though sugary drinks are linked to higher risk beyond their effect on weight
        correct: true
      - text: Sugar prevents diabetes
    explanation: Genetics, age, physical inactivity, and ethnic background all influence risk. South Asian, Black and Hispanic populations develop type 2 diabetes at lower BMIs on average.
  - id: cinnamon
    prompt: What is the evidence grade for cinnamon, bitter melon or apple cider vinegar as treatments for diabetes?
    options:
      - text: Established — they can replace medication
      - id: uncertain-small
        text: Uncertain — small, inconsistent effects on glucose; they cannot replace medication
        correct: true
    explanation: Cassia cinnamon in large amounts contains coumarin, which can harm the liver.
  - id: risk-foods
    prompt: Which dietary factors are associated with lower type 2 diabetes risk?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Whole grains and cereal fibre
        correct: true
      - text: Coffee
        correct: true
      - text: Yoghurt
        correct: true
      - text: Processed meat
      - text: Sugar-sweetened beverages
    explanation: Processed meat and sugary drinks are associated with higher risk. All of these are cohort associations of varying strength.
  - id: look-ahead
    prompt: The Look AHEAD trial of intensive lifestyle intervention in type 2 diabetes was stopped for futility. Why?
    options:
      - id: no-cv
        text: Despite weight loss and other benefits, it did not reduce cardiovascular events after about 10 years
        correct: true
      - text: Nobody lost weight
      - text: The intervention killed participants
    explanation: Participants did gain other benefits (less depression, better mobility, reduced need for medication). The usual-care group also received good medical care, which narrowed differences.
---
## Learning objectives

- Distinguish type 1 and type 2 diabetes
- Know the prevention and remission trials
- Recognise unsupported "cures"

## Prevention and remission

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Lifestyle intervention prevents or delays type 2 diabetes in high-risk adults | **Established** |
| Substantial weight loss can put early type 2 diabetes into remission | **Established** (DiRECT, bariatric surgery) |
| GLP-1 drugs and tirzepatide lower glucose and weight markedly | **Established** |
| Low-carbohydrate diets lower HbA1c in the short term | **Strong** |
| Any specific spice or supplement cures diabetes | **Not supported** |
| Diet can replace insulin in type 1 diabetes | **Not supported** — and dangerous |

## Sources

- Knowler WC et al. Reduction in the incidence of type 2 diabetes with lifestyle intervention or metformin (DPP). *NEJM* 2002. [doi:10.1056/NEJMoa012512](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa012512)
- Lean MEJ et al. Primary care-led weight management for remission of type 2 diabetes (DiRECT). *Lancet* 2018. [doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(17)33102-1](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(17)33102-1)
- Look AHEAD Research Group. Cardiovascular effects of intensive lifestyle intervention in type 2 diabetes. *NEJM* 2013. [doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1212914](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1212914)
- Tuomilehto J et al. Prevention of type 2 diabetes mellitus by changes in lifestyle (Finnish DPS). *NEJM* 2001.
- American Diabetes Association. Standards of Care in Diabetes. Updated annually.

title: Diet and cancer
questions:
  - id: obesity-cancers
    prompt: Excess body fatness is a cause of how many cancer types according to IARC's 2016 review?
    options:
      - text: None
      - id: thirteen
        text: At least 13, including oesophageal adenocarcinoma, colorectal, post-menopausal breast, endometrial, kidney, liver and pancreatic cancer
        correct: true
      - text: Only skin cancer
    explanation: After tobacco, excess weight and alcohol are among the largest modifiable causes of cancer in high-income countries.
  - id: established-causes
    prompt: Which dietary exposures are **Established** causes of human cancer?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Alcohol
        correct: true
      - text: Processed meat
        correct: true
      - text: Aflatoxin-contaminated foods (liver cancer)
        correct: true
      - text: Chinese-style salted fish (nasopharyngeal cancer)
        correct: true
      - text: Microwaved food
    explanation: Microwaving heats food by agitating water molecules. It does not make food radioactive or carcinogenic.
  - id: cure
    prompt: Can any diet cure established cancer?
    options:
      - text: Yes, alkaline diets cure cancer
      - text: Yes, juice fasting cures cancer
      - id: no-diet-cure
        text: No diet has been shown to cure cancer; people who choose alternative medicine instead of conventional treatment have substantially higher death rates
        correct: true
    explanation: A 2018 study in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute found that patients using alternative medicine alone had about 2.5 times the risk of death compared with conventional treatment. Nutrition support during treatment is important, but it does not replace treatment.
  - id: prevents
    prompt: Which factor has the strongest evidence of lowering colorectal cancer risk?
    options:
      - id: fibre-wholegrain
        text: Higher intake of fibre and whole grains, plus physical activity
        correct: true
      - text: Coffee enemas
      - text: Avoiding all cooked food
    explanation: WCRF rates whole grains and fibre as "probable" and physical activity as "convincing" protectors against colon cancer.
  - id: superfood-cancer
    prompt: Headlines often say a single food (turmeric, broccoli, blueberries) "fights cancer". What is the usual basis?
    options:
      - id: lab
        text: Cell or animal studies, or single cohort associations, not trials showing people eating the food get less cancer
        correct: true
      - text: Large RCTs in humans
      - text: Nobel Prize-winning discoveries
    explanation: Curcumin, for example, is poorly absorbed and has repeatedly been flagged as a "pan-assay interference compound" that gives false positives in lab assays.
  - id: wcrf
    prompt: Which recommendations are part of the World Cancer Research Fund's cancer prevention guidance?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Be a healthy weight and be physically active
        correct: true
      - text: Limit red meat and eat little, if any, processed meat
        correct: true
      - text: Limit alcohol; for cancer prevention, it is best not to drink
        correct: true
      - text: Do not use supplements for cancer prevention
        correct: true
      - text: Breastfeed if you can
        correct: true
    explanation: The WCRF recommendations are based on systematic, continuously updated reviews. All five statements are part of the guidance.
  - id: charred
    prompt: Do high-temperature cooking methods such as charring meat produce potential carcinogens?
    options:
      - id: yes-uncertain
        text: Yes — heterocyclic amines and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons form, and they are carcinogenic in animals; the size of the human risk at normal intakes is uncertain
        correct: true
      - text: No chemicals are formed
      - text: Charred meat is proven to prevent cancer
    explanation: A reasonable precaution is to avoid heavy charring. The evidence on human cancer from cooking methods is **Uncertain**.
---
## Learning objectives

- Rank dietary factors in cancer by strength of evidence
- Reject cancer-cure diets
- Understand why single-food claims mislead

## Estimated scale

In the UK, Cancer Research UK estimates about 4 in 10 cancer cases are preventable, with smoking first and
excess weight second. Alcohol, low fibre and processed meat each contribute a few percent.

## Evidence summary (WCRF/AICR and IARC)

| Exposure | Cancer | Grade |
|----------|--------|-------|
| Alcohol | Mouth, throat, oesophagus, liver, breast, colorectum | **Established** |
| Excess body fat | 13+ sites | **Established** |
| Processed meat | Colorectal | **Established** (Group 1) |
| Red meat | Colorectal | **Strong** (probable) |
| Aflatoxins | Liver | **Established** |
| Salt-preserved foods | Stomach | **Strong** |
| Whole grains, fibre | Colorectal (protective) | **Strong** (probable) |
| Dairy and calcium | Colorectal (protective) | **Strong** (probable) |
| Physical activity | Colon, breast, endometrium (protective) | **Established** to **Strong** |
| Very hot drinks above 65 °C | Oesophagus | **Strong** (IARC 2A) |
| Sugar "feeds" cancer | — | **Not supported** as a direct mechanism |
| Alkaline diet, juice fasts, apricot kernels (laetrile), coffee enemas | Cure | **Not supported**; laetrile can cause cyanide poisoning |

## Sources

- World Cancer Research Fund / AICR. *Diet, Nutrition, Physical Activity and Cancer: a Global Perspective.* Third Expert Report, 2018.
- Lauby-Secretan B et al. Body fatness and cancer — viewpoint of the IARC Working Group. *NEJM* 2016.
- Johnson SB et al. Use of alternative medicine for cancer and its impact on survival. *J Natl Cancer Inst* 2018.
- Nelson KM et al. The essential medicinal chemistry of curcumin. *J Med Chem* 2017.
- Brown KF et al. The fraction of cancer attributable to modifiable risk factors in the UK. *Br J Cancer* 2018.

---
title: The gut microbiome
questions:
  - id: established-microbiome
    prompt: Which microbiome-based treatment is **Established** by RCTs?
    options:
      - id: fmt
        text: Faecal microbiota transplantation for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection
        correct: true
      - text: Probiotics to cure autism
      - text: Kombucha to cure depression
    explanation: FMT cures a large majority of recurrent C. difficile infections — the clearest proof that the gut microbiome matters. Most other microbiome claims are early-stage.
  - id: probiotics-aad
    prompt: For which use do probiotics have the most consistent evidence?
    options:
      - id: aad
        text: Reducing antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (moderate certainty)
        correct: true
      - text: Weight loss in healthy adults
      - text: Preventing all infections
    explanation: Effects depend on the strain and dose; "probiotic" is not one thing. A 2018 study found that probiotics after antibiotics delayed the return of a person's normal microbiome compared with no treatment.
  - id: association
    prompt: Many studies show people with a disease have a different microbiome. What is the key limitation?
    options:
      - id: direction
        text: Differences may be a consequence of the disease, its treatment or diet, rather than a cause
        correct: true
      - text: The microbiome cannot be measured
      - text: Bacteria do not live in the gut
    explanation: Reverse causation applies here too. Causality requires interventions that change the microbiome and then change the outcome.
  - id: fibre-feeds
    prompt: What do gut bacteria produce when they ferment dietary fibre?
    options:
      - id: scfa
        text: Short-chain fatty acids such as butyrate, acetate and propionate
        correct: true
      - text: Vitamin C
      - text: Ethanol in dangerous amounts in everyone
    explanation: Butyrate is the main fuel for colon cells. This is one plausible mechanism for fibre's benefits.
  - id: tests
    prompt: What is the evidence grade for direct-to-consumer microbiome tests that recommend personalised diets?
    options:
      - text: Established
      - id: uncertain
        text: Uncertain at best — there is no agreed definition of a "healthy" microbiome, and test results vary between companies
        correct: true
      - text: Strong
    explanation: Research on personalised glucose responses (for example the Weizmann and PREDICT studies) is interesting, but consumer tests are ahead of the evidence.
  - id: leaky-gut
    prompt: Which statement about "leaky gut syndrome" is accurate?
    options:
      - text: It is a well-defined disease with a standard diagnostic test
      - id: not-diagnosis
        text: Increased intestinal permeability is a real, measurable phenomenon in some diseases, but "leaky gut syndrome" as a cause of a wide range of symptoms is not an established diagnosis
        correct: true
      - text: Intestinal permeability does not exist
    explanation: Products sold to "heal the leaky gut" generally lack trial evidence.
  - id: fermented
    prompt: In a 2021 Stanford trial, a diet high in fermented foods for 10 weeks compared with a high-fibre diet did what?
    options:
      - id: diversity
        text: Increased microbiome diversity and reduced several inflammatory markers
        correct: true
      - text: Caused weight gain of 10 kg
      - text: Had no measurable effect on anything
    explanation: It was a small (36 people) study. Interesting and plausible, but clinical outcomes were not measured. Grade - **Uncertain**.
---
## Learning objectives

- Separate established microbiome science from hype
- Understand the limitations of association studies
- Evaluate probiotic claims

## What is known

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Gut bacteria ferment fibre into short-chain fatty acids | **Established** |
| FMT cures recurrent C. difficile infection | **Established** |
| Antibiotics disrupt the microbiome | **Established** |
| Probiotics reduce antibiotic-associated diarrhoea | **Strong** (strain-dependent) |
| Microbiome differences cause obesity in humans | **Uncertain** |
| Fermented foods improve health outcomes | **Uncertain** |
| Probiotic supplements benefit healthy people | **Uncertain** |
| Consumer microbiome tests guide better diets | **Uncertain** to **Not supported** |
| Detox colon cleanses improve the microbiome | **Not supported** |

## Sources

- van Nood E et al. Duodenal infusion of donor feces for recurrent Clostridium difficile. *NEJM* 2013.
- Goldenberg JZ et al. Probiotics for the prevention of Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea. *Cochrane Database Syst Rev* 2017.
- Suez J et al. Post-antibiotic gut mucosal microbiome reconstitution is impaired by probiotics and improved by autologous FMT. *Cell* 2018.
- Wastyk HC et al. Gut-microbiota-targeted diets modulate human immune status. *Cell* 2021.
- Zeevi D et al. Personalized nutrition by prediction of glycemic responses. *Cell* 2015.

title: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and infancy
questions:
  - id: folic
    prompt: The 1991 MRC Vitamin Study found that folic acid supplementation before conception and in early pregnancy reduced recurrence of neural tube defects by about how much?
    options:
      - text: 5%
      - id: seventy-two
        text: 72%
        correct: true
      - text: 0%
    explanation: Neural tube closure happens around four weeks after conception, often before a pregnancy is known — which is why the advice applies to anyone who could become pregnant. Mandatory fortification of flour has reduced neural tube defects in over 80 countries.
  - id: avoid
    prompt: Which should be avoided during pregnancy?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Alcohol
        correct: true
      - text: Unpasteurised milk and soft cheeses made from it
        correct: true
      - text: High-mercury fish such as shark, swordfish, king mackerel and bigeye tuna
        correct: true
      - text: High-dose preformed vitamin A supplements and large amounts of liver
        correct: true
      - text: All fish
    explanation: Low-mercury fish such as salmon, sardines and cod are recommended 2–3 times weekly for omega-3 and other nutrients. Pregnant women are about 10 times more likely than the general population to get listeriosis (CDC).
  - id: weight-gain
    prompt: Is "eating for two" good advice?
    options:
      - text: Yes, energy needs double
      - id: modest
        text: No — extra energy needs are modest, about 340 kcal/day in the second trimester and 450 kcal/day in the third, with none extra in the first
        correct: true
    explanation: Recommended weight gain depends on pre-pregnancy BMI (US National Academies 2009). Nutrient needs (folate, iron, iodine) rise more than energy needs.
  - id: breastfeeding
    prompt: What does the WHO recommend for infant feeding?
    options:
      - id: exclusive-six
        text: Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, then continued breastfeeding with complementary foods up to two years or beyond
        correct: true
      - text: Cow's milk from birth
      - text: Solid food from one month
    explanation: Benefits for infections in infancy are **Established**; some long-term benefits seen in cohorts (IQ, obesity) are smaller in sibling and RCT analyses (PROBIT) and remain **Uncertain** in size. Infant formula is a safe, nutritionally complete alternative when breastfeeding is not possible.
  - id: leap
    prompt: What did the LEAP trial (2015) show about peanut introduction in high-risk infants?
    options:
      - text: Early peanut exposure caused more allergy
      - id: early-reduces
        text: Introducing peanut early (from 4–11 months) reduced peanut allergy by about 81% compared with avoidance
        correct: true
      - text: Peanuts should be avoided until age 10
    explanation: This reversed earlier avoidance advice — a good example of science updating guidance based on an RCT. Guidelines now recommend introducing allergenic foods early.
  - id: honey-infant
    prompt: Why must honey not be given to infants under 12 months?
    options:
      - id: botulism
        text: It can contain Clostridium botulinum spores, which can cause infant botulism
        correct: true
      - text: It causes diabetes
      - text: It contains gluten
    explanation: Older children and adults have mature gut flora that prevent the spores from colonising the gut.
  - id: cows-milk
    prompt: Why is cow's milk not recommended as a main drink before 12 months?
    options:
      - id: iron-kidney
        text: It is low in iron, can cause intestinal blood loss in young infants, and has a high protein and mineral load for immature kidneys
        correct: true
      - text: It is toxic at any age
      - text: Babies cannot taste it
    explanation: Small amounts in cooking are fine after about six months.
  - id: plant-milk-infant
    prompt: Are rice, almond or oat drinks suitable replacements for breast milk or infant formula?
    options:
      - text: Yes, they are healthier
      - id: dangerous
        text: No — they are nutritionally inadequate for infants, and their use has caused severe malnutrition and deaths
        correct: true
    explanation: Rice drinks are also not recommended for children under about five years in the UK because of arsenic content.
---
## Learning objectives

- Know the critical nutrients and hazards in pregnancy
- Understand infant feeding evidence
- Recognise how early-allergen guidance changed

## Pregnancy essentials

| Nutrient or practice | Recommendation | Grade |
|----------------------|----------------|-------|
| Folic acid | 400 µg/day from before conception through week 12 (higher doses for some) | **Established** |
| Iodine | 220 µg/day; many guidelines suggest a 150 µg supplement | **Strong** |
| Iron | 27 mg/day RDA; supplement if deficient | **Established** |
| Vitamin D | 10 µg (400 IU) daily in UK guidance | **Strong** |
| Alcohol | None | **Established** (harm), precautionary (low dose) |
| Caffeine | Below 200 mg/day | **Strong** |
| Low-mercury fish | 2–3 servings/week | **Strong** |
| Listeria-risk foods | Avoid unpasteurised dairy, deli meats unless reheated, refrigerated smoked fish | **Established** |

## Infancy

- Vitamin K injection at birth — **Established**
- Vitamin D 400 IU/day for breastfed infants — **Established**
- Solid foods around six months, not before four — **Strong**
- Early introduction of peanut and egg — **Established** for peanut in high-risk infants (LEAP)
- No honey before 12 months — **Established**
- No added salt or sugar — **Strong**

## Sources

- MRC Vitamin Study Research Group. Prevention of neural tube defects: results of the Medical Research Council Vitamin Study. *Lancet* 1991.
- Du Toit G et al. Randomized trial of peanut consumption in infants at risk for peanut allergy (LEAP). *NEJM* 2015. [doi:10.1056/NEJMoa1414850](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1414850)
- Kramer MS et al. Promotion of Breastfeeding Intervention Trial (PROBIT). *JAMA* 2001; *Arch Gen Psychiatry* 2008.
- Institute of Medicine. *Weight Gain During Pregnancy: Reexamining the Guidelines.* 2009.
- US FDA and EPA. Advice about eating fish. Updated 2022.
- WHO. Infant and young child feeding fact sheet.

title: Children, adolescents and older adults
questions:
  - id: stunting
    prompt: What is stunting?
    options:
      - id: low-height
        text: Low height for age caused by chronic undernutrition and repeated infection, especially in the first 1,000 days
        correct: true
      - text: Normal variation in height
      - text: A result of drinking coffee
    explanation: WHO and UNICEF estimate about 150 million children under five are stunted, with lasting effects on health and cognition.
  - id: double-burden
    prompt: What does the "double burden of malnutrition" refer to?
    options:
      - id: both
        text: Undernutrition and obesity coexisting in the same country, community or even household
        correct: true
      - text: Eating two dinners
      - text: Being deficient in two vitamins
    explanation: Many low- and middle-income countries now face both problems simultaneously.
  - id: picky
    prompt: How many times might a child need to be offered a new food before accepting it, according to feeding research?
    options:
      - text: Once
      - id: many
        text: Often 8–15 times
        correct: true
      - text: Never — preferences are fixed at birth
    explanation: Repeated, pressure-free exposure works better than forcing, bribing or rewarding with sweets.
  - id: sarcopenia
    prompt: Which combination best slows sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss)?
    options:
      - id: resistance-protein
        text: Resistance exercise combined with adequate protein
        correct: true
      - text: Collagen supplements alone
      - text: Bed rest
    explanation: Resistance training is the main driver; protein supports it. Supplements alone produce little benefit in people already eating enough.
  - id: older-risks
    prompt: Which nutritional problems are more common in older adults?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Vitamin B12 deficiency due to reduced stomach acid
        correct: true
      - text: Dehydration due to blunted thirst
        correct: true
      - text: Unintentional weight loss and undernutrition, especially in care homes
        correct: true
      - text: Scurvy from eating too many oranges
    explanation: In older adults, unintended weight loss is often more dangerous than modest excess weight; screening tools such as MUST help detect malnutrition.
  - id: obesity-paradox
    prompt: In older adults, a BMI in the "overweight" range is sometimes associated with lower mortality than "normal" BMI. What is a likely explanation?
    options:
      - id: confounding
        text: Reverse causation (illness causes weight loss) and poor measurement of body composition, though the true optimum BMI may shift somewhat upward with age
        correct: true
      - text: Fat is protective at every age
      - text: BMI cannot be measured in older people
    explanation: This "obesity paradox" is a genuine research debate. Grade for the optimal BMI in older adults - **Uncertain**.
  - id: school-meals
    prompt: What does evidence suggest about school meal and sugary-drink policies?
    options:
      - id: modest
        text: Healthier school food standards and sugar-drink taxes produce measurable, modest improvements in intake, with mixed evidence on obesity rates
        correct: true
      - text: They have been proven to eliminate childhood obesity
      - text: They have never been evaluated
    explanation: The UK Soft Drinks Industry Levy (2018) led manufacturers to reformulate, cutting sugar in drinks substantially. Health effects are still being evaluated.
---
## Learning objectives

- Know nutrition priorities in childhood and old age
- Understand undernutrition as well as overnutrition

## Children

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| The first 1,000 days (conception to age two) are critical for growth and brain development | **Established** |
| Repeated exposure increases acceptance of vegetables | **Strong** |
| Sugary drinks contribute to excess weight and tooth decay in children | **Strong** to **Established** |
| Fruit juice should be limited (AAP — none under 12 months; up to 120 ml for ages 1–3) | **Strong** |
| Sugar causes hyperactivity | **Not supported** |
| Children need special "toddler milks" | **Not supported** — these are unnecessary per WHO and AAP |

## Older adults

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Protein needs are higher (about 1.0–1.2 g/kg) | **Strong** |
| B12 deficiency is common and under-diagnosed | **Strong** |
| Vitamin D plus calcium reduces fractures in institutionalised elderly | **Strong** |
| Antioxidant supplements prevent dementia | **Not supported** |
| The MIND diet prevents dementia | **Uncertain** — a 2023 RCT found no significant cognitive benefit over a control diet with mild calorie restriction |

## Sources

- Victora CG et al. Revisiting maternal and child undernutrition in low-income and middle-income countries. *Lancet* 2021.
- UNICEF/WHO/World Bank. Joint Child Malnutrition Estimates. 2023.
- Cruz-Jentoft AJ et al. Sarcopenia: revised European consensus. *Age Ageing* 2019.
- Barnes LL et al. Trial of the MIND diet for prevention of cognitive decline in older persons. *NEJM* 2023.
- Rogers NT et al. Associations between trajectories of obesity prevalence in English primary school children and the UK soft drinks industry levy. *PLoS Med* 2023.

## Learning objectives

- Set protein and carbohydrate targets for athletes
- Identify the few supplements with good evidence
- Recognise low energy availability

## Targets

| Need | Guidance | Grade |
|------|---------|-------|
| Protein | 1.2–2.0 g/kg/day, about 0.3 g/kg per meal | **Strong** |
| Carbohydrate (daily) | 3–5 g/kg light training; 6–10 g/kg heavy; 8–12 g/kg very heavy endurance | **Strong** |
| Carbohydrate during long events | 30–90 g/hour depending on duration | **Strong** |
| Fluid | Drink to thirst; avoid weight gain during events | **Strong** |

## Supplements with evidence

| Supplement | Benefit | Grade |
|-----------|--------|-------|
| Caffeine 3–6 mg/kg | Endurance and some high-intensity performance | **Established** |
| Creatine | Strength, power, repeated sprints | **Established** |
| Nitrate | Endurance in non-elite athletes | **Strong** |
| Beta-alanine | Efforts of 1–10 minutes | **Strong** |
| Sodium bicarbonate | High-intensity efforts; gut side effects | **Strong** |
| BCAAs, glutamine, testosterone "boosters" | None meaningful | **Not supported** |

title: Food safety and foodborne illness
questions:
  - id: burden
    prompt: CDC estimates that foodborne illness in the US causes roughly how many illnesses each year?
    options:
      - text: About 4,800
      - id: forty-eight-million
        text: About 48 million, with about 128,000 hospitalisations and 3,000 deaths
        correct: true
      - text: About 3 billion
    explanation: These are 2011 estimates; WHO estimates about 600 million cases and 420,000 deaths globally each year.
  - id: danger-zone
    prompt: What is the bacterial "danger zone" for food temperature?
    options:
      - id: four-sixty
        text: About 4–60 °C (40–140 °F)
        correct: true
      - text: Below 0 °C
      - text: Above 100 °C only
    explanation: Perishable food should not sit in this range for more than two hours (one hour above 32 °C / 90 °F).
  - id: poultry-temp
    prompt: What internal temperature does USDA recommend for cooking poultry?
    options:
      - text: 50 °C (122 °F)
      - id: seventy-four
        text: 74 °C (165 °F)
        correct: true
      - text: 100 °C (212 °F) for one hour
    explanation: Ground meats should reach 71 °C (160 °F); whole cuts of beef, pork and lamb 63 °C (145 °F) with a three-minute rest. Colour is not a reliable indicator; use a thermometer.
  - id: washing-chicken
    prompt: Should you wash raw chicken before cooking?
    options:
      - text: Yes, it removes bacteria
      - id: no-splash
        text: No — washing does not reliably remove bacteria and splashes them around the kitchen; cooking kills them
        correct: true
    explanation: A 2019 USDA observational study found that a quarter of participants who washed poultry transferred bacteria to a salad they prepared afterwards.
  - id: listeria
    prompt: Which characteristics make Listeria monocytogenes particularly dangerous?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: It can grow at refrigerator temperatures
        correct: true
      - text: It can cause miscarriage, stillbirth and newborn infection
        correct: true
      - text: It has a high fatality rate in older and immunocompromised people
        correct: true
      - text: It is killed by refrigeration
    explanation: High-risk foods include unpasteurised dairy, soft cheeses, deli meats, refrigerated smoked fish and pre-cut melon.
  - id: five-second
    prompt: What did Rutgers researchers (Miranda and Schaffner, 2016) find about the "five-second rule"?
    options:
      - text: Food dropped for under five seconds is sterile
      - id: instant
        text: Bacterial transfer can begin in under one second; moisture and surface type matter more than time
        correct: true
      - text: Bacteria never transfer to food
    explanation: Wet foods like watermelon picked up the most bacteria; carpet transferred less than tile or steel.
  - id: botulism-home
    prompt: Which home practice carries a risk of botulism?
    options:
      - id: low-acid-canning
        text: Home-canning low-acid foods (vegetables, meats) without a pressure canner, or storing garlic in oil at room temperature
        correct: true
      - text: Freezing bread
      - text: Boiling water for tea
    explanation: Clostridium botulinum thrives in low-oxygen, low-acid conditions. Its toxin is among the most lethal substances known.
---
## Learning objectives

- Understand the scale of foodborne illness
- Apply the four core food-safety practices
- Identify high-risk foods and groups

## The four rules

| Rule | What it means |
|------|---------------|
| Clean | Wash hands, surfaces and produce (not raw meat) |
| Separate | Keep raw meat away from ready-to-eat foods |
| Cook | Use a thermometer to reach safe internal temperatures |
| Chill | Refrigerate at 4 °C (40 °F) or below within two hours |

## Major pathogens

| Pathogen | Typical sources | Notes |
|----------|-----------------|-------|
| Norovirus | Ill food handlers, shellfish | Most common cause of foodborne illness |
| Salmonella | Poultry, eggs, produce | Leading cause of hospitalisation and death in the US |
| Campylobacter | Undercooked poultry, raw milk | Can trigger Guillain-Barré syndrome |
| Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (O157:H7) | Undercooked ground beef, raw milk, leafy greens | Haemolytic uraemic syndrome and kidney failure in children |
| Listeria | Deli meats, soft cheese, raw milk | Dangerous in pregnancy |
| Clostridium botulinum | Improper home canning; honey for infants | Paralysis |

## High-risk groups

Pregnant people, infants and young children, adults over 65 and people with weakened immune systems are
at greatest risk. Their food-safety precautions are not optional extras.

## Sources

- Scallan E et al. Foodborne illness acquired in the United States — major pathogens. *Emerg Infect Dis* 2011.
- WHO. Estimates of the global burden of foodborne diseases. 2015.
- USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service. Safe minimum internal temperature chart.
- Miranda RC, Schaffner DW. Longer contact times increase cross-contamination of Enterobacter aerogenes from surfaces to food. *Appl Environ Microbiol* 2016.
- USDA FSIS. Food safety consumer research project: meal preparation experiment related to poultry washing. 2019.

---
title: Raw milk, sacred-animal remedies and the appeal to purity
questions:
  - id: pasteurisation
    prompt: What does standard high-temperature short-time (HTST) pasteurisation of milk involve?
    options:
      - id: seventy-two
        text: Heating to at least 72 °C (161 °F) for 15 seconds, then rapid cooling
        correct: true
      - text: Boiling milk for an hour
      - text: Adding antibiotics
    explanation: Pasteurisation kills the pathogens that historically made milk a major cause of tuberculosis, typhoid, scarlet fever, diphtheria and infant diarrhoea.
  - id: risk-ratio
    prompt: A 2017 analysis by Costard and colleagues estimated how unpasteurised milk compares with pasteurised milk per unit consumed in the US?
    options:
      - text: Equally safe
      - id: eight-forty
        text: About 840 times more illnesses and 45 times more hospitalisations
        correct: true
      - text: Raw milk is ten times safer
    explanation: CDC data for 1998–2018 attributed 202 outbreaks to raw milk, with 2,645 illnesses and 228 hospitalisations, despite only a small fraction of people drinking it. Children are disproportionately affected.
  - id: raw-claims
    prompt: Which common claims about raw milk are **Not supported**?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Pasteurisation destroys milk's nutritional value
        correct: true
      - text: Raw milk cures lactose intolerance
        correct: true
      - text: Raw milk's "good bacteria" make it safe
        correct: true
      - text: Raw milk boosts immunity in a way that outweighs its infection risk
        correct: true
    explanation: Pasteurisation causes only small losses of some heat-sensitive vitamins of which milk is not a major source. A 2014 Stanford randomised crossover trial found raw milk did not reduce lactose malabsorption or symptoms. Pathogens are not neutralised by other bacteria.
  - id: h5n1
    prompt: What happened with H5N1 avian influenza and raw milk in 2024?
    options:
      - text: Nothing — H5N1 cannot infect cattle
      - id: detected
        text: H5N1 spread in US dairy cattle, high virus levels were found in raw milk, farm cats died after drinking it, and raw-milk products were recalled; pasteurisation inactivates the virus
        correct: true
      - text: Raw milk was shown to cure H5N1
    explanation: CDC and FDA advise against raw milk, citing H5N1 among other risks. Retail testing of pasteurised milk found viral fragments but no infectious virus.
  - id: farm-asthma
    prompt: European studies (such as GABRIELA) found children on farms who drank farm milk had less asthma and allergy. What is the correct interpretation?
    options:
      - text: Proof that everyone should drink raw milk
      - id: association
        text: An association that may reflect the wider farm environment; the protective component has not been identified, and the infection risk is real — researchers have explicitly not recommended raw milk
        correct: true
      - text: The studies were faked
    explanation: Researchers are trying to find a way to preserve any protective factor while making milk safe. This is an honest example of **Uncertain** science that does not justify the health claims made by raw-milk advocates.
  - id: cow-urine
    prompt: What is the evidence grade for cow urine (gomutra) or panchagavya curing cancer, diabetes or infections in humans?
    options:
      - text: Established by large clinical trials
      - text: Strong
      - id: not-supported
        text: Not supported — there are no adequate human clinical trials showing such benefits
        correct: true
    explanation: The evidence base consists of laboratory and small, low-quality studies. Patents granted for cow-urine distillates are not evidence of clinical effectiveness; patents certify novelty, not that something works in patients. Religious significance is not evidence either.
  - id: urine-risk
    prompt: Which are documented health risks associated with ingesting animal urine or applying dung?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Leptospirosis can be transmitted through urine of infected animals, including cattle
        correct: true
      - text: Applying dung to a newborn's umbilical cord is a recognised cause of neonatal tetanus
        correct: true
      - text: Animal urine can contain pathogenic bacteria; a 2023 study by India's Indian Veterinary Research Institute reported harmful bacteria including E. coli in cow urine samples
        correct: true
      - text: Urine is always sterile and therefore harmless
    explanation: Urine is a waste product. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Indian medical associations publicly warned against cow dung and urine "therapies", which had no evidence of benefit.
  - id: special-pleading
    prompt: A remedy is defended with "you can't test it scientifically because it's sacred". Which reasoning error is this?
    options:
      - id: special-pleading
        text: Special pleading — exempting a claim from the standards applied to all other claims
        correct: true
      - text: Peer review
      - text: Statistical significance
    explanation: Any claim that a substance cures disease in human bodies is testable with a controlled trial, whatever its cultural or religious status. Respect for people's beliefs does not require pretending untested claims are proven.
---
## Learning objectives

- Explain why pasteurisation is one of public health's great successes
- Evaluate raw milk claims against data
- Apply the same standards to sacred and traditional remedies as to any other claim

## Why milk was pasteurised

In the 19th and early 20th centuries, milk was a leading vehicle for tuberculosis (Mycobacterium bovis),
typhoid, scarlet fever, diphtheria, brucellosis and infant diarrhoea. In the US in 1938, milk-borne outbreaks
caused about a quarter of all reported food- and water-borne outbreaks; today the share is below 1% (FDA), and
most dairy outbreaks involve unpasteurised products.

## Raw milk claims judged

| Claim | Grade | Evidence |
|-------|-------|----------|
| Raw milk carries a much higher risk of infection | **Established** | Outbreak surveillance; Costard 2017 |
| Pasteurisation substantially reduces nutritional value | **Not supported** | Small losses of vitamins C, B1, B12; milk's protein, calcium and fat are unaffected |
| Raw milk prevents lactose intolerance | **Not supported** | Mummah et al., randomised crossover trial, 2014 |
| Raw milk enzymes aid digestion | **Not supported** | Milk enzymes are digested like other proteins |
| Farm milk exposure is associated with less childhood asthma | **Uncertain** | Association in farming communities; not shown for shop-bought raw milk; not a recommendation |
| Raw milk is safe if the farm is clean | **Not supported** | Outbreaks occur at certified and "clean" farms; contamination comes from udder infection and faeces |

Groups most harmed — children, pregnant people, the elderly and the immunocompromised — are often the ones
encouraged to drink raw milk "for health".

## Sacred and traditional animal products

Many cultures attach religious or traditional significance to particular animals and their products. Such
beliefs are a matter of faith and deserve respect as beliefs. **Medical claims are different**: when someone
says a substance cures cancer, diabetes or infection, that claim is testable and must meet the same standard as
a drug.

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Cow urine or panchagavya cures cancer, diabetes, COVID-19 or other diseases | **Not supported** |
| Cow dung applied to skin or wounds protects against infection | **Not supported**; dung can carry tetanus spores |
| A product is safe because it comes from a revered animal | **Not supported** — sanctity is not sterility |
| Ingesting any animal's urine is a risk for zoonotic infection | **Strong** (leptospirosis and other pathogens) |

The same reasoning applies to rhino horn (keratin, like fingernails), bear bile, and countless other
traditional animal remedies whose demand drives species toward extinction without demonstrated benefit.

## Sources

- Costard S et al. Outbreak-related disease burden associated with consumption of unpasteurized cow's milk and cheese, United States, 2009–2014. *Emerg Infect Dis* 2017.
- Koski L et al. Foodborne illness outbreaks linked to unpasteurised milk and relationship to changes in state laws — United States, 1998–2018. *Epidemiol Infect* 2022.
- Mummah S et al. Effect of raw milk on lactose intolerance: a randomized controlled pilot study. *Ann Fam Med* 2014.
- Loss G et al. The protective effect of farm milk consumption on childhood asthma and atopy: the GABRIELA study. *J Allergy Clin Immunol* 2011.
- US FDA. Investigation of avian influenza A (H5N1) virus in dairy cattle. 2024–2025 updates.
- CDC. Raw milk: questions and answers.
- WHO. Neonatal tetanus elimination; leptospirosis fact sheets.

title: Detoxes, alkaline diets and other persistent myths
questions:
  - id: detox
    prompt: Which organs remove waste products and toxins from the body?

        correct: true
      - text: Juice cleanses and foot pads
      - text: Charcoal supplements taken daily
    explanation: A 2015 review found no rigorous clinical evidence that commercial detox diets eliminate toxins. Detox foot pads turn dark because of moisture and ingredients in the pad.
  - id: alkaline

        correct: true
    explanation: Blood pH outside this range is a medical emergency (acidosis or alkalosis). The "alkaline diet" is healthy only because it encourages vegetables and fruit.
  - id: msg
    prompt: What have double-blind, placebo-controlled studies found about MSG and "Chinese restaurant syndrome"?

      - text: MSG consistently causes headaches and palpitations in most people

        correct: true
      - text: MSG is banned worldwide
    explanation: Glutamate occurs naturally in tomatoes, Parmesan and human breast milk. The original 1968 "syndrome" letter and the reaction to it have been criticised as reflecting prejudice against Chinese cuisine.
  - id: late-eating
    prompt: Does eating after 8 pm cause weight gain regardless of total intake?
    options:
      - text: Yes, calories eaten late are stored as fat
      - id: total
        text: Not shown — total energy intake matters most; late eating may matter for some people because of extra snacking or effects on sleep, and the research on meal timing is still developing
        correct: true
    explanation: Grade - **Uncertain** for a specific effect of timing; **Not supported** for "late calories automatically become fat".
  - id: gluten-free
    prompt: For people without coeliac disease, wheat allergy or diagnosed sensitivity, is a gluten-free diet healthier?
    options:
      - text: Yes, gluten is toxic to everyone
      - id: no-benefit
        text: No evidence of benefit; gluten-free products are often lower in fibre and fortification and more expensive
        correct: true
    explanation: A large cohort study (Lebwohl 2017) found no link between gluten intake and heart disease in people without coeliac disease, and suggested avoiding gluten may reduce whole-grain intake.
  - id: colloidal-silver

    options:
      - id: argyria
        text: Argyria — permanent blue-grey discoloration of the skin
        correct: true
      - text: There are no harms
      - text: It cures all infections
    explanation: The FDA ruled in 1999 that over-the-counter colloidal silver products are not recognised as safe and effective for any disease.
  - id: celery-juice

    options:

        correct: true

  - id: homeopathy

        correct: true

  - id: myths-list
    prompt: Which statements are true?

    options:
      - text: Microwaving does not make food radioactive

      - text: Eating carrots helps vision only if you are vitamin A deficient; it will not give you night vision otherwise
        correct: true
      - text: Swallowed gum is not digested but passes through, usually within days
        correct: true
      - text: Spicy food causes stomach ulcers
    explanation: Most peptic ulcers are caused by Helicobacter pylori infection or NSAID drugs — a discovery that won Marshall and Warren the 2005 Nobel Prize.

## Learning objectives

- Recognise and refute common nutrition myths
- Understand why myths persist

## Myths judged

| Claim | Grade | Note |
|-------|-------|------|
| Detox diets, teas and cleanses remove toxins | **Not supported** | The liver and kidneys do this; no "toxin" is ever named or measured |
| Alkaline diet changes blood pH and prevents cancer | **Not supported** | Fenton & Huang 2016 systematic review |
| MSG is dangerous | **Not supported** | GRAS (FDA); double-blind trials inconsistent |
| Gluten-free is healthier for everyone | **Not supported** | Essential only for coeliac disease and related conditions |
| Eating late makes you fat independent of intake | **Uncertain** to **Not supported** | |
| Carbohydrates at night are worse | **Uncertain** | |
| Frequent small meals "stoke metabolism" | **Not supported** | Thermic effect depends on total intake |
| Microwaving destroys nutrients more than other cooking | **Not supported** | Short times and little water often preserve nutrients better than boiling |
| "Negative-calorie" foods (celery) | **Not supported** | Digestion costs only a fraction of the calories |
| Colloidal silver, homeopathy, celery juice cure disease | **Not supported** | |
| Spicy food causes ulcers | **Not supported** | H. pylori and NSAIDs are the main causes |
| Egg yolks or all fat must be avoided | **Not supported** in that absolute form | |

## Why myths persist

- **Placebo, natural recovery and regression to the mean:** people try remedies when they feel worst, so
  they usually feel better afterwards regardless
- **Confirmation bias:** successes are remembered, failures forgotten
- **Commercial incentives:** an unfalsifiable product never fails a trial
- **Identity:** diets become tribal, political or religious identities, which makes evidence feel like an attack

## Sources

- Klein AV, Kiat H. Detox diets for toxin elimination and weight management: a critical review of the evidence. *J Hum Nutr Diet* 2015.
- Fenton TR, Huang T. Systematic review of the association between dietary acid load, alkaline water and cancer. *BMJ Open* 2016. [doi:10.1136/bmjopen-2015-010438](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2015-010438)
- Geha RS et al. Review of alleged reaction to monosodium glutamate and outcome of a multicenter double-blind placebo-controlled study. *J Nutr* 2000.
- Lebwohl B et al. Long term gluten consumption in adults without celiac disease and risk of coronary heart disease. *BMJ* 2017.
- National Health and Medical Research Council (Australia). NHMRC information paper: evidence on the effectiveness of homeopathy for treating health conditions. 2015.
- US FDA. Over-the-counter drug products containing colloidal silver ingredients or silver salts. Final rule, 1999.

title: Additives, pesticides, contaminants and GMOs

    options:
      - id: no-evidence
        text: It found no substantiated evidence that foods from GE crops were less safe to eat than foods from conventionally bred crops
        correct: true
      - text: It found GE foods cause cancer
      - text: It did not assess food safety
    explanation: WHO, the European Commission's research programmes and many scientific academies have reached similar conclusions. Debates about patents, corporate concentration, herbicide use and labelling are real but are economic and environmental questions, not food-safety ones.
  - id: organic
    prompt: What did the Stanford systematic review (Smith-Spangler 2012) find about organic foods?
    options:
      - text: Organic foods are much more nutritious
      - id: residues
        text: There was little evidence that organic foods are more nutritious, though they had lower pesticide residues (conventional residues were usually within safety limits)
        correct: true
      - text: Organic foods are pesticide-free by definition
    explanation: Organic farming uses approved pesticides too, including natural ones such as copper sulphate. Whether lower residue exposure improves health outcomes is **Uncertain**.
  - id: mercury
    prompt: Which fish are highest in mercury and should be avoided by pregnant people and young children?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Shark
        correct: true
      - text: Swordfish
        correct: true
      - text: King mackerel
        correct: true
      - text: Bigeye tuna
        correct: true
      - text: Sardines
    explanation: Large, long-lived predatory fish accumulate methylmercury. Sardines, salmon and anchovies are low in mercury and high in omega-3.
  - id: arsenic-rice
    prompt: How can inorganic arsenic in rice be reduced at home?
    options:
      - id: excess-water
        text: Rinsing rice and cooking it in a large excess of water, then draining, reduces arsenic substantially (with some loss of B vitamins in enriched rice)
        correct: true
      - text: It cannot be reduced
      - text: By adding more salt
    explanation: Brown rice contains more arsenic than white because arsenic concentrates in the bran. Infant rice cereal is a particular concern; the FDA set an action level of 100 ppb in 2020.
  - id: glyphosate
    prompt: Why do IARC and regulators such as the US EPA and EFSA disagree about glyphosate?
    options:
      - id: hazard-risk
        text: IARC assesses hazard (can it cause cancer under some circumstances?), while regulators assess risk at realistic exposure levels; they also weighed some studies differently
        correct: true
      - text: One of them did not look at any data
      - text: They agree completely
    explanation: IARC classified glyphosate as Group 2A (probably carcinogenic) in 2015; EPA and EFSA concluded it is unlikely to pose a carcinogenic risk at expected exposures. Grade for dietary residues causing cancer - **Uncertain**, leaning **Not supported** at normal exposure.
  - id: e-numbers
    prompt: What does an "E number" on a food label in Europe indicate?
    options:
      - text: The additive is dangerous
      - id: approved
        text: The additive has been evaluated and approved for use in the EU
        correct: true
      - text: The food is genetically modified
    explanation: E300 is vitamin C (ascorbic acid); E330 is citric acid; E948 is oxygen. Approval does not mean every additive is beyond question — titanium dioxide (E171) was withdrawn by the EU in 2022 because genotoxicity could not be ruled out.
  - id: colours
    prompt: What did the 2007 Southampton study suggest about certain artificial food colours?
    options:
      - id: hyperactivity
        text: A mix of certain artificial colours plus sodium benzoate increased hyperactive behaviour slightly in some children
        correct: true
      - text: They cause cancer
      - text: They had no effect at all
    explanation: The EU then required a warning label on six colours. The effect size was small and its clinical significance debated — grade **Uncertain**. Several US states and the FDA have since moved to phase out some petroleum-based dyes.
  - id: acrylamide
    prompt: Acrylamide forms when starchy foods are fried, roasted or baked at high temperatures. What is the state of the evidence?
    options:
      - id: animal-uncertain
        text: It is carcinogenic in animals at high doses (IARC 2A), but human dietary studies have not shown consistent cancer increases
        correct: true
      - text: It is proven to cause most cancers
      - text: It does not exist
    explanation: Reasonable precautions include not over-browning toast and chips ("go for gold"). Grade for dietary harm at normal intakes - **Uncertain**.
---
## Learning objectives

- Apply hazard-versus-risk thinking to chemicals in food
- Know the main contaminants that matter
- Evaluate GMO and organic claims

## How additives are regulated

Regulators (FDA, EFSA, JECFA) set an **acceptable daily intake (ADI)** — usually the highest dose with no
observed adverse effect in animal studies divided by 100. Typical consumer intakes are generally far below
ADIs. Systems are not perfect: in the US, the "self-affirmed GRAS" pathway lets companies declare an ingredient
safe without notifying the FDA, which has been criticised by researchers and policymakers.

## Contaminants that matter

| Contaminant | Main sources | Health concern | Grade |
|------------|--------------|----------------|-------|
| Methylmercury | Large predatory fish | Fetal brain development | **Established** |
| Inorganic arsenic | Rice, some well water | Cancer, development | **Strong** at high exposure |
| Lead | Old pipes, some spices, contaminated products | Child neurodevelopment, no safe level | **Established** |
| Aflatoxins | Mouldy grains and nuts | Liver cancer | **Established** |
| Acrylamide | Fried and browned starches | Animal carcinogen | **Uncertain** for humans at dietary doses |
| Microplastics | Widespread | Unknown | **Uncertain** |
| PFAS | Packaging, water | Some immune, lipid and cancer effects | **Strong** for some PFAS at high exposures; dietary contribution **Uncertain** |

Lead deserves emphasis: the 2023 US recall of cinnamon applesauce pouches after children were poisoned, and
repeated findings of lead in imported spices and some traditional medicines, show that contamination risk is
real for "natural" and traditional products too.

## Biotechnology

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Approved GM foods are as safe to eat as conventional counterparts | **Established** scientific consensus |
| GM foods cause cancer, allergies or infertility | **Not supported** |
| Organic food is more nutritious | **Not supported** in any meaningful way |
| Organic food has lower pesticide residues | **Established** |
| Lower residues produce measurable health benefits | **Uncertain** |

## Sources

- National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. *Genetically Engineered Crops: Experiences and Prospects.* 2016. [doi:10.17226/23395](https://doi.org/10.17226/23395)
- Smith-Spangler C et al. Are organic foods safer or healthier than conventional alternatives? *Ann Intern Med* 2012. [doi:10.7326/0003-4819-157-5-201209040-00007](https://doi.org/10.7326/0003-4819-157-5-201209040-00007)
- McCann D et al. Food additives and hyperactive behaviour in 3-year-old and 8/9-year-old children (Southampton). *Lancet* 2007.
- IARC Monographs volume 112 (glyphosate), 2015; US EPA glyphosate interim decision, 2020; EFSA conclusion on glyphosate, 2023.
- EFSA. Safety assessment of titanium dioxide (E171) as a food additive. *EFSA J* 2021.
- US FDA. Inorganic arsenic in rice cereals for infants: action level guidance. 2020.
- US FDA and EPA. Advice about eating fish. 2022.

questions:

        text: No significant difference in weight loss or metabolic risk factors
        correct: true

  - id: adf

        correct: true
      - text: Alternate-day fasting produced three times the weight loss
      - text: Daily restriction caused no weight loss
    explanation: Intermittent fasting is a valid strategy, not a superior one. Adherence decides.
  - id: breakfast
    prompt: What did a 2019 BMJ meta-analysis of RCTs find about eating breakfast for weight control?

      - text: Breakfast causes major weight loss
      - id: no-help
        text: Adding breakfast did not help weight loss and slightly increased energy intake
        correct: true
      - text: Skipping breakfast always causes obesity
    explanation: The observational link between skipping breakfast and obesity is likely confounded. "Breakfast is the most important meal of the day" is a slogan popularised partly by cereal marketing.
  - id: autophagy

    options:

        correct: true
    explanation: Yoshinori Ohsumi's 2016 Nobel Prize was for autophagy mechanisms in yeast, not for fasting regimens.
  - id: risks

        correct: true

        correct: true
      - text: People with a history of eating disorders
        correct: true
      - text: Children and adolescents
        correct: true

  - id: tre-2024
    prompt: In 2024 an observational analysis presented at an American Heart Association meeting reported that an 8-hour eating window was associated with higher cardiovascular death. How should this be treated?
    options:
      - text: As proof that time-restricted eating kills
      - id: hypothesis

        correct: true

## Learning objectives

- Evaluate intermittent fasting against calorie restriction
- Judge breakfast and meal-timing claims

## Types of fasting

| Type | Description |
|------|-------------|
| Time-restricted eating (TRE) | Eating within a 6–10 hour window daily |
| 5:2 | Two non-consecutive low-calorie days (about 500–600 kcal) each week |
| Alternate-day fasting | Fasting or very low intake every other day |
| Prolonged fasting | More than 48 hours; requires medical supervision |

## Evidence

| Claim | Grade |
|-------|-------|
| Intermittent fasting produces weight loss | **Established** — through reduced intake |
| It beats equal-calorie daily restriction | **Not supported** |
| It improves insulin sensitivity beyond weight loss | **Uncertain** (some early TRE studies suggest yes) |
| Fasting extends human lifespan | **Uncertain** — animal data only |
| Breakfast is needed for weight control | **Not supported** |
| Eating in line with circadian rhythm (earlier in the day) is metabolically favourable | **Uncertain** to **Strong** for glucose; outcome data lacking |

## Sources

- Liu D et al. Calorie restriction with or without time-restricted eating in weight loss. *NEJM* 2022. [doi:10.1056/NEJMoa2114833](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2114833)
- Trepanowski JF et al. Effect of alternate-day fasting on weight loss, weight maintenance, and cardioprotection. *JAMA Intern Med* 2017. [doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2017.0936](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2017.0936)
- Lowe DA et al. Effects of time-restricted eating on weight loss and other metabolic parameters (TREAT). *JAMA Intern Med* 2020. [doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2020.4153](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2020.4153)
- Sievert K et al. Effect of breakfast on weight and energy intake: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. *BMJ* 2019. [doi:10.1136/bmj.l42](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.l42)
- Sutton EF et al. Early time-restricted feeding improves insulin sensitivity, blood pressure, and oxidative stress even without weight loss in men with prediabetes. *Cell Metab* 2018.

title: Food allergies, coeliac disease and intolerances
questions:
  - id: allergy-vs-intolerance
    prompt: What distinguishes a food allergy from a food intolerance?
    options:
      - id: immune
        text: An allergy involves the immune system (often IgE antibodies) and can cause anaphylaxis; an intolerance does not involve the immune system in that way and is not life-threatening
        correct: true
      - text: They are the same thing
      - text: Intolerances are always more severe
    explanation: Lactose intolerance is a digestive enzyme deficiency. Peanut allergy is an immune reaction that can kill.
  - id: anaphylaxis
    prompt: What is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis?
    options:
      - text: Antihistamine tablets
      - id: adrenaline
        text: Intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine), then emergency medical care
        correct: true
      - text: Drinking water
    explanation: Delays in adrenaline are associated with deaths. Antihistamines do not treat airway swelling or low blood pressure effectively.
  - id: coeliac
    prompt: Which statements about coeliac disease are correct?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: It is an autoimmune disease triggered by gluten in genetically susceptible people
        correct: true
      - text: It affects roughly 1% of many populations, and many cases are undiagnosed
        correct: true
      - text: Testing should be done while the person is still eating gluten
        correct: true
      - text: It can be cured with probiotics
    explanation: Treatment is a strict lifelong gluten-free diet. Going gluten-free before testing can produce false-negative results.
  - id: ncgs
    prompt: In a blinded crossover trial (Skodje 2018) in people with self-reported non-coeliac gluten sensitivity, what triggered symptoms?
    options:
      - text: Gluten, clearly
      - id: fructans
        text: Fructans (a FODMAP carbohydrate in wheat) rather than gluten
        correct: true
      - text: Placebo caused no symptoms at all
    explanation: Non-coeliac gluten or wheat sensitivity is a real complaint; its cause is **Uncertain** and may differ between people. Nocebo effects are also large in blinded challenges.
  - id: fodmap
    prompt: For which condition does the low-FODMAP diet have the best evidence?
    options:
      - id: ibs
        text: Irritable bowel syndrome, as a short-term elimination followed by structured reintroduction under guidance
        correct: true
      - text: Weight loss
      - text: Curing coeliac disease
    explanation: Long-term strict FODMAP restriction can reduce dietary diversity and beneficial gut bacteria, so reintroduction is part of the protocol.
  - id: igg-tests
    prompt: What do major allergy organisations say about IgG food-intolerance blood tests?
    options:
      - text: They are the gold standard
      - id: not-valid
        text: They are not valid for diagnosing food allergy or intolerance; IgG to foods usually reflects normal exposure
        correct: true
      - text: They diagnose anaphylaxis risk
    explanation: The American Academy of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology and the European Academy of Allergy and Clinical Immunology advise against them. Unnecessary elimination diets can cause nutritional problems, especially in children.
  - id: big-nine
    prompt: How many major food allergens must be declared on US labels since sesame was added in 2023?
    options:
      - text: Three
      - id: nine
        text: Nine — milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soy and sesame
        correct: true
      - text: Fourteen
    explanation: The EU requires 14 allergens to be declared, including celery, mustard, lupin, molluscs and sulphites.
---
## Learning objectives

- Distinguish allergy, autoimmune disease and intolerance
- Know validated diagnostic approaches
- Recognise invalid tests

## Comparison

| Condition | Mechanism | Diagnosis | Treatment |
|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| IgE food allergy | Immune (IgE) | History plus skin-prick or specific IgE; oral food challenge | Avoidance, adrenaline auto-injector; oral immunotherapy for some |
| Coeliac disease | Autoimmune | tTG-IgA blood test and intestinal biopsy, on a gluten-containing diet | Lifelong strict gluten-free diet |
| Lactose intolerance | Low lactase enzyme | Clinical history; hydrogen breath test | Limit lactose; lactase enzymes; lactose-free products |
| IBS (FODMAP-sensitive) | Gut sensitivity, motility | Clinical criteria (Rome IV) | Low-FODMAP diet with reintroduction, among others |
| Non-coeliac gluten/wheat sensitivity | Unclear | Exclusion of coeliac and wheat allergy | Individual trial of reduction |

## Invalid tests

Applied kinesiology, hair analysis, IgG food panels, electrodermal ("Vega") testing and pulse tests have no
diagnostic validity for food allergy or intolerance. Grade - **Not supported**.

## Sources

- Skodje GI et al. Fructan, rather than gluten, induces symptoms in patients with self-reported non-celiac gluten sensitivity. *Gastroenterology* 2018. [doi:10.1053/j.gastro.2017.10.040](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.gastro.2017.10.040)
- Muraro A et al. EAACI guideline: anaphylaxis (2021 update). *Allergy* 2022.
- Rubio-Tapia A et al. ACG guidelines update: diagnosis and management of celiac disease. *Am J Gastroenterol* 2023.
- Stapel SO et al. Testing for IgG4 against foods is not recommended as a diagnostic tool: EAACI task force report. *Allergy* 2008.
- US FDA. Food Allergy Safety, Treatment, Education, and Research (FASTER) Act of 2021.

title: The certainty scorecard
questions:
  - id: which-established
    prompt: Which of these claims are graded **Established** in this book?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Folic acid before conception reduces neural tube defects
        correct: true
      - text: Vegans need a reliable vitamin B12 source
        correct: true
      - text: Industrial trans fats increase heart disease
        correct: true
      - text: Alcohol causes several cancers
        correct: true
      - text: Low-carbohydrate diets produce more long-term weight loss than low-fat diets
    explanation: The low-carb versus low-fat claim is **Not supported** by long-term trials.
  - id: which-uncertain
    prompt: Which of these are graded **Uncertain**?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Whether moderate egg intake raises heart disease risk in healthy people
        correct: true
      - text: The long-term effects of non-sugar sweeteners
        correct: true
      - text: Whether specific emulsifiers harm human gut health
        correct: true
      - text: Whether vitamin C prevents scurvy
    explanation: Vitamin C preventing scurvy is about as Established as nutrition gets.
  - id: which-not
    prompt: Which of these are **Not supported**?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Detox teas remove toxins
        correct: true
      - text: Raw milk is healthier than pasteurised milk
        correct: true
      - text: Cow urine cures cancer
        correct: true
      - text: The alkaline diet changes blood pH
        correct: true
      - text: Sugary drinks contribute to weight gain
    explanation: The link between sugary drinks and weight gain is **Strong**.
  - id: uncertainty-honest
    prompt: Why is saying "we don't know yet" a strength of science, not a weakness?
    options:
      - id: calibrated
        text: Calibrated uncertainty tells you how much weight a claim can bear and where new evidence could change conclusions; false certainty is how people get hurt
        correct: true
      - text: Because scientists never know anything
      - text: Because all opinions are equally valid
    explanation: Admitting uncertainty does not make every alternative claim equally plausible. "We don't know the ideal omega-6 intake" is not the same as "we don't know whether raw milk carries infection risk".
  - id: reversals
    prompt: Which are genuine examples of nutrition advice changing because of better evidence?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Early peanut introduction replacing peanut avoidance for infants (LEAP)
        correct: true
      - text: Removal of the 300 mg/day dietary cholesterol cap from US guidelines in 2015
        correct: true
      - text: Recommendations against beta-carotene supplements after ATBC and CARET
        correct: true
      - text: Abandoning the germ theory of foodborne illness
    explanation: The germ theory has never been abandoned; it underpins all food safety. Real reversals come from better trials, not from social-media trends.
---
## Learning objectives

- Summarise the book's main conclusions by certainty
- Distinguish genuine scientific uncertainty from manufactured doubt

## Established

- Energy balance governs body-fat change; expenditure falls as weight falls
- Deficiency diseases: vitamin C (scurvy), thiamin (beriberi), niacin (pellagra), vitamin D (rickets), B12, iodine,
  iron, vitamin A
- Folic acid prevents neural tube defects; vitamin K at birth prevents bleeding; vegans need B12
- LDL cholesterol causes atherosclerosis; saturated fat raises LDL relative to unsaturated fat
- Industrial trans fats cause heart disease
- Sodium raises blood pressure; DASH lowers it
- Alcohol causes cancer and other harms with dose
- Processed meat causes colorectal cancer (small absolute risk)
- Free sugars cause tooth decay
- Lifestyle change prevents type 2 diabetes in high-risk adults; major weight loss can induce remission
- Pasteurisation prevents milk-borne disease; raw milk carries much higher infection risk
- High-dose beta-carotene increases lung cancer in smokers
- Early peanut introduction reduces peanut allergy in high-risk infants
- Approved GM foods are as safe as conventional foods

## Strong

- High fibre and whole grain intake lowers chronic-disease risk
- Mediterranean-style patterns reduce cardiovascular events
- Sugary drinks promote weight gain and type 2 diabetes
- Fruit, vegetables, legumes and nuts are associated with lower mortality
- Replacing red and processed meat with plant protein lowers risk
- Higher protein helps older adults and people losing weight retain muscle
- Moderate coffee and tea are safe for most adults
- Ultra-processed foods are associated with poor outcomes and can drive overeating

## Uncertain

- Health effects of eggs at moderate intake
- Effects of full-fat versus low-fat dairy
- Long-term effects of sweeteners and emulsifiers
- Role of the gut microbiome in most diseases; probiotics for healthy people
- Benefits of meal timing and fasting beyond calorie reduction
- Optimal vitamin D level; effect on cancer mortality
- Very-low-dose alcohol effects on total mortality
- Precise mechanisms of ultra-processed food harm
- Whether a defended body-weight "set point" exists
- Long-term safety of lifelong GLP-1 therapy

## Not supported

- Detoxes, cleanses, alkaline diets, blood-type diets
- Raw milk health claims
- Cow urine, dung and other sacred-animal medical remedies
- Diet cures for cancer or type 1 diabetes
- Antioxidant supplements for disease prevention
- Seed-oil toxicity at normal intakes
- MSG and sugar-hyperactivity scares
- Homeopathy, colloidal silver, IgG food-intolerance tests

## Sources

This chapter summarises the sources cited in previous chapters.

        correct: true

  - id: individual

    type: multiple

        correct: true

        correct: true

        correct: true

## Learning objectives

- Translate evidence into daily eating
- Read a nutrition label efficiently

## A practical summary

1. **Eat mostly plants** — vegetables, fruit, legumes, whole grains, nuts and seeds
2. **Choose fats well** — prefer olive, canola and other vegetable oils over butter, lard and tallow
3. **Pick protein sources thoughtfully** — legumes, fish, poultry, dairy and eggs; little processed meat
4. **Drink water** — limit sugary drinks; less alcohol is better, none is best for cancer risk
5. **Watch salt** — most comes from packaged and restaurant food
6. **Cook more, from minimally processed ingredients**, when you can
7. **Keep food safe** — pasteurised dairy, thorough cooking, cold storage
8. **Supplement only for a reason** — folic acid in pre-conception, B12 for vegans, vitamin D for infants and at-risk groups
9. **Ignore miracle claims** — no single food, ritual or product saves or ruins your health
10. **Find a pattern you can sustain** — adherence beats perfection

## Reading a label, in order

1. Serving size and servings per container
2. Calories per serving
3. Added sugars, sodium and saturated fat (lower is better)
4. Fibre (higher is better)
5. The ingredients list (first few ingredients make up most of the product)

## Sources

- Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health. Healthy Eating Plate.
- Public Health England. The Eatwell Guide. 2016.
- US FDA. How to understand and use the Nutrition Facts label.
- WHO. Healthy diet fact sheet.
- Drewnowski A. The cost of US foods as related to their nutritive value. *Am J Clin Nutr* 2010.

title: Cumulative review quiz
questions:
  - id: r-kcal
    prompt: A snack contains 10 g protein, 20 g carbohydrate and 10 g fat. Approximately how many kcal does it provide?
    options:
      - text: 160 kcal
      - id: two-ten
        text: 210 kcal
        correct: true
      - text: 400 kcal
    explanation: (10 × 4) + (20 × 4) + (10 × 9) = 40 + 80 + 90 = 210 kcal.

## How to use this review

These questions draw on every chapter. If you miss one, the explanation points to the relevant idea; revisit that
chapter before moving on. Several questions involve arithmetic — converting grams to calories, percentages to
grams, and relative to absolute risk — because numbers are the best defence against vague claims.

## Key numbers to remember

| Quantity | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Energy per gram | Carbohydrate 4, protein 4, fat 9, alcohol 7 kcal |
| Protein RDA | 0.8 g/kg/day |
| Fibre AI | 14 g per 1,000 kcal |
| Saturated fat | Below 10% of energy |
| Free sugars (WHO) | Below 10% of energy, ideally below 5% |
| Sodium (WHO) | Below 2 g/day (5 g salt) |
| Caffeine | Up to about 400 mg/day for healthy adults; below 200 mg in pregnancy |
| Folic acid | 400 µg/day before conception and in early pregnancy |
| Vitamin D | 600 IU adults (RDA); 400 IU breastfed infants |
| US standard drink | 14 g alcohol |
| Poultry cooking temperature | 74 °C (165 °F) |
| Pasteurisation (HTST) | 72 °C for 15 seconds |

FILE: content/books/solid-principles/01-foundations/01-why-design-principles.md
