---
title: Why design principles matter
questions:
  - id: cost-of-change
    prompt: What is the main problem that design principles such as SOLID try to address?
    options:
      - id: change
        text: Keeping the cost of changing software low as it grows
        correct: true
      - text: Making programs run faster on modern hardware
      - text: Reducing the number of classes in a codebase
      - text: Replacing the need for automated tests
    explanation: Most of a system's lifetime cost is change. SOLID is about structuring code so that changes stay local, predictable and cheap.
  - id: coupling-cohesion
    prompt: Which combination usually indicates a healthy design?
    options:
      - id: low-high
        text: Low coupling and high cohesion
        correct: true
      - text: High coupling and high cohesion
      - text: High coupling and low cohesion
      - text: Low coupling and low cohesion
    explanation: Modules should depend on each other as little as possible (low coupling) while the code inside each module should be strongly related (high cohesion).
  - id: rigidity-symptoms
    prompt: Which of these are symptoms of a rotting design?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: A small change forces edits in many unrelated places
        correct: true
      - text: Fixing a bug in one module breaks behaviour in another
        correct: true
      - text: A useful module cannot be reused because it drags in too many dependencies
        correct: true
      - text: The codebase has a comprehensive automated test suite
    explanation: Rigidity, fragility and immobility are the classic symptoms described by Robert C. Martin. A good test suite is a sign of health, not rot.
  - id: solid-origin
    prompt: Who coined the acronym "SOLID" for the principles popularised by Robert C. Martin?
    options:
      - text: Barbara Liskov
      - text: Bertrand Meyer
      - id: feathers
        text: Michael Feathers
        correct: true
      - text: Kent Beck
    explanation: Robert C. Martin described the principles around 2000; Michael Feathers later noticed the letters spelled SOLID.
---
Software rarely fails because it cannot be written. It fails because, after a few years, it can
no longer be **changed** safely. Design principles are a vocabulary for keeping change cheap.

## Learning objectives

- Explain coupling and cohesion and why they matter
- Recognise the symptoms of a design that resists change
- Name the five SOLID principles and their origins

## Coupling and cohesion

**Coupling** measures how much one module knows about another. **Cohesion** measures how
closely the responsibilities inside one module belong together.

```csharp
public class ReportService
{
    public string Build(Order order)
    {
        var connection = new SqlConnection("Server=prod;...");
        var smtp = new SmtpClient("mail.example.com");
        // query the database, format HTML, send e-mail, write a log file...
        return "done";
    }
}
```

This class is tightly coupled to SQL Server, SMTP and the file system, and it has low cohesion:
data access, formatting and delivery are unrelated jobs. Any change in any of those areas touches
this one class, and none of it can be tested without real infrastructure.

## Symptoms of rot

Robert C. Martin described four smells of a decaying design:

| Symptom | What it feels like |
|---------|--------------------|
| Rigidity | Every change cascades into many other changes |
| Fragility | Changes break things in places that seem unrelated |
| Immobility | Useful parts cannot be reused elsewhere |
| Viscosity | Doing the right thing is harder than hacking around it |

## The five principles

| Letter | Principle | One-line idea |
|--------|-----------|---------------|
| S | Single Responsibility | A module should have one reason to change |
| O | Open/Closed | Extend behaviour without modifying existing code |
| L | Liskov Substitution | Subtypes must be usable wherever their base type is expected |
| I | Interface Segregation | Clients should not depend on methods they do not use |
| D | Dependency Inversion | Depend on abstractions, not on concrete details |

The principles were collected by Robert C. Martin around 2000; Michael Feathers noticed the
acronym. Liskov substitution comes from Barbara Liskov (1987) and open/closed from Bertrand Meyer (1988).

> Principles are heuristics, not laws. Each chapter ends with the cost of applying the principle,
> because over-applying SOLID creates its own kind of rigidity.

FILE: content/books/solid-principles/01-foundations/02-abstractions-and-polymorphism.md

---
title: Abstractions and polymorphism in C#
questions:
  - id: interface-vs-abstract
    prompt: Which statement about C# interfaces and abstract classes is correct?
    options:
      - text: A class can inherit from several abstract classes
      - text: Interfaces cannot declare methods with a body in modern C#
      - id: multi-interface
        text: A class can implement many interfaces but inherit from only one class
        correct: true
      - text: Abstract classes cannot contain implemented methods
    explanation: C# has single class inheritance and multiple interface implementation. Since C# 8, interfaces may also contain default implementations.
  - id: polymorphism
    prompt: What does polymorphism let a caller do?
    options:
      - id: same-call
        text: Use one call site that behaves differently depending on the runtime type of the object
        correct: true
      - text: Call private methods of another class
      - text: Avoid declaring types for variables
    explanation: The caller depends only on the abstraction; the concrete type decides what actually happens.
  - id: good-abstraction
    prompt: Which are signs of a good abstraction?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: It is named after what callers need, not after how it is implemented
        correct: true
      - text: It exposes implementation details such as SQL connection strings
      - text: Several different implementations could reasonably satisfy it
        correct: true
      - text: It is small enough to be understood quickly
        correct: true
    explanation: Good abstractions are expressed in the caller's language, hide details and are small enough to implement in more than one way.
---
Every SOLID principle relies on two language features: **abstractions** (interfaces and abstract
classes) and **polymorphism** (calling through an abstraction and letting the runtime type decide).

## Learning objectives

- Choose between an interface and an abstract class
- Use polymorphism to remove type-checking conditionals
- Recognise what makes an abstraction useful

## Interfaces and abstract classes

```csharp
public interface IClock
{
    DateTimeOffset UtcNow { get; }
}

public abstract class Shape
{
    public abstract double Area();
    public override string ToString() => $"{GetType().Name} with area {Area():F2}";
}

public sealed class Circle(double radius) : Shape
{
    public override double Area() => Math.PI * radius * radius;
}
```

| Use an interface when… | Use an abstract class when… |
|------------------------|-----------------------------|
| You describe a capability (`IComparable`, `IDisposable`) | You share real implementation between related types |
| Unrelated types may implement it | Types form a genuine "is-a" family |
| You want a type to have several roles | You need constructors or protected state |

Since C# 8, interfaces may carry **default interface methods**, but they are best kept for
evolving published interfaces, not as a substitute for base classes.

## Polymorphism replaces conditionals

```csharp
double TotalArea(IEnumerable<Shape> shapes) => shapes.Sum(s => s.Area());
```

Compare that with a version that switches on a `Kind` property: every new shape forces a change
to every switch. Polymorphism moves the varying behaviour into the type that owns it.

## What makes a good abstraction

- It is named after the caller's need (`IOrderRepository`, `IClock`), not the technology (`ISqlHelper`)
- It is small — callers can understand it at a glance
- More than one implementation is plausible (including a test double)

> .NET 8 introduced `TimeProvider`, a built-in abstraction for time. Prefer it over hand-rolled
> `IClock` interfaces in new code.

---
title: One reason to change
questions:
  - id: definition
    prompt: In Robert C. Martin's refined wording, a module should be responsible to how many actors?
    options:
      - text: None
      - text: As many as needed, as long as the class is short
      - id: one
        text: One
        correct: true
      - text: Two — the developer and the user
    explanation: "\"A module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor.\" An actor is a group of stakeholders who would request changes for the same reason."
  - id: misconception
    prompt: Which statement about SRP is a misconception?
    options:
      - id: one-method
        text: Every class should have exactly one method
        correct: true
      - text: Code that changes for different reasons should be separated
      - text: Code that changes for the same reason should be kept together
    explanation: SRP is about reasons to change, not about counting methods. A cohesive class can have many methods serving one actor.
  - id: actors
    prompt: "An `Employee` class has `CalculatePay()` (used by finance), `ReportHours()` (used by operations) and `Save()` (owned by the DBA team). Which statements are true?"
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: The class serves three different actors
        correct: true
      - text: A change requested by finance could accidentally break the operations report
        correct: true
      - text: The class satisfies SRP because each method is short
      - text: Splitting by actor reduces the chance of accidental coupling
        correct: true
    explanation: This is Martin's own example. Three actors means three reasons to change living in one class.
---
The **Single Responsibility Principle** is the most quoted and most misunderstood SOLID principle.

## Learning objectives

- State SRP in terms of actors and reasons to change
- Identify mixed responsibilities in a class
- Avoid the "one method per class" misreading

## The definition

The original wording was *"a class should have only one reason to change."* Martin later sharpened
it: **a module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor.** An actor is a group of people
— finance, operations, a compliance team — who request changes for the same reason.

## A class with three masters

```csharp
public class Employee
{
    public decimal CalculatePay() { /* rules owned by finance */ return 0; }
    public string ReportHours()   { /* format owned by operations */ return ""; }
    public void Save()            { /* schema owned by the DBA team */ }
}
```

Suppose `CalculatePay` and `ReportHours` share a private helper `RegularHours()`. Finance asks
for a change to how overtime is counted, a developer updates the helper, and the operations
report silently changes too. Nobody asked for that.

## Separating by actor

```csharp
public sealed record EmployeeData(int Id, string Name, IReadOnlyList<TimeEntry> Entries);

public sealed class PayCalculator      { public decimal Calculate(EmployeeData e) => 0; }
public sealed class HoursReporter      { public string Report(EmployeeData e) => ""; }
public sealed class EmployeeRepository { public Task SaveAsync(EmployeeData e) => Task.CompletedTask; }
```

Each class now changes for one reason. The shared data is a plain record with no behaviour that
could couple the actors together.

## Finding responsibilities

Useful questions when reviewing a class:

- Who would ask for this code to change? If the answer is several unrelated groups, split.
- Does the class name need "And" or "Manager" to describe it?
- Do its tests need very different kinds of setup (a database *and* an SMTP server)?

> SRP applies at every level: functions, classes, modules and services. The same reasoning that
> splits a class also tells you where to draw microservice boundaries.

---
title: Refactoring toward SRP
questions:
  - id: first-step
    prompt: Before splitting a large class with mixed responsibilities, what should you have in place?
    options:
      - text: A new database schema
      - text: A microservice for each responsibility
      - id: tests
        text: Tests that pin down its current behaviour
        correct: true
      - text: A dependency injection container
    explanation: Characterisation tests let you refactor with confidence that behaviour has not changed.
  - id: facade
    prompt: After extracting responsibilities, existing callers still call `OrderProcessor.Process`. What is the role of `OrderProcessor` now?
    options:
      - text: It is dead code that should be deleted
      - id: coordinator
        text: A thin coordinator that delegates to focused collaborators
        correct: true
      - text: A violation of SRP because it calls several classes
    explanation: Orchestrating focused collaborators is itself a single responsibility — the workflow.
  - id: over-split
    prompt: Which are risks of splitting responsibilities too aggressively?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Logic that always changes together ends up scattered across many files
        correct: true
      - text: Readers must jump through many tiny classes to understand one behaviour
        correct: true
      - text: The compiler refuses to build classes with fewer than three methods
    explanation: Over-splitting lowers cohesion. Keep together what changes together.
---
Knowing the principle is easy; applying it to a 900-line class is the real skill.

## Learning objectives

- Refactor a mixed-responsibility class in small, safe steps
- Keep an orchestrating class thin
- Recognise when splitting has gone too far

## The starting point

```csharp
public class OrderProcessor
{
    public async Task ProcessAsync(Order order)
    {
        if (order.Lines.Count == 0) throw new InvalidOperationException("Empty order");
        var total = order.Lines.Sum(l => l.Price * l.Quantity);
        if (order.Customer.IsVip) total *= 0.9m;

        await using var connection = new SqlConnection(_connectionString);
        await connection.ExecuteAsync("INSERT INTO Orders ...", new { order.Id, total });

        using var smtp = new SmtpClient("mail.example.com");
        await smtp.SendMailAsync("shop@example.com", order.Customer.Email, "Thanks", $"Total {total}");
    }
}
```

Validation, pricing, persistence and notification all live together.

## Step 1 — pin the behaviour

Write characterisation tests around `ProcessAsync` (with a test database or by first extracting
seams). Refactoring without tests is just editing.

## Step 2 — extract one responsibility at a time

```csharp
public interface IPricingPolicy { decimal Total(Order order); }
public interface IOrderRepository { Task AddAsync(Order order, decimal total, CancellationToken ct); }
public interface IOrderNotifier { Task OrderPlacedAsync(Order order, decimal total, CancellationToken ct); }

public sealed class OrderProcessor(
    IPricingPolicy pricing,
    IOrderRepository orders,
    IOrderNotifier notifier)
{
    public async Task ProcessAsync(Order order, CancellationToken ct = default)
    {
        OrderValidator.EnsureValid(order);
        var total = pricing.Total(order);
        await orders.AddAsync(order, total, ct);
        await notifier.OrderPlacedAsync(order, total, ct);
    }
}
```

`OrderProcessor` still exists, but its only job is the **workflow**. Each collaborator can be
tested and replaced on its own.

## Knowing when to stop

Stop splitting when the pieces would always change together. A `PricingPolicy` that contains the
VIP discount, the volume discount and rounding rules is cohesive: all of it belongs to the people
who own pricing.

> Rule of thumb: separate code that changes for different reasons; keep together code that
> changes for the same reason. Both halves of the rule matter.

FILE: content/books/solid-principles/03-open-closed/01-open-for-extension.md

---
title: Open for extension, closed for modification
questions:
  - id: meaning
    prompt: What does "closed for modification" mean in practice?
    options:
      - text: The source file is marked read-only in source control
      - text: The class must be declared `sealed`
      - text: The code can never be changed, even to fix bugs
      - id: no-edit
        text: Adding a new variant of behaviour should not require editing existing, tested code
        correct: true
    explanation: Bugs still get fixed. OCP is about extending behaviour by adding new code rather than repeatedly editing a central switch.
  - id: smell
    prompt: Which code shape most often signals an OCP violation?
    options:
      - text: A class with a primary constructor
      - text: An interface with a single method
      - id: switch
        text: A `switch` on a type code that is duplicated across several methods
        correct: true
    explanation: Every new type code forces edits to every copy of the switch. Polymorphism or a lookup of strategies removes that.
  - id: meyer
    prompt: Who first formulated the open/closed principle?
    options:
      - text: Barbara Liskov, in a 1987 keynote
      - id: meyer
        text: Bertrand Meyer, in Object-Oriented Software Construction (1988)
        correct: true
      - text: Martin Fowler, in Refactoring (1999)
    explanation: Meyer described it using inheritance; Robert C. Martin later reframed it around abstractions and polymorphism.
  - id: mechanisms
    prompt: Which C# mechanisms can make code open for extension?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Interfaces with multiple implementations
        correct: true
      - text: Delegates such as `Func<T, TResult>` passed in by the caller
        correct: true
      - text: Registering implementations in a dependency injection container
        correct: true
      - text: Copying the class and editing the copy
    explanation: Interfaces, delegates and DI registrations all let you add behaviour without touching existing code. Copy-and-edit duplicates code instead.
---
## Learning objectives

- Explain the open/closed principle and its history
- Replace type-code switches with polymorphism
- Choose the right extension point instead of making everything pluggable

## The problem

```csharp
public decimal Shipping(Order order) => order.Method switch
{
    "standard" => 4.99m,
    "express"  => 14.99m,
    "pickup"   => 0m,
    _ => throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(order))
};
```

On its own this is fine. It becomes a problem when the same `switch` appears in `EstimatedDays`,
`Label` and `CanShipTo`. Adding "drone" means finding and editing every copy.

## Making it open

```csharp
public interface IShippingMethod
{
    string Code { get; }
    decimal Cost(Order order);
    int EstimatedDays(Address destination);
}

public sealed class ExpressShipping : IShippingMethod
{
    public string Code => "express";
    public decimal Cost(Order order) => 14.99m;
    public int EstimatedDays(Address destination) => 1;
}

public sealed class ShippingCalculator(IEnumerable<IShippingMethod> methods)
{
    private readonly Dictionary<string, IShippingMethod> _byCode =
        methods.ToDictionary(m => m.Code, StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

    public decimal Cost(Order order) =>
        _byCode.TryGetValue(order.Method, out var method)
            ? method.Cost(order)
            : throw new UnknownShippingMethodException(order.Method);
}
```

Adding drone delivery is now a new class plus one registration:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IShippingMethod, DroneShipping>();
```

`ShippingCalculator` is **closed**: it never changes. The system is **open**: it gains behaviour.

## Strategic closure

No design is closed against every change. Predict which axis is likely to vary — new shipping
methods, new report formats — and make *that* axis open. Wait for the second or third real
variation before introducing the abstraction; until then, a simple `switch` is easier to read.

title: Strategies, decorators and pipelines

    explanation: A decorator implements the same interface, wraps the original and adds behaviour before or after delegating.
  - id: pipeline

    options:
      - id: middleware
        text: The middleware pipeline, where new behaviour is added with `app.Use...` calls
        correct: true
      - text: Hard-coding authentication inside every controller action
      - text: The `web.config` file
    explanation: New middleware extends request processing without modifying the framework or existing middleware.
  - id: strategy-facts
    prompt: Which statements about the strategy pattern are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: It encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface
        correct: true
      - text: In C#, a simple strategy can be a delegate such as `Func<Order, decimal>`
        correct: true
      - text: It requires inheritance from a common abstract base class
    explanation: An interface or a delegate is enough; no base class is needed.

## Learning objectives

- Apply the strategy and decorator patterns to achieve OCP
- Recognise pipeline-style extensibility in .NET
- Use delegates when an interface would be overkill

## Strategy

A strategy is an interchangeable algorithm. In modern C#, a delegate is often the lightest strategy:

```csharp
public sealed class PriceCalculator(Func<Order, decimal> discount)
{
    public decimal Total(Order order) => order.Subtotal - discount(order);
}

var blackFriday = new PriceCalculator(o => o.Subtotal * 0.25m);
var none = new PriceCalculator(_ => 0m);
```

Use an interface when the strategy has several members, needs dependencies, or deserves a name.

## Decorator

A decorator wraps an implementation of the same interface:

```csharp
public sealed class CachedProductRepository(IProductRepository inner, IMemoryCache cache)
    : IProductRepository
{
    public async Task<Product?> GetAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct) =>
        await cache.GetOrCreateAsync($"product:{id}", _ => inner.GetAsync(id, ct));
}
```

The original repository is unchanged, and caching can be removed by changing one registration.
Cross-cutting concerns — caching, logging, retries, metrics — are natural decorators.

## Pipelines

ASP.NET Core's middleware is OCP at framework scale:

```csharp
app.UseExceptionHandler();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    context.Response.Headers["X-Content-Type-Options"] = "nosniff";
    await next(context);
});
```

Each `Use` adds behaviour around the next step. The same idea appears in `HttpClient`
`DelegatingHandler`s and in MediatR-style pipeline behaviours.

> Patterns are tools for OCP, not goals. If only one implementation will ever exist, the
> abstraction adds indirection without paying for itself.

title: Behavioural subtyping
questions:
  - id: definition
    prompt: What does the Liskov Substitution Principle require?
    options:
      - text: Every subclass must override every virtual method
      - text: Subclasses must not add new methods
      - id: substitutable
        text: Objects of a subtype must be usable wherever the base type is expected without breaking the program's correctness
        correct: true
      - text: A base class must know about all of its subclasses
    explanation: LSP is about behaviour. Code written against the base type must keep working when handed any subtype.
  - id: contracts
    prompt: According to design-by-contract rules for subtypes, which are correct?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: A subtype must not strengthen preconditions
        correct: true
      - text: A subtype must not weaken postconditions
        correct: true
      - text: A subtype must preserve the invariants of the base type
        correct: true
      - text: A subtype may throw new kinds of exceptions that callers of the base type do not expect
    explanation: Subtypes may demand less and promise more, never the reverse. Unexpected exceptions break callers.
  - id: square
    prompt: "Why is `Square : Rectangle` (with settable `Width` and `Height`) a classic LSP violation?"
    options:
      - text: Squares have fewer sides than rectangles
      - id: setter
        text: Code that sets width and height independently, then checks the area, breaks for a square
        correct: true
      - text: C# does not allow a class to inherit from a class with properties
    explanation: A mutable square must keep width equal to height, which violates the rectangle's implicit promise that the two vary independently.
  - id: year
    prompt: When did Barbara Liskov introduce the idea in a keynote titled "Data Abstraction and Hierarchy"?
    options:
      - text: "1972"
      - id: y1987
        text: "1987"
        correct: true
      - text: "2000"
    explanation: The 1987 OOPSLA keynote introduced it; Liskov and Jeannette Wing formalised it in 1994.
---
## Learning objectives

- State LSP and its contract rules
- Spot "is-a" relationships that are not behaviourally substitutable
- Use tests to verify substitutability

## The principle

Barbara Liskov introduced the idea in 1987. Informally: **if code works with a base type, it must
keep working with any subtype.** "Is-a" in the real world is not enough — the subtype must keep
the base type's *behavioural* promises.

## The rectangle and the square

```csharp
public class Rectangle
{
    public virtual int Width { get; set; }
    public virtual int Height { get; set; }
    public int Area => Width * Height;
}

public class Square : Rectangle
{
    public override int Width  { set { base.Width = value; base.Height = value; } }
    public override int Height { set { base.Width = value; base.Height = value; } }
}

void Resize(Rectangle r)
{
    r.Width = 5;
    r.Height = 4;
    Debug.Assert(r.Area == 20);
}
```

`Resize(new Square())` produces an area of 16. Geometrically a square *is* a rectangle; as a
**mutable** object it does not honour the rectangle's contract.

The fix is to not model it with inheritance — for example, immutable records with a shared
`IShape` interface:

```csharp
public interface IShape { double Area { get; } }
public sealed record Rect(double Width, double Height) : IShape { public double Area => Width * Height; }
public sealed record Sq(double Side) : IShape { public double Area => Side * Side; }
```

## The contract rules

| Rule | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| Preconditions cannot be strengthened | A subtype cannot demand more from callers |
| Postconditions cannot be weakened | A subtype cannot promise less |
| Invariants must be preserved | What is always true of the base stays true |
| No new unexpected exceptions | Callers should not need to catch surprises |
| History constraint | A subtype cannot allow state changes the base forbids |

## Testing substitutability

Write the base type's contract as an abstract test class and run it against every implementation:

```csharp
public abstract class ShapeContractTests
{
    protected abstract IShape Create();

    [Fact]
    public void Area_is_never_negative() => Assert.True(Create().Area >= 0);
}

public sealed class RectTests : ShapeContractTests { protected override IShape Create() => new Rect(2, 3); }
```

title: LSP in the .NET libraries
questions:
  - id: readonly-collection
    prompt: "`ReadOnlyCollection<T>` implements `ICollection<T>`. What happens when you call `Add` on it through the `ICollection<T>` interface?"
    options:
      - text: The item is added silently
      - id: throws
        text: It throws `NotSupportedException`
        correct: true
      - text: It does nothing and returns false
      - text: It fails to compile
    explanation: "The interface promises `Add`, but the implementation refuses it. Callers must check `IsReadOnly` — a widely cited LSP smell in the BCL."
  - id: stream
    prompt: How does `System.IO.Stream` reduce surprises for callers when not every stream supports every operation?
    options:
      - text: It forbids subclasses from throwing any exception
      - text: It provides separate abstract classes for every combination of capabilities
      - id: capability
        text: It exposes capability properties such as `CanRead`, `CanWrite` and `CanSeek` as part of its contract
        correct: true
    explanation: Because the capability checks are part of the documented contract, a caller who honours them is not surprised. Splitting into smaller interfaces would be the ISP-style alternative.
  - id: fixes
    prompt: Which are good ways to fix a subtype that cannot support an inherited operation?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Split the base interface so the subtype only implements what it supports
        correct: true
      - text: Replace inheritance with composition
        correct: true
      - text: Override the method to throw `NotImplementedException` and hope nobody calls it
    explanation: Throwing from an inherited member pushes the problem onto every caller. Narrower interfaces or composition remove it at the source.
---
## Learning objectives

- Recognise LSP trade-offs in the base class library
- Distinguish "refused bequest" from legitimate capability checks
- Fix violations with narrower interfaces or composition

## A famous compromise

```csharp
ICollection<int> numbers = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 }.AsReadOnly();
numbers.Add(4); // NotSupportedException
```

`ICollection<T>` has an `IsReadOnly` property, so technically the contract allows refusal. In
practice, many callers never check it, which is why later versions of .NET added
`IReadOnlyCollection<T>` and `IReadOnlyList<T>`. Prefer those in your own APIs:

```csharp
public IReadOnlyList<OrderLine> Lines => _lines;
```

## Capability properties

`Stream` exposes `CanRead`, `CanWrite`, `CanSeek` and `CanTimeout`. A network stream throws
`NotSupportedException` from `Seek`, but only after declaring `CanSeek == false`. Code that
honours the capability flags keeps working with any stream, so the contract holds.

## Refused bequest

When a subclass inherits a member it does not want and throws from it, that is a **refused
bequest**:

```csharp
public class Bird { public virtual void Fly() { } }
public class Penguin : Bird
{
    public override void Fly() => throw new NotSupportedException();
}
```

## Fixing it

```csharp
public abstract class Bird { public abstract void Eat(); }
public interface IFlyer { void Fly(); }

public sealed class Sparrow : Bird, IFlyer { public override void Eat() { } public void Fly() { } }
public sealed class Penguin : Bird { public override void Eat() { } }
```

Code that needs flight asks for `IFlyer`. The compiler now prevents the bug that the exception
used to report at runtime — and that is LSP and ISP working together.

title: Client-specific interfaces
questions:
  - id: definition
    prompt: What does the Interface Segregation Principle state?
    options:
      - text: Every class must implement exactly one interface
      - id: clients
        text: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use
        correct: true
      - text: Interfaces must live in a separate assembly from their implementations
      - text: Interfaces should never inherit from other interfaces
    explanation: Fat interfaces couple clients to members they never call, so changes to those members ripple into unrelated clients.
  - id: who-owns
    prompt: Who should an interface be shaped around?
    options:
      - text: The class that implements it
      - text: The database schema
      - id: client
        text: The client that uses it
        correct: true
    explanation: Interfaces describe what a client needs. One implementation can satisfy several client-shaped interfaces.
  - id: symptoms
    prompt: Which are symptoms of a fat interface?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Implementations throw `NotImplementedException` for several members
        correct: true
      - text: Test doubles must stub many methods the test never touches
        correct: true
      - text: Most clients call only a small subset of the members
        correct: true
      - text: The interface has a descriptive name
    explanation: Unused members show up as stubs, throwing implementations and clients that only use a slice of the interface.
---
## Learning objectives

- State the interface segregation principle
- Split a fat interface into role interfaces
- Let one class implement several small interfaces

## A fat interface

```csharp
public interface IMultiFunctionDevice
{
    void Print(Document d);
    void Scan(Document d);
    void Fax(Document d);
    void Staple(Document d);
}

public sealed class BasicPrinter : IMultiFunctionDevice
{
    public void Print(Document d) { /* ... */ }
    public void Scan(Document d)   => throw new NotImplementedException();
    public void Fax(Document d)    => throw new NotImplementedException();
    public void Staple(Document d) => throw new NotImplementedException();
}
```

`BasicPrinter` is forced to lie, and every client that only prints still recompiles and redeploys
whenever the fax signature changes.

## Segregated interfaces

```csharp
public interface IPrinter { void Print(Document d); }
public interface IScanner { void Scan(Document d); }
public interface IFax     { void Fax(Document d); }

public sealed class BasicPrinter : IPrinter { public void Print(Document d) { } }
public sealed class OfficeMachine : IPrinter, IScanner, IFax
{
    public void Print(Document d) { }
    public void Scan(Document d) { }
    public void Fax(Document d) { }
}
```

The same `OfficeMachine` instance can be registered under several interfaces:

```csharp
builder.Services.AddSingleton<OfficeMachine>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IPrinter>(sp => sp.GetRequiredService<OfficeMachine>());
builder.Services.AddSingleton<IScanner>(sp => sp.GetRequiredService<OfficeMachine>());
```

## ISP and LSP

Fat interfaces tend to cause LSP violations, because implementations throw for members they cannot
support. Segregation removes the temptation: if you cannot fax, you simply do not implement `IFax`.

## Learning objectives

- Split repositories and services by how they are used
- Recognise role interfaces in the base class library
- Avoid over-fragmentation

## Read and write roles

```csharp
public interface IOrderReader
{
    Task<OrderDto?> FindAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct);
    Task<IReadOnlyList<OrderSummary>> ListForCustomerAsync(int customerId, CancellationToken ct);
}

public interface IOrderWriter
{
    Task<int> AddAsync(Order order, CancellationToken ct);
    Task CancelAsync(int id, CancellationToken ct);
}

public sealed class SqlOrderStore : IOrderReader, IOrderWriter { /* ... */ }
```

The reporting page asks for `IOrderReader`. It cannot accidentally write, and its tests only need
a fake with two methods.

## Interfaces in the base class library

The BCL is full of tiny role interfaces: `IDisposable` (one method), `IAsyncDisposable`,
`IComparable<T>`, `IEquatable<T>`, `IEnumerable<T>`. Their smallness is exactly why so many types
can implement them and so much generic code can rely on them.

## Interfaces shaped for consumers

```csharp
public sealed class InvoiceEmailer(IOrderReader orders, IEmailSender email)
{
    public async Task SendAsync(int orderId, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var order = await orders.FindAsync(orderId, ct) ?? throw new OrderNotFoundException(orderId);
        await email.SendAsync(order.CustomerEmail, "Your invoice", InvoiceTemplate.Render(order), ct);
    }
}
```

## Balance

Do not create an interface per method by reflex. Group members by the clients that use them
together. A good test: could you describe the interface's role in a short noun phrase —
"order reader", "email sender"? If so, it is probably the right size.

title: Inverting dependencies
questions:
  - id: definition
    prompt: Which pair of statements makes up the Dependency Inversion Principle?
    options:
      - text: Classes should create their own dependencies; dependencies should be static.
      - id: dip
        text: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. Abstractions should not depend on details; details should depend on abstractions.
        correct: true
      - text: Every class must be registered in a container; every constructor must take an interface.
    explanation: This is Robert C. Martin's two-part formulation.
  - id: ownership
    prompt: In a design that follows DIP, which layer should own the `IOrderRepository` interface?
    options:
      - text: The infrastructure layer that contains the SQL implementation
      - text: A shared "Interfaces" project referenced by everything
      - id: application
        text: The domain or application layer that uses it
        correct: true
    explanation: The inversion is about source-code dependency direction. The policy layer defines the abstraction; the detail implements it and depends on the policy layer.
  - id: not-same
    prompt: Which statements are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: Dependency injection is a technique that helps implement dependency inversion
        correct: true
      - text: You can follow DIP without using a DI container
        correct: true
      - text: Using a DI container automatically means you follow DIP
      - text: "`new`-ing up a stable type like `List<T>` violates DIP"
    explanation: A container is optional plumbing. DIP is about the direction of dependencies on volatile details; stable framework types are fine to depend on directly.
---
## Learning objectives

- State the dependency inversion principle
- Explain which layer owns an abstraction
- Distinguish DIP, dependency injection and DI containers

## The problem

```csharp
public sealed class CheckoutService
{
    private readonly SqlOrderRepository _orders = new("Server=prod;...");
    private readonly StripeGateway _payments = new("sk_live_...");
}
```

Checkout — the business policy — depends on SQL Server and Stripe. To test it you need both; to
change payment providers you must edit the business logic.

## The principle

> High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.
> Abstractions should not depend on details. Details should depend on abstractions.

```csharp
namespace Shop.Application;

public interface IOrderRepository { Task AddAsync(Order order, CancellationToken ct); }
public interface IPaymentGateway { Task<PaymentResult> ChargeAsync(Money amount, CardToken card, CancellationToken ct); }

public sealed class CheckoutService(IOrderRepository orders, IPaymentGateway payments)
{
    public async Task CheckoutAsync(Cart cart, CardToken card, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var result = await payments.ChargeAsync(cart.Total, card, ct);
        if (!result.Succeeded) throw new PaymentDeclinedException(result.Reason);
        await orders.AddAsync(Order.From(cart, result.TransactionId), ct);
    }
}
```

```csharp
namespace Shop.Infrastructure;

public sealed class StripePaymentGateway(StripeClient client) : Application.IPaymentGateway { /* ... */ }
```

## Why "inversion"

Without DIP, source-code dependencies point the same way as the flow of control: policy → detail.
With DIP, the interface lives *with the policy*, so the infrastructure project references the
application project — the source-code arrow is **inverted** against the flow of control.

## DIP, DI and containers

| Term | What it is |
|------|------------|
| Dependency inversion | A design principle about dependency *direction* |
| Dependency injection | A technique: pass dependencies in, usually through the constructor |
| DI container | A library that builds object graphs (e.g. `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection`) |

You can follow DIP with plain constructor calls in `Main`. A container is a convenience.

> Do not abstract everything. `List<T>`, `string` and `DateOnly` are stable; depend on them
> directly. Invert dependencies on things that are **volatile**: databases, networks, clocks,
> file systems, third-party services.

FILE: content/books/solid-principles/06-dependency-inversion/02-composition-root.md

---
title: The composition root and DI containers
questions:
  - id: composition-root
    prompt: Where should object graphs be composed in an ASP.NET Core application?
    options:
      - text: Inside each domain class, using `new`
      - text: In a static `ServiceLocator` called from anywhere
      - id: program

        correct: true
    explanation: The composition root is the one place that knows about concrete implementations. Everywhere else depends on abstractions.
  - id: service-locator
    prompt: Why is calling `serviceProvider.GetService<T>()` from deep inside business classes considered an anti-pattern?
    options:
      - text: It is slower than reflection
      - id: hidden
        text: It hides dependencies, so a class's constructor no longer tells you what it needs
        correct: true
      - text: It is not supported in .NET 10
    explanation: Service location makes dependencies implicit, harder to test and easy to get wrong at runtime.
  - id: lifetimes
    prompt: Which statements about Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection lifetimes are true?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: A singleton is created once for the root container
        correct: true
      - text: In ASP.NET Core, a scoped service is created once per HTTP request
        correct: true
      - text: A transient service is created every time it is resolved
        correct: true
      - text: Injecting a scoped service into a singleton is always safe
    explanation: A singleton holding a scoped service keeps it alive beyond its scope — a captive dependency. Scope validation in Development detects this.
---
## Learning objectives

- Compose object graphs in a single composition root
- Avoid the service locator anti-pattern
- Pick correct lifetimes and avoid captive dependencies

## The composition root

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, SqlOrderRepository>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IPaymentGateway, StripePaymentGateway>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<CheckoutService>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton(TimeProvider.System);

var app = builder.Build();
app.MapPost("/checkout", (CheckoutRequest req, CheckoutService checkout, CancellationToken ct) =>
    checkout.CheckoutAsync(req.Cart, req.Card, ct));
app.Run();
```

Only `Program.cs` knows that `IPaymentGateway` means Stripe. Swapping providers is a one-line change.

## Lifetimes

| Lifetime | Created | Typical use |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| Singleton | Once | Stateless services, caches, `TimeProvider` |
| Scoped | Once per scope (per request in ASP.NET Core) | `DbContext`, unit of work |
| Transient | Every resolution | Lightweight stateless helpers |

A **captive dependency** happens when a longer-lived service holds a shorter-lived one, such as a
singleton holding a `DbContext`. ASP.NET Core enables scope validation in the Development
environment, which throws when a scoped service is resolved from the root provider.

## Service locator

```csharp
public sealed class CheckoutService(IServiceProvider services)
{
    public Task CheckoutAsync(Cart cart) =>
        services.GetRequiredService<IPaymentGateway>().ChargeAsync(/* ... */);
}
```

The constructor lies about what the class needs. Ask for `IPaymentGateway` directly instead.
Resolving from `IServiceProvider` is acceptable only in infrastructure code such as factories and
middleware, where creating scopes is the actual job.

title: "Case study: a notification service"
questions:
  - id: which-principle

  - id: lsp-check
    prompt: "`PushChannel.SendAsync` silently does nothing when the user has no device registered, while other channels throw. Which principle is at risk?"
    options:

      - id: lsp

    type: multiple

        correct: true
      - text: The service can be tested with fake channels and no network
        correct: true
      - text: New channels require no changes to the dispatcher
        correct: true
      - text: The number of classes in the system decreased
    explanation: The design traded a few more types for isolation, testability and extensibility.
---
## Learning objectives

- Apply the five principles together on a realistic example
- Recognise which principle each design decision supports

## Before

```csharp
public class NotificationService
{
    public void Notify(User user, string message)
    {
        if (user.PrefersEmail)
            new SmtpClient("smtp.example.com").Send("noreply@example.com", user.Email, "Notice", message);
        else if (user.PrefersSms)
            TwilioClient.Send(user.Phone, message);
        File.AppendAllText("notifications.log", $"{DateTime.Now}: {user.Id} {message}\n");
    }
}
```

## After

```csharp
public sealed record DeliveryResult(bool Delivered, string? Reason = null);

public interface INotificationChannel
{
    string Name { get; }
    bool CanDeliverTo(User user);
    Task<DeliveryResult> SendAsync(User user, string message, CancellationToken ct);
}

public sealed class EmailChannel(IEmailSender sender) : INotificationChannel
{
    public string Name => "email";
    public bool CanDeliverTo(User user) => user.PrefersEmail && user.Email is not null;
    public async Task<DeliveryResult> SendAsync(User user, string message, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        await sender.SendAsync(user.Email!, "Notice", message, ct);
        return new DeliveryResult(true);
    }
}

public sealed partial class NotificationService(
    IEnumerable<INotificationChannel> channels,
    ILogger<NotificationService> logger)
{
    public async Task NotifyAsync(User user, string message, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        foreach (var channel in channels.Where(c => c.CanDeliverTo(user)))
        {
            var result = await channel.SendAsync(user, message, ct);
            LogDelivery(user.Id, channel.Name, result.Delivered);
        }
    }

    [LoggerMessage(Level = LogLevel.Information, Message = "Notified {UserId} via {Channel}: {Delivered}")]
    private partial void LogDelivery(int userId, string channel, bool delivered);
}
```

## Mapping decisions to principles

| Decision | Principle |
|----------|-----------|
| Each channel has its own class | SRP |
| New channels are new classes plus a registration | OCP |
| Every channel returns a `DeliveryResult` instead of throwing or silently skipping | LSP |
| `IEmailSender` exposes only sending, not mailbox management | ISP |
| `NotificationService` depends on interfaces composed in `Program.cs` | DIP |

FILE: content/books/solid-principles/07-solid-in-practice/02-pitfalls-and-balance.md
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
---
title: Pitfalls and balance
questions:
  - id: yagni
    prompt: You are writing the first and only implementation of a report exporter, and there is no known need for another. What is the most pragmatic choice?
    options:
      - text: Create an interface, an abstract base class, a factory and a plugin loader up front
      - text: Put the exporter code directly in the controller
      - id: simple
        text: Write the concrete class cleanly and extract an abstraction when a second need appears
        correct: true
    explanation: YAGNI — "you aren't gonna need it". Clean concrete code is easy to refactor later; speculative abstractions cost something every day.
  - id: header-interfaces
    prompt: What is a "header interface"?
    options:
      - id: mirror
        text: An interface that mirrors every public member of a single class, created by reflex rather than from client needs
        correct: true
      - text: An interface that only declares properties
      - text: An interface declared at the top of a file
    explanation: Header interfaces add indirection without providing a real abstraction. They often violate ISP because they are shaped around the implementation.
  - id: when-apply
    prompt: Which situations justify investing in SOLID-style abstractions?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - text: The code talks to volatile infrastructure such as databases, queues or third-party APIs
        correct: true
      - text: There are already two or three variations of the same behaviour
        correct: true
      - text: You need to unit test business rules without real infrastructure
        correct: true
      - text: A one-off script that will be deleted next week
    explanation: Abstractions pay for themselves where change, variation or testing pressure exists.
---
## Learning objectives

- Recognise over-engineering driven by SOLID
- Apply YAGNI and the rule of three
- Decide when an abstraction pays for itself

## Over-engineering

The most common failure with SOLID is not ignoring it — it is applying it everywhere:

```csharp
public interface IStringFormatterFactoryProvider
{
    IStringFormatterFactory GetFactory(FormatterKind kind);
}
```

If there is one formatter and no plan for another, every reader now navigates three files to
discover that a string is upper-cased.

## Useful counterweights

| Heuristic | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|
| YAGNI | Do not build for needs you do not have yet |
| Rule of three | Extract an abstraction on the third repetition, not the first |
| KISS | The simplest design that works is usually the right first design |
| Keep things that change together, together | Cohesion beats fragmentation |

## Header interfaces

Creating `IFoo` for every `Foo`, with identical members, is a ritual, not a design. Abstractions
should come from **clients** (ISP) and from **volatility** (DIP). Modern mocking libraries and
in-memory fakes mean you rarely need an interface purely for testing a stable, pure class.

## A practical checklist

- Does this code depend on something volatile? → invert the dependency
- Do I already have variations? → introduce a strategy or polymorphism
- Would a change requested by one group break another? → split responsibilities
- Are implementations throwing for members they cannot support? → segregate interfaces
- None of the above? → write clear, concrete code and move on

> SOLID is a means to an end: code that is easy to understand, test and change.

title: Where geothermal energy comes from
questions:
- id: q1
  prompt: What are the two sources of geothermal energy?
  type: multiple
  options:
  - text: "Heat trickling through the mantle from the earth's core"
    correct: true
  - text: Friction from ocean currents
  - text: Sunlight absorbed by the ground
  - text: "Radioactive decay in the earth's crust"
    correct: true
  explanation: "**p. 96:** “Geothermal energy comes from two sources: from radioactive decay in the crust of the earth, and from heat trickling through the mantle from the earth’s core.”"
- id: q2
  prompt: "Besides the earth's original heat, what tops up the heat in the core?"
  options:
  - text: Burning of fossil fuels
  - text: "Tidal friction, as the earth flexes under the moon's and sun's gravity"
    correct: true
  - text: Volcanic eruptions
  - text: Cosmic rays
  explanation: "**p. 96:** “the heat in the core is also being topped up by tidal friction: the earth flexes in response to the gravitational fields of the moon and sun”."
- id: q3
  prompt: Why is geothermal an attractive renewable?
  options:
  - text: It is the cheapest form of energy
  - text: It works best in Britain
  - text: "It is \"always on\", independent of the weather, and can follow demand"
    correct: true
  - text: It requires no drilling
  explanation: "**p. 96:** “Geothermal is an attractive renewable because it is ‘always on,’ independent of the weather; if we make geothermal power stations, we can switch them on and off so as to follow demand.”"
- id: q4
  prompt: What analogy does MacKay use for unsustainable geothermal extraction?
  options:
  - text: Sucking a crushed-ice drink through a straw until you get air
    correct: true
  - text: Squeezing an orange
  - text: Draining a bath
  - text: Charging a battery
  explanation: "**p. 96:** “It’s like trying to drink a crushed-ice drink through a straw … after a little more sucking, you find you’re sucking air.”"
- id: q5
  prompt: What limits the rate at which heat can be sustainably extracted?
  options:
  - text: The speed at which heat travels through solid rock
    correct: true
  - text: The depth we can drill
  - text: The boiling point of water
  - text: The cost of pumps
  explanation: "**p. 96:** “the speed at which heat travels through solid rock limits the rate at which heat can be sustainably sucked out of the red-hot interior of the earth.”"
- id: q6
  prompt: What average geothermal electricity did Iceland generate in 2006?
  options:
  - text: "300 MW — 24 kWh/d per person"
    correct: true
  - text: "30 MW — 2.4 kWh/d per person"
  - text: "300 kW"
  - text: "3000 MW — 240 kWh/d per person"
  explanation: "**Figure 16.3, p. 97:** “Average geothermal electricity generation in Iceland (population, 300 000) in 2006 was 300 MW (24 kWh/d per person). More than half of Iceland’s electricity is used for aluminium production.”"

title: Geothermal power that would be sustainable forever

    correct: true
  explanation: "**p. 97:** “the heat flow from the centre coming through the mantle is about 10 mW/m2. The heat flow at the surface is 50 mW/m2. So the radioactive decay has added an extra 40 mW/m2”."

  - text: It is too high-grade
  - text: It is radioactive

  - text: About 1400 °C

  explanation: "**p. 97:** “The temperature increases with depth … reaching a temperature of about 500 ◦C at a depth of 40 km.”"

  - text: About 15 km — 17 mW/m²
    correct: true
  explanation: "**p. 98:** “I calculated that the optimal depth is about 15 km. Under these conditions, an ideal heat engine would deliver 17 mW/m2.”"
- id: q5

  options:
  - text: World 100 kWh/d; UK 20 kWh/d

    correct: true
  - text: World 1 kWh/d; UK 0.2 kWh/d

- id: q6

    correct: true
  - text: Perfect power stations
    correct: true

    correct: true
  - text: Exploiting hot spots like Iceland
  explanation: "**p. 98:** “ignoring hot spots, assuming perfect power stations, assuming every square metre of continent is exploited, and assuming that drilling is free. And that it is possible to drill 15-km-deep holes.”"

title: The physics of deep-water waves
questions:
- id: q1
  prompt: In what two forms does a wave contain energy?
  type: multiple

    correct: true
  - text: Chemical energy of salt
  - text: Kinetic energy — the water moving around
    correct: true
  - text: Thermal energy of warm water
  explanation: "**p. 307:** “Waves contain energy in two forms: potential energy, and kinetic energy. The potential energy is the energy required to move all the water from the troughs to the crests. The kinetic energy is associated with the water moving around.”"

  prompt: "Does the water in a wave crest travel across the ocean at the crest's speed?"

  - text: Only the wind speed

  explanation: "**p. 307:** “v = gT/2π … if T = 10 seconds, then v = 16 m/s. The wavelength of such a wave … is λ = vT = gT²/2π = 160 m.”"

  explanation: "**p. 308:** “Waves have kinetic energy as well as potential energy, and, remarkably, these are exactly equal”."
- id: q6
  prompt: Why must the first estimate of wave power be halved?

  - text: "Machines are 50% efficient"

    prompt: A team adds `WITH (NOLOCK)` to every query and splits every report into a cursor loop because "that is how we tuned SQL Server 2000". Which word best describes applying this technique to a 2026 application?
    options:
      - text: Factoid
      - text: Polymorphic
      - id: anachronistic
        text: Anachronistic
        correct: true
      - text: Idempotent
    explanation: An anachronism is something that belongs to a period other than the one in which it exists. The technique may have been reasonable for its era and hardware; transplanted into today's engine, optimizer and workload, it is out of time.
  - id: factoid-origin
    prompt: In its original sense, what is a *factoid*?
    options:
      - text: A small but true and interesting fact
      - text: A fact that has been peer reviewed
      - id: repeated-falsehood
        text: A piece of unreliable or false information repeated so often that it becomes accepted as fact
        correct: true
      - text: A fact that only applies to one version of a product
    explanation: Norman Mailer coined the word in 1973 for "facts which have no existence before appearing in a magazine or newspaper". The later "trivia" meaning is a drift; this book uses the original one.
  - id: dogma-def
    prompt: Which statement is the clearest example of *legacy dogma*?
    options:
      - text: "We measured both options with BenchmarkDotNet and kept the faster one."
      - text: "We use records for DTOs because value equality makes our tests simpler."
      - text: "We target .NET 10 because it is the current LTS release."
      - id: never-question
        text: "Every class must have an interface. That is the rule here; it has always been the rule."
        correct: true
    explanation: Dogma is a rule held as incontrovertible and repeated after the conditions that justified it have gone. "It has always been the rule" is the tell — no reason is offered, and none is allowed to be questioned.
  - id: vestige-def
    prompt: A codebase still calls `GC.Collect()` after every request "to keep memory low", a habit that began during a leak investigation years ago. The leak was fixed long ago. What is the `GC.Collect()` call?
    options:
      - text: An anachronism, because GC did not exist when it was written
      - text: A factoid, because it is a false statement
      - id: vestigial
        text: Vestigial — a surviving remnant of an earlier stage that no longer serves a purpose
        correct: true
      - text: A dogma, because it is written in code
    explanation: Like the appendix, the call survived the conditions that produced it. It now costs something (forced full collections hurt throughput) and buys nothing.
  - id: relationships
    prompt: Which statements about how these four ideas relate are accurate?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: factoid-feeds-dogma
        text: A factoid often supplies the "reason" that keeps a dogma alive
        correct: true
      - id: vestige-was-useful
        text: A vestigial practice usually *was* useful once; that is what distinguishes it from a plain mistake
        correct: true
      - text: An anachronism is always wrong in every context
      - id: time-dimension
        text: All four involve time — something that was once true, once believed or once needed is carried past its moment
        correct: true
    explanation: Anachronism is relative to context; a technique can be right in its own era. The four words are useful precisely because they share a time dimension, which tells you where to look for the evidence — at what changed.
  - id: not-everything-old
    prompt: Which of these is *not* an example of a vestige or anachronism?

        correct: true
      - text: "Who on the team wrote it?"
      - text: "Is it older than five years?"
      - text: "Does a blog post say it is bad?"

## Learning objectives

- Define *anachronism*, *dogma*, *factoid* and *vestige* precisely
- Recognize each in real codebases and code reviews
- Use the vocabulary to have calmer, evidence-based design discussions

## Why a book about .NET starts with vocabulary

Software ages unevenly. The C# compiler, the runtime and the libraries change every year;
the advice people repeat about them changes far more slowly. A great deal of friction in
teams is not about code at all — it is about which era's rules everyone is playing by.

Having precise words for "this was once true" lets us separate the *idea* from the *person*
holding it. "That rule is vestigial" is a claim about history that can be checked. "That rule is
dumb" is an insult that cannot.

The real-world scenarios throughout this book are composites of common incidents, written to
teach; they do not describe specific organizations.

## The four words

**Anachronism** *(adj. anachronistic)* — something that belongs to a period other than that in
which it exists. Applying a 1998 database optimization to a 2026 .NET application is
*anachronistic*: the optimizer, the plan cache, the hardware and the workload are all different.

**Dogma (legacy dogma)** — a rule held as incontrovertible truth, repeated long after the
conditions that made it sensible have vanished. The sign of dogma is not that the rule is wrong;
it is that the rule cannot be questioned.

**Factoid** — in Norman Mailer's original 1973 sense, a piece of unreliable or false information
repeated so often that it becomes accepted as fact. "Stored procedures are faster because they are
precompiled" is a classic .NET-world factoid (Chapter 10 takes it apart).

**Vestige** *(adj. vestigial)* — borrowed from biology, a remnant of an earlier stage of evolution
that serves no current purpose. A vestigial belief or practice was usually useful once.

## How they show up in .NET code

| Symptom in a codebase | Likely category | What changed |
|---|---|---|
| `AutoMapper` profiles for one-to-one DTO copies | Vestige | Records, `with`, extension members, source generators, compile-time safety |
| "Always `ConfigureAwait(false)`" in ASP.NET Core app code | Dogma | ASP.NET Core has no `SynchronizationContext` |
| "Stored procedures are precompiled, so they are faster" | Factoid | Parameterized SQL plans have been cached and reused since SQL Server 7.0 |
| `Newtonsoft.Json` added to a new .NET 10 project by habit | Anachronism | `System.Text.Json` ships in the box, with source generation |
| One interface per class, every class | Dogma | Interfaces exist for substitution; most classes are never substituted |
| `Task.Run(() => httpClient.GetAsync(...))` in a web app | Vestige | Async I/O frees the thread already; `Task.Run` just borrows another |
| `lock (this)` / `lock (typeof(X))` | Anachronism | Private lock objects (and `System.Threading.Lock` since .NET 9) |
| Hand-rolled `IDateTimeProvider` interfaces | Vestige | `TimeProvider` in the BCL since .NET 8 |

None of these is malicious. Each was good advice somewhere, sometime, for someone.

## The anatomy of a factoid

Factoids survive because they are *nearly* true and easy to repeat. They tend to have:

1. **A kernel of historical truth.** SQL Server 6.5 really did treat procedures specially.
2. **A plausible mechanism.** "Precompiled" sounds like how compilers work.
3. **No date attached.** The claim is stated in the present tense forever.
4. **Social reinforcement.** Senior people repeat it, so juniors do too.

The antidote is to attach a date and a mechanism to every performance or design claim:
*when* was this true, *why* was it true, and has that mechanism changed?

## A worked example: the "every class gets an interface" rule

```csharp
public interface IInvoiceTotalCalculator
{
    decimal Calculate(Invoice invoice);
}

public sealed class InvoiceTotalCalculator : IInvoiceTotalCalculator
{
    public decimal Calculate(Invoice invoice) => invoice.Lines.Sum(l => l.Quantity * l.UnitPrice);
}
```

Ask the historical question: *what problem did the interface solve?* In 2008 the answer was
often "Rhino Mocks and Moq can only fake interfaces and virtual members, and we want to mock
this". But a pure calculation needs no mocking — you test it directly with real invoices. The
interface is vestigial for this class. It costs a file, an indirection, and a registration.

```csharp
public static class InvoiceMath
{
    public static decimal Total(this Invoice invoice) => invoice.Lines.Sum(l => l.Quantity * l.UnitPrice);
}
```

Contrast a payment gateway client: it talks to the network, is slow, costs money, and has
several real implementations (sandbox, production, fake). There the interface earns its keep.
The rule is not "never use interfaces" — that would be a new dogma. The rule is "know the reason".

## Language for code review

- "What problem does this solve today?"
- "When was this measured, and on what runtime?"
- "Is this still true on .NET 10?"
- "What would break if we deleted it?"

These questions are hard to take personally and easy to answer with evidence.

## Sources

- Merriam-Webster, "factoid" — <https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/factoid>
- D. L. Parnas, "On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules", *CACM* 1972 — <https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/361598.361623>
- Microsoft Learn, `TimeProvider` — <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.timeprovider>
- Stephen Toub, "ConfigureAwait FAQ" — <https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/configureawait-faq/>

title: A field guide to .NET vestiges
questions:
  - id: newtonsoft
    prompt: You are starting a new ASP.NET Core project on .NET 10. A colleague adds `Newtonsoft.Json` "because it is the standard JSON library". What is the most accurate response?
    options:
      - text: Agree; `System.Text.Json` cannot serialize records
      - text: Agree; Microsoft deprecated `System.Text.Json` in .NET 9
      - id: stj-default
        text: "`System.Text.Json` is built in, is the framework default, supports records, polymorphism and source generation; add Newtonsoft only for a specific feature you actually need"
        correct: true
      - text: Use both, configured to run in sequence, for safety
    explanation: Newtonsoft.Json was the de facto standard before .NET Core 3.0. It remains a fine library, but adding it by reflex to a new project is anachronistic — a second serializer with different defaults is a source of bugs.
  - id: task-run-io
    prompt: "Why is `await Task.Run(() => _http.GetStringAsync(url))` in an ASP.NET Core endpoint a vestige?"
    options:
      - text: Because `Task.Run` was removed in .NET 8
      - text: Because it makes the call synchronous
      - text: Because it causes a compile error with nullable reference types
      - id: borrows-thread
        text: Because the I/O is already asynchronous; `Task.Run` only queues extra work to another thread-pool thread and adds overhead
        correct: true
    explanation: "`Task.Run` exists to move CPU-bound work off a thread that must stay responsive (like a UI thread). Server code has no such thread, and async I/O needs no thread while it waits."
  - id: datetime-now
    prompt: Which modern replacement makes the vestigial hand-rolled `IClock`/`IDateTimeProvider` interface unnecessary in most codebases?
    options:
      - text: "`DateTime.UtcNow`"
      - text: "`Stopwatch.GetTimestamp()` only"
      - id: timeprovider
        text: "`TimeProvider`, built into .NET 8 and later, with `FakeTimeProvider` for tests"
        correct: true
      - text: "`Environment.TickCount`"
    explanation: "`TimeProvider` abstracts wall-clock time, timestamps and timers. `FakeTimeProvider` (Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing) lets tests advance time deterministically, including `Task.Delay` and `CancellationTokenSource.CancelAfter` when created with the provider."
  - id: string-concat
    prompt: "A reviewer rejects `var label = $\"{first} {last}\";` and demands `StringBuilder` \"because string concatenation is slow\". Which statements are accurate?"
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: small-fine
        text: For a handful of pieces, interpolation is clear and efficient; the compiler uses `DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler`
        correct: true
      - id: loops
        text: "`StringBuilder` (or `string.Join`/`string.Create`) still matters when building a string in a loop with many iterations"
        correct: true
      - text: "`StringBuilder` is always faster than interpolation"
      - id: overgeneralized
        text: The reviewer's rule is an over-generalized kernel of truth — a classic factoid shape
        correct: true
    explanation: The true part is "repeated concatenation in a loop is quadratic". The false generalization is "all concatenation is slow". Since C# 10, interpolated strings compile to an efficient handler.
  - id: repository-over-ef
    prompt: A team wraps EF Core's `DbContext` in a generic `IRepository<T>` with `GetAll()`, `Add()` and `Save()` "so we can swap the ORM later". What is the main problem?
    options:
      - text: Generic types cannot be registered in DI
      - id: leaky-and-redundant
        text: "`DbContext` already is a unit of work and `DbSet<T>` a repository; the generic wrapper hides useful features (projection, `AsNoTracking`, `Include`) and the swap rarely happens"
        correct: true
      - text: EF Core forbids wrapping `DbContext`
      - text: There is no problem; this is always best practice
    explanation: The pattern made more sense with older ORMs and pre-LINQ data access. A *specific*, query-shaped abstraction (an `IOrderQueries` with `GetOpenOrdersForCustomer`) can still be valuable at a boundary; the generic CRUD wrapper usually is not.
  - id: lock-object
    prompt: What is the modern replacement for `private readonly object _gate = new();` used with `lock` on .NET 9 and later?
    options:
      - id: lock-type
        text: "`private readonly Lock _gate = new();` — the `System.Threading.Lock` type, which the `lock` statement recognizes"
        correct: true
      - text: "`Monitor.Enter(this)`"
      - text: "`Mutex`"
      - text: "`SemaphoreSlim(1)` in all cases"
    explanation: "`System.Threading.Lock` (.NET 9, C# 13) gives the `lock` statement a dedicated, faster primitive. `SemaphoreSlim` is still the tool when you must `await` inside the critical section."
  - id: still-valid
    prompt: Which of these practices is still valid in 2026 — *not* a vestige?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: dispose
        text: Disposing `IDisposable` resources deterministically with `using`
        correct: true
      - text: Calling `GC.Collect()` at the end of each web request
      - id: httpclientfactory
        text: Using `IHttpClientFactory` or a long-lived `HttpClient` instead of creating and disposing one per request
        correct: true
      - id: parameterize
        text: Parameterizing every SQL statement that includes user input
        correct: true
    explanation: Deterministic disposal, connection reuse and parameterization address problems that still exist. Forced GC addresses a problem the runtime solves better on its own.
  - id: sealed
    prompt: "Marking classes `sealed` by default: vestige, dogma, or still sensible?"
    options:
      - id: sensible
        text: Still sensible — it states design intent (not built for inheritance) and lets the JIT devirtualize calls
        correct: true
      - text: Vestige — sealing stopped mattering after .NET Framework 2.0
      - text: Dogma — `sealed` makes classes untestable
      - text: Anachronism — C# 14 removed `sealed`
    explanation: Designing for inheritance is a deliberate act (Framework Design Guidelines). Sealing what was not designed for it is honest, and the runtime's devirtualization work since .NET 5 means it can also be slightly faster.
---
## Learning objectives

- Recognize the most common vestigial patterns in .NET codebases
- Know the modern replacement for each
- Avoid replacing one dogma with another

## The catalogue

Each entry has the same shape: what people do, why it once made sense, what changed, and what
to do now.

### Newtonsoft.Json by reflex

- **Then:** Before .NET Core 3.0 (2019) there was no high-performance JSON in the box.
- **Changed:** `System.Text.Json` became the framework default, then gained source generation,
  polymorphism (`[JsonDerivedType]`), `required` support, and (in .NET 11) union support.
- **Now:** Use `System.Text.Json`. Add Newtonsoft only for a feature you have identified.

```csharp
[JsonSerializable(typeof(OrderDto))]
[JsonSerializable(typeof(List<OrderDto>))]
internal partial class AppJsonContext : JsonSerializerContext;

var json = JsonSerializer.Serialize(order, AppJsonContext.Default.OrderDto);
```

### Task.Run around I/O on a server

```csharp
var before = await Task.Run(() => _http.GetStringAsync(url));
var after = await _http.GetStringAsync(url, ct);
```

The first line was copied from desktop code, where moving work off the UI thread mattered. On a
server it borrows a second thread to wait for work that needed no thread at all.

### `new HttpClient()` per call

```csharp
using var client = new HttpClient();
```

Creating and disposing clients per request can exhaust sockets; a single static client can miss
DNS changes. `IHttpClientFactory` (or a long-lived client with
`SocketsHttpHandler.PooledConnectionLifetime`) addresses both. This one is *not* vestigial — the
problem is real, and the fix is current.

### Hand-rolled clock interfaces

```csharp
public sealed class TrialService(TimeProvider time)
{
    public bool IsExpired(DateTimeOffset startedAt) =>
        time.GetUtcNow() - startedAt > TimeSpan.FromDays(30);
}

builder.Services.AddSingleton(TimeProvider.System);
```

In tests:

```csharp
var time = new FakeTimeProvider(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero));
var sut = new TrialService(time);
time.Advance(TimeSpan.FromDays(31));
Assert.True(sut.IsExpired(new DateTimeOffset(2026, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, TimeSpan.Zero)));
```

### `lock (this)` and `object` gates

```csharp
private readonly Lock _gate = new();

public void Add(Item item)
{
    lock (_gate)
    {
        _items.Add(item);
    }
}
```

### Generic repositories over EF Core

`DbContext` is a unit of work; `DbSet<T>` is a repository. A generic `IRepository<T>` usually
hides features and adds nothing. Query-shaped interfaces at real boundaries are a different and
often good idea.

### AutoMapper for DTO copies

Covered in full in Chapter 8. In short: explicit mapping methods are shorter to read, safer to
refactor, faster, AOT-friendly, and no longer require a commercial licence decision.

### `ConfigureAwait(false)` everywhere in app code

Covered in Chapter 5. In ASP.NET Core application code it does nothing useful; in reusable
libraries it remains good practice.

### Defensive `GC.Collect()`

The garbage collector tunes itself using allocation rates and memory pressure. Forcing full
collections usually lowers throughput. If memory is a problem, find the allocation with a
profiler (`dotnet-counters`, `dotnet-trace`, `dotnet-gcdump`).

## Do not make a new dogma

It is tempting to turn this catalogue into a list of "never" rules. Resist. Each entry has an
exception:

- Newtonsoft is still right for a project relying on `JObject` dynamic manipulation everywhere.
- `Task.Run` is still right for CPU-heavy work in a desktop app.
- An interface is still right when there are, or will plausibly be, several implementations.

The goal is reasons, not rules.

## Sources

- Microsoft Learn, "Migrate from Newtonsoft.Json to System.Text.Json" — <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/serialization/system-text-json/migrate-from-newtonsoft>
- Microsoft Learn, "Use IHttpClientFactory" — <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/http-requests>
- Microsoft Learn, `System.Threading.Lock` — <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.lock>
- Microsoft Learn, `TimeProvider` — <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.timeprovider>
- David Fowler, "ASP.NET Core Diagnostic Scenarios: Async Guidance" — <https://github.com/davidfowl/AspNetCoreDiagnosticScenarios/blob/master/AsyncGuidance.md>

questions:
  - id: benchmark-tool

      - id: bdn

    explanation: BenchmarkDotNet handles warm-up, JIT tiering, outliers, statistical analysis and memory diagnostics. A `Stopwatch` loop in Debug measures the debugger as much as your code.
  - id: release-mode
    prompt: Why are measurements taken in a Debug build misleading?
    options:
      - text: Debug builds use a different garbage collector
      - text: Debug builds run on a different CLR version
      - id: no-opts
        text: The JIT disables most optimizations so code can be stepped through, which distorts relative costs
        correct: true
      - text: They are not misleading
    explanation: Inlining, loop optimizations and register allocation are largely disabled. Always measure Release builds, ideally with BenchmarkDotNet's harness.
  - id: dated-claims

    type: multiple

        correct: true

      - text: Apply it everywhere, since a measured claim is true forever
      - id: readability
        text: Prefer the readable version unless a profiler shows this loop is hot
        correct: true
    explanation: Performance claims have a half-life. Date them, re-measure the ones that matter, and default to clarity.
  - id: profiler-first
    prompt: An endpoint is slow. What is the best first step?
    options:

        correct: true

      - text: Convert all classes to structs
      - text: Add `ConfigureAwait(false)` to every await
    explanation: Most real latency is I/O — a missing index, a chatty N+1 query, a slow downstream service. Micro-optimizations made blind usually change nothing measurable.
  - id: primary-sources

    type: multiple

      - id: learn

        correct: true
      - text: An undated answer on a Q&A site with many upvotes

  - id: chesterton

    options:
      - text: Delete it immediately; unknown code is dead code
      - text: Never touch it
      - id: find-reason

        correct: true
