## Learning objectives

- Turn opinions about code into testable claims
- Measure correctly with BenchmarkDotNet
- Use primary sources to settle disputes

## Every claim has a date

A useful habit: when you hear a rule, silently append "...as of when, on what?"

- "Exceptions are slow" — as of when? Throwing is expensive relative to a return value, which is
  why exceptions are for exceptional cases; .NET 9 also made exception handling itself
  substantially faster. Neither fact justifies returning error codes everywhere.
- "LINQ is slow" — on what? LINQ has been heavily optimized across .NET 7–10; for typical
  business code its cost is noise next to a single database round trip.

## Measuring properly

```csharp
using BenchmarkDotNet.Attributes;
using BenchmarkDotNet.Running;

BenchmarkRunner.Run<LabelBenchmarks>();

[MemoryDiagnoser]
public class LabelBenchmarks
{
    private readonly string _first = "Ada";
    private readonly string _last = "Lovelace";

    [Benchmark(Baseline = true)]
    public string Interpolation() => $"{_first} {_last}";

    [Benchmark]
    public string Builder() => new StringBuilder().Append(_first).Append(' ').Append(_last).ToString();
}
```

```bash
dotnet run -c Release
```

Read the *Allocated* column as carefully as the *Mean* column; allocations drive GC cost under load.

## The order of evidence

1. **Production telemetry** (OpenTelemetry traces, metrics) — what is actually slow
2. **Profiles** (`dotnet-trace`, Visual Studio profiler, PerfView) — where the time goes
3. **Benchmarks** — whether a specific change helps
4. **Documentation and source** — why it behaves that way
5. **Folklore** — a hypothesis to test, never a conclusion

## A short case study

A team spent a sprint replacing LINQ with hand-written loops in an order export, citing "LINQ is
slow". Export time did not change. A trace later showed 97% of the time in 4,000 individual
`SELECT` statements — one per order line. A single set-based query fixed it in an afternoon. The
factoid cost a sprint; the measurement cost ten minutes.

## Sources

- BenchmarkDotNet — <https://benchmarkdotnet.org/>
- Microsoft Learn, ".NET diagnostic tools" — <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/>
- Stephen Toub, "Performance Improvements in .NET 10" (and earlier annual posts) — <https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/performance-improvements-in-net-10/>
- dotnet/runtime on GitHub — <https://github.com/dotnet/runtime>

## Learning objectives

- Explain the yearly release cadence and LTS/STS support windows
- Choose a target framework deliberately
- Keep a codebase on a supported runtime without heroics

## The rhythm

| Version | Released | Type | Support ends (approx.) |
|---|---|---|---|
| .NET 8 | Nov 2023 | LTS | Nov 2026 |
| .NET 9 | Nov 2024 | STS | Nov 2026 |
| .NET 10 | Nov 2025 | LTS | Nov 2028 |
| .NET 11 | Nov 2026 | STS | Nov 2028 |
| .NET 12 | Nov 2027 (expected) | LTS (by pattern) | Nov 2030 (by pattern) |

Confirm dates against the official support policy page; the table is a teaching aid, not a contract.

## The timeless lesson: upgrade is a routine, not a project

Teams that treat each upgrade as a project fall behind and end up on unsupported runtimes. Teams
that treat it as a routine — a tracked chore every November — spend a day or two per year.

What makes upgrades cheap:

- A **`global.json`** that pins the SDK, so builds are reproducible
- **Central package management**, so one file controls versions
- **Warnings as errors** and analyzers, so obsolete APIs are visible immediately
- **Good tests**, so you can upgrade with confidence
- **Few dependencies**, especially few reflection-heavy ones

```json
{
  "sdk": {
    "version": "10.0.100",
    "rollForward": "latestFeature"
  },
  "test": {
    "runner": "Microsoft.Testing.Platform"
  }
}
```

`rollForward: latestFeature` lets machines with a newer 10.0.x feature band build, while still
preventing an accidental jump to an 11.0 SDK.

## Target framework monikers

```xml
<TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
```

Libraries that serve a wide audience may multi-target:

```xml
<TargetFrameworks>net10.0;net8.0;netstandard2.0</TargetFrameworks>
```

Applications should target exactly one framework. Multi-targeting an application multiplies test
and deployment work for no benefit.

## Real-world scenario: the forgotten .NET 6 service

A payments reconciliation service was "done" in 2022 and nobody touched it. In 2025 a container
scan flagged unpatched vulnerabilities; .NET 6 had been out of support since November 2024. The
upgrade to .NET 8 took three weeks because of a stale ORM and an abandoned logging package. The
upgrade from 8 to 10 the following year took one afternoon — because they had fixed the habits,
not just the version.

- .NET and .NET Core official support policy — <https://dotnet.microsoft.com/en-us/platform/support/policy/dotnet-core>

## Learning objectives

- Set up a repository so upgrades are cheap
- Use central package management, shared build properties and analyzers
- Use file-based apps for scripts

## A repository skeleton that ages well

```text
/
  global.json
  Directory.Build.props
  Directory.Packages.props
  MyCompany.Orders.slnx
  src/
    Orders.Api/
    Orders.Core/
  tests/
    Orders.Tests/
```

### Directory.Build.props

```xml
<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <AnalysisLevel>latest-recommended</AnalysisLevel>
    <EnforceCodeStyleInBuild>true</EnforceCodeStyleInBuild>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

### Directory.Packages.props

```xml
<Project>
  <PropertyGroup>
    <ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>true</ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageVersion Include="Dapper" Version="2.1.89" />
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.Data.SqlClient" Version="6.1.2" />
    <PackageVersion Include="xunit.v3" Version="4.0.2" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
```

Versions shown are illustrative; pin to what you have tested.

### A project file becomes almost empty

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Dapper" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Data.SqlClient" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
```

### The solution file

```xml
<Solution>
  <Folder Name="/src/">
    <Project Path="src/Orders.Api/Orders.Api.csproj" />
    <Project Path="src/Orders.Core/Orders.Core.csproj" />
  </Folder>
  <Folder Name="/tests/">
    <Project Path="tests/Orders.Tests/Orders.Tests.csproj" />
  </Folder>
</Solution>
```

## File-based apps: C# as a scripting language

```csharp
#:package Dapper@2.1.89
#:package Microsoft.Data.SqlClient@6.1.2

using Dapper;
using Microsoft.Data.SqlClient;

var connectionString = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("ORDERS_DB")
    ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("ORDERS_DB is not set");

await using var connection = new SqlConnection(connectionString);
var stuck = await connection.QueryAsync<(int Id, string Status)>(
    "select Id, Status from dbo.Orders where Status = @status and UpdatedAt < @cutoff",
    new { status = "Pending", cutoff = DateTime.UtcNow.AddDays(-3) });

foreach (var (id, status) in stuck)
{
    Console.WriteLine($"{id}\t{status}");
}
```

```bash
dotnet run find-stuck-orders.cs
```

Real-world use: the support team's "find stuck orders" script lives in the repository, is
type-checked, uses the same data access library as production, and runs on any machine with the
SDK.

## The dependency budget

Treat third-party packages like hiring: each one has ongoing costs. In 2025 alone, AutoMapper and
MediatR introduced commercial editions, and Fluent Assertions v8 moved to a paid licence for
commercial use. Earlier, Moq's SponsorLink episode (2023) taught the community that a test
dependency can become a privacy and compliance question overnight. None of these projects did
anything wrong by seeking funding — but a codebase that needs fewer of them is more resilient.

title: Records — value semantics on purpose
questions:
  - id: equality
    prompt: "Given `public record Money(decimal Amount, string Currency);`, what does `new Money(10m, \"EUR\") == new Money(10m, \"EUR\")` return?"
    options:
      - text: "`false`, because they are different objects"
      - text: It does not compile
      - id: true-value
        text: "`true`, because records compare by the values of their members"
        correct: true
      - text: It throws `InvalidOperationException`
    explanation: Records generate `Equals`, `GetHashCode`, `==` and `!=` that compare member values. `record` is a reference type (`record class`), so `ReferenceEquals` would still be `false`.
  - id: with
    prompt: "What does `var discounted = price with { Amount = price.Amount * 0.9m };` do?"
    options:
      - text: Mutates `price` in place
      - id: copy
        text: Creates a shallow copy of `price` with `Amount` replaced; `price` is unchanged
        correct: true
      - text: Creates a deep copy of every nested object
      - text: Only works on structs
    explanation: "Non-destructive mutation. It is a *shallow* copy: reference-type members (like a `List<T>`) are shared between the original and the copy."
  - id: list-equality
    prompt: "`public record Basket(string Owner, List<string> Items);` — two baskets with the same owner and lists containing the same strings, but different list instances. Are they equal?"
    options:
      - text: Yes, records compare collections element by element
      - id: no-reference
        text: No — `List<string>` uses reference equality, so the generated `Equals` sees two different lists
        correct: true
      - text: Only if the lists are sorted
      - text: It depends on the culture
    explanation: Record equality delegates to each member's `Equals`. Collections in records are a common trap; use an immutable collection with value semantics you write yourself, or override equality, or keep collections out of value-object records.
  - id: ef-entities
    prompt: Why are records usually a poor fit for EF Core entities?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: identity
        text: Entities have identity (two rows with equal data are still different rows); records define equality by value
        correct: true
      - id: tracking
        text: EF Core's change tracker relies on reference identity and mutation, while records encourage replacing instances with `with`
        correct: true
      - text: EF Core cannot read records at all
      - id: hashcode
        text: Mutable members participating in `GetHashCode` can break `HashSet`/`Dictionary` lookups as the entity changes
        correct: true
    explanation: Records are excellent for DTOs, messages, value objects and query results. Entities are about identity over time — a different concept.
  - id: positional
    prompt: For a *positional* `record class`, what does the compiler generate for each positional parameter?
    options:
      - text: A public field
      - text: A private readonly field only
      - text: A public `set` property
      - id: init-prop
        text: A public `init`-only property, plus a constructor and a `Deconstruct` method
        correct: true
    explanation: "`record struct` positional parameters generate *mutable* (`get; set;`) properties unless you declare `readonly record struct`."
  - id: tostring
    prompt: What does a record's generated `ToString()` produce, and what is a real-world risk?
    options:
      - text: Only the type name, like a class
      - text: JSON
      - text: An empty string
      - id: members-leak
        text: "Something like `User { Email = a@b.com, PasswordHash = ... }` — every public member, which can leak secrets into logs"
        correct: true
    explanation: The printing is great for debugging and tests, and dangerous for records holding secrets or personal data. Override `PrintMembers` or keep sensitive values out of records that might be logged.
  - id: when-records
    prompt: Which are good uses of records?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: dto
        text: API request and response DTOs
        correct: true
      - id: messages
        text: Commands, events and messages
        correct: true
      - id: value-objects
        text: Small value objects such as `Money`, `DateRange` or `EmailAddress`
        correct: true
      - text: Long-lived services registered in DI
    explanation: Services have behavior and dependencies, not values. Records shine where the *data* is the identity.
  - id: sealed-record
    prompt: Why might you declare `public sealed record OrderPlaced(...)`?
    options:
      - text: Sealed records cannot be serialized
      - text: To make the record a value type
      - text: Because records cannot have methods otherwise
      - id: equality-contract
        text: To prevent derived records, which simplifies the equality contract (`EqualityContract`) and states intent
        correct: true
    explanation: Record inheritance works but complicates equality (a derived record is never equal to its base). Most DTOs and messages should be sealed.
---
## Learning objectives

- Explain what the compiler generates for a record
- Use `with` and positional records correctly
- Avoid the collection, entity and logging traps

## What a record is

A record is a class (or struct) for which the compiler writes the boring parts: value-based
equality, `GetHashCode`, `ToString`, a copy constructor for `with`, and — for positional
records — properties, a constructor and `Deconstruct`.

```csharp
public sealed record Money(decimal Amount, string Currency)
{
    public static Money Zero(string currency) => new(0m, currency);

    public Money Add(Money other) =>
        other.Currency == Currency
            ? this with { Amount = Amount + other.Amount }
            : throw new InvalidOperationException($"Cannot add {other.Currency} to {Currency}");
}
```

## The four flavors

| Declaration | Kind | Positional properties | Equality |
|---|---|---|---|
| `record` / `record class` | reference | `init` | value |
| `readonly record struct` | value | `init` | value |
| `record struct` | value | `get; set;` | value |
| `class` | reference | — | reference |

## Validation in records

Positional records are concise, but validation needs a little more:

```csharp
public sealed record EmailAddress
{
    public string Value { get; }

    public EmailAddress(string value)
    {
        ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace(value);
        if (!value.Contains('@')) throw new ArgumentException("Not an email address", nameof(value));
        Value = value.Trim().ToLowerInvariant();
    }

    public override string ToString() => Value;
}
```

Note that `with` bypasses the constructor and copies fields directly. If invariants matter,
validate in property `init` accessors (C# 14's `field` keyword makes this concise — see Chapter 4),
or avoid exposing `with`-able properties.

## The collection trap

```csharp
public sealed record Basket(string Owner, IReadOnlyList<string> Items);

var a = new Basket("ada", ["tea", "milk"]);
var b = new Basket("ada", ["tea", "milk"]);
Console.WriteLine(a == b);
```

This prints `False`. One fix is to implement equality for the collection member:

```csharp
public sealed record Basket(string Owner, IReadOnlyList<string> Items)
{
    public bool Equals(Basket? other) =>
        other is not null && Owner == other.Owner && Items.SequenceEqual(other.Items);

    public override int GetHashCode()
    {
        var hash = new HashCode();
        hash.Add(Owner);
        foreach (var item in Items) hash.Add(item);
        return hash.ToHashCode();
    }
}
```

## The logging trap

```csharp
public sealed record LoginRequest(string Email, string Password);

logger.LogInformation("Login attempt {Request}", request);
```

The log now contains the password. Real incident reports contain this exact bug. Mitigate by
logging specific fields, or by overriding the printer:

```csharp
public sealed record LoginRequest(string Email, string Password)
{
    private bool PrintMembers(StringBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.Append($"Email = {Email}, Password = ***");
        return true;
    }
}
```

## Real-world scenario: idempotent message handling

Records make "have I seen this message?" trivial when the message *is* its data:

```csharp
public sealed record InvoicePaid(Guid InvoiceId, decimal Amount, DateOnly PaidOn);

private readonly HashSet<InvoicePaid> _processed = [];

public void Handle(InvoicePaid message)
{
    if (!_processed.Add(message)) return;
    Apply(message);
}
```

- Microsoft Learn, "Use record types" tutorial — <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/tutorials/records>

title: Choosing a type, and primary constructors
questions:
  - id: pc-readonly
    prompt: "In `public sealed class OrderService(IOrderStore store) { ... }`, is the captured parameter `store` read-only?"
    options:
      - id: mutable
        text: No — in a class or struct primary constructor the parameter is a mutable captured variable; it can be reassigned inside the class
        correct: true
      - text: Yes, primary constructor parameters are always `readonly` fields
      - text: Only if the class is sealed
      - text: It is a public property
    explanation: This surprises many developers. If immutability matters, assign it to an explicit `private readonly` field, or rely on the analyzer warning when you reassign it.
  - id: pc-vs-record
    prompt: How do primary constructors on a *class* differ from positional parameters on a *record*?
    options:
      - text: There is no difference
      - text: Classes generate `Deconstruct`; records do not
      - id: no-properties
        text: A class's primary constructor parameters do not become public properties; a record's positional parameters do
        correct: true
      - text: Records cannot have primary constructors
    explanation: For classes, primary constructor parameters are simply in scope for the body — ideal for dependency injection. For records, they define the public shape of the data.
  - id: struct-when
    prompt: When is a `struct` (or `readonly record struct`) a better choice than a class?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: small

        correct: true
      - id: immutable
        text: It is logically immutable
        correct: true
      - id: many-instances
        text: Large numbers are created in hot paths and heap allocations matter
        correct: true
      - text: It needs inheritance
    explanation: Structs avoid heap allocation but are copied on assignment. Large or mutable structs cause subtle bugs and extra copying.
  - id: default-struct
    prompt: What is a real hazard of value types such as `public readonly record struct OrderId(Guid Value);`?
    options:
      - text: They cannot be used as dictionary keys
      - id: default
        text: "`default(OrderId)` exists and bypasses any constructor validation, so `Guid.Empty` can sneak in"
        correct: true
      - text: They are always slower than classes
      - text: They cannot implement interfaces
    explanation: Every struct has a default value. Arrays, uninitialized fields and `default` all produce it. Design strongly-typed ids so that the default is detectable or harmless.
  - id: required
    prompt: What does the `required` modifier do?
    options:
      - text: Throws at runtime if the property is null
      - id: object-initializer
        text: Makes the compiler insist that callers set the member in an object initializer (or a constructor marked `[SetsRequiredMembers]`)
        correct: true
      - text: Marks a parameter as non-optional in ASP.NET Core
      - text: Makes the property `readonly`
    explanation: "`required` is a compile-time contract for construction. `System.Text.Json` also honors it, failing deserialization when the property is missing from the JSON."
  - id: strong-ids

    options:
      - text: SQL injection
      - id: swap
        text: Accidentally passing an order id where a customer id is expected, as in `GetOrders(orderId)`
        correct: true
      - text: Deadlocks
      - text: Null reference exceptions
    explanation: The compiler can only catch mixed-up arguments if they have different types — a cheap, timeless technique ("primitive obsession" is the smell it cures).

## Learning objectives

- Choose between `class`, `struct`, `record` and `record struct` with reasons
- Use primary constructors for services and know their mutability caveat
- Use `required`, `init` and strongly-typed identifiers

## A decision table

| You are modeling… | Prefer |
|---|---|
| A service with dependencies and behavior | `sealed class` with a primary constructor |
| A DTO, message, or query result | `sealed record` |
| A small immutable value (id, coordinate, money in a hot path) | `readonly record struct` |
| An entity with identity and a lifecycle | `class` |
| A closed set of alternatives | `abstract record` with derived records (today), `union` (C# 15) |

## Primary constructors for services

```csharp
public sealed class InvoiceSender(
    IInvoiceRepository invoices,
    IEmailGateway email,
    ILogger<InvoiceSender> logger)
{
    public async Task SendAsync(InvoiceId id, CancellationToken ct)
    {
        var invoice = await invoices.GetAsync(id, ct)
            ?? throw new InvalidOperationException($"Invoice {id} not found");
        await email.SendAsync(invoice.CustomerEmail, invoice.ToEmail(), ct);
        logger.LogInformation("Sent invoice {InvoiceId}", id);
    }
}
```

This removes the vestigial ceremony of `private readonly` fields assigned in a constructor —
seven lines per dependency in 2015-era code.

### The caveat, made concrete

```csharp
public sealed class Counter(int start)
{
    public int Next() => ++start;
}
```

This compiles: `start` is mutable captured state. For services that is rarely a problem, but if
you want an enforced invariant, be explicit:

```csharp
public sealed class PriceCalculator(TaxTable taxes)
{
    private readonly TaxTable _taxes = taxes;
}
```

## Strongly-typed ids

```csharp
public readonly record struct CustomerId(Guid Value)
{
    public static CustomerId New() => new(Guid.CreateVersion7());
    public override string ToString() => Value.ToString();
}

public readonly record struct OrderId(Guid Value)
{
    public static OrderId New() => new(Guid.CreateVersion7());
    public override string ToString() => Value.ToString();
}

public Task<IReadOnlyList<Order>> GetOrdersAsync(CustomerId customer, CancellationToken ct);
```

`Guid.CreateVersion7()` (.NET 9) produces time-ordered GUIDs, which index far better than random
v4 GUIDs in clustered indexes — an old database problem with a new, built-in answer.

## `required` and `init`

```csharp
public sealed class CreateCustomerRequest
{
    public required string Name { get; init; }
    public required string Email { get; init; }
    public string? Phone { get; init; }
}

var request = new CreateCustomerRequest { Name = "Ada" };
```

The last line fails to compile: `Email` is required. This replaces the vestigial pattern of a
constructor with nine parameters, or a mutable object half-filled by mistake.

title: Pattern matching and closed sets of alternatives
questions:
  - id: switch-expr
    prompt: What is the main advantage of a `switch` *expression* over a chain of `if`/`else if` for mapping inputs to outputs?
    options:
      - text: It runs on a different thread
      - id: expression
        text: It is an expression that must produce a value for every input, and the compiler warns when cases are not exhaustive
        correct: true
      - text: It is required for async code
      - text: It avoids allocations in all cases
    explanation: Exhaustiveness checking turns "forgot a case" from a runtime bug into a compiler warning (CS8509), which you should treat as an error.
  - id: property-patterns
    prompt: "What does `order is { Status: OrderStatus.Paid, Total: > 1000m }` check?"
    options:
      - text: Only that `order` is not null
      - text: It assigns `Paid` to `Status`
      - id: both
        text: That `order` is not null, its `Status` is `Paid`, and its `Total` is greater than 1000
        correct: true
      - text: It does not compile; patterns cannot use relational operators
    explanation: Property patterns test nested members; relational patterns (`>`, `<=`) and logical patterns (`and`, `or`, `not`) compose them.
  - id: closed-today
    prompt: Before C# 15, what is the common idiom to model a closed set of alternatives such as `PaymentResult` = Approved | Declined | RequiresAction?
    options:
      - text: An `enum` with a `Dictionary<string, object>` payload
      - id: abstract-record
        text: An abstract base record with a private constructor and nested sealed derived records
        correct: true
      - text: A class with nullable fields for every possible case
      - text: Throwing a different exception type for each case
    explanation: A private constructor prevents derivation outside the type, so the set really is closed. The compiler still cannot prove exhaustiveness, so a discard arm is needed; C# 15's `closed` and `union` remove that limitation.
  - id: list-patterns
    prompt: "What does `args is [\"--verbose\", .. var rest]` match?"
    options:
      - text: Any array containing `--verbose` anywhere
      - id: first
        text: A sequence whose first element is `--verbose`, capturing the remaining elements in `rest`
        correct: true
      - text: Only an array of exactly one element
      - text: A string that starts with `--verbose`
    explanation: List patterns (C# 11) match sequences by shape. `..` is a slice pattern.
  - id: illegal-states
    prompt: "Which design follows \"make illegal states unrepresentable\"?"
    options:
      - text: "`class Shipment { bool IsShipped; DateTime? ShippedAt; string? TrackingNumber; }`"
      - text: "`class Shipment { string State; }` with comments explaining allowed values"
      - text: "`Dictionary<string, object?>` named `ShipmentData`"
      - id: cases
        text: "`abstract record Shipment` with `Pending()` and `Shipped(DateTimeOffset At, string TrackingNumber)` cases"
        correct: true
    explanation: With booleans and nullables, `IsShipped = true` with no tracking number is representable — so someday it will exist in production. With cases, it cannot be constructed.
  - id: enum-trap
    prompt: Why is a `switch` over an `enum` never fully exhaustive in C#?
    options:
      - text: Enums are reference types
      - text: Enums cannot be used in switch expressions
      - id: any-int
        text: Any integer value of the underlying type can be cast to the enum, such as `(OrderStatus)42`
        correct: true
      - text: It is exhaustive; there is no trap
    explanation: Even with every named member covered, the compiler asks for a discard. Throw `UnreachableException` (or `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`) in that arm.
---
## Learning objectives

- Use switch expressions, property, relational and list patterns
- Model closed sets of alternatives with records today
- Apply "make illegal states unrepresentable"

## Patterns in practice

```csharp
public static decimal ShippingCost(Order order) => order switch
{
    { Total: >= 100m } => 0m,
    { Destination.Country: "US", Weight: <= 1.0m } => 4.99m,
    { Destination.Country: "US" } => 9.99m,
    { IsExpress: true } => 29.99m,
    _ => 19.99m,
};
```

Patterns are evaluated top to bottom; the compiler reports arms that can never match.

## Closed alternatives, today

```csharp
public abstract record PaymentResult
{
    private PaymentResult() { }

    public sealed record Approved(string AuthorizationCode) : PaymentResult;
    public sealed record Declined(string Reason) : PaymentResult;
    public sealed record RequiresAction(Uri RedirectTo) : PaymentResult;
}

public static IResult ToHttp(PaymentResult result) => result switch
{
    PaymentResult.Approved a => Results.Ok(new { a.AuthorizationCode }),
    PaymentResult.Declined d => Results.UnprocessableEntity(new { d.Reason }),
    PaymentResult.RequiresAction r => Results.Accepted(r.RedirectTo.ToString()),
    _ => throw new UnreachableException(),
};
```

The nested types can call the private constructor; nobody else can derive. In C# 15 the same
idea becomes `closed` or `union` and the compiler checks exhaustiveness (Chapter 13).

## Real-world scenario: replacing boolean soup

```csharp
public sealed class Subscription
{
    public bool IsTrial { get; set; }
    public bool IsCancelled { get; set; }
    public DateTime? TrialEnds { get; set; }
    public DateTime? CancelledAt { get; set; }
    public DateTime? RenewsOn { get; set; }
}
```

Five fields allow 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32 combinations of null/non-null and true/false, of which
perhaps four are meaningful. A support ticket reading "customer is both cancelled and renewing"
is the inevitable result.

```csharp
public abstract record SubscriptionState
{
    private SubscriptionState() { }
    public sealed record Trial(DateOnly EndsOn) : SubscriptionState;
    public sealed record Active(DateOnly RenewsOn) : SubscriptionState;
    public sealed record Cancelled(DateOnly CancelledOn, DateOnly AccessUntil) : SubscriptionState;
}
```

title: Extension members
questions:

    prompt: What do C# 14 extension members add beyond classic `this`-parameter extension methods?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: props

        correct: true

        text: An `extension(Receiver r) { ... }` block that groups members for one receiver
        correct: true

  - id: compat
    prompt: Are existing `this`-parameter extension methods compatible with C# 14?
    options:
      - text: No, they must be rewritten as extension blocks
      - text: Only in .NET Framework

        correct: true
      - text: Only if marked `[Obsolete]`
    explanation: The language team designed the feature so that libraries can move to the new syntax without breaking callers.
  - id: receiver-name
    prompt: "In `extension(Order order) { public bool IsLarge => order.Total > 1000m; }`, what is `order`?"
    options:

      - text: A new instance created for each call
      - text: A static property
      - id: receiver

        correct: true

      - id: no-storage
        text: Extension members cannot add storage to the receiver; there is nowhere for the value to live
        correct: true
      - text: There is no problem
    explanation: Extension properties are computed. Attaching data needs a real member, a wrapper, or (for advanced cases) `ConditionalWeakTable`.
  - id: when

        correct: true
      - id: interface-helpers

        correct: true

## Learning objectives

- Write extension blocks with properties, methods and static members
- Know what extensions cannot do
- Use extensions for mapping and fluent APIs

## From extension methods to extension members

Classic extension methods (C# 3, 2007) only allowed methods:

```csharp
public static class OrderExtensions
{
    public static bool IsLarge(this Order order) => order.Total > 1000m;
}
```

C# 14 introduces extension blocks:

```csharp
public static class OrderExtensions
{
    extension(Order order)
    {
        public bool IsLarge => order.Total > 1000m;

        public bool IsOverdue(TimeProvider time) =>
            order.DueDate < DateOnly.FromDateTime(time.GetUtcNow().UtcDateTime) && !order.IsPaid;

        public OrderSummary ToSummary() => new(order.Id, order.CustomerName, order.Total);
    }

    extension(Order)
    {
        public static Order Empty(CustomerId customer) => new(OrderId.New(), customer, []);
    }
}
```

Callers write `order.IsLarge`, `order.ToSummary()` and `Order.Empty(customerId)`.

## Extending interfaces and sequences

```csharp
public static class EnumerableExtensions
{
    extension<T>(IEnumerable<T> source)
    {
        public bool IsEmpty => !source.Any();

        public IEnumerable<T[]> InBatchesOf(int size) => source.Chunk(size);
    }
}

if (pendingEmails.IsEmpty) return;
foreach (var batch in pendingEmails.InBatchesOf(100))
{
    await sender.SendBatchAsync(batch, ct);
}
```

## Real-world scenario: a value-object API you do not own

Your company's shared library exposes a `Money` type you cannot change. You need
`Money.Zero(currency)` and `money.IsZero` everywhere:

```csharp
public static class MoneyExtensions
{
    extension(Money)
    {
        public static Money Zero(string currency) => new(0m, currency);
    }

    extension(Money money)
    {
        public bool IsZero => money.Amount == 0m;
    }
}
```

## Limits worth remembering

- No instance state: extensions cannot add fields
- Resolution is static: no virtual dispatch on the receiver's runtime type
- A real member on the type always wins over an extension with the same signature
- Discoverability depends on `using` directives — keep extensions in predictable namespaces

- Microsoft Learn, "What's new in C# 14" — <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/whats-new/csharp-14>
- Microsoft Learn, "Extension members" — <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/programming-guide/classes-and-structs/extension-methods>

title: field, null-conditional assignment, spans and the rest
questions:
  - id: field-keyword
    prompt: "What does `field` refer to in `public string Name { get; set => field = value.Trim(); }`?"
    options:
      - id: backing
        text: The compiler-generated backing field of the property
        correct: true
      - text: A new public field named `field`
      - text: The `value` parameter
      - text: A field on the base class
    explanation: The `field` contextual keyword lets you add logic to one accessor without declaring a backing field by hand. If you already have a member named `field`, use `@field` or `this.field` to disambiguate.
  - id: null-cond-assign
    prompt: "What does `customer?.LastSeen = now;` do in C# 14?"
    options:
      - text: Throws if `customer` is null
      - text: Assigns null to `customer`
      - text: It does not compile in any C# version
      - id: assign-if-not-null
        text: Assigns `now` to `LastSeen` only if `customer` is not null; otherwise does nothing, and the right side is not evaluated
        correct: true
    explanation: Null-conditional member access can now appear on the left of assignments (and compound assignments like `+=`). Increment and decrement (`++`, `--`) are not allowed.
  - id: spans
    prompt: What do C# 14's first-class span conversions provide?
    options:
      - text: Spans can now be stored in fields of classes
      - id: implicit
        text: Implicit conversions between arrays, `Span<T>` and `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, so span-based overloads and extension methods apply naturally
        correct: true
      - text: Spans become reference types
      - text: Automatic parallelization of span loops
    explanation: Library authors can now offer a single `ReadOnlySpan<T>` overload, and calls with arrays or strings bind to it, including as extension receivers.
  - id: nameof-unbound
    prompt: What does `nameof(List<>)` produce in C# 14?
    options:
      - text: "`\"List<T>\"`"
      - id: list
        text: "`\"List\"`"
        correct: true
      - text: A compile error, as in earlier versions
      - text: "`\"System.Collections.Generic.List`1\"`"
    explanation: Unbound generic types are now allowed in `nameof`. Previously you had to write `nameof(List<int>)` with an arbitrary type argument.
  - id: lambda-modifiers
    prompt: "Which lambda is newly legal in C# 14 given `delegate bool TryParse<T>(string text, out T result);`?"
    options:
      - text: "`TryParse<int> parse = async (text, out result) => ...;`"
      - id: modifiers-no-types
        text: "`TryParse<int> parse = (text, out result) => int.TryParse(text, out result);`"
        correct: true
      - text: "`TryParse<int> parse = text => true;`"
      - text: None — lambdas still require explicit types for `out` parameters
    explanation: C# 14 allows parameter modifiers such as `out`, `ref`, `in` and `scoped` on lambda parameters without spelling out their types.
  - id: partial-ctors
    prompt: Who benefits most from partial constructors and partial events?
    options:
      - text: Developers writing simple console apps
      - id: generators
        text: Source generators, which can implement a constructor or event that the user declared
        correct: true
      - text: Developers targeting .NET Framework
      - text: Nobody — they are deprecated
    explanation: Partial members let a declaration in your code be implemented in generated code — the pattern behind high-performance logging, regex and interop generators.
  - id: compound-ops
    prompt: What is the benefit of user-defined compound assignment operators such as `public void operator +=(Vector other)`?
    options:
      - text: They are required for all structs
      - text: They replace `IEquatable<T>`
      - id: in-place
        text: The type can update itself in place instead of allocating a new instance for `a = a + b`
        correct: true
      - text: They make operators virtual
    explanation: For large mutable numeric types, matrices or buffers, in-place updates avoid copying and allocation.

## Learning objectives

- Use the `field` keyword for validation and normalization
- Use null-conditional assignment
- Know what span conversions, unbound `nameof`, lambda modifiers, partial constructors/events and
  compound operators are for

## The field keyword

Before C# 14, adding one line of logic to an auto-property meant writing the backing field:

```csharp
private string _email = "";
public string Email
{
    get => _email;
    set => _email = value.Trim().ToLowerInvariant();
}
```

Now:

```csharp
public string Email
{
    get;
    set => field = value.Trim().ToLowerInvariant();
}
```

Validation in `init` accessors works the same way, which also protects records against invalid
`with` expressions:

```csharp
public sealed record Percentage
{
    public required decimal Value
    {
        get;
        init => field = value is >= 0m and <= 100m
            ? value
            : throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(Value));
    }
}
```

## Null-conditional assignment

```csharp
if (session is not null)
{
    session.LastActivity = time.GetUtcNow();
}
```

becomes

```csharp
session?.LastActivity = time.GetUtcNow();
```

Use it where "nothing to update" is legitimately normal. If `session` being null is a bug, an
explicit check that throws is more honest.

## First-class spans

```csharp
public static class Checksums
{
    public static int Sum(ReadOnlySpan<byte> data)
    {
        var total = 0;
        foreach (var b in data) total += b;
        return total;
    }
}

byte[] payload = File.ReadAllBytes("message.bin");
var sum = Checksums.Sum(payload);
```

One overload serves arrays, `Span<byte>`, slices and stack memory alike.

## Unbound generic `nameof`

```csharp
logger.LogDebug("Resolving {Type}", nameof(IRepository<>));
```

## Lambda parameter modifiers

```csharp
TryParse<decimal> parse = (text, out result) => decimal.TryParse(text, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, out result);
```

## Partial constructors and events

```csharp
public partial class Telemetry
{
    public partial Telemetry(ILogger logger);
    public partial event EventHandler<Measurement>? Measured;
}
```

A source generator supplies the implementing declarations.

## User-defined compound assignment

```csharp
public sealed class Histogram
{
    private readonly long[] _buckets = new long[64];

    public void operator +=(int sample) => _buckets[Math.Clamp(sample, 0, 63)]++;
}

histogram += latencyMs;
```

- Microsoft Learn, "field keyword" — <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/keywords/field>
- dotnet/csharplang proposals — <https://github.com/dotnet/csharplang/tree/main/proposals>

title: What a Task is (and is not)
questions:
  - id: task-not-thread
    prompt: Which statement best describes a `Task`?
    options:
      - id: promise
        text: An object representing an operation that will complete in the future, with a result or an exception
        correct: true
      - text: A thread with a nicer API
      - text: A unit of work that always runs on the thread pool
      - text: A synonym for `Thread.Start`
    explanation: A task is a promise of a result. Some tasks represent CPU work queued to the thread pool; most in server code represent I/O, during which *no thread* is running for that operation.
  - id: hot
    prompt: "When does the HTTP request start in `var t = http.GetStringAsync(url);`?"
    options:
      - text: When `await t` is executed
      - text: When `t.Start()` is called
      - text: When the garbage collector runs
      - id: immediately
        text: Immediately — tasks returned from async methods are "hot"; awaiting only observes completion
        correct: true
    explanation: This is why starting several operations and then awaiting them gives concurrency. Calling `Start()` on a task from an async method throws.
  - id: no-thread
    prompt: Stephen Cleary's well-known article is titled "There Is No Thread". What does it explain?
    options:
      - id: io-no-thread
        text: That during a true asynchronous I/O operation no thread is blocked waiting for it; the OS signals completion
        correct: true
      - text: That .NET does not use threads
      - text: That `Task.Run` never uses a thread
      - text: That async methods run on the UI thread only
    explanation: The device driver and OS complete the I/O; a thread-pool thread is borrowed only briefly to run the continuation.
  - id: taskcompletionsource
    prompt: What is `TaskCompletionSource<T>` for?
    options:
      - text: Running CPU work in parallel
      - id: bridge
        text: Creating a task whose completion you control manually — bridging callback- or event-based APIs into `await`
        correct: true
      - text: Cancelling tasks
      - text: Logging task exceptions
    explanation: Construct it with `TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously` to avoid running awaiters' continuations inline on the thread that calls `SetResult`.
  - id: valuetask-rules
    prompt: Which are rules for consuming a `ValueTask<T>`?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: once
        text: Await it at most once
        correct: true
      - id: no-concurrent
        text: Do not await it concurrently from multiple places
        correct: true
      - id: astask
        text: If you need to do either of those, call `.AsTask()` once and use the resulting `Task`
        correct: true
      - text: Always prefer `ValueTask` over `Task` for every public API
    explanation: "`ValueTask` can be backed by a pooled, reusable object. Using it twice may observe another operation's result. Default to `Task`; use `ValueTask` for hot paths that frequently complete synchronously."
  - id: completed-task
    prompt: A method implementing an async interface has nothing asynchronous to do. What should it return?
    options:
      - text: "`Task.Run(() => result)`"
      - text: "`new Task<T>(() => result)`"
      - text: "`null`"
      - id: fromresult
        text: "`Task.FromResult(result)` (or `Task.CompletedTask` for non-generic `Task`)"
        correct: true
    explanation: Returning `null` from a `Task`-returning method makes the caller's `await` throw `NullReferenceException`. `Task.Run` wastes a thread hop.
  - id: exceptions
    prompt: "An async method throws before its first `await`. When does the caller see the exception?"
    options:
      - id: stored
        text: When the returned task is awaited — the exception is stored in the task
        correct: true
      - text: Immediately, as a synchronous throw from the call
      - text: Never; it is swallowed
      - text: On the finalizer thread
    explanation: Everything inside an `async` method, including argument validation, is captured in the task. If you need eager validation, validate in a non-async wrapper that then calls a private async core.

## Learning objectives

- Describe a task as a promise, not a thread
- Distinguish I/O-bound and CPU-bound work
- Use `Task.FromResult`, `TaskCompletionSource` and `ValueTask` correctly

## Promises, not threads

```csharp
Task<string> pending = http.GetStringAsync("https://example.org/rates");
DoOtherWork();
string rates = await pending;
```

From the moment `GetStringAsync` returns, the request is in flight. While the network does its
work, no thread in your process is dedicated to it. `await` subscribes a continuation and returns
control to the caller.

## Two kinds of work

| | I/O-bound | CPU-bound |
|---|---|---|
| Examples | HTTP, database, file, queue | Image resize, compression, hashing large data |
| Uses a thread while waiting? | No | Yes, the whole time |
| Right tool | Async APIs + `await` | Synchronous code; `Task.Run` or `Parallel` to offload where a thread must stay free |
| Scales with | Concurrency (thousands in flight) | Cores |

Server code is overwhelmingly I/O-bound. That is why async matters so much there: a thread pool of
a few dozen threads can service thousands of concurrent requests that are mostly waiting.

## Bridging old APIs with TaskCompletionSource

```csharp
public static Task<ScanResult> ScanAsync(this BarcodeScanner scanner, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var tcs = new TaskCompletionSource<ScanResult>(TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously);

    void OnScanned(object? sender, ScanResult result)
    {
        scanner.Scanned -= OnScanned;
        tcs.TrySetResult(result);
    }

    scanner.Scanned += OnScanned;
    var registration = ct.Register(() =>
    {
        scanner.Scanned -= OnScanned;
        tcs.TrySetCanceled(ct);
    });
    _ = tcs.Task.ContinueWith(_ => registration.Dispose(), TaskScheduler.Default);

    scanner.Start();
    return tcs.Task;
}
```

## Eager validation with an async core

```csharp
public Task<Invoice> GetInvoiceAsync(InvoiceId id, CancellationToken ct)
{
    ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfEqual(id.Value, Guid.Empty);
    return GetInvoiceCoreAsync(id, ct);
}

private async Task<Invoice> GetInvoiceCoreAsync(InvoiceId id, CancellationToken ct)
{
    await using var connection = await dataSource.OpenConnectionAsync(ct);
    return await connection.QuerySingleAsync<Invoice>(
        new CommandDefinition("select * from Invoices where Id = @Value", id, cancellationToken: ct));
}
```

Most application code does not need this split; it is a library-quality nicety.

## ValueTask: a measured optimization

```csharp
public ValueTask<Rate> GetRateAsync(string currency, CancellationToken ct)
{
    if (_cache.TryGetValue(currency, out var rate))
    {
        return ValueTask.FromResult(rate);
    }
    return new ValueTask<Rate>(LoadRateAsync(currency, ct));
}
```

When the cache hit rate is 99%, this avoids a `Task<Rate>` allocation on almost every call.

title: How await works, and the truth about ConfigureAwait
questions:
  - id: state-machine
    prompt: What does the compiler turn an `async` method into?
    options:
      - text: A new thread per method
      - text: A synchronous method with `.Wait()` calls
      - id: state-machine
        text: A state machine that records where it paused and resumes there when an awaited operation completes
        correct: true
      - text: A `Parallel.For` loop
    explanation: Each `await` is a potential suspension point. If the awaited task has already completed, execution continues synchronously without suspending.
  - id: sync-context
    prompt: What is a `SynchronizationContext` used for in the context of `await`?
    options:
      - id: resume-where
        text: Deciding where the continuation runs — for example back on the UI thread in WPF or WinForms
        correct: true
      - text: Synchronizing access to static fields
      - text: Encrypting task results
      - text: Choosing which CPU core runs a method
    explanation: By default `await` captures the current context (or `TaskScheduler`) and posts the continuation back to it.
  - id: aspnetcore-context

    options:
      - text: Yes, the same as classic ASP.NET
      - text: Only in Blazor Server

        text: No — continuations run on thread-pool threads, so `ConfigureAwait(false)` has no practical effect in ASP.NET Core application code
        correct: true
    explanation: Classic ASP.NET (System.Web) had `AspNetSynchronizationContext`, which caused the infamous `.Result` deadlocks. ASP.NET Core removed it. Note that Blazor (Server and WebAssembly) does have its own renderer synchronization context.
  - id: when-cfa
    prompt: Where is `ConfigureAwait(false)` still recommended?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: libraries

        correct: true
      - id: ui-background
        text: In UI apps, in code after an `await` that does not need to touch UI elements
        correct: true
      - text: Everywhere in ASP.NET Core controllers, as a mandatory style rule
      - text: Before `await Task.Yield()`
    explanation: The rule "always use `ConfigureAwait(false)`" is library guidance that hardened into dogma for application code. It is harmless there but adds noise.
  - id: deadlock
    prompt: Why does `var data = GetDataAsync().Result;` deadlock in a WPF button handler?
    options:
      - text: Because `.Result` is not allowed in WPF
      - id: ui-blocked
        text: The UI thread blocks waiting for the task, while the task's continuation waits to be posted back to that same blocked UI thread
        correct: true
      - text: Because the garbage collector pauses the UI thread
      - text: It does not deadlock
    explanation: Each side waits for the other. The fix is `await` all the way up; `ConfigureAwait(false)` inside `GetDataAsync` would only patch the symptom.
  - id: runtime-async

      - text: A way to run async code without tasks
      - id: runtime-native

        correct: true
      - text: A garbage collector mode
    explanation: Your `async`/`await` code stays the same; the mechanics underneath move into the runtime. This is a good example of why writing idiomatic code ages well — the platform improves underneath it.
  - id: completed-fast-path

    options:

      - text: An exception is thrown
      - text: The method restarts from the beginning

        correct: true
    explanation: This synchronous fast path is why cached results and buffered streams make async code cheap.

## Learning objectives

- Describe the async state machine at a conceptual level
- Explain synchronization contexts and when `ConfigureAwait(false)` matters
- Identify the classic sync-over-async deadlock

## The mechanics in one picture

```csharp
public async Task<decimal> GetTotalAsync(OrderId id, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var order = await _orders.GetAsync(id, ct);
    var rate = await _rates.GetAsync(order.Currency, ct);
    return order.Total * rate.ToUsd;
}
```

Conceptually the compiler produces:

1. **State 0**: call `_orders.GetAsync`. If it is not complete, store state = 1, register a
   continuation and return an incomplete task to the caller.
2. **State 1**: read the order, call `_rates.GetAsync`. If not complete, store state = 2, register,
   return.
3. **State 2**: compute, set the task's result.

Local variables that live across awaits are hoisted into the state machine.

## Where the continuation runs

| Environment | Context captured by `await` | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| WPF / WinForms / MAUI | UI `SynchronizationContext` | Continuation returns to the UI thread |
| Classic ASP.NET (System.Web) | `AspNetSynchronizationContext` | One-at-a-time request context; `.Result` deadlocks |
| ASP.NET Core | none | Continuation on any thread-pool thread |
| Console / worker service | none | Thread pool |
| Blazor | renderer context | Continuation on the renderer's logical thread |

## ConfigureAwait: a dogma case study

In 2012–2016, much .NET code ran under classic ASP.NET or WPF, and libraries were called from
both. Library authors were told "use `ConfigureAwait(false)` everywhere so your library cannot
deadlock someone's UI". Good advice for libraries.

The advice then spread, without its reason, into application code — including ASP.NET Core
applications, which have no context to capture. Today you can find codebases with
`.ConfigureAwait(false)` on every line of controller code, enforced by a rule nobody can explain.
That is legacy dogma.

**Rules of thumb in 2026:**

- Writing a reusable NuGet library: use `ConfigureAwait(false)` (an analyzer such as CA2007 can
  enforce it in library projects only).
- Writing ASP.NET Core, worker service or console application code: omit it.
- Writing UI code: omit it where you need the UI thread afterwards; use it in non-UI helpers.
- Never use it to "fix" a deadlock caused by blocking — remove the blocking instead.

.NET 8 added `ConfigureAwaitOptions` for advanced cases:

```csharp
await task.ConfigureAwait(ConfigureAwaitOptions.SuppressThrowing);
```

## Real-world scenario: the Friday deadlock

A WinForms tool called a shared library's `GetCustomersAsync().Result` in a `Form_Load` handler.
It worked for months — until the library added its first real `await` on network I/O. The UI
froze on startup. Two fixes were proposed: add `ConfigureAwait(false)` throughout the library, or
make `Form_Load` `async void` and `await` the call. The second fixes the cause; the first hides it
and leaves the next blocking call to deadlock elsewhere. (Do both if you own the library.)

## Learning objectives

- Start independent operations concurrently and await them together
- Bound concurrency correctly
- Choose between `WhenAll`, `WhenAny`, `WhenEach`, `Parallel.ForEachAsync` and channels

## Sequential versus concurrent

```csharp
var customer = await customers.GetAsync(id, ct);
var orderList = await orderStore.ListForAsync(id, ct);
```

```csharp
var customerTask = customers.GetAsync(id, ct);
var ordersTask = orderStore.ListForAsync(id, ct);
await Task.WhenAll(customerTask, ordersTask);
var customer = await customerTask;
var orderList = await ordersTask;
```

Awaiting an already completed task is free and avoids `.Result` (which is safe here but trains
bad habits).

**Caution with shared resources:** an EF Core `DbContext` or a single `DbConnection` cannot run two
commands concurrently. Concurrency across one connection needs separate connections.

## Bounded concurrency

```csharp
await Parallel.ForEachAsync(
    invoiceIds,
    new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 8, CancellationToken = ct },
    async (id, token) =>
    {
        var pdf = await renderer.RenderAsync(id, token);
        await storage.UploadAsync($"invoices/{id}.pdf", pdf, token);
    });
```

The SemaphoreSlim equivalent, useful when you also need the results:

```csharp
using var gate = new SemaphoreSlim(8);
var tasks = invoiceIds.Select(async id =>
{
    await gate.WaitAsync(ct);
    try
    {
        return await renderer.RenderAsync(id, ct);
    }
    finally
    {
        gate.Release();
    }
});
byte[][] pdfs = await Task.WhenAll(tasks);
```

## As they complete

```csharp
var lookups = providers.Select(p => p.QuoteAsync(shipment, ct)).ToList();
await foreach (var finished in Task.WhenEach(lookups))
{
    var quote = await finished;
    progress.Report(quote);
}
```

## First one wins, with cleanup

```csharp
using var cts = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(ct);
var primary = primaryDns.ResolveAsync(host, cts.Token);
var secondary = secondaryDns.ResolveAsync(host, cts.Token);
var winner = await Task.WhenAny(primary, secondary);
await cts.CancelAsync();
return await winner;
```

Always cancel the losers; otherwise they keep consuming resources after you have returned.

## Channels for pipelines

```csharp
var channel = Channel.CreateBounded<OrderEvent>(new BoundedChannelOptions(1_000)
{
    FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait,
    SingleReader = true,
});

async Task ProduceAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    await foreach (var evt in broker.SubscribeAsync(ct))
    {
        await channel.Writer.WriteAsync(evt, ct);
    }
    channel.Writer.Complete();
}

async Task ConsumeAsync(CancellationToken ct)
{
    await foreach (var evt in channel.Reader.ReadAllAsync(ct))
    {
        await projector.ApplyAsync(evt, ct);
    }
}
```

## Streaming with IAsyncEnumerable

```csharp
public async IAsyncEnumerable<Product> GetAllAsync([EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct = default)
{
    string? cursor = null;
    do
    {
        var page = await api.GetProductsAsync(cursor, ct);
        foreach (var product in page.Items) yield return product;
        cursor = page.NextCursor;
    } while (cursor is not null);
}
```

## Real-world scenario: the nightly export that took down a partner

A nightly job called a partner's API for 120,000 shipments with `Task.WhenAll`. On day one it
worked — the partner's sandbox was small. In production, the burst triggered the partner's DDoS
protection and blocked the company's IP for a day. `Parallel.ForEachAsync` with a degree of 10,
plus a resilience pipeline that honored `Retry-After`, made the job polite and only 4 minutes
slower.

- Microsoft Learn, `Task.WhenEach` — <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.task.wheneach>
- Microsoft Learn, "System.Threading.Channels" — <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/extensions/channels>
- Microsoft Learn, "Generate and consume async streams" — <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/asynchronous-programming/generate-consume-asynchronous-stream>

title: Async mistakes that still ship to production
questions:
  - id: async-void-crash
    prompt: What happens when an exception escapes an `async void` method in an ASP.NET Core or worker service process?
    options:
      - text: It is logged and ignored
      - text: It is stored in a task nobody awaits
      - id: crash
        text: It is rethrown on the thread pool with no caller to catch it, which typically terminates the process
        correct: true
      - text: The method retries automatically
    explanation: "`async void` has no task to carry the exception. Event handlers are the only legitimate use, and they should catch their own exceptions."
  - id: fire-forget
    prompt: An endpoint does `_ = emailSender.SendWelcomeAsync(user);` and returns immediately. Which problems can this cause?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: lost-errors
        text: Exceptions are silently lost
        correct: true
      - id: disposed-scope
        text: Scoped services (such as a `DbContext`) used by the background work may be disposed when the request ends
        correct: true
      - id: shutdown
        text: Work in flight is lost when the process restarts or scales in
        correct: true
      - text: The response is delayed until the email is sent
    explanation: Use a queue (a `Channel` consumed by a `BackgroundService` for in-process work, or a durable broker for work that must survive restarts).
  - id: sync-over-async
    prompt: Why is `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` in an ASP.NET Core request path harmful even though there is no synchronization context?
    options:
      - text: It always deadlocks
      - id: starvation
        text: It blocks a thread-pool thread while waiting; under load this causes thread-pool starvation and latency collapse
        correct: true
      - text: It does not compile
      - text: It changes the exception type
    explanation: The thread pool grows slowly. When many requests block, new work queues behind them and the service stalls — a classic production incident pattern.
  - id: elide
    prompt: "When is it safe to drop `async`/`await` and return the task directly, as in `Task<User> GetAsync(Guid id) => _inner.GetAsync(id);`?"
    options:
      - text: Always, it is strictly better
      - id: simple-passthrough
        text: In a simple pass-through with no `using`, `try`/`catch`, or code after the call
        correct: true
      - text: Never, it does not compile
      - text: Only inside `using` blocks
    explanation: Inside a `using`, returning the task without awaiting disposes the resource before the operation finishes. Exceptions also surface differently. When in doubt, keep `async`/`await` — the overhead is small.
  - id: lazy-async-init
    prompt: Why should constructors not start asynchronous work (for example `_ready = LoadAsync();`)?
    options:
      - text: Constructors run on a separate thread
      - text: The compiler forbids it
      - text: Tasks cannot be stored in fields
      - id: unobserved
        text: Exceptions become unobserved or surface at surprising times, and DI resolution cannot await; use an explicit `InitializeAsync`, a factory, or a hosted service
        correct: true
    explanation: Construction should be cheap and side-effect free. Asynchronous start-up belongs in `IHostedService.StartAsync` or in lazily awaited initialization.
  - id: asynclocal
    prompt: What is `AsyncLocal<T>` used for?
    options:
      - text: Storing data per thread
      - text: Making fields thread-safe
      - id: flows
        text: Storing ambient data that flows with the logical async call path, such as a correlation id or `Activity.Current`
        correct: true
      - text: Caching tasks
    explanation: "`ThreadStatic` breaks across awaits because continuations can run on different threads. `AsyncLocal` flows with the `ExecutionContext`. Use sparingly — ambient state is hidden coupling."
  - id: backgroundservice
    prompt: In a `BackgroundService`, what should `ExecuteAsync` do with its `stoppingToken`?
    options:
      - text: Ignore it
      - text: Call `Environment.Exit` when it fires
      - text: Store it in a static field
      - id: pass-it
        text: Pass it to every async call in the loop and exit the loop when it is cancelled
        correct: true
    explanation: The host signals shutdown through this token and waits (by default 30 seconds since .NET 6) for services to stop.

## Learning objectives

- Recognize `async void`, fire-and-forget and sync-over-async in code review
- Move background work to a proper queue and hosted service
- Know when eliding `async` is safe

## A gallery of bugs

### async void

```csharp
public async void OnOrderPlaced(object? sender, OrderPlaced e)
{
    await _billing.ChargeAsync(e.OrderId);
}
```

If `ChargeAsync` throws, the process may terminate. If you must use an event handler, catch:

```csharp
public async void OnOrderPlaced(object? sender, OrderPlaced e)
{
    try
    {
        await _billing.ChargeAsync(e.OrderId, CancellationToken.None);
    }
    catch (Exception ex)
    {
        _logger.LogError(ex, "Charging order {OrderId} failed", e.OrderId);
    }
}
```

### Fire-and-forget from a request

```csharp
app.MapPost("/users", async (CreateUser cmd, AppDb db, IEmailSender email) =>
{
    var user = await db.CreateAsync(cmd);
    _ = email.SendWelcomeAsync(user);
    return Results.Created($"/users/{user.Id}", user);
});
```

### The fix: a channel-backed queue and a hosted service

```csharp
public sealed class EmailQueue
{
    private readonly Channel<WelcomeEmail> _channel = Channel.CreateBounded<WelcomeEmail>(10_000);
    public ValueTask EnqueueAsync(WelcomeEmail email, CancellationToken ct) => _channel.Writer.WriteAsync(email, ct);
    public IAsyncEnumerable<WelcomeEmail> ReadAllAsync(CancellationToken ct) => _channel.Reader.ReadAllAsync(ct);
}

public sealed class EmailWorker(EmailQueue queue, IServiceScopeFactory scopes, ILogger<EmailWorker> logger)
    : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        await foreach (var email in queue.ReadAllAsync(stoppingToken))
        {
            try
            {
                await using var scope = scopes.CreateAsyncScope();
                var sender = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<IEmailSender>();
                await sender.SendAsync(email, stoppingToken);
            }
            catch (Exception ex) when (ex is not OperationCanceledException)
            {
                logger.LogError(ex, "Welcome email to {UserId} failed", email.UserId);
            }
        }
    }
}

builder.Services.AddSingleton<EmailQueue>();
builder.Services.AddHostedService<EmailWorker>();
```

For work that must survive a restart (payments, compliance emails), use a durable queue — Azure
Service Bus, Amazon SQS, RabbitMQ — or the transactional outbox pattern.

### Sync over async

```csharp
public IActionResult Get(int id)
{
    var product = _catalog.GetAsync(id).GetAwaiter().GetResult();
    return Ok(product);
}
```

Make the action `async Task<IActionResult>` and `await`. Every framework entry point in modern
.NET — controllers, minimal APIs, hosted services, `Main`, xUnit tests — accepts async.

### Returning a task from inside a using

```csharp
public Task<string> ReadAsync(string path)
{
    using var reader = new StreamReader(path);
    return reader.ReadToEndAsync();
}
```

The reader is disposed while the read is still in flight. Add `async` and `await`.

## A checklist for code review

- [ ] No `async void` except event handlers that catch everything
- [ ] No `.Result`, `.Wait()`, `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` on incomplete tasks
- [ ] No discarded tasks (`_ =`) without a deliberate, logged, owned lifetime
- [ ] Every async method accepts and passes a `CancellationToken` where the caller can cancel
- [ ] No `Task.Run` around I/O in server code
- [ ] Unbounded `WhenAll` over user-controlled sizes has a concurrency limit

## Sources

- David Fowler, "Async Guidance" — <https://github.com/davidfowl/AspNetCoreDiagnosticScenarios/blob/master/AsyncGuidance.md>
- Microsoft Learn, "Background tasks with hosted services" — <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/host/hosted-services>
- Stephen Cleary, "Eliding Async and Await" — <https://blog.stephencleary.com/2016/12/eliding-async-await.html>
- Microsoft Learn, "Debug thread-pool starvation" — <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/core/diagnostics/debug-threadpool-starvation>

title: What a cancellation token is
questions:
  - id: cooperative
    prompt: What kind of cancellation model does .NET use?
    options:
      - text: Preemptive — the runtime stops the thread at any point
      - id: cooperative
        text: Cooperative — code observes a token and chooses where to stop
        correct: true
      - text: Signal-based — the OS sends SIGKILL to the task
      - text: Exception-based — the runtime injects an exception anywhere
    explanation: Nothing is forcibly interrupted. Cancellation only happens where code checks the token or passes it to an API that does.
  - id: source-vs-token
    prompt: What is the difference between `CancellationTokenSource` and `CancellationToken`?
    options:
      - text: They are the same type with different names
      - id: roles
        text: The source has the power to cancel; the token can only observe. You hand out tokens and keep the source
        correct: true
      - text: The token can cancel; the source can only observe
      - text: The source is for threads and the token is for tasks
    explanation: Separating the two roles means a callee cannot cancel its caller's other work. It is a capability design.
  - id: struct
    prompt: "`CancellationToken` is a struct. What does `default(CancellationToken)` (also `CancellationToken.None`) represent?"
    options:
      - text: A token that is already cancelled
      - text: An invalid token that throws when used
      - text: The current request's token
      - id: never
        text: A token that can never be cancelled
        correct: true
    explanation: "`CanBeCanceled` is `false` for it. That is why `CancellationToken ct = default` is a safe optional parameter."
  - id: oce
    prompt: Which exception signals that an operation was cancelled?
    options:
      - id: oce
        text: "`OperationCanceledException` (and its subclass `TaskCanceledException`)"
        correct: true
      - text: "`TimeoutException`"
      - text: "`ThreadAbortException`"
      - text: "`ObjectDisposedException`"
    explanation: Catch `OperationCanceledException`, not `TaskCanceledException`, so you handle both. A task that ends with this exception transitions to the *Canceled* state rather than *Faulted*.
  - id: observe-ways
    prompt: Which are legitimate ways for code to observe a token?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: pass
        text: Passing it to async APIs that accept a token
        correct: true
      - id: throwif
        text: Calling `ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` between units of work in a loop
        correct: true
      - id: register
        text: "`ct.Register(callback)` to bridge into APIs that have their own cancel mechanism"
        correct: true
      - text: Calling `Thread.Abort()` when `ct.IsCancellationRequested` is true
    explanation: "`Thread.Abort` is not supported on modern .NET and throws `PlatformNotSupportedException`."
  - id: linked
    prompt: What does `CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(a, b)` produce?
    options:
      - text: A source that cancels `a` and `b`
      - id: either
        text: A source whose token is cancelled when either `a` or `b` is cancelled, or when it is cancelled itself
        correct: true
      - text: A token that requires both to be cancelled
      - text: A copy of `a`
    explanation: Linking combines "the caller gave up" with "my own timeout" or "the app is shutting down". Dispose linked sources — they register callbacks on their parents.
  - id: dispose-cts
    prompt: Why should you dispose a `CancellationTokenSource` you create?
    options:
      - text: Undisposed sources cancel themselves after 60 seconds
      - id: timers-registrations
        text: It may own a timer (from `CancelAfter`) and linked registrations on parent tokens, which otherwise live longer than needed
        correct: true
      - text: It holds an OS thread
      - text: Disposal is required to read `IsCancellationRequested`
    explanation: A long-lived parent token (like the host's shutdown token) with thousands of undisposed linked children is a real memory leak pattern.

## Learning objectives

- Explain the cooperative cancellation model
- Use `CancellationTokenSource`, tokens, linking and registration
- Handle `OperationCanceledException` correctly

## The model in four sentences

1. Someone who might want to stop work owns a **`CancellationTokenSource`**.
2. They hand its **`CancellationToken`** to the work.
3. The work **checks** the token at safe points (or passes it on to APIs that check it).
4. When cancelled, the work stops and signals it by throwing **`OperationCanceledException`**.

```csharp
using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();
var work = ImportAsync(file, cts.Token);

Console.CancelKeyPress += (_, e) =>
{
    e.Cancel = true;
    cts.Cancel();
};

try
{
    await work;
}
catch (OperationCanceledException) when (cts.IsCancellationRequested)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Import cancelled by user.");
}
```

## Checking in CPU-bound loops

```csharp
public static int CountPrimes(int limit, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var count = 0;
    for (var n = 2; n < limit; n++)
    {
        if ((n & 0xFFFF) == 0) ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
        if (IsPrime(n)) count++;
    }
    return count;
}
```

Check often enough to be responsive and rarely enough to be cheap.

## Bridging with Register

```csharp
public static async Task<Process> RunAsync(ProcessStartInfo info, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var process = Process.Start(info) ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("Process did not start");
    await using var registration = ct.Register(() =>
    {
        if (!process.HasExited) process.Kill(entireProcessTree: true);
    });
    await process.WaitForExitAsync(ct);
    return process;
}
```

## Linking and timeouts

```csharp
public async Task<Quote> GetQuoteAsync(Shipment shipment, CancellationToken ct)
{
    using var timeout = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(ct);
    timeout.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(3));
    try
    {
        return await carrier.QuoteAsync(shipment, timeout.Token);
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) when (!ct.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        throw new TimeoutException("Carrier did not quote within 3 seconds");
    }
}
```

The `when` filter distinguishes "our timeout fired" from "our caller gave up" — a distinction
that matters for logging, metrics and HTTP status codes.

## Useful members added in modern .NET

| Member | Since | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `CancellationTokenSource.CancelAsync()` | .NET 8 | Cancel without running callbacks synchronously on the caller |
| `CancellationTokenSource.TryReset()` | .NET 6 | Reuse a source that was not cancelled (pooling) |
| `Task.WaitAsync(TimeSpan, CancellationToken)` | .NET 6 | Stop *waiting* for a task (does not stop the task) |
| `CancellationToken.UnsafeRegister` | .NET 5 | Register without flowing `ExecutionContext` |
| `new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan, TimeProvider)` | .NET 8 | Timeouts that tests can control |

- Stephen Toub, "Recommended patterns for CancellationToken" — <https://devblogs.microsoft.com/premier-developer/recommended-patterns-for-cancellationtoken/>

title: What cancellation is NOT
questions:
  - id: not-abort
    prompt: Your code calls a third-party SDK method `Compute(input)` that accepts no token and takes 10 minutes. You cancel your token after 5 seconds. What happens to `Compute`?
    options:
      - text: It stops immediately
      - id: keeps-running
        text: It keeps running to completion; tokens cannot stop code that does not observe them
        correct: true
      - text: The runtime aborts its thread
      - text: It throws `OperationCanceledException` at its next line
    explanation: Cancellation is a request, not an abort. If you must hard-stop uncooperative work, isolate it in a separate process you can kill.
  - id: waitasync-not-stop
    prompt: "What does `await slowTask.WaitAsync(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5))` do when the timeout elapses?"
    options:
      - id: stops-waiting
        text: Throws `TimeoutException` to *you*, while `slowTask` continues running in the background
        correct: true
      - text: Cancels `slowTask`
      - text: Blocks for 5 seconds then returns null
      - text: Restarts `slowTask`
    explanation: "`WaitAsync` abandons the wait, not the work. That is sometimes exactly what you want — but understand that the work still consumes resources and may still have side effects."
  - id: not-rollback
    prompt: A method writes three rows and is cancelled after the second write. What does cancellation do to the first two rows?
    options:
      - text: Rolls them back automatically
      - text: Marks them as deleted
      - id: nothing
        text: Nothing — cancellation does not undo side effects; atomicity needs a transaction (or idempotent, compensatable steps)
        correct: true
      - text: Moves them to a dead-letter queue
    explanation: If the three writes must be all-or-nothing, put them in one transaction. A cancelled `await` inside the transaction leads to disposal without commit, which rolls back.
  - id: not-a-guarantee
    prompt: You cancel an HTTP POST that charges a credit card. The `await` throws `OperationCanceledException`. Was the card charged?
    options:
      - id: unknown
        text: Unknown — the request may have reached the server and completed; cancellation only tells you that *you* stopped waiting
        correct: true
      - text: No, cancellation guarantees the server did nothing
      - text: Yes, always
      - text: Only if the response status was 200
    explanation: This is why payment APIs use idempotency keys. Retrying with the same key is safe whether or not the first attempt succeeded.
  - id: point-of-no-return
    prompt: In a checkout flow, after the payment provider has confirmed a charge, which token should the code use to save the order?
    options:
      - text: The request's `HttpContext.RequestAborted` token
      - id: none
        text: "`CancellationToken.None` (or a token tied only to application shutdown) — the user closing the tab must not stop us recording a payment we already took"
        correct: true
      - text: A token that cancels after 1 millisecond
      - text: No token; the method should not be async
    explanation: Past the point of no return, honoring the client's cancellation creates inconsistent state. Choose tokens deliberately per step, not mechanically.
  - id: not-error
    prompt: How should ASP.NET Core log a request that ended because the client disconnected?
    options:
      - text: As an error with a stack trace and an alert to on-call
      - text: It should crash the process
      - id: not-error
        text: As informational or debug at most — a client going away is not a server fault
        correct: true
      - text: As a security incident
    explanation: Treating cancellations as errors floods dashboards and pages people at 3 a.m. for users closing their browser. Filter with `catch (OperationCanceledException) when (ct.IsCancellationRequested)`.
  - id: not-swallow
    prompt: "What is wrong with `catch (OperationCanceledException) { return Array.Empty<Order>(); }` deep inside a data access method?"
    options:
      - text: "`Array.Empty` allocates"
      - text: It cannot compile
      - id: lies
        text: It converts "cancelled" into "no results", so callers proceed as if the query succeeded — possibly caching or acting on empty data
        correct: true
      - text: Nothing is wrong with it
    explanation: Let cancellation propagate. Only the code that *initiated* the cancellation (or a framework boundary) should decide what it means.
  - id: myths
    prompt: Which statements are myths?
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: myth-timeout
        text: "\"A token is a timeout.\" (A token is a signal; a timeout is one *reason* a source might signal.)"
        correct: true
      - id: myth-threads
        text: "\"Cancelling a token frees threads immediately.\""
        correct: true
      - text: "\"Cancellation is cooperative.\""
      - id: myth-optional
        text: "\"If my method accepts a token, callers are guaranteed fast cancellation.\" (Only if the method actually observes it everywhere.)"
        correct: true
    explanation: Cooperative is the one true statement. The others confuse the signal with its effects.
