    prompt: "To supply a test version of `fit.Parse` in `FitFilter`, where is the seam and where is the enabling point?"
    options:
      - id: o52368f
        text: "Seam — `main`; enabling point — `argv`"
      - id: classpath
        text: "Seam — the `new Parse` call in `process`; enabling point — the classpath"
        correct: true
      - id: o0e71dc

  - id: tell-interface

  - id: link-enabling

    options:
      - id: o26a369
        text: "Yes — every virtual call is a seam"
      - id: oab1ee4
        text: "Yes — the enabling point is the `Cell` base class"

    explanation: "“Is the call to Recalculate an object seam? No. There is no enabling point.” — “The class of the cell is decided when the object is created, and we can’t change it without modifying the method.”"
  - id: param-seam

      - id: o48c7e9

    explanation: "“In this example, the enabling point is the argument list of buildMartSheet.”"

    options:
      - id: o5ed91d

      - id: protected-virtual
        text: "Making the method protected and non-static lets a test subclass override it without editing `buildMartSheet`"
        correct: true
      - id: o8f3719
        text: "Static methods can be replaced at runtime by any test framework"
    explanation: "“Is the call to Recalculate in buildMartSheet a seam? Yes. We don’t have to edit buildMartSheet to change behavior at that call.   - id: three-seams
    prompt: "Which seam types are available at the `PostReceiveError` call in `CAsyncSslRec::Init`?"
    type: multiple

      - id: object

        correct: true

  - id: which-best
    prompt: "Which seam type does Feathers recommend in object-oriented languages, and when should the others be used?"
    options:
      - id: o990778
        text: "Link seams always, because they need no code changes"
      - id: object-best
        text: "Object seams in general; reserve preprocessing and link seams for pervasive dependencies with no better alternative"
        correct: true
      - id: o13e3bf
        text: "Preprocessing seams, because they are most explicit"
    explanation: "“In general, object seams are the best choice in object-oriented languages.” and “I like to reserve preprocessing seams and link seams for cases where dependencies are pervasive and there are no better alternatives.” They are “not as explicit” and tests on them “can be hard to maintain.”"
  - id: csharp-virtual
    prompt: "In C#, methods are non-virtual unless marked `virtual`. A legacy class calls its own non-virtual `SendAlert()` method. What does this mean for the object seam technique shown with `Recalculate`?"
    options:
      - id: oa2dce3
        text: "Nothing — C# overrides non-virtual methods automatically in subclasses"
      - id: od48fde
        text: "Object seams are impossible in C#"
      - id: mark-virtual
        text: "You must make the method `virtual` (and accessible to a subclass) before a testing subclass can override it"
        correct: true
    explanation: "The book's Java example removes `static` and makes the method `protected` so it can be overridden: “If we delete the keyword static on Recalculate and make it a protected method instead of a private method, we can subclass and override it”. In C# you also need `virtual`, because `new` on a non-virtual method only hides it."
---
## Learning objectives

- Identify preprocessing, link and object seams and their enabling points
- Decide which seam type to use and why
- Spot calls that look like seams but are not

## In a nutshell

| Seam | Build step | Enabling point | Recommendation |
|------|------------|----------------|----------------|
| Preprocessing | Before compilation (C/C++) | Preprocessor define | Last resort; obscures code |
| Link | Linking / class loading | Build script, classpath | Last resort; easy to miss |
| Object | Runtime dispatch | Where the object is created or passed | Default choice in OO code |

A call is an object seam only if something outside the method can choose which implementation
runs. A `new` in the same method kills the seam.

## Connections to today

- **C# virtual-by-opt-in.** Unlike Java, C# methods are non-virtual by default and many classes
  are `sealed`. Interfaces and constructor injection are the usual way to create object seams.
- **Conditional compilation.** `#if DEBUG` and custom `DefineConstants` are .NET's preprocessing
  seam. The same warning applies: two programs in one file.
- **Runtime detours.** Microsoft Fakes shims (Visual Studio Enterprise) and similar tools rewrite
  calls at run time, much like a link seam whose enabling point is the test context. They help
  with untouchable statics, but the dependency remains in the design.
- **Dependency injection containers** are enabling points expressed as configuration. Keep the
  test/production difference obvious, as the link-seam usage tip advises.

## Learning objectives

- State what makes a change a refactoring
- Explain how a "safe" tool refactoring can still change behaviour
- Run quick sanity checks on a refactoring tool

## In a nutshell

Automated refactorings are huge time savers if — and only if — they preserve behaviour. Know
what your tool checks, test it on tricky cases, and have tests around code before relying on it.

## Connections to today

- Roslyn-based refactorings in Visual Studio and Rider are far more capable than 2004 tools, yet
  side effects, reflection, `dynamic`, source generators and serialisation by member name can all
  defeat a tool's analysis.
- AI "refactor this" suggestions are not refactorings in Fowler's sense unless something verifies
  behaviour preservation. Treat them as hand edits.

## Learning objectives

- Explain the role of stand-ins when dependencies are removed
- Distinguish value-supplying stand-ins from effect-sensing ones

## Connections to today

| Need | Typical .NET choice |
|------|---------------------|
| Return canned values | Hand-written stub, `Substitute.For<T>().Returns(...)` |
| Record calls for assertions | Hand-written spy, `Received()`/`Verify()` |
| Replace time | `FakeTimeProvider` |
| Replace HTTP | Fake `HttpMessageHandler` |

Prefer state checks on a simple fake over deep interaction verification; over-specified mocks
make refactoring harder, which defeats the point in legacy work.

- Explain the xUnit design and its isolation guarantee
- Justify `setUp`/`tearDown` in JUnit's design
- Map the book's harnesses to today's .NET frameworks

## In a nutshell

Feathers found free xUnit harnesses more effective than costly GUI-driven tools. xUnit's power is
simplicity: tests in your language, isolated, grouped and rerunnable.

## Connections to today

- .NET has three mainstream xUnit-family frameworks: xUnit.net, NUnit and MSTest. All mark tests
  with attributes, as the book's NUnit example shows.
- Microsoft.Testing.Platform turns test projects into executables, echoing CppUnitLite's
  "just compile and run" simplicity.
- Playwright and similar tools have made UI tests far more reliable, but Feathers' caution about
  distance from the logic still applies to legacy work.

## Learning objectives

- Argue for or against test investment under deadline pressure
- Describe the team experiment and "getting over the hump"
- Recognise when to try getting the class under test before sprouting

## In a nutshell

The cost of tests is visible; the savings are counterfactual. Changes cluster, so tests tend to
pay back quickly. Teams that commit to "no change without tests" feel pain at first and then do
not want to go back. When you really cannot get the class under test, write the change as new
code: sprout or wrap.

## Connections to today

- "We'll fix it in the next sprint" is the 5:00 emergency. Tracking the follow-up as a ticket
  rarely beats getting the change tested now.
- A useful team agreement: any PR touching legacy code must either add a test or explain in the
  description why it couldn't — the modern form of "call a quick meeting".

## Learning objectives

- Apply the six Sprout Method steps
- Choose fallbacks when the source class cannot be instantiated
- Weigh the advantages and disadvantages

## In a nutshell

1. Find the change point.
2. Write a commented-out call to the new method.
3. Pass needed locals as arguments.
4. Capture a return value if needed.
5. Develop the sprout with TDD.
6. Uncomment the call.

## Connections to today

```csharp
public void PostEntries(IReadOnlyList<Entry> entries)
{
    var entriesToAdd = UniqueEntries(entries);
    foreach (var entry in entriesToAdd)
        entry.PostDate();
    _transactionBundle.ListManager.Add(entriesToAdd);
}

internal IReadOnlyList<Entry> UniqueEntries(IEnumerable<Entry> entries) =>
    entries.Where(e => !_transactionBundle.ListManager.HasEntry(e)).ToList();
```

- `internal` plus `InternalsVisibleTo` lets the test project call the sprout without making it
  public API.
- A sprouted `public static` helper in C# is easy to test and is often the seed of a later
  domain service.

## Learning objectives

- Recognise when to escalate from Sprout Method to Sprout Class
- Name sprouted classes so they join existing concepts
- Explain the trade-off of conceptual complexity

## In a nutshell

When the source class can't even compile into a harness, put the new logic in a new class,
develop it test-first, and instantiate it from the old code. Start with an awkward name if you
must, but look for the concept it belongs to.

## Connections to today

- In .NET, a sprouted class is usually a small service in a new file, injected or `new`-ed at
  the call site. If the old class isn't using DI, a direct `new` is fine for now — that line is a
  future seam.
- Project-level build cost is the .NET analogue of the C++ header benefit: putting new logic in a
  separate, lightly referenced project can keep incremental builds and test runs fast.

## Learning objectives

- Apply both forms of Wrap Method
- Explain temporal coupling
- Choose between Sprout Method and Wrap Method

## In a nutshell

Rename the old method, create a new one with the original signature that calls the new tested
behaviour and the old code. Or add a new explicitly named method that does both. New behaviour
must come before or after the old — never interleaved.

## Connections to today

```csharp
public void Pay()
{
    LogPayment();
    DispatchPayment();
}

private void DispatchPayment() { }
private void LogPayment() { }
```

- ASP.NET Core middleware, MediatR pipeline behaviours and `DelegatingHandler`s are
  architecture-level "wrap" mechanisms for before/after behaviour.
- Watch for temporal coupling in event handlers: "on order placed, also do X" accumulates exactly
  the way Feathers describes.

## Learning objectives

- Implement Wrap Class as a decorator and as a non-decorator wrapper
- Decide between the two forms based on the number of call sites
- Recognise when Wrap Class's higher threshold is met

## In a nutshell

Wrap the existing class in a new one that does the new work and delegates to the old. Use a
decorator (same interface, transparent to callers) when many callers need the behaviour, and a
plain wrapper when only one or two places do.

## Connections to today

```csharp
public sealed class LoggingEmployee(IEmployee inner, ILogger<LoggingEmployee> log) : IEmployee
{
    public void Pay()
    {
        log.LogInformation("Paying {Employee}", inner.Name);
        inner.Pay();
    }

    public string Name => inner.Name;
}
```

- DI containers such as Scrutor's `Decorate<TService, TDecorator>()` register decorators without
  touching call sites.
- Resilience pipelines (Polly, `Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience`) are decorator stacks.
  Feathers' onion warning applies when debugging them.

## Learning objectives

- Choose among the four techniques for a given scenario
- Explain how small, consistent improvements change a team's beliefs

## Decision guide

| Situation | Technique |
|-----------|-----------|
| Class is testable or nearly so; change is a distinct step | Sprout Method |
| Class can't be compiled or instantiated in a harness | Sprout Class |
| New behaviour must run before/after every call; method name should stay | Wrap Method |
| Same, but class is untestable or too large to grow | Wrap Class |

## Learning objectives

- Distinguish learning cost from change cost
- Connect understandability to small, well-named pieces

## In a nutshell

All systems have a learning cost. Legacy systems add a change cost on top, and the learning does
not accumulate into wider understanding.

## Connections to today

Code search, "go to implementation", AI summarisation and architecture diagrams generated from
code all reduce learning cost. None of them reduce change cost if the code itself is tangled.

## Learning objectives

- Use interfaces and packages to cut recompilation
- Explain why average build time matters more than full rebuild time
- Apply the Dependency Inversion Principle to build speed

## In a nutshell

Get the cluster into a harness, then extract interfaces at its boundaries — for what it uses and
for what uses it. Move the cluster into its own package. Full builds may get slightly slower;
everyday builds get dramatically faster.

## Connections to today

- In .NET, project boundaries are the compilation unit. A test project that references only an
  `OpportunityProcessing` project and an abstractions project builds in seconds; one that
  references the web host builds everything.
- Reference assemblies let MSBuild skip rebuilding dependents when only a referenced project's
  implementation (not its public surface) changes — a tooling version of the "compilation firewall".
- Interface-only "Abstractions" packages (for example `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions`)
  are this chapter's package structure applied at ecosystem scale.

    prompt: "Why is TDD's focus on one thing at a time especially valuable in legacy code?"
    options:
      - id: separate-activities
        text: "You are either writing code or refactoring, never both — so new code can be written independently, then duplication with old code refactored away"
        correct: true
      - id: of7b6a8
        text: "It avoids the need for any refactoring"
      - id: o86cbca
        text: "It lets you skip compiling"
    explanation: "“We are either writing code or refactoring; we are never doing both at once.” and “After we have written some new code, we can refactor to remove any duplication between it and the old code.” (The printed sidebar says “write new code independently of new code”, which reads as a slip for old code.)"
---
## Learning objectives

- Run the TDD cycle, including the legacy step 0
- Use copy-then-deduplicate safely
- Reason about what a test actually asserts, not what prose says

## In a nutshell

Write the test for the method you wish existed, make it compile with a failing stub, make it
pass, then remove duplication. In legacy code, first get the class under test and avoid changing
old code while making the new test pass.

## Connections to today

```csharp
[Fact]
public void First_moment_about_point()
{
    var calc = new InstrumentCalculator();
    calc.AddElement(1.0);
    calc.AddElement(2.0);
    Assert.Equal(-0.5, calc.FirstMomentAbout(2.0), precision: 10);
}

[Fact]
public void Throws_with_no_elements() =>
    Assert.Throws<InvalidBasisException>(() => new InstrumentCalculator().FirstMomentAbout(0.0));
```

`Assert.Throws<T>` replaces the try/fail/catch idiom and removes the ambiguity discussed in the
quiz.

## Learning objectives

- Add a feature by subclassing, pin it with a test, then refactor away the subclass
- Recognise the "one feature per subclass" trap
- Evolve configuration data into a behavioural class

## In a nutshell

Subclass, override, pass the test. Then use that test to move the behaviour into a better place —
configuration, then a class with real responsibilities, then a good name.

## Connections to today

- In C#, overriding requires the base member to be `virtual`, and `protected` is usually needed —
  the same two edits as Java's `private` → `protected`.
- Options objects (`IOptions<MailingOptions>`) are the modern properties collection. When the
  option starts driving behaviour, it is time for a `MailingList`-style class.

  - id: mechanical

      - id: o73a052

## Learning objectives

- Diagnose an LSP violation from client expectations
- Apply the two rules of thumb for overriding
- Normalise a hierarchy

## In a nutshell

Programming by Difference often overrides concrete methods — the classic route to LSP surprises.
Keep the override short-lived, or normalise: abstract base, one implementation per method.

## Connections to today

- C#'s `sealed override`, `abstract` members and the `virtual`-opt-in default nudge toward
  normalized hierarchies.
- Records with `with` expressions sidestep the Rectangle/Square mutator problem by not having
  setters.

## Learning objectives

- Classify an instantiation problem into one of the four categories
- Use the rest of the chapter as a case library

## Case map

| Case | Core problem | First techniques |
|------|--------------|------------------|
| Irritating Parameter | Hard-to-build argument | Extract Interface, Pass Null, Subclass and Override |
| Hidden Dependency | Constructor creates a resource | Parameterize Constructor |
| Construction Blob | Many nested creations | Extract and Override Factory Method, Supersede Instance Variable |
| Irritating Global | Singleton/global use | Introduce Static Setter |
| Horrible Includes | C++ header web | Fakes header, separate test program |
| Onion Parameter | Objects needing objects | Pass Null, Extract Interface on nearest dependency |
| Aliased Parameter | Interface can't fit a class-typed field | Subclass and Override Method |

## Learning objectives

- Use a construction test to discover dependencies
- Choose among Extract Interface, Pass Null and Subclass and Override Method
- Keep Pass Null out of production code

## Connections to today

- C# nullable reference types (`<Nullable>enable</Nullable>`) flag `null!` in tests — that's
  fine; the warning is about production code, which matches Feathers' rule.
- `null!` or a `default!` argument is the C# spelling of Pass Null. A `NullLogger<T>.Instance`
  from `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions` is a ready-made Null Object.

    explanation: "“This refactoring is even easier in languages such as C# and Java because we can call constructors from other constructors in those languages.”"
  - id: when-easy
    prompt: "When is Parameterize Constructor a very easy technique to apply?"
    options:
      - id: o590825
        text: "When the object has many construction dependencies of its own"
      - id: no-ctor-deps
        text: "When the object created in the constructor has no construction dependencies itself"
        correct: true
      - id: o75e730
        text: "When the class is a singleton"
    explanation: "“When an object is created in a constructor and it doesn’t have any construction dependencies itself, Parameterize Constructor is a very easy technique to apply.”"
---
## Learning objectives

- Recognise a hidden constructor dependency
- Apply Parameterize Constructor without breaking existing clients

## Connections to today

```csharp
public class MailingListDispatcher
{
    private readonly IMailService _service;

    public MailingListDispatcher() : this(new MailService()) { }

    public MailingListDispatcher(IMailService service)
    {
        _service = service;
    }
}
```

This "poor man's DI" constructor pair is a legitimate stepping stone. Once a composition root
exists, the parameterless constructor can be deleted.

## Learning objectives

- Explain why singletons hinder isolated tests
- Apply Introduce Static Setter, `resetForTesting` and testing subclasses
- Plan the longer-term move away from a global

## Connections to today

- Static `DbContext` accessors, `HttpContext.Current`, `ConfigurationManager.AppSettings` and
  service locators are common .NET globals. `IHttpContextAccessor`, `IOptions<T>` and constructor
  injection are the long-term fixes; a static setter is the short-term bridge.
- xUnit runs test classes in parallel by default. A static testing instance shared across tests
  can make results flaky unless those tests share a non-parallel collection.

        text: "Break Out Method Object, if the method is long and hard to deal with"
        correct: true
      - id: o71d945
        text: "Pass Null"
    explanation: "“If the method doesn’t use much instance data, we can use Expose Static Method (345) to get access to the code. If the method is pretty long and difficult to deal with, we can use Break Out Method Object (330) to move the code to a class that we can instantiate more easily.”"
  - id: second-part
    prompt: "According to the chapter opening, what is \"the second part of the battle\"?"
    options:
      - id: o2a5936
        text: "Getting code review approval"
      - id: methods
        text: "Writing tests for the methods you need to change, after instantiation"
        correct: true
      - id: ob1ffe3
        text: "Deploying the change"
    explanation: "“Instantiating a class is often only the first part of the battle. The second part is writing tests for the methods we need to change.”"
---
## Learning objectives

- Classify a method-level testing obstacle
- Know when to skip instantiation entirely

## Case map

| Case | Obstacle | Techniques |
|------|----------|------------|
| Hidden Method | Private access | Test through public; make public; move to new class; make protected + testing subclass |
| "Helpful" Language Feature | Sealed/final library types | Adapt Parameter, Skin and Wrap the API |
| Undetectable Side Effect | No observable result | Extract Method, Command/Query Separation, Subclass and Override |

## Learning objectives

- Choose between testing through public methods and exposing a private one
- Use protected access plus a testing subclass when public access is dangerous

## Connections to today

- C#'s `internal` + `[InternalsVisibleTo("MyApp.Tests")]` is a middle ground the book doesn't
  cover: visible to tests, invisible to other assemblies.
- `UnsafeAccessor` (.NET 8+) and reflection reach private members. Feathers' sidebar applies
  word for word: handy for breaking in, but don't let such tests linger.

## Learning objectives

- Work around sealed library types with Adapt Parameter and Skin and Wrap the API
- Explain why direct library dependencies are the real problem

## Connections to today

- Microsoft later shipped exactly this wrapper idea: `System.Web.Abstractions` added
  `HttpPostedFileBase` and an `HttpPostedFileWrapper` for ASP.NET MVC testability.
- ASP.NET Core went further: uploaded files arrive as `IFormFile`, an interface you can fake
  directly. Library design caught up with Feathers' complaint.
- Many .NET analyzers now recommend sealing classes for performance. That is fine for your own
  leaf types; just keep library-facing code behind your own abstractions.

- Extract GUI-dependent code into command and query methods
- Test remaining logic with a testing subclass
- Name extracted methods by role, not by widget

## Connections to today

- MVVM in WPF/MAUI and component logic split from markup in Blazor are this refactoring made

- bUnit can render Blazor components in tests, but extracting the logic is still cheaper and
  faster than rendering.

## Learning objectives

- Trace a change's chain of effects to system boundaries
- Draw an effect sketch
- Use immutability to prune effect analysis

## Connections to today

- Feathers wished for an IDE that lists everything affected by selected code. "Find all
  references", call hierarchy and Roslyn-based dependency views go part way; none fully trace
  effects through mutable state.
- `readonly`, `init`-only properties, records and `IReadOnlyList<T>` turn many effect arrows into
  "can't happen", shrinking the sketch.

```csharp
[Fact]
public void Generated_index_lists_existing_elements()
{
    var dir = new InMemoryDirectory();
    dir.AddElement(new Element("a"));
    dir.AddElement(new Element("b"));
    dir.GenerateIndex();
```

## Connections to today

- Aspect-like mechanisms in .NET — middleware, filters, interceptors, source generators, EF Core

  won't reveal.
- Static `ActivitySource`, `Meter`, `ILogger` and ambient `AsyncLocal<T>` values are global
  channels. They're usually harmless, but a test that asserts on them must know they exist.

## Learning objectives

- Use access modifiers and immutability as effect firewalls
- Know which language guarantees can be circumvented

## Know your language — C# edition

| Construct | Narrows effects? | Caveat |
|-----------|------------------|--------|
| `private` field | Yes | Reflection, `UnsafeAccessor`, `InternalsVisibleTo` for `internal` |
| `readonly` field | Reference can't change | Object it points to may be mutable |
| `record` / `init` | Shallow immutability | Collections inside may still mutate |
| `in` / `ref readonly` parameters | Caller's variable protected | Reference types' contents still mutable |
| `static` field | Widens effects | Shared across tests running in parallel |

    prompt: "After adding supplier get/set used by both `InventoryControl` and `BillingStatement`, what is the pinch point?"
    options:
      - id: oa82663

  - id: tangled
    prompt: "If an effect sketch looks like a large tangled tree with no pinch point, what should you do?"
    type: multiple

      - id: oc12cd4

## Learning objectives

- Identify pinch points from effect sketches
- Handle cases with multiple or no pinch points

## In a nutshell

A pinch point is an interception point that sees many changes. It depends on *which* changes you
plan, so recompute it when the plan changes.

- Avoid letting pinch-point tests become the permanent suite
- Apply different rules to new code and existing code

## Connections to today

Large, slow "service tests" that nobody dares delete are the pinch-point trap in many .NET code
bases. Track their run time; when finer unit tests cover an area, retire the broad test.

## Learning objectives

- Write characterization tests with the fail-first trick
- Explain why characterization tests carry no moral authority
- Decide when you have enough characterization

## In a nutshell

Assert something you know is wrong, read the failure, paste in the real value. Repeat until you
understand the code and your tests would notice the change you plan.

## Connections to today

```csharp
[Fact]
public Task Generates_page_for_base_row()
{
    var generator = new PageGenerator();
    generator.Assoc(RowMappings.GetRow(Page.BaseRow));
    return Verify(generator.Generate());
}
```

- Snapshot/approval tools such as **Verify** and **ApprovalTests** automate step 3–4: the first
  run writes a `.received` file, you approve it, and later runs compare against it. That is
  characterization testing at scale.
- Property-based testing (FsCheck, CsCheck) can explore inputs, but characterization still needs
  you to decide which recorded outputs matter for the change.

## Learning objectives

- Apply the four characterization heuristics
- Organise characterization tests as readable documentation
- Decide how to handle discovered bugs

## Connections to today

- Name suspicious tests explicitly, e.g. `Rounds_half_down_SUSPICIOUS_see_ticket_123`, or tag them
  with a trait so they surface in reports.
- Snapshot tests are great for breadth but poor at intent. Add a few named, hand-written tests
  for the main intent at the top of the file, as Feathers suggests.

## Learning objectives

- Target tests at exactly the code you will change
- Pick inputs that exercise conversions
- Check existence and connection of moved behaviour

## Connections to today

Java lets `long cost; cost += 1.2 * totalPrice;` compile with a hidden narrowing conversion,
which is exactly the trap in the book. C# rejects that line without an explicit cast, so the
compiler catches more of these. The risk moves to casts you add while extracting —
`(long)(1.2 * totalPrice)` or `(int)amount` on a `decimal` — and those still need inputs with
fractional results to be exercised.

        text: "Write tests for the area where you'll make changes — as many as you need to understand it"
        correct: true
    explanation: "“1. Write tests for the area where you will make your changes. Write as many cases as you feel you need to understand the behavior of the code.”"

      - id: ob75105

    explanation: "“2. After doing this, take a look at the specific things you are going to change, and attempt to write tests for those.”"
  - id: step3
    prompt: "When extracting or moving functionality, what should step 3 tests verify?"
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: exercise-move

        correct: true
      - id: conversions
        text: "That conversions are exercised"
        correct: true
      - id: o363539

      - id: existence
        text: "Existence and connection of the behaviours, case by case"
        correct: true
    explanation: "“write tests that verify the existence and connection of those behaviors on a case-bycase basis. Verify that you are exercising the code that you are going to move and that it is connected properly. Exercise conversions.”"
  - id: scenario
    prompt: "You'll move a discount calculation from `OrderService` to `Customer`. You have 15 characterization tests, all with whole-dollar prices. What does the heuristic suggest adding?"
    options:

## Learning objectives

- Apply the three-step heuristic to a planned change

## Checklist

1. Understand the area.
2. Pin the specific behaviours you'll touch.
3. For moves and extractions: existence, connection, conversions.

## Learning objectives

- Recognise the cost of scattering library calls
- Explain the once and restricted-override dilemmas
- Choose wrappers and conventions to keep seams available

## Connections to today

- Cloud SDKs (Azure, AWS), payment providers and LLM APIs are today's high-risk libraries. A thin
  internal interface (`IBlobStore`, `IPaymentGateway`, `IChatModel`) keeps vendor churn and pricing
  changes from becoming rewrites.
- Many modern SDKs now ship mockable abstractions (for example, Azure SDK clients have virtual
  methods and protected constructors for mocking). Check before wrapping — but wrapping still buys
  you vocabulary and isolation.

## Learning objectives

- Choose between Skin and Wrap the API and Responsibility-Based Extraction
- Combine thin and high-level wrappers

## Connections to today

```csharp
public interface IInvoiceArchive
{
    Task SaveAsync(InvoiceId id, Stream pdf, CancellationToken ct);
}

public sealed class BlobInvoiceArchive(BlobContainerClient container) : IInvoiceArchive
{
    public Task SaveAsync(InvoiceId id, Stream pdf, CancellationToken ct) =>
        container.GetBlobClient($"{id}.pdf").UploadAsync(pdf, overwrite: true, ct);
}
```

`IInvoiceArchive` is a responsibility-based interface: it speaks your domain, not the SDK's. A
thin skin over `BlobContainerClient` is rarely needed because the SDK is already mockable.

        text: "A gross mistake may give you a false view of what the system does"
        correct: true
    explanation: "“The first risk is that we make some gross mistake when we refactor that leads us to think that the system is doing something that it isn’t.” “We could get so attached to the way that the code turns out that we start to think about it in those terms all the time.”"
  - id: why-not-same
    prompt: "Why might the real refactoring end up structured differently from the scratch one?"
    type: multiple
    options:
      - id: o201bcd
        text: "Refactoring tools produce random structure"
      - id: better-way
        text: "You may see a better way later"
        correct: true
      - id: code-changes
        text: "The code may change in the meantime, bringing different insights"
        correct: true
    explanation: "“We might see a better way of structuring the code later. Our code could change between now and then, and we might have different insights.”"
  - id: benefit
    prompt: "What psychological benefit does Scratch refactoring offer?"
    options:
      - id: oc9d037
        text: "It replaces the need for tests"
      - id: confidence
        text: "It convinces you that you understand the most important things — you feel there isn't something scary behind every corner"
        correct: true
      - id: o9f6d90
        text: "It improves code coverage"
    explanation: "“Scratch refactoring is a good way to convince yourself that you understand the most important things about the code” — “You feel reasonably confident that there isn’t something scary behind every corner”."
  - id: modern
    prompt: "Using git, which workflow best matches Scratch refactoring?"
    options:
      - id: o70c815
        text: "Refactor on main and revert if tests fail"
      - id: oe8290d
        text: "Squash the scratch commits into the feature PR"
      - id: discard
        text: "Create a throwaway branch or stash, refactor freely, then delete it and start the real work from the main branch"
        correct: true
    explanation: "The essence is “just don’t check it in again. Throw that code away.” A throwaway branch is the version-control equivalent."
---
## Learning objectives

- Use throwaway refactoring to learn code quickly
- Guard against false views and attachment

## Connections to today

Asking an AI assistant to "restructure this for readability" in a scratch branch is a fast scratch
refactoring — with the same two risks, amplified: the assistant may misread behaviour, and its
tidy structure may anchor you.

      - id: oa8f85f
        text: "They don't support functions"
      - id: few-seams
        text: "They often lack the seams that OO and many functional languages have, so few techniques introduce unit tests"
        correct: true
    explanation: "“the number of things you can do to introduce unit tests in procedural languages is pretty small.” and “Procedural languages often just don’t have the seams that OO (and many functional) programming languages do.”"
  - id: strategy
    prompt: "What is the standard strategy for procedural legacy code?"
    options:
      - id: o0d5a82
        text: "Rewrite in an OO language before testing"
      - id: ob30977

  - id: easy

  - id: typical

## Learning objectives

- Explain why procedural code has fewer seams
- Recognise functions that are already testable

## Connections to today

Static utility classes in C# behave like procedural modules: no object seam, only "link-like"
options (wrapping, `Func<>` parameters, or runtime detours). Pure static functions, though, are
the easiest code of all to test — like `set_writetime`.

## Connections to today

```csharp
public sealed record LoanDatabase(
```

static legacy helpers without inventing an interface hierarchy. Functional-core/imperative-shell
architecture is the `form_command`/`send_command` split as a design principle.

```csharp
public interface IJobController
```

## Learning objectives

- Choose incremental strategy over refactoring binges
- Perform Extract Class without tests using the `MOVING` prefix procedure

## The MOVING procedure (summary)

1. Pick a responsibility.
2. Group the instance variables to move.
3. Extract bodies of whole methods into `MOVING*` methods.
4. Extract partial bodies into `MOVING*` methods.
5. Text-search class and subclasses for variable uses — no compiler leaning.
6. Move to the new class; instantiate it; lean on the compiler for call sites.
7. Drop the `MOVING` prefix.

## Connections to today

C# warns about member hiding (CS0108) and requires `new`/`override`, so some shadowing traps are
compiler-visible. Reflection- or string-based access (serialisers, `nameof`-free bindings) still
escapes the compiler — text search remains essential.

    explanation: "“When two methods look roughly the same, extract the differences to other methods. When you do that, you can often make them exactly the same and get rid of one.”"

## Learning objectives

- Pull shared behaviour into a base class step by step
- Use abstract hooks for differing data
- Judge when tiny subclasses are fine

## Connections to today

```csharp
public abstract class Command
{
    private static readonly byte[] Header = [0xde, 0xad];
    private static readonly byte[] Footer = [0xbe, 0xef];
    protected List<string> Fields { get; } = [];
    protected abstract byte CommandChar { get; }
    protected virtual void WriteBody(Stream output) { foreach (var f in Fields) WriteField(output, f); }
    private static void WriteField(Stream output, string field) { output.Write(Encoding.ASCII.GetBytes(field)); output.WriteByte(0); }
}
```

Today you might prefer composition (a `CommandWriter` plus data records) over inheritance, but the
duplication-driven discovery of "field" and "body" concepts is the same.

        correct: true
      - id: o2f3e81
        text: "Deleting unused imports"
      - id: o98d812
        text: "Collecting all dependencies into one class"
    explanation: "“You write tests for the logic that you need to preserve. Afterward, you extract things that the tests do not cover. When you do this, you can at least have confidence that you are preserving the important behavior.”"
  - id: gleaning-why
    prompt: "Why is gleaning acceptable even though it feels like a cop-out?"
    options:
      - id: o5e5392
        text: "Display code never has bugs"
      - id: unequal
        text: "Not all behaviours are equal — errors in display code show up fast, errors in add logic may hide for a long time"
        correct: true
      - id: o2fc460
        text: "Tests are optional"
    explanation: "“If we make a mistake with the display code, we’ll see it pretty quickly. An error in the add logic, though, is something that might take quite a while to find.” “But not all behaviors are equal in an application.”"
  - id: method-object
    prompt: "Why choose Break Out Method Object over turning locals into instance variables?"
    options:
      - id: o2b096b
        text: "Locals can't be read by tests"
      - id: production-vars
        text: "Instance variables shared only by the monster and its extractions are confusing; a method object makes those variables legitimately part of a class you can sense through, with tests you can keep"
        correct: true
      - id: oe6899d
        text: "Method objects are faster"
    explanation: "Turning locals into fields “can be confusing.” With a method object, “We can turn the temporary variables in the method into instance variables and sense through them” and “unlike introducing a sensing variable, the variables that you are using are needed for production. This allows you to build up tests that you can keep.”"
---
## Learning objectives

- Choose low-coupling extractions and compute coupling counts
- Protect critical behaviour with Gleaning Dependencies
- Know when to break out a method object

## Connections to today

C#'s "Extract Method" dialog shows parameters and return values — your coupling count at a glance.
Local functions can be a stepping stone: extract to a local function first, then promote it.

title: "Strategy"
questions:
  - id: skeletonize
    prompt: "What is skeletonizing?"
    options:
      - id: ob25511
        text: "Extract the condition and body together"
      - id: separate
        text: "Extract the condition and the body into separate methods, leaving only control structure and delegations"
        correct: true
      - id: od852a8
        text: "Delete all comments"
    explanation: "“If you extract the condition and the body to two different methods, you are in a better position to reorganize the logic of the method later” — “all that is left in the method is a skeleton: the control structure and delegations to other methods.”"
  - id: sequences
    prompt: "What is \"finding sequences\"?"
    options:
      - id: ocb4a3b
        text: "Finding loops"
      - id: together
        text: "Extract the condition and body together, to reveal the method as a clear sequence of operations"
        correct: true
      - id: ofd935c
        text: "Sorting methods alphabetically"
    explanation: "“If you extract the condition and the body to the same method, you are in a better position to identify a common sequence of operations”."
  - id: which
    prompt: "Feathers admits his advice conflicts. How does he choose?"
    options:
      - id: o99729e
        text: "Flip a coin"
      - id: o38e5ae
        text: "Always skeletonize"
      - id: depends
        text: "Skeletonize when control structure will need refactoring (snarled methods); find sequences when an overarching sequence clarifies (bulleted methods)"
        correct: true
    explanation: "“I skeletonize when I feel that the control structure will need to be refactored after it is clarified. I attempt to find sequences when I feel that identifying an overarching sequence will make the code clearer.   - id: current-class
    prompt: "A chunk wants to be called `recalculateOrder` and clearly belongs on `Order`. What should you do first?"
    options:
      - id: awkward
        text: "Extract it to the current class with the awkward name; move it later when the direction is clear"
        correct: true
      - id: odb13a7
        text: "Extract it directly into `Order`"
      - id: o9a6dfa
        text: "Leave it inline"
    explanation: "“Although it is tempting to extract directly to another class, don’t do it. Use the awkward name first.” — “extracting to the current class moves us forward and it is less error prone.”"
  - id: name-hint
    prompt: "What strong indication suggests extracted code belongs on another class?"
    options:
      - id: o567303
        text: "It's longer than 10 lines"
      - id: o2ea621
        text: "It has a loop"
      - id: variable-name
        text: "You're tempted to name it after one of the variables it uses"
        correct: true
    explanation: "“If you look at a piece of code and you are tempted to use the name of one of the variables you are using in it, chances are good that the code belongs on the class of that variable.”"
  - id: small
    prompt: "Why extract small pieces first rather than large chunks?"
    options:
      - id: details
        text: "Small extractions change how you see the method; big chunks are less safe and easier to miss details that make the code work"
        correct: true
      - id: o9a90cb
        text: "Tools only extract small pieces"
      - id: o45f6b5
        text: "Small methods are faster"
    explanation: "“After you extract more pieces, you’ll probably see the original method in a different way.” “Too often that isn’t as easy as it looks; it isn’t as safe. It’s easier to miss the details, and the details are what make the code work.”"
  - id: redo
    prompt: "Are extractions you later undo wasted effort?"
    options:
      - id: o0a872f
        text: "Only if tests fail"
      - id: o6c7201
        text: "Yes — undone work is waste"
      - id: insight
        text: "No — they gave insight into the old design and a better way forward"
        correct: true
    explanation: "“Sometimes the best way to move forward is to undo an extraction or two and re-extract. When you do this, it doesn’t mean that the first extractions were wasted effort. They gave you something very important: insight into old design and into a better way of moving forward.”"
---
## Learning objectives

- Choose between skeletonizing and finding sequences
- Extract to the current class first, small pieces first, and be ready to redo

## Connections to today

Version control makes "be prepared to redo" cheap: commit each extraction, and use interactive
rebase or a fresh branch to try a different slicing.

    explanation: "“As you start to take control of your code base, you’ll start to develop oases of good code. Work can really be enjoyable in them.”"

## Learning objectives

- Recognise the green-field illusion
- Choose concrete actions to rebuild team morale

## Connections to today

"Strangler fig" migrations (Fowler) are the healthier alternative to the big-bang replacement team:
the new system grows around the old one incrementally, guided by the same tests-first habits.

## Learning objectives

- Explain the purpose and limits of the catalog

## Technique map

| Group | Techniques |
|-------|-----------|
| Parameters | Adapt Parameter, Primitivize Parameter, Parameterize Constructor, Parameterize Method |
| Method-level isolation | Break Out Method Object, Expose Static Method, Extract and Override Call |
| Creation | Extract and Override Factory Method, Extract and Override Getter, Supersede Instance Variable |
| Interfaces | Extract Interface, Extract Implementer |
| Globals and statics | Encapsulate Global References, Introduce Static Setter, Introduce Instance Delegator, Replace Global Reference with Getter |
| Inheritance | Subclass and Override Method, Pull Up Feature, Push Down Dependency |
| Build-level (C/C++) | Definition Completion, Link Substitution, Replace Function with Function Pointer, Template Redefinition, Text Redefinition |

- Wrap a hard-to-fake parameter behind a narrow, responsibility-named interface

## Learning objectives

- Encapsulate related globals or free functions behind a class
- Use the compiler to redirect references safely

## Steps

1. Identify the globals.
2. Create a class to reference them from.
3. Copy the globals in; handle initialisation.
4. Comment out the originals.
5. Declare a global instance of the new class.
6. Lean on the Compiler for unresolved references.
7. Prefix each with the instance name.
8. Add a seam for fakes (static setter, parameterize, getter).

## Connections to today

`static class AppSettings { public static string ConnectionString; }` is a modern global. Wrap it
in an `IAppSettings` (or `IOptions<T>`) instance first, then inject it.

## Learning objectives

- Isolate a single static or global call behind an overridable method

## Connections to today

```csharp
public class PageLayout
{
    protected void RebindStyles() => _styles = FormStyles(_template, _id);
    protected virtual IList<Style> FormStyles(StyleTemplate template, int id) =>
        StyleMaster.FormStyles(template, id);
}
```

Remember `virtual` in C#. If the class is `sealed`, use a delegate parameter instead.

- Extract an interface incrementally using the compiler
- Avoid the non-virtual method trap

## Connections to today

C# explicit interface implementation and the fact that interface dispatch never changes calls
made through the concrete type (Feathers' "C# is safer" note) make this the default .NET seam.

## Learning objectives

- Replace a singleton instance in tests safely
- Manage shared static state across tests

## Connections to today

xUnit.net runs test classes in parallel by default. Tests that set a static instance must share a

## Learning objectives

- Substitute functions at link time and sense calls through them

## Steps

1. Identify the functions or classes to fake.
2. Produce alternative definitions.
3. Adjust the build to include them instead of production versions.

## Connections to today

In .NET, swapping a referenced assembly in a test project is possible but rare; strong naming,
NuGet and DI make object seams far easier. Link-time tricks survive in native interop: a fake
native DLL with the same exports for P/Invoke tests.

      - id: many-calls

        correct: true
    explanation: "From Extract and Override Call: “I tend to use it unless there are many different calls against the same global. If there are, I often use Replace Global Reference with Getter (399) instead.”"
  - id: steps

## Learning objectives

- Funnel global access through an overridable getter

## Connections to today

```csharp
protected virtual Inventory Inventory => Inventory.Current;
```

A virtual property is the C# getter. If `Inventory` is sealed or a static class, combine with Extract
Interface or Introduce Instance Delegator.

## Learning objectives

- Parameterize a class over its dependency type to swap in fakes

## Connections to today

C# generics can do this (`AsyncReceptionPort<TSocket> where TSocket : ISocket`), and `using

## Learning objectives

- Use the book's vocabulary precisely

## Quick reference

| Term | One-line meaning |
|------|------------------|
| Seam | Place to vary behaviour without editing there |
| Enabling point | Where you choose which behaviour a seam uses |
| Change point | Where you must change code |
| Interception point | Where a test can sense effects |
| Pinch point | Narrow interception point covering many changes |
| Characterization test | Pins current behaviour |
| Coupling count | Params (+1 if a return value) |
| Fake / mock | Impersonating collaborator / one that asserts internally |
| Testing subclass | Subclass made to allow testing |

FILE: export.sh
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ===========================================================================
# export.sh — Export git-tracked project files to docs/llm/dump.txt
#
# Blog posts (content/blog/*.md): only front matter is included; the
# markdown body is omitted to save context space. Every other git-tracked
# file is exported in full.
#
# Excluded from export:
#   - The docs/ directory itself (to avoid recursion / stale LLM context)
#   - Binary files (images, fonts, etc.)
#
# Usage:
#   bash export.sh            # writes docs/llm/dump.txt
#   bash export.sh -o out.txt # writes to a custom path
# ===========================================================================

set -euo pipefail

# ── Configuration ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

OUTPUT_FILE="docs/llm/dump.txt"
BLOG_DIR="content/blog"
SEPARATOR="-------------------------------------------------------------------------------"
WIDE_SEP="==============================================================================="

# Binary file extensions to skip (lowercase comparison)
BINARY_EXTENSIONS="png jpg jpeg gif ico bmp svg webp woff woff2 ttf eot otf mp3 mp4 wav ogg pdf zip tar gz"

# ── Parse arguments ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

while [[ $# -gt 0 ]]; do
    case "$1" in
        -o|--output)
            OUTPUT_FILE="$2"
            shift 2
            ;;
        -h|--help)
            echo "Usage: bash export.sh [-o OUTPUT_FILE]"
            echo "  Exports git-tracked project files to docs/llm/dump.txt"
            echo "  Blog posts include front matter only (body omitted)."
            exit 0
            ;;
        *)
            echo "Unknown argument: $1" >&2
            exit 1
            ;;
    esac
done

# ── Helpers ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

is_binary_extension() {
    local file="$1"
    local ext="${file##*.}"
    ext="${ext,,}" # lowercase
    for bin_ext in $BINARY_EXTENSIONS; do
        if [[ "$ext" == "$bin_ext" ]]; then
            return 0
        fi
    done
    return 1
}

is_blog_post() {
    local file="$1"
    [[ "$file" == ${BLOG_DIR}/*.md ]]
}

is_excluded_dir() {
    local file="$1"
    [[ "$file" == docs/* ]]
}

# Extract only the YAML front matter (between first --- and second ---).
# Prints the front matter block including delimiters.
extract_front_matter() {
    local file="$1"
    local in_front_matter=0
    local found_start=0

    while IFS= read -r line; do
        if [[ "$found_start" -eq 0 && "$line" == "---" ]]; then
            found_start=1
            in_front_matter=1
            echo "$line"
            continue
        fi
        if [[ "$in_front_matter" -eq 1 && "$line" == "---" ]]; then
            echo "$line"
            return
        fi
        if [[ "$in_front_matter" -eq 1 ]]; then
            echo "$line"
        fi
    done < "$file"
}

# ── Collect git-tracked files ────────────────────────────────────────────────

mapfile -t ALL_FILES < <(git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard | sort)

# ── Counters ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

total_files=0
blog_front_matter_only=0
full_content_files=0
binary_skipped=0

# ── Ensure output directory exists ───────────────────────────────────────────

mkdir -p "$(dirname "$OUTPUT_FILE")"

# ── Write output ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

{
    # Header
    echo "$WIDE_SEP"
    echo "PROJECT EXPORT: terlingua.github.io"
    echo "DATE: $(date -u '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S UTC')"
    echo "$WIDE_SEP"
    echo ""

    # Directory tree
    echo "$WIDE_SEP"
    echo "DIRECTORY TREE (all git-tracked files)"
    echo "$WIDE_SEP"
    echo ""

    # Use tree if available, otherwise fall back to a simple listing
    if command -v tree &>/dev/null; then
        # Build a temp file list for tree --fromfile
        printf '%s\n' "${ALL_FILES[@]}" | tree --fromfile --charset utf-8 -a 2>/dev/null || {
            # Fallback: just print the sorted file list as an indented tree
            echo "."
            printf '%s\n' "${ALL_FILES[@]}" | sed 's|^|├── |'
        }
    else
        echo "."
        printf '%s\n' "${ALL_FILES[@]}" | sed 's|^|├── |'
    fi

    echo ""

    # File contents
    for file in "${ALL_FILES[@]}"; do
        # Skip files in docs/ directory
        if is_excluded_dir "$file"; then
            continue
        fi

        # Skip binary files
        if is_binary_extension "$file"; then
            binary_skipped=$((binary_skipped + 1))
            total_files=$((total_files + 1))
            continue
        fi

        # Skip the export script itself
        if [[ "$file" == "export.sh" ]]; then
            # Still include it — it's useful context for the LLM
            :
        fi

        echo ""
        echo "$SEPARATOR"

        if is_blog_post "$file"; then
            # Blog post: front matter only
            echo "FILE: ${file}  [FRONT MATTER ONLY — body omitted to save context space]"
            echo "$SEPARATOR"
            extract_front_matter "$file"
            echo ""
            blog_front_matter_only=$((blog_front_matter_only + 1))
        else
            # All other files: full content
            echo "FILE: ${file}"
            echo "$SEPARATOR"
            cat "$file"
            echo ""
            full_content_files=$((full_content_files + 1))
        fi

        total_files=$((total_files + 1))
    done

    # Footer
    echo ""
    echo "$WIDE_SEP"
    echo "EXPORT COMPLETED"
    echo "Total Files Exported: ${total_files}"
    echo "  Blog posts (front matter only): ${blog_front_matter_only}"
    echo "  Full content files: ${full_content_files}"
    echo "  Binary files skipped: ${binary_skipped}"
    echo "Output File: ${OUTPUT_FILE}"
    echo "$WIDE_SEP"

} > "$OUTPUT_FILE"

echo "Export complete: ${OUTPUT_FILE}"
echo "  Total files: ${total_files}"
echo "  Blog posts (front matter only): ${blog_front_matter_only}"
echo "  Full content files: ${full_content_files}"
echo "  Binary files skipped: ${binary_skipped}"

FILE: .github/workflows/deploy.yml
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
name: Deploy to GitHub Pages

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 6 * * *'
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: false

env:
  DOTNET_NOLOGO: true
  DOTNET_CLI_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT: true
  TESTINGPLATFORM_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT: true

jobs:
  build-and-deploy:
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Setup .NET
        uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v6
        with:
          dotnet-version: '11.0.x'

      - name: Restore
        run: dotnet restore

      - name: Process content
        run: dotnet run --project tools/ObserverMagazine.ContentProcessor --no-restore

      - name: Restore audio cache
        id: audio-cache
        uses: actions/cache@v6
        with:
          path: .audio-cache
          key: audio-v1-${{ hashFiles('content/blog/**/*.md') }}
          restore-keys: |
            audio-v1-

      - name: Copy cached audio to output
        run: |
          mkdir -p src/ObserverMagazine.Web/wwwroot/blog-data
          shopt -s nullglob
          files=(.audio-cache/*.mp3 .audio-cache/audio-manifest.json)
          if (( ${#files[@]} )); then cp "${files[@]}" src/ObserverMagazine.Web/wwwroot/blog-data/; fi
          echo "Restored ${#files[@]} cached audio file(s)"

      - name: Setup Python
        if: steps.audio-cache.outputs.cache-hit != 'true'
        uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: '3.13'
          cache: pip
          cache-dependency-path: tools/requirements-audio.txt

      - name: Install system dependencies
        if: steps.audio-cache.outputs.cache-hit != 'true'
        run: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y espeak-ng ffmpeg

      - name: Cache Hugging Face model
        if: steps.audio-cache.outputs.cache-hit != 'true'
        uses: actions/cache@v6
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/huggingface
          key: hf-kitten-tts-nano-0.8

      - name: Install Python audio dependencies
        if: steps.audio-cache.outputs.cache-hit != 'true'
        run: pip install onnxruntime -r tools/requirements-audio.txt

      - name: Generate TTS audio
        if: steps.audio-cache.outputs.cache-hit != 'true'
        run: python tools/generate_audio.py --content-dir content/blog --output-dir src/ObserverMagazine.Web/wwwroot/blog-data --voice Bella --model KittenML/kitten-tts-nano-0.8

      - name: Update audio cache
        if: steps.audio-cache.outputs.cache-hit != 'true'
        run: |
          mkdir -p .audio-cache
          shopt -s nullglob
          files=(src/ObserverMagazine.Web/wwwroot/blog-data/*.mp3 src/ObserverMagazine.Web/wwwroot/blog-data/audio-manifest.json)
          if (( ${#files[@]} )); then cp "${files[@]}" .audio-cache/; fi
          echo "Cached ${#files[@]} audio file(s)"

      - name: Test
        run: dotnet test --solution ObserverMagazine.slnx --no-restore

      - name: Publish
        run: dotnet publish src/ObserverMagazine.Web/ObserverMagazine.Web.csproj -c Release -o publish

      - name: Prepare site
        run: cp publish/wwwroot/index.html publish/wwwroot/404.html

      - name: Setup Pages
        uses: actions/configure-pages@v6

      - name: Upload artifact
        uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v5
        with:
          path: publish/wwwroot

      - name: Deploy
        id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v5

FILE: README.md
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Terlingua Magazine

A free, open-source Blazor WebAssembly application deployed to GitHub Pages.

Built with **.NET 11** and **C# 15**. Targets the current stable releases of evergreen browsers only
(Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari); there are no polyfills, vendor prefixes or legacy fallbacks.

## Features

- **Blog** — Write posts in Markdown with YAML front matter; compiled to static JSON at build time
- **RSS Feed** — Auto-generated `feed.xml`
- **Books & Quizzes** — Multi-chapter books with single- and multiple-answer quizzes; reading progress stored in the browser (localStorage)
- **Responsive Tables** — Sortable, filterable data tables that work on mobile
- **Master-Detail Flow** — Click a list item to view full details
- **OpenTelemetry-ready Logging** — Structured logging via `ILogger`
- **Full Test Suite** — bUnit component tests + xUnit.net v3 integration tests, running on Microsoft.Testing.Platform

## Quick Start

`global.json` asks for SDK `11.0.100-rc.3` or any later 11.0.1xx SDK, so the Fedora RC 3 SDK works
locally and CI uses the latest .NET 11 GA SDK.

```bash
# Process blog posts and books
dotnet run --project tools/ObserverMagazine.ContentProcessor

# Run the app locally
dotnet run --project src/ObserverMagazine.Web

# Run all tests
dotnet test
```

## Books

Books live under `content/books/` and are compiled by the content processor into
`wwwroot/book-data/` (git-ignored) at build time.

```
content/books/
  blazor-basics/                  # book slug (lowercase, digits, hyphens)
    book.yml                      # title, author, summary, date, tags, image, draft
    01-getting-started/           # NN-chapter-slug; the number sets the order
      chapter.yml                 # title, summary, draft
      01-what-is-blazor.md        # NN-subchapter-slug.md
      02-project-structure.md
    02-components/
      ...
```

Chapters and subchapters are numbered 1, 2, 3… in the order of their prefixes, so gaps
(`01`, `05`, `10`) are fine. Drafts and future-dated books are skipped.

### Subchapter format

```markdown
---
title: What is Blazor WebAssembly?
questions:
  - id: runtime                   # optional, defaults to q1, q2…; keep stable once published
    prompt: Where does the C# code run?
    explanation: Shown after a correct answer.   # optional
    options:
      - text: On the server
      - text: In the browser
        correct: true
  - id: hosting
    prompt: Which statements are true?
    type: multiple                # optional: single | multiple
    options:
      - id: static                # optional, defaults to a, b, c…
        text: It can be served from GitHub Pages
        correct: true
      - text: It needs ASP.NET Core on the server
---
Markdown body…
```

- `type` is inferred when omitted: more than one correct option means `multiple`.
  Set `type: multiple` explicitly to use checkboxes even when only one option is correct.
- Prompts, options and explanations support Markdown (inline code, emphasis, links).
- Question and option ids are what reader progress is keyed on. Changing them resets
  progress for that question.
- Invalid content (no correct option, fewer than two options, unnumbered files, missing
  `chapter.yml`, bad YAML, duplicate ids) fails the build with a list of errors.

Content guidelines for new sections:

- Open with a "Learning objectives" list and keep each section focused on one concept
- Prefer small, compilable code snippets with a language on every code fence
- Write three or more questions per section, mixing single- and multiple-answer questions,
  with an `explanation` on every question
- Vary the position of the correct option; the UI does not shuffle options
- Companions to published books follow the original chapter and section order, quote only short passages, and put each quotation inside “ ” in the `explanation` so it can be checked against the source
- Non-software books may grade claims by certainty; `nutrition-science` uses Established, Strong, Uncertain and Not supported, and cites sources at the end of each section
- Quote option text that YAML would read as a boolean, number or null (`"Yes"`, `"50"`), and avoid `yes`, `no`, `null`, `true` and `false` as ids
- Quote YAML values that contain `: `, ` #` or start with a backtick or `@`

### Progress and analytics

- A section is complete when every question has been answered correctly, or, if it has
  no questions, once it has been opened.
- Progress is saved per book in `localStorage` under `book:<slug>`. If storage is
  unavailable (blocked storage, quota) the app falls back to in-memory storage and tells
  the reader that progress will not persist.
- When the analytics backend is reachable, the reader count of a book and of each
  section is shown. A reader is counted once per book and once per section, using the
  local progress record to avoid counting repeat visits. Quiz answers are sent as
  interaction events. Nothing is shown and nothing breaks when the backend is down.

## Front end

- The site ships no JavaScript of its own. The only interop is `localStorage` through
  `LocalBrowserStorage` (`IBrowserStorage`), which wraps every call in `try`/`catch` as
  analyzer BL0016 requires.
- Code blocks are highlighted at build time by `SyntaxHighlighter` in the content processor,
  plugged into Markdig as `SyntaxHighlightingExtension`. The `hl-*` colour classes live in
  `app.css`.
- Horizontally scrolling code blocks show edge shadows with pure CSS
  (`background-attachment: local`).
- Themes are CSS custom properties. `MainLayout` renders `data-theme` on `.page` and saves the
  choice in `localStorage` (`observer-theme`). The default `system` theme uses `light-dark()`
  and `color-scheme`, so it follows the OS setting live. The loading screen always uses the
  system theme.
- The audio player uses the browser's native controls, including playback speed, and stays
  hidden until the MP3's metadata loads.
- `OverrideHtmlAssetPlaceholders` fingerprints the framework files (`dotnet.js` is published as
  `dotnet.<hash>.js`) and fills the `<script type="importmap">` placeholder in `index.html`,
  which is how `blazor.webassembly.js` finds them. Keep that placeholder, and don't modify files
  under `_framework` after publish, because the import map can carry integrity hashes for them.
  A 404 for `/_framework/dotnet.js` on the live site is expected.
- GitHub Pages deep links work because CI copies the published `index.html` to `404.html`.

## Testing

Tests run on **Microsoft.Testing.Platform (MTP)**, not VSTest. The opt-in lives in
`global.json`:

```json
{ "test": { "runner": "Microsoft.Testing.Platform" } }
```

Test projects are ordinary executables, so each one can also be run on its own:

```bash
# Whole solution
dotnet test --solution ObserverMagazine.slnx

# One project
dotnet test --project tests/ObserverMagazine.Web.Tests

# Filter by class, or by trait
dotnet test --filter-class ObserverMagazine.Web.Tests.Services.BlogServiceTests
dotnet test --filter-trait Category=Integration

# Run a test project directly, no dotnet test involved
dotnet run --project tests/ObserverMagazine.Integration.Tests
```

Run `dotnet test -?` from the repo root for the full option list, which is built
from whichever MTP extensions the test projects reference.

xUnit configuration for MTP lives in `testconfig.json` next to a test project
(not `xunit.runner.json`, which is the VSTest-era file).

@inject IAnalyticsService Analytics
@inject ILogger<BlogTtsPlayer> Logger

<div class="tts-player" hidden="@(!_available)">
    <span class="tts-icon" aria-hidden="true">🔊</span>
    <span class="tts-label">Listen to this post</span>

    <audio controls
           preload="metadata"
           src="@AudioUrl"
           @onloadedmetadata="OnLoadedMetadata"
           @onplay="OnPlay"
           @onpause="OnPause"
           @onended="OnEnded"></audio>

    <a class="tts-direct-link" href="@AudioUrl" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"
       title="Open audio file directly in a new tab">
        Open audio ↗
    </a>
</div>

@code {
    [Parameter, EditorRequired]
    public string Slug { get; set; } = "";

    private string? _currentSlug;
    private bool _available;

    private string AudioUrl => $"blog-data/{Slug}.mp3";

    protected override void OnParametersSet()
    {
        if (Slug == _currentSlug)
        {
            return;
        }

        _currentSlug = Slug;
        _available = false;
    }

    private void OnLoadedMetadata() => _available = true;

    private async Task OnPlay()
    {
        Logger.LogInformation("TTS play: {Slug}", Slug);
        await Analytics.TrackInteractionAsync("TTS.Play", Slug);
    }

    private async Task OnPause()
    {
        Logger.LogInformation("TTS pause: {Slug}", Slug);
        await Analytics.TrackInteractionAsync("TTS.Pause", Slug);
    }

    private async Task OnEnded()
    {
        Logger.LogInformation("TTS finished: {Slug}", Slug);
        await Analytics.TrackInteractionAsync("TTS.Finished", Slug);
    }
}

@code {
    private const string StorageKey = "observer-products-v1";

    private enum ViewMode { Idle, Viewing, Editing, Adding }

    private List<Product>? _products;
    private Product? _selected;
    private ViewMode _viewMode = ViewMode.Idle;

    // Edit form fields
    private string _editName = "";
    private string _editCategory = "";
    private decimal _editPrice;
    private int _editStock;
    private double _editRating;
    private string _editDescription = "";
    private bool _showValidation;

    // Confirmation dialog
    private string _confirmTitle = "";
    private string _confirmMessage = "";
    private string _confirmButton = "";
    private Func<Task>? _confirmAction;

    protected override async Task OnInitializedAsync()
    {
        Logger.LogInformation("Loading product data for master-detail");
        await LoadProducts();
    }

    private async Task LoadProducts()
    {
        try
        {
            // Try localStorage first
            var saved = await Js.InvokeAsync<string?>("localStorage.getItem", StorageKey);
            if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(saved))
            {
                _products = System.Text.Json.JsonSerializer.Deserialize<List<Product>>(saved,
                    new System.Text.Json.JsonSerializerOptions { PropertyNameCaseInsensitive = true });
                Logger.LogInformation("Loaded {Count} products from local storage", _products?.Count ?? 0);
            }
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            Logger.LogDebug(ex, "Could not read from local storage");
        }

        if (_products is null || _products.Count == 0)
        {
            try
            {
                var loaded = await Http.GetFromJsonAsync<Product[]>("sample-data/products.json");
                _products = loaded?.ToList() ?? [];
                Logger.LogInformation("Loaded {Count} products from JSON", _products.Count);
            }
            catch (Exception ex)
            {
                Logger.LogError(ex, "Failed to load products");
                _products = [];
            }
        }
    }

    private async Task SaveProducts()
    {
        if (_products is null) return;
        try
        {
            var json = System.Text.Json.JsonSerializer.Serialize(_products,
                new System.Text.Json.JsonSerializerOptions { PropertyNamingPolicy = System.Text.Json.JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase });
            await Js.InvokeVoidAsync("localStorage.setItem", StorageKey, json);
            Logger.LogInformation("Saved {Count} products to local storage", _products.Count);
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            Logger.LogWarning(ex, "Could not save to local storage");
        }
    }

    private async Task SelectProduct(Product product)
    {
        if (_viewMode is ViewMode.Editing or ViewMode.Adding) return;
        _selected = product;
        _viewMode = ViewMode.Viewing;
        Logger.LogInformation("Selected product: {Name}", product.Name);
        await Analytics.TrackInteractionAsync("ProductSelect", product.Name);
    }

    // ---- CRUD operations ----

    private void StartAdd()
    {
        _selected = null;
        _editName = "";
        _editCategory = "";
        _editPrice = 0;
        _editStock = 0;
        _editRating = 0;
        _editDescription = "";
        _showValidation = false;
        _viewMode = ViewMode.Adding;
    }

    private void StartEdit()
    {
        if (_selected is null) return;
        _editName = _selected.Name;
        _editCategory = _selected.Category;
        _editPrice = _selected.Price;
        _editStock = _selected.Stock;
        _editRating = _selected.Rating;
        _editDescription = _selected.Description;
        _showValidation = false;
        _viewMode = ViewMode.Editing;
    }

    private async Task SaveEdit()
    {
        _showValidation = true;
        if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(_editName)) return;

        if (_viewMode == ViewMode.Adding)
        {
            var newProduct = new Product
            {
                Id = Guid.NewGuid(),
                Name = _editName.Trim(),
                Category = _editCategory.Trim(),
                Price = _editPrice,
                Stock = _editStock,
                Rating = Math.Clamp(_editRating, 0, 5),
                Description = _editDescription.Trim()
            };
            _products!.Add(newProduct);
            _selected = newProduct;
            Logger.LogInformation("Added product: {Name}", newProduct.Name);
            await Analytics.TrackInteractionAsync("ProductAdd", newProduct.Name);
        }
        else if (_viewMode == ViewMode.Editing && _selected is not null)
        {
            var idx = _products!.FindIndex(p => p.Id == _selected.Id);
            if (idx >= 0)
            {
                var updated = _selected with
                {
                    Name = _editName.Trim(),
                    Category = _editCategory.Trim(),
                    Price = _editPrice,
                    Stock = _editStock,
                    Rating = Math.Clamp(_editRating, 0, 5),
                    Description = _editDescription.Trim()
                };
                _products[idx] = updated;
                _selected = updated;
                Logger.LogInformation("Updated product: {Name}", updated.Name);
                await Analytics.TrackInteractionAsync("ProductUpdate", updated.Name);
            }
        }

        await SaveProducts();
        _viewMode = ViewMode.Viewing;
        _showValidation = false;
    }

    private void CancelEdit()
    {
        _viewMode = _selected is not null ? ViewMode.Viewing : ViewMode.Idle;
        _showValidation = false;
    }

    private void ConfirmDelete()
    {
        if (_selected is null) return;
        _confirmTitle = "Delete Product";
        _confirmMessage = $"Are you sure you want to delete \"{_selected.Name}\"? This cannot be undone.";
        _confirmButton = "Delete";
        _confirmAction = ExecuteDelete;
    }

    private async Task ExecuteDelete()
    {
        if (_selected is not null && _products is not null)
        {
            var name = _selected.Name;
            _products.RemoveAll(p => p.Id == _selected.Id);
            _selected = null;
            _viewMode = ViewMode.Idle;
            await SaveProducts();
            Logger.LogInformation("Deleted product: {Name}", name);
            await Analytics.TrackInteractionAsync("ProductDelete", name);
        }
        _confirmAction = null;
    }

    private void ConfirmReset()
    {
        _confirmTitle = "Reset to Defaults";
        _confirmMessage = "This will discard all your changes and restore the original product data. Continue?";
        _confirmButton = "Reset";
        _confirmAction = ExecuteReset;
    }

    private async Task ExecuteReset()
    {
        try
        {
            await Js.InvokeVoidAsync("localStorage.removeItem", StorageKey);
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            Logger.LogDebug(ex, "Could not clear local storage");
        }

        _products = null;
        _selected = null;
        _viewMode = ViewMode.Idle;
        await LoadProducts();
        Logger.LogInformation("Reset products to defaults");
        await Analytics.TrackInteractionAsync("ProductReset", "");
        _confirmAction = null;
    }

    private void CancelConfirm()
    {
        _confirmAction = null;
    }

    private async Task ExecuteConfirm()
    {
        if (_confirmAction is not null)
        {
            await _confirmAction();
        }
    }
}
